title: {Editorial: Common Ground}
body:
It's a good moment to consider again what community means 
and what our individual responsibilities are to the village and to 
each other. Perhaps you feel that this does not apply to you. 
Perhaps you think your home is your castle and it's well forti-
fied. You're not on a water hookup, you don't expect to have an 
accident or have your house catch on fire. You don't care what is 
built where or how Galisteo changes so long as it's out of sight. 
You're too busy with your own life to bother with what goes on 
around you. If so, that's a pity. It's even dangerous. Not just for 
you, but for all of us. 

A place where a few do the work and many contribute noth-
ing is only real estate, not a community. To have no opinion, to 
put in no time, is to be powerless. We often don't realize how 
many dedicated people it takes to keep Galisteo as we see it 
today. Some of them are virtually invisible and ask for no credit. 
They work for love of the village. Those of us who are relatively 
new here don't always know who has done a lot of work in the 
past. We need others to step into their shoes. You know who you 
are -
whether you have contributed or not. 

Change is not bad, but it must be thoughtful change, agreed 
upon by at least a majority of those whom it affects. A few hours 
a month seems a relatively small price in exchange for the beauty 
of this place, for the hardworking Fire Department, Water Asso-
ciation, and GCA Board, for the fundraisers (and -
yes -
the 
newsletter volunteers!) 

In EL PUENTE's first issue, Barbara Cooper wrote, "Com-
munity is a powerful thing. It enfolds us in tradition, making us 
an important part of history, and urgently involves us in plan-
ning for a future we will be proud to pass along to the next 
generation .... May we all benefit from the new energy of others 
who have lost their hearts to Galisteo, and from the advice and 
council of those who have spent a lifetime here." 

That is the ideal makeup of the GCA Board -
representatives both of the longtime community and of newcomers will-
ing to do their part. Santa Clara Pueblo writer Rina Swentzell 
defines community as "something you can't walk away from." 
It is also a place you can't be passive about. The backbone of 
community is caring -
for the people and for the place.

title: El Rinconcito: Dichos y Cuentos de Amor
body:
from Anna Cardenas

Amor con amor se paga. 
Love is paid with Love. One good turn deserves another. 

Amor de lejos es pa los pendejos. 
Love at a distance is for fools. 

Amor que ha sido brasa de repente vuelve a arder. 
Where there's smoke, there's fire. 

Con amor y aguardiente, nada se siente. 
There's no defense against love and fate. 
Love always finds a way. 

De amor y amor, solo amor. 
Only love is given away freely. 

Donde hay amor no hay temor. 
Where there's love; there's no fear. 

Quien bien ama nunca olvida. 
He who truly loves never forgets. 

FELIZ DIA DE SAN VALENTINE!

title: Going to the Dogs (Again)
body:
This is the beginning of an occasional series about what we do in Galisteo.

Dogtrainer Evelyn Gregory's mailbox sports a metal Bassett 
Hound, and her house is decorated with four live ones (plus a 
coon hound and occasional boarders). She and her husband 
J.C. lived in El Paso for 23 years before they retired to New 
Mexico, where their daughter lives, bringing 8 dogs with them. 
After a year in Eldorado, they found a house on Phil McKee's 
land, where his son had lived. Evelyn fell in love with the out-
crop of white sandstone next to it. They had been in Galisteo 
almost ten years when J.C. Gregory died after a long illness in 
1996. 

Evelyn has been an active member of the community, and 
many of us remember her courageous appearance as a Board 
member at a GCA meeting, the day after her husband died. Now 
she keeps herself good and busy with three part-time jobs. (I 
hounded her for months to get this story.) 

She chose the sad-faced Bassetts (trained as "slow track-
ers" so hunters could follow on foot) "because they have a sense 
of humor and they make me laugh." She says her dogs are like 
the shoemaker's children who have no shoes. She's so tired of 
training when she gets home, her pets get away with murder. 
The favorite is clearly Cracker, whose kennel name and title 
is Champion Bugle Bay's Fire Cracker because he was born on 
July 4 and the woman who bred him named all her dogs after 
food. (His son is called Biscuit.) And Cracker is a real ham, who 
loves to perform and be shown. He has starred in a Pillsbury 
Dough Boy commercial for crescent rolls, and in an ad for the 
pet boutique in Sanbusco. In a TV commercial for the Santa Fe 
Animal Shelter, he even appeared in costume. 

When Evelyn came to Santa Fe, the Santa Fe Dog Obedi-
ence Club was "on its knees." She helped get it back on all four 
feet and now trains some 400 dogs a year. One of her jobs is 
teaching classes there. 

She is also a paid employee and adoption counselor at the 
Santa Fe Animal Shelter on Cerrillos Road, matching people 
with dogs, which she finds fascinating: "Sometimes people just 
want the wrong dogs for the wrong reasons. The Dalmatian craze 
is diminishing but the dogs of choice around here are Chows, 
Rottweilers, and Pit Bulls. People want watch dogs, guard dogs, 
but where will it sleep? Will it have room to run? You have to 
screen people very carefully," she says. "We make home visits 
to see how the animal's going to be kept, and talk to personal 
references and vets. No yard, no dog." 

Gregory has "mixed feelings" about no-kill shelters. They 
often have high ideals, but unadoptable animals spend the rest 
of their lives in cages, with no human contact except when they 
are fed. This is inhumane, she insists: 
"Our shelter takes anything, no matter what its health. Strays 
are kept five days and put up, if adoptable. If it's healthy and we 
have the space, we'll keep it as long as possible - one or two 
months. When we get crowded we have to choose: Soon we're 
getting a new state-of-the-art shelter, including a clinic and train-
ing facility, low-cost spaying and neutering services. Challenge 
New Mexico wants to have their horse facility there [a riding 
program for the developmentally disabled].Hopefully the land 
will be donated." 

Her third job is working part time for Dr. Phillip Hinko, the 
much-respected veterinarian at the Shelter. She gives private les-
sons and helps clients with dog problem-solving. Sometimes 
behavior problems can be solved in one visit, and sometimes 
they can last for months. Problems arise, she says, from "unbal-
anced relationships between dog and owner stemming from co-
dependency or just neglect. It's really psychology. You watch 
the interactions between people and animals and teach owners 
how to work with their pets. Often people's ex-pectations are way 
beyond where the animal is." 

Some words of wisdom from the expert: "New dogs don't 
get along with old ones. It's not a good idea to have two dogs of 
the same sex and age. You can't leave a dog alone all the time. 
Dogs are naturally pack animals and they need family, even wild 
strays need others and end up in packs. You are your dog's pack 
and somebody's got to be the alpha, the leader." 

Evelyn opposes letting dogs run loose, citing the "unleashed 
is unloved" maxim. "They shouldn't be chained up all the time 
either, but kept in a fenced yard - no matter how much land 
you may own. An animal on a chain with no human companion-
ship is the cruelest life. They're better off dead." 

She is also adamant about owners' responsiblity to "spend a 
couple of bucks on a large, readable ID collar with a phone num-
ber." (I agree; a dog followed me home from a walk recently 
and spent 24 hours outside my door in the cold; finally with 
some help from a neighbor I managed to read her tags and got 
hold of the vet, who recognized her and found the owners.) 

Evelyn is not a cat person, but she agrees with Shelter policy, 
which is not to adopt out cats if they are going to be let outdoors. 
(A local veterinarian told me that in some circumstances it would 
be okay to let cats out during the daytime, but not after dark. 
Some people lose one cat after another to coyotes, and keep re-
turning to the shelter for replacements.) 

When it comes to horses, Evelyn says she feels terrible 
when she sees a horse confined in a small space without excercise, 
with no chance to use their muscles. If they're left standing in 
mud they may get thrush. And once they are let out, they are so 
excited that they can be very hard to handle. 

Need advice? Call Evelyn at 466-1875.

title: Plans Presented for El Tanque Viejo
body:
On February 9, at a well-attended meeting at the Community Center, partners Mike and Dora Anaya and Hansi and Asi Mohn presented the plans for a new building in front of the 
former Anaya home on Route 41, just south of the Church. El 
Tanque Viejo (named for an old water structure once on the site) 
will contain three businesses, including the Anaya-Mohn firm 
Electrical Concepts, now housed in a tiny structure on the site. 
The one-story building with portal and terrace or garden in 
front will be 3,750 square feet., set back 25' from the property 
line. They have received a 30' easement at the north side from 
the highway department. There will be two water runoff areas, 
trees planted as a buffer around the edges, and a 22-place 
basecourse parking lot in front. 

The project calls for County rezoning from domestic to com-
mercial status, but it is not clear whether this would simply in-
volve a waiver to current laws or whether it would open up more 
of Galisteo to commercial zoning. 

There was a lot of interest in what the other two businesses 
would be. The partners hope to attract a coffee house/gallery 
and a restaurant. Other possibilities were a feedstore, a general 
store, a grocery store, a bakery, a small retail store, or storage 
lockers. 

The coffee shop and gallery idea sounded good to many. 
We could use a gathering place and we certainly have artists. 
If a restaurant were to come in, it would be open nights. At 
first the closing hour was stated as midnight; after some worried 
comments from those present, and a plea from Harmony 
Hammond for a closing hour more like restaurants in town, Mike 
agreed to l O PM. Priscilla Hoback asked about traffic impact 
and parking. Anna Cardenas asked about drainage. Valentine 
Riddell and Joe Cooper asked about zoning precedents, while 
others asked about lighting. There will be freestanding lights 
pointed down, and a 5' high lighted sign pointing up, with 50-
120 watt maximums in different areas. 

Several people wondered about liquor licenses. Mike said 
that was down the road; community input and approval would 
again be sought. (Apparently neighbors are sometimes a decid-
ing factor in liquor license hearings; this includes beer and wine 
for a restaurant.) Although the property is adjacent to the church, 
it is 450' away, so it is not affected by the law that says no liquor 
can be sold within 200' of a church. 

There remains the ticklish question of water. In December, 
the Board of the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers' 
Association (without submission to the membership) approved 
the transferral of Mike's domestic hookup from one house to 
the three-unit commercial building. (He is drilling a well to cover 
the needs of the rental house behind the new building.) 

Mela Montoya pointed out that the Water Association's 1996 
policy paper stated unequivocally "No approval for commercial 
or rental use." Galisteo uses all of its allotted 42.58 acre-feet. 
Water Board President Steve Moya (who was out of town and 
could not attend this meeting) has stated that there will be no 
more hookups of any kind permitted, although there are a num-
ber of people on the waiting list who have been there for years. 

Despite the apparent irregularity of the water permit awarded 
this project, we assume that the Water Board had logical rea-
sons for its actions. In the interest of mutual trust, the commu-
nity - especially Water Association members- needs to hear 
what they are. EL PUENTE welcomes comment in future is-
sues. 

If the Anaya-Mohn project is approved by the CDRC 
(County Development Review Committee) and then by the 
County Commissioners, the partners will have a year to build 
and a year's extension if necessary. Thanks were expressed to 
Mike, Dora, and the Mohns for bringing their plans to the com-
munity before going on to the County hearings. 

The first hearing is on Thursday, February 26, 4:00 PM, 
at the County Courthouse. The Anayas and Mohns welcome 
community presence and support. If you will be out of town, 
and have something to say, you can write a letter to the CDRC 
before the hearing.

title: Protecting Our Assets
body:
by Joe Cooper

For most of us, our biggest investment is the house we 
live in and the land it sits on. We protect this investment and try 
to increase its value by making repairs and improvements. The 
condition of our community as a whole and the quality of life it 
offers also affect our property values. It follows that we shouid 
put some of our time and effort toward improving Galisteo as 
well. If you've thought about doing this, but don't quite know 
where to start, here are some ideas. 

This is the time of year for some major meetings, for the 
Galisteo Community Association (March 4) and the Galisteo 
Water Association (in March, but not yet scheduled). Sometimes 
there aren't enough people at these meetings to conduct busi-
ness, much less express the views of residents who might make 
a real contribution. We should all go to meetings, learn the is-
sues and speak up and vote for what we think is best. We can 
even run for office. But the starting point is to go and make one's 
feelings known. If we don't do that, we can't affect the outcome, 
and have no right to complain. 

The organizations which work for Galisteo can only im-
prove things if they have enough people to do their jobs. If we 
won't do it, who will? For example, the Galisteo Volunteer Fire 
& Rescue needs more people. If we have a fire that could dam-
age our property, or a medical emergency, we expect them to be 
there for us. But how can they meet our needs and protect us if 
there are not enough people trained and equipped to do so? 

The last thought is that we should all share our part of the 
cost. Most of what Galisteo needs costs money and we should 
consider our contributions as the opportunity to protect our in-
vestment here. If we can't spare the money, we can contribute 
our labor and our energy. The point is that we shouldn't depend 
on our neighbors to fulfill our obligations. 

There's a story about a very religious man who prayed for 
hours every day. At the end of each prayer, he asked God to help 
him win the lottery. After years of this, God said to him: "You're 
a good man and I'd really like to help you win the lottery. But 
first you have to buy a ticket." 

Isn't it time that everyone in Galisteo bought a ticket?

title: Letter to the Editor: Bartering System Proposal
body:
My family and I are newcomers to Galisteo and feel very 
fortunate to be living here. Since we arrived last spring, I've 
become aware of how many talented people there are living in 
and next to the village who, as a group, can provide the service 
for just about anything that anyone needs. 

I'd like to put an idea on the table for discussion: What about 
setting up a bartering system here so that we could trade talents 
whenever possible? There could be two lists: the first a base 
naming different people and what they can do; the other a run-
ning list of who needs what. Then people could compare the 
two, make their own connections, and work out the logistics them-
selves. Maybe the lists could be published in EL PUENTE. Uncle 
Sam is generally not very supportive of ideas like this, but as far 
as I understand, so long as you keep records of value received 
and value given, all this is perfectly legal. 

I've mentioned this idea to a few people so far and the re-
sponse has been positive. It seems to me that this goes back to 
how villages originally worked. What do you think? 

Ted Fleming, 466-2363

title: New Galisteo Community Association Board
body:
PRESIDENT: Maria Padilla; VICE PRESIDENT: Wendy Monroe; SECRETARY: Barbara Cooper; TREASURER: Suzi Calhoun; NEW BOARD MEMBERS: Woody Gwyn and Munson Hunt; CONTINUING BOARD MEMBERS: Anna Cardenas, Florence Sohn, Mela Montoya, and CO-SECRETARY Barbara Holloway.

The slate above was elected at the March 4 meeting of the Community Association, attended by around 30 people. Many thanks went to outgoing board members: President Mike Anaya, Michael Datoli, Evelyn Gregory, Secretary Linda McKee, and Joette Trofimuk, who did heroic time as Treasurer for ten years. ("I was a young woman when I began," she laughed.)

The other major news at the meeting was about the paving of our end of County Road 42, which may go out to contract as early as May 1. Rather than paving the road by the church, this section, up to the Pattons' curve, will be basecourse, maintaining the character of the center of the village. Paving will then run from the curve to 200 feet past the railroad tracks. They will try to put the new water lines at the sides of the road.

The Bosque ownership dispute is still in the courts.

A fuller report on this meeting will appear in the April issue of EL PUENTE, which went to press the morning after.

title: From the Water Board
body:
On Monday, March 16, at 7PM, the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers' Association, Inc. will hold its annual meeting for members only at the Community Center. Members present will elect a new President, the Foreman, one Board Member and one Alternate, will consider a request for commercial use, and will deal with a long-standing violation of the Bylaws.

Board officers will make annual reports on finances, the system, and plans to improve it, and will hear members' comments, complaints and suggestions.

There are 57 water association members. We need one-fourth of them (15) to hold a legal meeting. Each year we have to go out and beat the bushes to make that quorum, so we can have a meeting we are required by law to hold. Please, members, PLAN TO ATTEND ON MONDAY, MARCH 16.

Any member interested in serving on the Board, especially as President, please call Steve Moya, 466-1544, Moira Walden, 466-4097, or any other Board Member. Such service is unpaid. We are all volunteers.

For the information of the community, our well is metered and the gallons used are reported monthly to the County and quarterly to the State Engineer, so we know how much water the system is using. Our water right, granted to us in 1962, is for 42.58 acre feet a year, or 13,874,735 gallons. Because we are very close to that limit with our current usage, we regret to inform those of you who are on a waiting list for a hookup that there can be no new hookups.

M. Walden, Treasurer

title: Open Letter to Steve Moya, President, and Board Members of the Galisteo Water Association
body:
Steve and Board members:

We find it hard to believe that the board members would allow Mike Anaya and his partners to transfer his water hookup from his house to the business he attempts to open. In the first place, that partner of his is not a resident of Galisteo. And secondly you will not open water hookups for residents of Galisteo that need or want it. Yet you will allow Mike Anaya to use his water hookup for his business. You know he will be using up a lot of water. He will have to have bathrooms in his commercial building according to Code.

Another thing, you did not have the decency to let members know what was going on. I think a lot of us learned about it the night of the meeting.

I think by letting Mike use his water hookup for his commercial business you have opened a can of worms. I understand we are already using our allotted water acre feet. So is that the reason you will not open the water hookups? And yet you will allow Mike to transfer his water hookup from his house to this commercial building. We sure would like to know why!

Mela and Onesimo Montoya

title: The Ancient Ones
body:
We cannot imagine how dark it was - darker than any night most of us have ever known even in the depths of what's left of the "wilderness," where noisy lighted airplanes continually cross the sky at night. And by day vast silent spaces shimmered in the sun between the small bands of people under skies unmarred by jet trails.

But the land in this basin we now call the Galisteo was not empty: deer, rabbits, mountain sheep, bear, turtles and mountain lions, rattlesnakes and eagles lived here in abundance. For the people of the basin and elsewhere these creatures were not just animals to be exploited or feared, they were ambassadors from the spirit world. The rattlesnake lived in the ground, the underworld, place of death and of the origin of life. The eagle lived in the sky, the home of Tlaloc the rain god who controlled the clouds and storms which brought life-giving rain.

Over the millennia people continued to live here using water from the river, building pit houses and eventually fortified stone pueblos to guard against invaders from the north.

In the basin along the spined ridges called crestones, the south side of the rocks is dark with desert varnish. It is here that the people chose to depict their world view: Kokopelli, the humpbacked god of fertility, mountain sheep, spirals, hands, often displaying six or more digits; mountain lion claws, roadrunner tracks, bear claws, masks, horned serpents, just to name a few. Little is truly known about these drawings, but what we do know is that they are not "writing" nor are they "pictures" in the sense of illustrations. Perhaps the closest we can come to an explanation for these petroglyphs is that they are "magic." And as sacred work they deserve to be respected, admired with awe, and preserved. Which brings up a difficult question. Most of the petroglyphs in the Galisteo Basin are on private land and therefore not legally accessible to those who wish to see them.

On the other hand, this inaccessibility helps to protect them from vandalism. Hopefully, some day this question of inaccessibility and protection can be addressed. They are all we have left to learn something of an ancient lifeway so very different from our own. (To the right: A Galisteo Basin petroglyph)

title: From the Kids: A Vibrant Little Town
body:
I'm writing this so people in Greece can know what my little town of two hundred fifty people is like!

When you hear that, you'll probably think that my town is pretty dull. Actually something is always happening here.

I live two miles outside of Galisteo, but I'm still considered a resident. I live on a twelve-acre parcel of land that has intrigued people from around the world to write my family a letter asking if we could trade houses. One of the reasons my family moved to the house I am describing to you is because the landscape looked a lot like Greece. My family is Greek. We have relatives in a town called Eritini on the Gulf of Corinth. My name is Athanasious Merehoulias.

Back to my house and land. I have seventeen apple trees, one pear tree, and twenty one cottonwood trees. We have an arroyo going right along the property. An arroyo is a dried up river bed. In the summer when New Mexico gets its monsoons, walls of water come pouring down the arroyos at tremendous speed. The arroyo at my house [Arroyo de los Angeles] can be fifty feet wide and have four foot rapids. Every year people try to drive through the rushing water, but each time the car gets carried down the arroyo about 100', only to be smashed up and stuck on rocks.

The town of Galisteo is a little but very festive town. Almost everybody is friends. A few years ago Galisteo started a Volunteer Fire Department. This got the town really going. Every year fundraisers are held for the fire department. One is called G.A.G.A. Gala-- Great Array of Galisteo Artists. It is an auction where Galisteo artists donate their work to the Galisteo Fire Department. There is a really fun party. The fire fighters of Galisteo don't get paid. They volunteer to help out their community.

The Galisteo Fiesta is another fundraiser for the Fire Department. It is an outdoor party with food, games, and live bands playing. Most of the bands are pretty good. Some of the music the adults dance to. The bands also agree to play for free. Another way the Fire Department makes money is that they hold a raffle for great prizes. I've never won any of the prizes but I hope my luck will change this year.

Another fundraiser is the Studio Tour which is a great chance for Galisteo artists to sell their work. People come from all over the state to see this tour. It is a great time for meeting people and having fun.

One of the reasons the town of Galisteo is able to do these fundraisers together is because of the amount of people. Everybody knows everybody. It's the kind of town when you drive through it you wave at almost everybody you see. The people of Galisteo are great people who are all willing to make our little village better.

There is also a lot of things that I like to do on my free time in Galisteo. In the center of town there is a river called the Galisteo River that runs through part of New Mexico. It is more like a stream. Down by the river there is a huge rope swing. You sit in a loop in the rope and run off a hill. You fly down all the way over the river. It is the biggest rope swing I have seen in my life.

Another thing I like to do is mountain bike along the railroad tracks that go to another town about four miles away. There is a volcanic dike behind my house. It's like a rough hill with boulders, rocks, and sandcliffs. I like to go up there and jump off the sand cliffs into piles of sand.

This is how I view my town and my home, my Galisteo.

Athan is twelve years old and goes to Sante Fe Prep. He is the son of Shaun Gilmore and Nick Merrick.

title: Letter to the Community from State Historic Preservation Division
body:
To Members of the Board, Galisteo Community Association, March 3, 1998:

The Galisteo Historic District (State Register #129) was listed on the State Register of Cultural Properties in 1969. Enclosed is a copy of the 1969 correspondence from the State Planning Office, HPD's predecessor, announcing the historic designation and stating that documentation of the site will be necessary in the future. The Historic Preservation Division (HPD) has been aware for some time that the 1969 historic designation was not accompanied by a nomination form as intended by the Cultural Properties Act (18-6-1 through 22, NMSA 1978). HPD does not have in its files a narrative account of the history of Galisteo, descriptions of the historic buildings and features of the village, or a boundary description for the historic district. Because the documentation and a State Register nomination form were never completed by the State Planning Office, HPD has decided that it is necessary to complete what was started in 1969.

As part of our 1998 Historic Preservation Division Fund grant program for research and planning, HPD has sent out a Request for Proposals for "Preparation of Galisteo Village Inventory and District Nomination." To inform the community of this project I am sending this letter to your organization with copies to the Galisteo Volunteer Fire Department, the Galisteo Domestic Water Users Association, and to the editor of El Puente de Galisteo for inclusion in that newsletter.

The purpose of the proposed Inventory and State Register nomination is to provide the community and our office with documentation on the buildings and features that contribute to the historical character of Galisteo. For example, from the New Mexico State Highway and Transportation Department, HPD is aware of two projects proposed by the Santa Fe County for Galisteo: 1) assistance for the improvement of the Galisteo community water system and 2) improvements to County Road 42. Once HPD has entered into a contract with a consultant to perform the Galisteo Village Inventory and State Register nomination, we will encourage the consultant to visit with people in the community about this project. We hope that the residents of Galisteo will welcome this project and offer their assistance to the consultant and HPD for its successful completion. Thank you for your cooperation. If you have questions regarding this correspondence, please contact my office at (505) 827-6320.

Sincerely,
Lynne Sebastian, Ph.D.; State Historic Preservation Officer.

EDITOR'S NOTE: Listing on the State Register does not affect a property owner's rights on decisions regarding their property unless it is a project involving State or Federal funding.

[* The GCA Board has a copy of the proposal, and a 1969 letter to Jose Ortiz y Pino confirming the state registry. Applications are due at 5 PM, March 27. EL PUENTE editor Lucy Lippard is applying to do this inventory, working with an experienced architectural historian. Wish me luck! ]

title: La Cuaresma
body:
With Lent upon us I thought I'd remind our Catholic villagers of the coming events. Good Friday is April 10. It was and is customary among some of the village to share the lenten foods with one another. Those foods were prepared before 12 o'clock, served in small dishes, put on a tray, and the older children or adults would take them to their neighbors. The neighbor did the same. Some of the foods were: chile con torta, arroz dulce, salmon. panocha, and sopa. These were dishes handed down from mother to daughter. 

After lunch the people would join at the church to observe the three hours Christ hung on the cross. To announce the services the matracas (a wooden slate with attached wooden beads that hit against the wood to produce a rattling sound) would be used instead of ringing the bell. The Stations of the Cross, or estaciones would be prayed, followed by other prayers. Easter Sunday is April 12 and mass begins at 12 o'clock. Feliz Dia de Pasqua a todos.

title: CDRC Approves Preliminary Plan for El Tanque Viejo
body:
The County Development Review Committee meeting on March 26 at the County Courthouse was attended by several Galisteo residents. Asi Mohn and Mike Anaya stood as applicants for the El Tanque Viejo project, "in Galisteo Village within Section 36 Township 14N Range 9E (Commission District 5) a 3,500 square foot project on .0822 acres." Chairman Steve Moya recused himself from voting on his brother-in-law's proposal. Anaya and Mohn stated that one third of the building would be for their business, Electrical Concepts, and two thirds would be rented out, perhaps as a gallery and coffee shop. Mike said the community seemed to think it would be a good place for people to stop for coffee before work, and "My sister needs a place to show her artwork."

The staff case planner was Development Review Specialist I Vicki Lopez. The Staff recommended .approval subject to a number of conditions too long to list here in detail, including standard regulations for driveway permit, master plan, underground utilities, dumpster fence, fire hydrant and other fire considerations. Among them: "The minimum water main size shall be 8" and shall be capable of providing 1000 ( +) gallons per minute to the attached hydrant with a residual pressure of 20 PSI"; "fire licenses shall not be granted until the fire suppression sprinkler system and alarm system have been tested and approved by the Fire Marshal." And "Prior to final approval, the applicant must submit an approved Environment Department permit for a waste water system. The system shall serve the entire project and must reduce nitrogen per Article VII, Section 2.7."

The.staff recommended that the proposed development be given 1.39 acre-feet of water per year which was approved by County hydrologist Jack Frost. The Galisteo Water Association was not consulted on the amount. Our domestic hookups allow for 169,000 gallons per year: 42.58 acre feet divided by 80 hookups. (The city of Santa Fe recommends 8,000 to 12,000 gallons per month, or 96,000-144,000 per year.)

The final condition for the Anaya-Mohn project states: "The water budget must be honored. A meter shall be installed with water use reported every 6 months, and any overuse shall be made up by conservation in the six months following over-consumption. Landscaping and water use must follow the County Terrain Management Requirements."

Richard Griscom asked whether this commercial approval established a precedent for other development in Galisteo. The reply was yes, (politically if not legally) but if a Community Land Use Plan were adopted to modify zoning, it would override this and other precedents.

The Anaya-Mohn project is scheduled to be heard for final approval by the Board of County Commissioners on April 14, 1998, 6PM. If you have questions, call Vicki Lopez at 986-6222.

title: {Gateway to Galisteo}
body: The cross on the Creston or hogback east of Route 41 was erected by Jose Ortiz y Pino and his brother John on Good Friday around 1955. The two young men made it as "a little sacrifice for Easter, a reminder of the Passion." They constructed it in two pieces on the family ranch ( where Vista Clara is now) and it took them half a day to carry it up the hill and raise it.

title: From the Minutes of the Annual Meeting of the Water Association
body:
On Monday, March 16, at 7PM, the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers' Association, Inc. held its annual meeting for members only (there are 57 members) at the Community Center. The following was submitted to EL PUENTE for public information.by Gary Grimm, Secretary.

Members Present: Steve Moya, Gary Grimm, Michael D. Anaya, Lisa Griego, Moira Walden, Roman Attenberger, Antonio Chavez, Priscilla Hoback, Scott Diffrient, Barbara Cooper, Teresa Montoya, Rod Hall, Anna Cardenas, Onesimo Montoy.a, Anastacio Sandoval, Romona Scholder, Elayne Patton, Bobbi Anaya, and Barbara Holloway. (19 members total).

1. New Storage Tank Update:
We have just recently received final approval from the County. The job should go out to bid within 30 days, and construction most likely will begin in early May. With the new tank, we will have 65,000 gallons of storage (15,000 in old tank and 50,000 in new one). The new tank will be made of plexiglas and will be able to be painted any color the membership chooses. New system will assist Fire Department with greater water supply and more fire hydrants, will give the Association more water storage,and it will ensure fewer breaks. ISO rating is now down to 9 and we hope that when system is finished and inspected it could go as low as 7.

2. Frankie and Tacho Sandoval's Request for a Variance:
Discussion began by looking at feasibility of leasing or selling a hook-up rather than granting a variance. Anna Cardenas made a motion to sell to Frankie Sandoval one hook-up that the Association now owns (sold back to us by Alvaro Lopez-Waterman), provided that Frankie submit a permit of approval to the board based on having received final inspection from state on having a legal septic system and leach line, showing that he is now in compliance with all state health codes regarding septic. Motion was approved by members present voting 10 in favor and 9 opposed. Priscilla Hoback then made a motion to sell Frankie this hookup for $500. Anna seconded this motion, which was approved unanimously by membership.

3. MikeAnaya's Proposed Commercial Plan:
Mike explained that due to needing sufficient water pressure to operate a sprinkler system (Fire code requirement), he could not use his well to supply this new building. Mike answered further questions of water usage, noting CDRC meeting on March 26. Barbara Cooper moved to ha\'e Board consider the possibility of metering the 2 non-residential users (Chris Griscom and Mike Anaya) in order to determine and monitor their water usage. Motion was approved by the membership.

4. By-Law Change:
Anna moved that we propose to change Article III, paragraph H, to read: "Water hookups provided by the Association shall be used for domestic purposes only, unless special approval ·is given by a majority vote of a legal meeting (no fewer than 15 members present) of the general membership ... " Proposal approved. Letter will be sent out .to general membership this week to vote on this issue.

[Nos. 5-6 not received].

7. Elections:
Mike Anaya moved to re-elect Steve Moya as President. Steve Moya moved to re-elect Roman Attenberger as Foreman. Moira moved to re-elect Lisa Griego to a 2-year term as Member of the Board. Anna Cardenas moved to re-elect Teresa Montoya to a 2-year term as Alternate Board Member.

[All these motions were approved unamimously.]

Meeting adjourned at 9:15 PM.

title: Letter to the Editor - Change is Difficult
body:
The recent flap about Mike Anaya's pror,..,sed development of his Galisteo property- and water rights rebted to this development -
illustrates one very simple thing: ..:h:rnge is difficult. Folks like to believe that the way things are is the way they will remain. Those of us who have been around fL,r several decades can testify to the fact that this is not the case -
quite to the contrary! In delicate situations like this one. ~c,ple are tempted to take sides -
shall we support an issue? Sh:111 we oppose it? Shall we ride the fence?

But will our stance, in the Jong run. make' any difference? Change is inevitable, whether we support. L'Ff'.' $e. or ignore it. Wouldn't it be more practical to lay aside our differences in fa-
vor of a much more pressing need: the need to unite, as a community, behind a plan to embrace and prepare for positive change, to create for our children a future which ensures that they will enjoy the pleasures which brought us to Galisteo in the first place clean air, plenty of space, the support of neighbors and friends in a peaceful and natural setting?

Far more critical than Mike Anaya's plan to switch the wa-
ter hookup from his house to his proposed commercial building is the obvious threat that faces us all: Eldorado-type development headed this way.

How can we protect Galisteo from suburban sprawl? Can we work together to solve this potential problem? Can we ac-
cept the challenge, the responsiblity to prepare for this change? There are solutions out there. People are.already employing them in other small rural communities. Have we the determination, the patience, the faith in each other it will take to find our solu-
tions? I hope so!

title: Letter to the Editor - Water Association Concerns
body:
It's too bad the membership of the Galisteo Water Association is not concerned about our water. They didn't come to the hearing about Mike Anaya's proposal for a commercial building.

Seems to me that Mike Anaya deceived the Board members about what he was going to build on his commercial building ..

I talked to Moira Walden because I really wanted to know exactly why there are no more water hookups available and she plainly said there is no more water available. I asked if they knew that, why did they approve Mike Anaya the transfer of his hookup from his house to use it on his commercial building? title: Letter to the Editor - Community Harmony and Open Dialogue
body:
I was excited when EL PUENTE started. I think a newspaper like this has the potential to create and even heal community. Unfortunately it has the power also to destroy community and hurt individuals. When I read "Open Letter to Steve Moya and Board Members ... " [from Mela and Onesimo Montoya, in March] I was disappointed that this letter was printed without an equal simultaneous voice for the members of the Board.

When there is conflict like we have in Galisteo right now over this proposed zoning change, there are only a few possible outcomes: I. One side wins, the other side loses. 2. Withdrawal (neither achieves goal) 3. Compromise (both sides give up something) 4. A solution· where all needs and interests are met and village harmony is enhanced. Which outcome does EL PUENTE want to support?

I have followed this zoning change request fairly closely. If Mike Anaya or Steve Moya have done anything unethical or illegal, I am not aware of it. Let them have a voice. This is not the way to thank these people for the services they have provided us. If our residents serve the community on boards, follow the rules they've been given and then are called publicly without warning into question, there will come a day when no one will serve. It felt to me that by only printing one side of the conflict and not allowing a simultaneous voice to the people whose integrity was being called into question, El PUENTE may have inadvertently escalated an already difficult situation.

You can bet that one day there will be a restaurant (in addition to the Inn) in Galisteo. If there is only room for one, I prefer that it be in Mike Anaya's control, rather than in the control of some person we havenft even met yet.

title: EL PUENTE Reply to Nancy Fischer
body:
I'm not sure Nancy read the February or the March issues. The Water Board was in fact given first say in March. The same with this April issue. This is what they chose to print. EL PUENTE has been in contact with Moira and Steve all along. And we. print all Letters to the Editor that are received.

The newspaper exists so all sides can be heard. This is not inadvertent but intentional. Open discussion of controversy is healthier than false harmony and buried resentments.

EL PUENTE has never spoken against Mike Anaya's development and has in fact supported the coffee shop/gallery idea. We are interested in the water situation because it ultimately affects the entire community and not just the members of the water association. In the interest of harmony it is important for everyone in the community to be well informed and for all the facts to be out in the open.

title: The Greening of Galisteo
body:
Just three days after many wore green to celebrate St. Patrick's Day, Kaye Sandford gave a community party to announce plans for the ecological future of Vista Clara Ranch. Permaculture expert and Living Systems Designer Thomas Mack presented a visionary program for creating a thriving ecosystem where the soil and its dependents, animal and vegetable, will work in harmony with the human goals of physical and spiritu.al wholeness. Organic farmer Rob Roy (the man, not the cocktail) then described how this would provide a wide range of natural bounty, including fruits and vegetables, herbs and spices, small animals, poultry and fish.

Creating this Eden won't be easy, but with Kaye's cominit-
ment and the expertise and energy of her staff, it surely seems attainable. Tackling the challenge involves checking erosion and creating productive soil to replace what's blown or wasted away. Digging swales or shallow trenches along the land contours catches and holds the water as berms jn between are planted with hardy native plants to anchor and enrich the soil. This makes it attractive for trees like Cottonwoods rather than the Salt Cedar (Tamarisk) and Russian Olive that have taken over.

The guiding principle is to make nature our ally by turning negatives into positives that work interactively. It is better to find constructive uses for pests rather than just getting rid of them. That way-some creature you want to have around can eat, say, grasshoppers, turning them into a resource rather than a burden. That approach, repeated over and over with various plants, animals, birds, and insects, makes the program efficient.

All this takes water and the challenge is to save and re-use it to the fullest. Rain will be channelled from roofs and organized drainage into rock-lined ponds containing reeds to cleanse and preserve it. Systems to re-use "gray water" will mean drawing minimal water from the ground. Drought-tolerant plants will nurture and sustain each other as in the brother/sister relationship of the pinon and juniper. As the land heals, vegetables and herb gardens, orchards, beehives, small animals and poultry can thrive in interdependence.

Just as one hand washes the other, the various species will grow and thrive, giving and taking as nature intended.This will provide natural beauty as well as healthy foods and healing herbs for chefs Steven and Kirstin Jarrett to prepare and to use in teaching others. Vista Clara does not intend to keep all these benefits for themselves. Kaye has offered to share the expertise and energy of her advisors and staff with the entire community so that we all benefit. Supporting the project can help us extend the greening all over Galisteo. Call Kaye Sandford if you are interested (466-0597).

title: {The GCA Report}
body:
The new Board of the Galisteo Community Association held its first meeting on March 24. It was recommended and approved that major issues considered by the Board be written up regularly in a column in EL PUENTE. This will give us a much-needed opportunity to communicate with the community at large. All members will continue to receive the minutes of each Board meeting. This column by the Secretary will simply expand on the minutes and give a more detailed account of matters considered by the Board.

In our attempt to increase general communication and further broader-based community participation in events and issues of importance to us all, the Board decided that the first half hour of each Board meeting would be an open forum, encouraging anyone in town to come and speak about issues of importance to them.No written request will be required and you are all encouraged to share your concerns with us. With the exception of the April meeting which will be Tuesday night, April 21 at 6:30 PM in the Community Center, the meetings are generally held on the third Wednesday of each month at 6:30.

The newly formed Action Committee [formerly the Advisory Committee] will be headed by Wendy Monroe. This group will consist of members of the community who are willing to volunteer their services for special events or projects which Board members cannot undertake due to time and energy commitments. While we have several names of those willing to serve in this way, we could use a few more people to come and "fill the gaps." Call Wendy if you would like to help in this way. You may choose thr. time and project on which you would like to work and your help and advice will be greatly appreciated.

At the moment, we are in need of two people to organize our annual Flea Market on a Saturday morning in early June (date not yet determined). This involves publicizing the event, collecting booth fees, arranging for food and space for all participants. It is a great all-community event and we do need your . help.

We would all like to thank Joette and Nick Trofimuk for their gift of a Sharp copier to the community.

title: Gravestone of Carolina Granito
body: One of the most handsome stones in the old graveyard is that of a young woman who died of consumption less than a month after her marriage. Her marker features a tree stump (symbolizing a life cut short), an anchor (perhaps her immigration from Italy) and a fern. The sad story is told in the inscription: En Memoria de Carolina nacio Carolina Granito el dia primero de marzo de 1888, nacio en Petina Italia. De tres meses de nacida, vino a los estados unidos, fue educada en el convento de las Hermanas, en Albuquerque, New Mex. Fue casada con Pedro Ortiz y Pino, el dia primero de Agosto de 1908. Fallecio el dia 25 del mismo mes, a la edad de 20 anos, 5 meses, 25 dias. Hija de Rafael Granito y de Permenia P. De Granito. (Photo: Richard Shuff)

title: GCA Doings
body:
by Barbara Cooper, GCA Secretary

We were pleased to welcome eight members of the community to our April 21 Board meeting. Rob Roy, the farm manager of Vista Clara and Kaye Sandford, spa director, distributed flyers about Nolo-Bate, the biological grasshopper control. Copies of this memo have been distributed to all residents and it is urgently requested that all in the village take part in this project to ensure its success. Nolo-Bate may be purchased from Rob Roy at Vista Clara ( 466-4772) at wholesale prices.

Janice Felty and Dick Griscom expressed their concern that lumber has been dumped in the arroyo at the Bosque, posing a potential fire hazard.

Valentine and Lou Riddell asked that the entrance to the Bosque be blocked to vehicular traffic ( cars and motorbikes) due, again, to the possibility of sparks igniting fires. The Board agreed to their suggestion and the road will be blocked.

Richard Shuff has volunteered to run the Flea Market which will be held on Saturday June 6.

Florence Sohn, Wendy Monroe and Woody Gwyn are the members of the committee to design and arrange to have constructed cabinets for our archives which will be displayed in the new room at the Community Center. They would welcome bids from anyone interested in constructing these cabinets. Bids should be submitted in writing by June 1. This project, as well as a conference table, will be funded by a generous grant recently received from the McKee Foundation of El Paso.

We are in the process of soliciting bids for a new roof for the Community Center. After twenty years, there are leaks and problems which warrant this new roof. We would welcome suggestions of reliable roofing contractors and personal recommendations to aid us in the selction process. Please contact Maria Padilla if you can offer names of tried and true contractors. We are anxious to proceed with this project before the onset of the rainy season.

As this project represents a sizable financial investment and one not covered by any allocated funds, we would welcome donations for the new roof in any amount. It appears that the cost will be between $3500 and $5000 and due to our limited resources, we would prefer to provide matching funds from the treasury for donations received. This is a project of concern to us all!

title: Linda Durham's New Gallery Building
body:
Linda Durham's new gallery building may be open as early as the end of this month. Durham's pioneering role as a representative of New Mexico contemporary art was written up in Pasatiempo. One colleague was quoted as saying she has been as important as Gerald Peters in the Santa Fe art scene. (Some would say more so.) "She has 'discovered' many artists now recognized as important and showed their work consistently even when it didn't necessarily sell." On the list of well-known artists who have shown at Durham's gallery was Galisteo's Harmony Hammond (who is currently exhibiting a group of paintings in New York).

Durham's first gallery opened in Santa Fe, March 1978, on El Caminito and then moved to a prime spot on Canyon Road. Three years ago, when the rent went astronomical, she moved the gallery to Galisteo; when Woody Gwyn bought the hacienda, she decided to stay and build her own space, designed by Santa Fe architect Beverly Spears. It is being built by Ray Valdez, using Rastra, a new building material made from recycled materials.

In the Pasatiempo article, Hollis Walker says Durham has "found her niche, hewed to her vision and plunged ahead, even when anyone who's ever taken Business 101 would have recommended she close her doors."

title: Past Lives/Present Concerns
body:
Galisteo has become home to many of us from "elsewhere" who have left past lives behind, fallen in love with the village, and, in a sense, begun again. Our collective past lives could probably fill several books. These personal histories are important because they have given us all talents, energies, experiences and knowledge acquired worldwide and brought here.

Not all of our past lives are spoken about or generally known. Even after years of friendship, it is not always easy to weave together the strands of another's life, the "what makes her tick." In the case of Lucy Lippard we are being treated to an insider's view of her thirty years in a small loft in SoHo in New York City. "Sniper's Nest:Art that has Lived with Lucy R. Lippard" is an astounding group of artworks, posters, memorabilia and favorite things that fills the new wing of the Museum of Fine Arts throughout the summer. The show, curated by Neery Melkonian, has been travelling around the U.S. to college museums for the past two years. Now the artwork has been donated by Lucy to the Museum of New Mexico's Museum of Fine Arts in Santa Fe. It represents the work of many famous and not-so-famous artists who have been and are Lucy's friends and gave her these treasures over the past forty years. They represent Lucy's many interests and reflect her work as a respected art critic, free-lance writer, activist, and author of 18 books (many of which are in the Santa Fe Public Library).

"Almost everything here was found or was a gift," she says. "Attached as I am to these objects, they don't form an image of my taste, but of my life."

The artworks and treasures surrounded you in that New York loft .Sometimes hung haphazardly,sometimes painted on the very walls or stacked around the room,never organized and always cherished, they formed a fascinating background for the people who came and went.

Now reframed, cleaned, selected and grouped by Melkonian with carefully chosen excerpts from Lucy's writings, these same objects give us an intimate look at the life of an avant-garde art writer, curator, and lecturer. (Lucy designed and hung the Santa Fe show herself.)

Lucy has been coming to New Mexico since 1972, often to visit her longtime friends Harmony Hammond and Judy Chicago. On her first trip to Galisteo in 1986 she sat on the hogback at night to watch Halley's Comet. She "fell for Galisteo" in daylight a couple of years later. Between 1992 and 1994 she lived here part time and built her house ( off the grid, plugging the whole thing into her car at first). Then she moved here, entrusting to others her "stuff," which would not become part of her new life.

Lucy was born in New York City in 1937 and graduated as an art history major from Smith College, where she won the creative writing prize her senior year. She went on to earn a Master's degree from the Institute of Fine Arts at New York University and has since received several honorary Doctorates of Fine Arts from American art schools.

Her summers have always been spent at her family homestead in Georgetown, Maine, where she sails a 12-foot sailboat She returns there each year to be with her partner, Peter Woodruff (who is a shipyard mechanic, photographer and archaeologist) and to be close to her son Ethan Ryman, a hiphop musician, producer, and audio engineer, his wife Kyla Adams, an elementary school teacher, and their two year old son, Samuel Justice. Lucy is deeply involved in researching the local history of her place in Maine as well as th,at of Galisteo. Years ago she spent time in Mexico and Central America and was "once pretty fluent" in Spanish.

In her present life in Galisteo, Lucy is creating a new environment in her cozy little house and newly-added workroom. She has an extraordinary library, filling a 24-foot wall floor to ceiling with books on art, politics, Hispanic and Native American cultures, feminism, and fiction. She invites anyone in the village who is interested to borrow from this "Galisteo branch library."

Needless to say all our past lives color our new ones here. Our deepest interests continue to excite us and we search for ways to connect in Galisteo. Lucy said it was hard at first but she found her niche after joining the Fire Department auxiliary and soon afterwards beginning EL PUENTE. As a writer, historian and journalist, this was exactly the opportunity she sought. She continues to work for a living ("free-lance writers die with their boots on"), spending six to eight hours a day on her articles and books in progress, hiking in the afternoons through the village and surrounding area, and working on EL PUENTE. She continues to lecture nationally at colleges, museums and art schools. Over the years her interest has shifted from conceptual and minimalist art, feminist art, activist art and multicultural art to a concern for place, land use, and public art. Her fascination with the history of Galisteo has led her to collect material from local archives which will be added to the history section in the Community Center when it is completed. Her most recent book The Lure of the Local- contains some Galisteo pictures and references.

The past and present lives of Lucy Lippard are beginning to seem of a piece. She brings to Galisteo tremendous energy, an urgent sense of engagement in the community past and present, and an open mind. We look forward to weaving the strands of her past lives as seen in the museum exhibition with those of her present life as we have come to know her.

title: El Cardinal
body:
by Tana Cardenas

Rojo como una rosa
Elegante como un rey
Se llama Cardinal.
Le gusta bailar en
mi jardin presumiendo
sus colores.
Se sienta en su cerco
cantanando su cancion
Canta por manana y por la tarde
Pero la noche
se cuesta a dormir.
En la noche suena de canciones
para cantar el segundo dia.
Canta por su pajorita presumiendo sus colores.
El cardinal baila por la compaiiera de su vida.

title: {Editorial}
body:
Over the summer might be a good time to think about the possibility of a Galisteo Community Plan (See Griscom article below). It's an idea that has been raised and faded away before. But the issue of planning becomes more urgent as the 285 sprawl comes our way like a great blob from the north, as the King development hovers to the south, as County Road 42 is paved, and as the development north of the Galisteo hogback ("Haciendas Tranquilas") seems to be rising again with a fancy gate. Change may be inevitable, but Galisteans should call the shots about what and how things will change. It seems important for the village to take a look at where we are and where we are going. Even if we never manage to set a formal Community Plan in motion, we can at least get an idea of what we as a community would like to see happen in the next decade. Maybe next fall we could convene a meeting to discuss the pros and cons.

EL PUENTE is about to take the summer off again. The next issue will appear in late September and will catch up on July-August events. Please send info and articles to Lucy Lippard, Route 2, Box 70, Georgetown, Maine, 04548 or call 207-371-2760 or use Box 77 after Sept. 16.

EVERYBODY HAVE A GOOD, WET, HAPPY SUMMER!

title: Community Planning
body:
At its April 1998 meeting, the Board of County Commissioners (BCC ) of Santa Fe County approved an ordinance adding a new section to the Land Use Development Code which outlines a process whereby communities can develop their own plans. The ordinance will become effective June 21, 1998. The intent is to encourage communities to identify their problems and to propose solutions to them in the form of a Community Plan.

The first step in the process is for a community to name a planning committee to work on the community's plan in conjunction with Santa Fe County staff. The planning committee would apply to the BCC to proceed with the Community Plan. The applications should include an indication of wide and diverse community participation in the development of the Plan.

The BCC would then hold a hearing on the application to decide whether to proceeed with the Community Plan and what elements the Plan should include. At a minimum the Plan would have to identify problems and issues, indicate the reasons for needing a Community Plan, and state how the Plan wi II conform to the County General Plan.

Once the Plan is developed, with the as<>i.;:.ince of County staff, it would be presented at another hearing before the BCC. Once approved by the BCC, it would cun'>titute an amendment to the County General Plan.

The County staff is currently assisting eight different communities in the development of their Plans - including Cerrillos, Madrid, La Cienaga, and Aqua Fri a. Since the staff i:; currently spread so widely, it may not be able to provide much assistance to Galisteo in the immediate future. This does not mean that we can't start thinking and discussing the broad outlines of what such a plan might mean to us.

title: The Last Vaquero
body:
He was born Sarapio Montoya 71 years ago to Isabel and Luis Montoya on a small ranch near Leyba, New Mexico. He was the second of seven children.

When he was ten years old a sheep-herder with a big flock came through, as they often did in those clays, and because his family needed the money, Sarapio hired on at $12.50 a month, walking [from White Lakes to Buckman behind the sheep and then by train] to Laramie, Wyoming.

He is my abuelo (grandfather) by choice not by birth. He was my father's ranch foreman for 25 years and I grew up calling him "Abuelo" and his wife "Abuelita" (little grandmother). He is still remarkably handsome, a small dark man with graying hair and moustache. I remember when his hair was as black as his eyes.

As a child I was convinced there was nothing that my Abuelo couldn't do. He could pull windmills or calves, break horses, make harnesses, braid rawhide lariats and quirts and horsehair hat bands. He co~ld fix any motor, car, truck, tractor or bulldozer; wire a barn or build a house. He could rope, head or heel, and throw the hulahan.

He could flank and brand, dehorn and castrate, doctor sick animals, dam up arroyos or build a dirt tank. He could make roads, fix fences and witch for water. He could weld, tan hides, and be patient with little children. He could also knit and crochet and didn't care who knew. The one thing he couldn't do was stop getting older.

Sitting in his kitchen over a cup of rich, dark coffee, I asked him to turn his dark flashing eyes back over the years to remember ...

It was May when he started out to Wyoming with those sheep. It was November when he got there. He stayed through the winter, working for the sheep-herder. In the spring he got a job with a rancher [named Fletcher] who was shipping a herd of cattle to New Mexico on the narrow gauge. He rode back in the cattle cars with the herd and unloaded them at what is now Buckman, west of Santa Fe.

He got a job with a rancher named Fisher who had some cattle in the Lamy Box area, now part of the Eldorado Wilderness. There were few fences in those days and ranchers' cattle roamed the open ranges with just brands and ear marks to tell them apart. Each cowboy had a string or two of three horses, and covered a designated area. Sarapio said he'd tire a horse out in half a day in that rough country [ ..... ]

Sarapio doesn't remember how long he worked for Mr. Fisher, but he was about 17 when he went back to Moriarty to · · his family. About this time he went to work for "Ol' Man" ,1:,>" ] Ortiz on his ranch near Clines Corners. Seiior Ortiz was patriarch of the Ortiz family of Galisteo. There Sarapio met an absolutely beautiful girl. She was tiny, had red hair and white, white skin. Her father, who was foreman at the Ortiz ranch, was French and her mother Spanish. Sarapio fell deeply in love with Polly Archiveque, then 16, and married her.

Polly moved to Galisteo with him, where he worked laying track for the railroad. It was nice, safe work and Polly prayed he would stay with it. To please her, he did so for several years. Then the open range called him again.

In 1946 he went to work for Mr.McKinley on what is now the Thornton Ranch, just below Eldorado. He made a dollar a day and had a small one-room house.

Later, Polly followed him to Colorado, where he worked se:veral big ranches. Cowboys broke and trained horses as they worked, often spending all summer or winter alone in the mountains. Most of these wandering young men were not married, and those that were usually left their wives home. But Polly always refused to be separated from Sarapio and went with him from ranch to ranch, making a home of the little floorless shacks they were usually given to live in. She taped his broken ribs, put aloe juice on his rope-burned hands, and prayed, always prayed, that when he rode off in the morning, he'd come back again.

From Colorado they moved back to New Mexico, and Sarapio went to work for Philip McKee, near Galisteo.

September I, 1959, he went to work for my father on the Thornton Ranch. He and my Daddy were a perfect pair. Sarapio was proud and didn't like being told what to do, a trait that lost him more than one job. My father was an unassuming man, quiet to a fault. He'd find out in the first week if a new man knew what he was doing. Ifhe didn't, Dad fired him. Ifhe did, Dad left him alone from then on. Dad rode out with Sarapio every day, either in the pickup or on horseback, but in all those years, I never remember Dad giving him an order. They just worked together.

Dad was an old time cattleman. His father had been a Texas cowboy, the son of one of the last trail drivers. Dad knew straight up about cattle and horses and land, but he didn't have a mechanical bone in his body. Gracias a Dios for Sarapio, a wonderful mechanic.

Polly and Sarapio never had any children of their own. Maybe that was why they were so fond of my brother and me. All my life I'll remember the smell and taste of Polly's tortillas and green chi le, the warmth of their house, the feel of their strong hands as they held mine and led me up the steps into the little church at Galisteo. The service was always in.Latin and Spanish and I never understood a word, but I loved going. Those beautiful native people taught me real devotion.

That little church, with its wood stove, brightly painted saints in their nichos along the walls, and the row of flickering candles, wrapped its thick arms around us and made me feel the timelessness of these people and their land. Its grace and comfort reached out across the miles to warm my soul on the day my father died. As I sat alone in the house I heard its bell tell me again, "there is a time to be born and a time to die."

Sarapio helped us to go on without Dad. He told me, "the night your father die I don't sleep," his eyes pleading with me to understand his pain.

Last September [ 1982] we stood together on a little hill overlooking the sleepy village below and listened to Los viejos (the old ones) singing softly, "Adios, adios, adios," until the very wind whispered it. We helped Sarapio lay Polly in the ground and cover her grave. I watched him hold his head up, turn his back, walk away for the first time in 50 years without her at his side.

Time and the world that made him will never be the same again. He's the last of his kind, the last vaquero.

[Sarapio Montoya (Onesimo's older brother) still iives in his house on the east side of Galisteo. His father was born in Galisteo and his mother, Isabel Baca Montoya, was born in Cerrillos. Although his health is bad, his memory is very sharp.The bracketed corrections are from a conversation with him June 12. ]

Genora Moore is Gene Thornton's sister. She was raised on the Thornton Ranch in Galisteo/Lamy. This memoir is excerpted with permission from Eldorado Update, 1985, and Windmills and Dreams: A History of the Eldorado Community and Neighboring Areas, Eldorado: ECIA: 1997, p.75-76.

title: El Tanque Viejo Hearing
body:
On June 9 at around 10PM at the County Courthouse, the County Commissioners considered the Anaya-Mohn El Tanque Viejo proposal. Richard Griscom was the only member of the Water Association to attend other than the Anaya family. Commissioner Paul Duran moved to accept the proposal with two modifications in the conditions: the first concerned drainage plans; the second concerned water. Commissioners Joe Grine and Marcos Trujillo (Javier Gonzales attended most of the hearing but was out of the room for this vote) joined Duran to vote unanimously for approval

The Commissioners had received letters from Galisteo residents and a petition signed by 32 of the 57 members of the Water Association, protesting the CDRC's approval of the 1.39 acre feet of water per year Mike Anaya had applied for. "We object to this illegal and unequal allocation of our water," reads the petition. "We ask the Board of County Commissioners to recognize our rights and to include in any action it takes regarding the Tanque Viejo Project the condition that water from our Association will be limited to .53 acre ft./yr., the amount to which each member [ one hookup] is entitled" ( 42.58 acre feet divided by the 80 hookups).

However, letters and petitions were apparently ignored. The Commissioners did not consider the amount. In fact, they cancelled the CDRC's condition that El Tanque Viejo's water must be metered and overuse be compensated for, apparently on the basis that Chris Griscom's Light Institute - Galisteo's other commercial hookup - was not metered. (A simple solution might be for the Water Association to meter both/all commercial hookups; they now pay $50/month, not for added water, but for the commercial variance.)

The problem remains of the unprecedented amount of water approved for El Tanque Viejo. At one point during the proceedings, Commissioner Trujillo turned to his staff and asked if they had ever told a local water provider how much water to provide? The answer was no.

There are legitimate questions as to whether certain commercial uses would take any more water than most domestic hookups, given the amount used on drip irrigation for gardens and lawns. We have no idea how much water anyone uses. Eventually domestic hookups and private wells may also have to be metered, so that Galisteo has some idea of how much water is used and how to fairly distribute it. There is justified anxiety about general metering because it could raise prices for many who can barely pay what is charged now by a volunteer water board. Is there any possibility that government funding could be found to cover the cost of the meters themselves, without raising charges?

The crucial issue raised by this hearing is: Who controls our water? Is it Galisteo's Water Association (which leaves all private wells off the hook as well as off the hookups)? Is it the CDRC and County Commissioners, who do not usually interfere in local water quantities, but have done so in this case and can do so again? Do local associations have to abide by this?

Surely these issues should be discussed by all users of the water available to Galisteo, Water Association members or not.

title: {GCA Doings}
body:
Our new Open Forum segment of each board meeting is working. On May 18, Jim Fickey came to speak of his concerns about the landfill by the bridge. It is impinging upon his fenceline and recently substantial quantities of household trash have been dumped there. After discussion, the Board voted to close the landfill and fence it off to all further dumping.

Although it was previously reported that we were going to block the entrance to the Bosque to vehicular traffic, we did some research and discovered that legally we are unable to do so until our current litigation is resolved. It was also brought to our attention that it would be unwise to limit fire departrment access to the Bosque. So the road remains open, but cars are strongly discouraged.

By this time you have all seen the new pro-panel roof on the Community Center. We are extremely proud of this new capital improvement and hope it lasts for many years to come.

New tables have been purchased for the Community Center. Jim Sloan will soon start grading; screen doors will be installed; and in the near future gravel and landscaping for the new playground will be in place.

In order to check the safety of the old bridge, it was decided to call Robert Martinez, who is in charge of county roads, and to discuss it with the County Manager. The County will also be contacted about the poor condition of the road by Sandovals'.

Frank Hirsch has generously donated I 00 prints of a painting of the Galisteo Church by James McComb, an artist from Chicago who spent time here several years ago. Roman Attenberger will frame one for permanent display in the Community Center and the rest will be offered for sale for $30 apiece. We thank Frank for this handsome gift to us all.

We are excited about the real progress we have made and the community participation we have received.

Note: Board meetings have been changed to the third Monday of each month beginning with open forum at 6:30-7:00. Feel free to come and share your views.

title: From the Fire Department
body:
In case you are wondering what the fire engine was doing outside Mike Anaya's last month, while people in bulky bunker gear tripped over long hoses, spraying each other in the dark, that was GVFR staging a fire drill.

GVFR volunteers normally attend at least two trainings a month-one for fire, one for medical. This month's fire training was in the "burn building" (an old boxcar) at the Eldorado Transfer Station on June 9. Next month we plan to hold a fire drill (no fires allowed) in the Bosque-:-- just in case! It's very dry now and extreme caution should be exercised in the area.

In addition to those regular trainings, members frequently attend special classes - certification for new skills or re-certification for those already learned. For example, this month medical volunteers will attend four nights of PHTLS (Pre-Hospital Trauma Life Support) classes in Eldorado. These are required for First Responders, EMTs and Paramedics, but all members may attend.

Harmony Hammond will be taking her Swift Water Rescue Technician I training June 12-14th - a weekend on the Pecos and Rio Grande Rivers learning how to save the unfortunate few who don't heed the "Watch for Water!" signs at the arroyos. Swift Water Rescue is a very rigorous training and technicians are much sought after for mutual aid in other New Mexico counties during the monsoons.

We're lucky to have such a dedicated bunch of volunteers most of them hard-working folks who spend carefully guarded family and leisure time to learn skills which may some day save our lives. HATS OFF TO GVFR!

title: Public Information Meeting on Santa Fe County Library
body: At 7PM, on July 9, there will be a Public Information Meeting at the Galisteo Community Center for community input about the Santa Fe County Library to be built in Eldorado for the area from Galisteo to Glorieta. The building will stand on rent-free County land next to the Eldorado school. $250,000 has been budgeted by the legislature and some day, when there is a fully qualified librarian and it is open 20 hours a week, the State will provide some operating money. Until then funds must be raised from the communities involved.This library will be especially handy for those in the area with kids who need basic information for school projects. Andy Winnegar ( 466-6563) will facilitate the Galisteo meeting and encourages everyone to attend.
