title: Editorial: Community Action on Open Lands
body:
What a community can do when it gets together! Thanks to a large and eloquent turnout on June 7 at the public hearing of COLTPAC (County Open Lands and Trails Committee), the committee voted 8 to 1 to acquire a second parcel of land from the subdividing Thornton Ranch to our north and west. The chairman cited community support as a deciding factor.

This will add 640 acres to public open space in the Galisteo Basin (non-existent before the 1998 open land bond issue that spawned COLTPAC). A total of around 3000 acres are now saved in combined County, State and BLM lands.

Supporting speakers included Paul Williams, an archaeologist with the BLM, Jan Willem Jansens of the Galisteo Watershed Restoration Project, Cherie Scheick of the Rio Grande Foundation, County Planner Jack Kolkmeyer, and Jenny Parks from the Trust for Public Land (TPL). Our County Commissioner, Jack Sullivan, attended to observe.

This acquisition provides crucial leverage for TPL's ambitious plan to provide another 4000-plus acres of open land on both sides of route 42 (mostly on the northeast) bordering the railroad tracks. They plan a cluster development (rather than scattered ranchettes taking up all the land) off CR 42 on the west.

Few of us want to see development increase at all, but it's coming; and cluster is the best bet for conservation of land, water, and resources. TPL is now negotiating with the Thorntons for the details of a 3-year option - a condition for final purchase of this current parcel. On June 12 the County Commissioners approved all of COLTPAC's recommendations.

Many thanks to everyone who wrote letters, made phone calls, and attended the hearings. It worked.

title: La Lanera: History of the Old Wool Warehouse
body:
In 1989 I bought the old stone lanera (wool warehouse) from Peter Gould and moved here from La Cieneguilla. I lived in an added part of the space and used the long stone building for studio and storage. Now, 12 years later, I have expanded the living area into the lanera and renewed my interest in the history of the building. I am especially curious about the names and numbers painted on the trusses, window sills, and some of the stones.

On June 2, I talked on the phone with Jose Ortiz y Pino III, whose grandfather, Don Jose Ortiz y Pino, owned this property and had the lanera built around the turn of the century. The following history comes from pages 39 and 87 of Jose's book, Don Jose: The Last Patron, and from our phone conversation.

Don Jose controlled one of the largest herds of sheep in New Mexico and the lanera was suggested to him by Robert Seligman, a wool buyer from Boston who wanted to buy wool direct and have it shipped by rail from Lamy. Don Jose thought it was a good idea and called in his carpenter, Juan Martinez, to make "a large building constructed from stone, with good ventilation and wooden floors .... East of the stable, close to the alameda on the river front." Flat roofs tend to leak a lot, so the lanera was built with one of the earliest pitched, corrugated metal roofs in Galisteo. [The tin sheets are marked: "Patented May 1915, American Sheet & Tin Co., Pittsburgh."]

The lanera housed a wool cooperative where Don Jose brokered wool from his own sheep and those of neighbors and others around the state. He could get better prices for everyone if he pooled the wool and sold it in large quantities. Each family had a stall-like area in the warehouse where their wool was stored. (Once Don Jose was forced to report some of his men for robbing the wool warehouse, since some of the wool belonged to other sheepmen.)

He did a lot of business with the Bond Brothers in Espanola. The wool was shipped out of Kennedy. In fact Don Jose's men built the stone train station there specifically for this purpose. When wool prices dropped, Kennedy became a ghost town.

Seasonal shearing started June 1. The wool was kept in huge burlap sacks marked with the family brands. The sacks were 10 x 12 feet long and about 5 feet in diameter. It took four men to lift one, so they were mostly rolled. Each family had its own way of marking and counting the bags stacked high in the lanera. Jose speculates that the men probably used the black paint for marking bags to write their names on the trusses and window sills.

Here are the signatures and Jose's information on the people who "signed" the building:

Dan A. Chavez, one of Don Jose's main foremen; Feliberto N. Anaya: clever, a good worker, his family was from Cerrillos; Isabel Adams, "held in esteem" by Don Jose. "He was half-Indian and an all around handyman. He chopped wood, tended to the fireplaces in the main buildings. A very quiet man, never a step away from the Patron when he was in Galisteo"; Clemente Martinez; Juan Martinez built the lanera and lived in Galisteo. Glennes Parker, a homesteader in Moriarty who drove a truck to bring wool to Kennedy around 1940. Juan Montoya; Romolo Leyba; Betty and Tony Garcia, 1947; Tony liked his booze and women.; Pite (Pepito) lived and worked in Galisteo. He was very short, about 4' tall, had a hunchback and one arm. He chopped wood with this arm and could beat anyone arm wrestling.; Mateo; Felipe Chavez; Jack Salter (memorial 1937), a well-driller from Stanley/Moriarty who had sheep. Jose recalls that something strange happened to him but can't remember what.

Many people in the area raised sheep. During World War II there was such a need for wool that you could get a draft exemption for producing it. After the war, when the demand and prices dropped and synthetic fibers were becoming widely available, it became less profitable. The lanera was used to store wool until about 1950. Don Jose passed away in 1951. After that the building was used only for storage.

On May 26, 2001, sitting in my new kitchen in the old lanera, Priscilla Hoback graciously talked about the building's more recent history. In 1978 she bought the cluster of buildings on Via La Puente with property that extended to the south bridge on highway 41. She named it Quartermill Farm. The former owner was Linley Soleri, who bought it, she thinks, from Philip McKee (his in-laws, the Hovers, lived there). McKee bought it from Jose. Gradually, the southern parcels were sold off.

Priscilla says that the place was run-down and the land was so overgrown you couldn't walk across it. Many of the buildings had not been used for years. When she bought it, the lanera was filled with junk, garbage, and critters; a family of rattlesnakes lived by the door. (See her book, Living Clay, for more details.)

Gradually Priscilla and her friend (later husband) Peter Gould cleaned out and fixed up the buildings. They ran electricity and water to the lanera. For some 6 years the well-known sculptor Tony Price (whose materials came from Los Alamos dumps) lived and worked there. Christina Hagman also used it as a studio. Russ Letlow and his two daughters lived there briefly and around 1984 Peter used it as a wood shop and added on a little living area. I bought it in 1989.

Does anyone out there know anything else about the lanera's history? Do you recognize these names or know anything more about the numbers? Do you know the family brands? If you have any information, stories, or memories about working, playing, partying, or hanging out there, please call me (466-3932).

title: Fire Department News
body:
The GVFR welcomes two new members: Miguel Padilla and Doug Brenner. The new secretary is John Fitch.

Chris Fields, Linda Anaya and Steve Moya passed their Red Card test - a grueling physical trial. And Chris also got his Swiftwater Rescue certificate. With other Fire Department members who have also passed these tests, they are the people who will save our lives and property. It's hard to overstate the time and energy they put into these unpaid jobs.

Jan Willem Jansens of the Galisteo Watershed Restoration Project will come to the next GVFR meeting to explain the work being done along the creek, which will hopefully improve fire risk as well as conserving the bosque. In early June, a big batch of school children came to plant seedballs and do other preliminary work in and around the creek and were also given a tour of the fire station.

Hot Shot James Steinepreis will be living in the Fire Station off and on this summer. There is a new motion sensor light outside the station.

One very easy way to express your gratitude for the GVFR's hard work is to go to the Fiesta on August 18th, which benefits the Fire Department. And once again, they do all the work. Bob Harte is waiting for more recipes for the Fire Department Cook Book. Bring one to the Fiesta and receive a free raffle ticket.

"Andy and I plan to keep on going until we can't anymore," she said. Needless to say, the village hopes that time is not coming soon. La Tienda has been in its present location since 1986. title: Yard Guard: Outdoor Work and Exercise
body:
For the last 90 days or so, I have been designing and working hard on our yard. Moving heavy rock, pulling weeds, making stone paths ... My obsession has given me little time to exercise. We have all heard, and said, that we are exercising while working outside. The President's Council on Physical Fitness tells us that walking the dog is exercise. This seems to mean that just about anything is exercise. It is true that I maintained my weight and, to a certain extent, did a form of strength training.

The problem was that I lost some definition in my muscles and became less flexible. It has been my experience that a program of weight training with concentration on isolated muscle groups will shape and contour the body better than anything else.

I have achieved one important goal that I set for myself, which was to get outdoors more. Don't misunderstand me about the value of outdoor work. I'm just saying that it could have more value within a formal exercise routine. Happy Trails.

title: Letter to the Editor: Cats Needing Homes
body:
Dear Fellow Galisteans,

Lewis and I will be moving to Berkeley at the end of July, so that I can finish work on a degree in psychology. Over four years a number of Galisteo's cats have found their way to our casita and I have cared for them. Now this cat family needs new homes.

We have several precious kittens who will be ready for adventure in a few more weeks and two affectionate young mothers (just over a year old) each of whom would bring joy to a loving home. All are litter-box trained (don't ask me how this happened!) All are excellent mousers, healthy outdoor cats. So long as they have a safe place to sleep, they're pretty savvy about coyotes and owls. I wish I could take them with me, but Galisteo cats would be miserable in Berkeley. There is always the Animal Shelter but it's sad to think of these beautiful free-spirited creatures shut up in cages. Please call and claim your new furry friend!

-Valentine McKay-Riddell, 466-1791.

title: {Editorial}
body:
In the past year there have been some muted calls for a
"positive gossip column." Won't the current "Pedacitos/Bits and
Pieces" do it? It would be livelier if you would send me your
own items. As it stands now, I dig them up in newspapers and
hearsay, and I can miss a lot. Let me know about events and

title: Rudy Sena Honored at 31st Rodeo
body:
His daughters Amy Rogers, and Audra Baca, and son Clint
Sena now run the Rodeo de Galisteo, but Rudy Sena, who
founded it in 1970, is very much a presence at the annual event,
greeting friends and patrolling on horseback. This year he is
formally retiring at age 65 and was given a commemorative belt
buckle made by Mark Lee of Lamy. Rodeo announcer Joe Dan
Riggensberg came out of his own retirement to make the
presentation on behalf of Galisteo village. We turned out in force
on July 21-22, along with the biggest crowd ever - capping last
year's attendance of 2,000.

First came the parade Saturday morning, which was short
but very sweet, and included local riders on handsome horses,
kids, llamas, the Fire Department, and "floats" - one of which
advertised "brown water rafting" in the Galisteo Creek.

Bronc Riding, Bull Riding, Calf Roping, Barrel Racing,
Team Roping, and other events were exciting - and difficult.
Bad Moon Rodeo provided the feisty stock, which often got the
best of their human adversaries. (EMTs from the GVFR were
on hand to cope with injuries - all relatively minor this year.)
One big bull, having easily divested himself of his rider, decided
not to return to the pen, lying down in the ring (and virtually
smiling) whenever he was roped. His pursuers gave up and two
cowboys guarded him as the event continued in another part of
the arena. On Saturday none of the roping teams managed to
rope a calf both head and tail. Barrel racers, however, did fine
against their inanimate obstacles. Mostly women, their ages
ranged from 7 to forty-something. Sheri Ralston took the prize.

The children's events were great fun. Girls and boys
participated in Mutton Busting-where they burst out of the chute
on the back of a sheep- and the Calf Scramble - where hordes
of kids, some barely walking, confront hordes of calves, and try
to grab ribbons off their tails to win a prize. Sunday night the
trailers pulled out of the Rodeo Grounds. All those except the
severely bruised must be looking forward to next year.

title: The Other Galisteo
body:
There is something haunting about a namesake. Last April,
I was in Spain for work and I had to see the other Galisteo,
although aside from the name, its connections to our village are
tenuous. Our Galisteo is successor to the Tano Pueblo just to our
north, which was named Santa Cruz de Galisteo in 1581 by an
expedition led by Fray Agustín Rodriguez and soldier Francisco
Sanchez Chamuscado (not a name but a nickname: he was
apparently called El Chamuscado — the Singed One-because
he had a flaming red beard).

Many hope ancestors came from the Spanish Galisteo. But many of the early
explorers and settlers of New Spain and then New Mexico did
come from the same province - Cáceres in the Estremadura —
a rugged region of western Spain that borders on Portugal. In
the 13th century, huge tracts of land were granted to knights and
nobility for grazing livestock, especially sheep, which left the
rest of the population scant means to make a living. So when
Fray Nicolas de Ovando from Cáceres was named Governor of
the Indies in 1501, many of the 2500 Spaniards who followed
him to the Caribbean were Estremeños, among them Francisco
Pizarro, conqueror of the Incas, and, later, Hernan Cortes, who
subdued the Aztec empire. Hernando de Soto, the first European
to discover the Mississippi, and Francisco de Orellana, who found
the Amazon, were among others who left the Estremadura to try
their luck in the Americas.

I wondered which member of the Rodriguez expedition came
from Galisteo or environs. Luckily, it was a small group: nine
soldiers and three friars with nineteen Mexican Indian servants
and one unnamed mestizo, so searching the documents for their
Spanish hometowns was not a huge job. (They did not travel
light; 90 horses and 600 head of stock accompanied them.)

It turned out that of those listed, only Chamuscado was from
Cáceres. According to the 16th century chronicler Obregón, he was
"a native of the bishopric of Coria, Cáceres, Estremadura," born
in Arroyo del Puerto. Perhaps his parents or wife were from
Galisteo. For whatever reason, he named two Galisteo Basin
pueblos Galisteo and Malpartida (a nearby Spanish village) and
two pueblos he came upon elsewhere after other nearby Spanish
towns: Cáceres and Rinconada. The Rio Grande was named the
Guadalquivir, after the big river that runs through Sevilla, where
one of the friars came from. In Galisteo's case alone, the name
stuck. The Tano pueblo was still called Galisteo by Oñate in 1598.

The Gallegos Relación of the Rodriguez-Chamuscado
expedition reads: "About five leagues [c.14 miles) from the
Guadalquivir River we discovered another valley which we called
San Mateo [the Galisteo Basin]. Here we found four pueblos,
the first of which had three hundred houses, five stories high.
We named it Piedra Hita because it was built entirely of rock.
[This may have been San Cristóbal, or Pecos.] The second had
one hundred and forty houses four stories high. We named it
Galisteo. The third had one hundred houses three stories high.
We called it Malpartida [probably San Marcos]. The fourth had
eighty houses three stories high. We named it Malagón [San
Lazaro or possibly San Cristóbal]."

Some historians have suggested that Malpartida was named
after the "bad departure" from that pueblo of Father Juan de
Santa Maria, who was killed by Indians as he headed back to
Mexico. (Chamuscado himself died on Easter Sunday, April 15,
1582, before the expedition made it back to Mexico City.)

But the geographical explanation makes more sense when
combined with multiple Estremadura references. (There is also
a Rio de los Angeles there, which might be the source of our
arroyo, appropriately a.k.a. Arroyo del Infierno in the early days.)
In addition, the Rodriguez-Chamuscado expedition was the first
to name Nuevo Mexico.

Back to the Estremadura in 2001. On the eastern border of
Cáceres, we spent the night at the Sanctuary of Guadalupe (where,
ironically, given the recent controversy over Alma Lopez's
modernized version of Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe, there were
bare-breasted nudes all over the dense "grotesque" decorations
of one seventeenth-century room). Then we drove northwest
through a mountainous, wooded landscape with deep ravines.
Although we had heard that western Spain resembled New
Mexico, this part was so green that the only similarity was a
wild landscape, sparse population, and isolation. Dehesas
(pasturelands) dotted with evergreen oaks did recall our own
piñon-dotted rangeland, although the ancient buildings were gray
stone rather than adobe.

In the Tajo Valley, we passed through the national Parque
Natural Monfragüe, known for its birds of prey. A precipitous
dirt road wound through wild green hills dotted by sheep. Just
before the town of Plasencia we turned west at the first road sign
to mention Galisteo. My heart beat faster, but the landscape was
deteriorating. The road led through vast agricultural fields dotted
with curious two-story stone barns with open gridded walls (we
finally figured out they were tobacco barns) and patches of less-
than-picturesque agricultural/industrial areas. My friend began
to worry that I'd be disappointed if Galisteo weren't beautiful.
We got closer and closer until we could see in the distance a
walled village perched on a small hill.

The approach to Galisteo from the east is indeed not scenic.
The town is being developed as a tourist attraction. A huge ugly
brick hotel named the Medina Ghaliaya after an ancient Arab
fortress was under construction on the flatland below the hill
(next to the welcome sign, shown in the picture in last summer's
issue of EL PUENTE, where I'm holding up a photo of this
Galisteo). But the village itself is lovely, unique in its fully
surrounding Almohad (Moorish) wall dating from the 11th to 14th
centuries. There were once many such villages, but most retain
only remnants of their ramparts. The European Union provided
funds to restore those at Galisteo.

The village is entered through a mighty wooden gate that
opens onto a different world. The two-and-three storied houses,
all whitewashed, are crowded wall-to-wall along the narrow
winding streets. Just inside the gate, there was a very steep, worn
stone staircase. We climbed it with caution and found we could
walk along the top of the wall almost all the way around the
village, which we did, enjoying the view across a sea of red tile
roofs and peering down into people's back yards with ancient
stone outbuildings, chickens, and tiny gardens— a far more
intimate view than the closed facades on the street.

A stork was nesting in one of the turrets, and an octagonal
14th century tower called the Picota loomed over the ruins of a
Moorish Alcázar (fort) at the west end of the village. The old
church, with a mudéjar brick apse and a baroque retablo, huddles
within the village. There is a little plaza, occasional Moorish
decorations, and outside of the walls to the south, a sweet little
park and refreshment stand at the confluence of two rivers (the
Alagón and the Jerté), over which arches a medieval bridge (El
Puente de Galisteo!). It was Sunday, and the park was crowded
with local fishermen and picnicers.

Janice and Dick Griscom have also made the pilgrimage to
Galisteo, Spain. And when Bruce Nauman had a big exhibition
in Madrid, the Mayor of Galisteo showed up and gave him a
Chamber of Commerce video about the town. I will put my copy
in the Community Center for loans, but please return it, since it
belongs in the Archive.

title: Goose Downs Event
body:
The Event at Goose Downs has become a premier
international attraction. Held at the end of July and beginning of
August, it attracted competitors from ten states and five countries:
Canada, Mexico, France, England and Germany. Riders ranged
in age from teens to seventies. The first weekend 139 horses
participated, including many local riders and many new to
eventing. The second weekend there were 125 horses, and about
500 spectators came out each weekend.

The first weekend was marred by a fall in which the horse
was killed and the rider was helicoptered to Albuquerque after
what Jeffray Ryding recalls as "superb care by our Galisteo and
Eldorado paramedics. If you ever wondered about emergency
care in your village, wonder no more. It's the best."

Evelyn Bemis, member of the event's Organizing
Committee, won the Advanced Class on her New Mexico-born-
and-raised thoroughbred Tolstoy. For many the height of fun
on both weekends was the Event Team Challenge. Each of the
three teams was made up of an international rider, 2 pony
clubbers, and a Challenge New Mexico rider.

The Event at Goose Downs is a unique mixture. There are
high-powered world-class riders racing around a grueling cross-
country course, over intimidating obstacles with names like The
Big Burrito or Liam's Delight (which featured a huge log
mounted with a wooden deer head that alarmed several horses).
There is dressage (intricate maneuvers performed by highly
trained horses in the ring), show jumping, Pony Club classes,
and Olympic level competitions.

And perhaps best of all, there are events for the Disabled,
developed from a program with Challenge New Mexico now in
its second year. Riders with multiple sclerosis, Downs Syndrome,
and other afflictions, find a new freedom on horseback. It's called
hippotherapy (no hippopotamuses involved), and it can improve
mobility, speaking ability and flexibility. Challenge New Mexico
is always looking for more volunteers and calm older horses.
(Call 988-7621).

(Thanks to Jeffray Ryding and to Staci Matlock's article in the
New Mexican August 8).

title: Bear Sightings and Safety
body:
A bear and her cubs were sighted just west of Ranchitos (as well as in Eldorado, Villa Linda Mall and Camino del Monte Sol). Thanks to drought and a late spring frost that ruined the acorn and berry crops, bears are starving to death. They need some 45 pounds of food a day to survive hibernation, which begins in late October or November. Now they are forced to come down out of the mountains to search for food and are being injured and killed in record numbers.

Don't leave garbage, barbecues, birdseed, hummingbird feeders and petfood outdoors. Don't compost sweet things (like melons). Put electric fencing around beehives and chickens. If you meet a bear, don't get between it and the food source and don't run. Look as big as you can, wave your hands slowly over your head and back away. If attacked, fight back. (Good luck!)

If you feel for the bears, who have no choice but to seek food, send a donation to the Wildlife Center in Española, which is caring for the injured ones: POB 246, Española, NM 87532.

body: Galisteans have been speaking their mind in the New Mexican. Joette Trofimuk wrote to deplore the picture covering the Santa Fe High School graduation, which she felt demeaned the ceremony and education itself. Chris Fields wrote an eloquent plea for environmental education. (And a picture of him and Alison Tinsley with directors of the Tucson-based Center for Biological Diversity appeared in that organization's publication on the occasion of a benefit for the Gray Wolf at their home in May 2000.) The editors cut out the paragraph that said over 70 residents of Galisteo and Ranchitos had signed a similar letter to the County Commissioners.

title: Bridge Incident from 100 Years Ago
body: From the New Mexican 100 Years Ago, July 3, 1901: "A bridge 35 feet long and 40 feet wide burned down night before last at Lamy [caused by sparks from an engine]. It took the repair crew just 45 minutes to build a new bridge. Trains were delayed only that length of time by the incident." Those were the days! The same week a century later, there was another accident at Lamy in which one train backed into another and several people were injured. The delay was much longer.

title: John Massee Art Exhibition

title: Pamela Markoya at O'Keeffe Museum

title: Obituary: Joe (José Manuel) Anaya
body:
Joe Anaya died of a lung disease on June 30. He had just turned 67. Although he was raised in Stanley (in the little house next to the former Landon Store), schooled there, and lived on the ranch there much of his life, his family was from Galisteo and he never broke his ties with the village, where four of his children have lived.

In 1960 Joe and his wife Mary Ann Anaya lived here in the Contreras's house (which had been moved up from Kirtland Air Force Base), while they were fixing up the old adobe his father (Basilio Anaya) had left him. Their third child, Jean Anaya Moya, was born in the ancestral home and she and her family now live there. Remedios Chavez recalls that "they were very good neighbors. Joe was a very warm person. We owe him a lot. He was so good to the people. We're missing him so much, especially in church."

He was a devoted member of Nuestra Señora de los Remedios and was active in the Sociedad de San José. Clarita Anaya recalls that "he was a good Catholic," and just before his death he was instrumental in getting new heaters in the church. Clarita knew Joe since he was a little boy: "He was my madrina's son; his mom and dad baptized me and married Manuel and me. He was like a little brother to me. Joe was very friendly, and a good cousin, a good man."

Joe Anaya was born June 24, 1934 in Santa Fe, the youngest of nine children. In 1955 he married Mary Ann Phillips, "the love of his life," and they had six children. (Mike, Robert, and Mark live on the ranch with their own children; Jean lives in Galisteo and Mike's electrical business is here.) Joe graduated from St. Michael's College in 1957 with a BA in biology. For 30 years he worked in the New Mexico State Highway Department, Traffic Services Division. In 1990 he was appointed by Governor Bruce King to the New Mexico State Highway Commission and served as its chairman in his last year, 1994-1995. He was also reserve conservation officer for the state department of Game and Fish and he was active in the Elks, who presided among others at his burial.

Joe Anaya was best known in Galisteo as founder of the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Waterusers Association and was its president for 20 years. "If it wasn't for him we might still not have running water," say both Remy Chavez and Clarita Anaya. Jean Moya found out after his death that he had been Chief in one of the Galisteo/Lamy Fire Department's earlier temporary incarnations; he was certainly proud of his family's involvement in the current GVFR.

I owe my own debt to Joe Anaya for introducing me to Simona Baros Garcia, whom I often quote in these pages and has become a friend as well as an important source on Galisteo history. She was named after Joe Anaya's grandmother, her aunt, and recalls that he "was a wonderful person and had a good push. He was a good Democrat." (This from a lifelong Republican!)

Joe M. Anaya's funeral service was held at the Cathedral in Santa Fe on July 5. Childhood friend Bruce King spoke at length. Then his body was transported to Galisteo where it was blessed in the church he had always attended and was laid to rest in the "new" graveyard on the hill. A meal at the Community Center afterwards celebrated this life well lived.

title: Obituary: Lynn Ackerman Hirsch
body: Lynn Hirsch, who, with her husband Franklin, built a modern house up against the Galisteo hogback on the north side of County Road 42 a few years ago, died of cancer on August 6 at the age of 63 at her home in Northfield, Illinois. A successful stage actress under the name Lynn Franklin, she also raised American saddlebred horses and loved gardening. When she was ill, Frank reported, she enjoyed reading El Puente, and had looked forward to living in Galisteo. She is survived by her husband, their three children, and four grandchildren.

title: Haciendas Tranquilas Rises Again
body: There's a new permit sign on the gate to the ever-pending Haciendas Tranquilas development north of the village. This time the new owner, Victor Ballas from Dallas, (who also owns a home in Ranchitos but gave his address as "Entrada Tranquila on NM 41") is applying for subdivision of 293.59+ acres into five lots. The administrative review (not a public hearing because they are held only for subdivisions over five lots) was held August 31. At that time Emilio Gonzales of the County Land Use Administration informed Ballas that the one existing well can only supply four lots of any size. So the application process continues. Gonzales told EL PUENTE that summary review subdivisions (5 lots or under) "don't impact too much" and that the village should get concerned about water when buyers of these lots want to subdivide further, which often happens. We will publish an update when more information is available.

title: Fire Department News
body:
The annual Fiesta was very successful and thanks are owed again to Kaye Sandford who donated Vista Clara's facilities as well as food and assistance. The very popular Lumbre del Sol provided music for dancing. Alan Langer chaired the event with Ways and Means Committee Chair Bob ("Where are your recipes?") Harte. The GVFR is also grateful to the fifty-some contributors of raffle prizes, to those who donated food and labor, and to the tireless efforts of GVFR members - too many to list here, but you know who you are. You made it happen.

Over $4,000 was raised for fire department operations and expenses. Why, someone asked, do the GVFR members have to provide fire and rescue services for the community, but also raise the funds to do so, spend all day and night in the kitchen, tend bar, clean up, etc. etc.? Good question.

A farewell gift (one of Richard Shuff's Galisteo panorama photographs) was given GVFR members Valentine and Lou Riddell, who left town for California in July. Valentine did a yeoman's job as the department secretary for around three years. Their dedication will be missed. And what will the village cats do now?

At the August 7th meeting, Jan-Willem Jansens, Director of Earth Works Institute's Galisteo Watershed Restoration Project, was the guest speaker. He gave a history of the Galisteo Watershed and recommended various procedures for its health. Among them were education for children and work with landowners, pruning piñon and juniper to encourage the growth of grass, and water catchment. Project goals include restoring vegetation and eventually raising the water table. (EL PUENTE plans a longer piece on Jansens' work in Galisteo sometime soon. See also the Dec. 1999 issue. If you need more information, call him at 982-9806.)

Chief Steve Moya attended the National Chiefs Association conference in New Orleans in August. A new sign for the firehouse will be placed near the entrance. A contract has been awarded for the long-awaited stucco coat on the exterior.

On July 25, the New Mexican's Eldorado edition ran a story headlined "Galisteo Fire Department Saves, Changes Lives." It ended with Linda Anaya saying, "When the pager goes off, my 2-year old says, 'Mommy, we have a call.' I look forward to the day when she can be there."

Arrimate a los buenos y seras uno de ellos. (Keep company with good people and you will be one of them (You are judged by the company you keep.) (Dicho courtesy of Anna Cárdenas)

Dan will come out for a delightful visit as he assesses your backyard habitat. When he visited with me, we had a great time discussing suggestions for the availability of the 4 basics: food, water, shelter, nesting sites. - Jan Saunders

title: Editorial: September 11 and Our Volunteer Fire Department
body:
The trauma of the last three weeks has marked the country. For some in Galisteo it may have seemed far away (not for me; my grandson and daughter-in-law were at a public school in the shadow of the World Trade Center ... and got out in time). But the heroism and sacrifice of the New York City firefighters, EMTs, and rescue workers should make us appreciate even more the risks our own volunteer fire department is willing to take for us.

Raffle tickets for great prizes to benefit New York Fire Fighters' families are available from GVFR members; winner to TBA at Studio Tour.

Soon after the disaster, former Galisteo firefighter Michael Datoli took this picture of the Galisteo Volunteer Fire and Rescue as they paid homage to their comrades in New York City's Ladder Company 20, on Lafayette Street in downtown Manhattan. The company lost 14 members on September 11. One female firefighter, who survived, is a friend of Datoli's. He says this picture "represents the bigger picture, and the strong bond between firefighters, wherever they are."

title: Studio Tour Weekend: Oct. 20-21, 9-5
body:
More than thirty artists will display their work on the 14th annual Galisteo Studio Tour, one of the first and longest-running in what is now a large number of Northern New Mexico area-art tours. You can get a map in front of the church as usual on that weekend, or you can get one early by calling 466-3099. See also the web site at www.galisteostudiotour.com.

This year will be even more mouth-watering than usual with a lot of food for the tummy as well as for the heart and the eye. The epicurean epicenter will still be Cocina de Mela serving hearty traditional New Mexican dishes at the Community Center. In addition, the Felty-Griscom house will offer coffee and muffins in the morning and then veggie burgers and turkey dogs; the Coopers and their daughter will serve cheeseburgers, bratwurst, and beverages; Janie Katz and Suzi Calhoun will offer stews and soups in Suzi's ceramic bowls, with cold drinks and dessert; and the Galisteo Inn will be selling green chile stew and roasted corn. Buen apetito.

title: Red Cross Fundraising by Local High School Student
body: Josephine and Andres Anaya's granddaughter Yvette Anaya, a junior at Santa Fe High, conceived the idea of collecting money for the Red Cross and the victims of September's terrorist attacks. She and two friends went into action with ribbons and coffee cans and raised $3,000 in one day. It was then matched by Eddie Bauer, raising the total to an amazing $6,000. The Albuquerque Journal North ran a story and picture of the three girls, who continued to make ribbons and sell them. They reported that having been able to respond to the situation made everybody feel much better.

title: Fly Me on the Moon
body:
I've always admired the courage of acrobats who fly through the air so effortlessly, fearlessly. All in a day's work. A snap. I discovered this summer that flying through the air with the greatest of ease is not a snap. It's a terrifying experience.

July: I am singing the role of "Miss Universe" in the Philip Glass/Robert Wilson opera White Raven, part of the Lincoln Center Festival 2001 in New York City. It has been decided that the best perch for Miss Universe is on the moon. The moon, of course, should be swinging in mid-air high above the stage. This is called "flying" in stage terminology. Is this in my contract? Is this entirely necessary? Gulp.

My feat of courage starts nightly when, in tight sequined gown and grotesque blonde wig (make-up to match), I climb a ladder and step onto a tiny metal platform just large enough for my feet, which is attached to a very large crescent moon, placing me in the curve of the moon. Get the picture? It is a huge moon. I am safely belted onto a rod attached to it. Even if I faint I won't fall. Very reassuring. Unfortunately, the question in the back of my mind keeps repeating, "What if the entire moon falls?"

Once an opera starts, there's no turning back. It's like a machine that grinds forward, propelled by the music, not concerning itself with queasy stomachs or fluttering hearts. The moon and I slowly rise. I smile weakly at everyone below- my dresser, my wig lady, the stage manager, stagehands, all becoming smaller and smaller.

Eventually the moon and I come to rest in the fly space - the area above a stage where dusty curtains and backdrops are stored. A glamorous place to wait for an entrance. They say it is forty feet up. I know it's higher. The singers on stage below look pea-size. I swallow hard, tear my eyes from the singers and look straight ahead into the dusty curtains five inches from my face. A less terrifying sight. Three stagehands on a catwalk nearby greet my arrival and crack a joke. I give an obligatory chuckle, then steel myself for a plunge into another reality.

The moon and I jerk and sway horizontally, positioning for the descent. I take a few deep breaths, my heart leaping anew when I hear the music signal my scene. I'll soon be lowered into view of the audience. Is my memory secure? Is there a frog in my throat?

I assume my stance with raised arm, switch my weight to my left foot, lift my chin and try not to hyperventilate as I descend. I realize I'm eye-level with the highest box seats in the theater. This terrifying sight is blotted from my vision when the full force of the lights hits me. All I can see now are the tiny musicians illuminated by their music-stand lights and the tiny conductor waving wildly. Too far away. Too far below.

After singing in Portugese about the mysteries of the Universe, I am again hoisted into the stratosphere before descending for the Finale. The best part of the scene is when I shakily climb off that tiny platform and wobble to my dressing room. It's stage magic, and I am a cog in a very large wheel.

title: Cemetery Update
body:
We have started collecting donations again to finish the restoration of the south side of the Old Cemetery wall. It was mowed once this summer, and some of the headstones have been repaired. Lucy Lippard has recorded the writing on each headstone and I have recorded them on digital camera floppy disc to be printed and given to St. Joseph's Parish in Cerrillos. (The Archives of the Archdiocese in Santa Fe also wants copies of both records.)

A new cemetery commission was set up on September 16, 2001 by Father Donnan Herbe of St. Joseph's Parish in Cerrillos. Father Donnan, Robert Anaya, Joe E. Chavez, Rudy Sandoval and myself were named for the cemeteries here in Galisteo. We are in the process of asking for donations to clean and fix up the new cemetery (on the north side of CR 42) as well as the old one.

Many of the surviving families take care of the newer graves, but the older ones closer to the road have been overgrown with chamiso and caved in by gopher holes. We have raised some money to start the clean-up process, and Richard Shuff has started the process of digging up the bushes and cactus. It will take a while, but as long as the donations are coming in, we will get it in beautiful condition and continue yearly maintenance for the years to come.

Donations of any amount will be greatly appreciated. Please make out checks either to "Old Galisteo Cemetery" or to "New Cemetery Maintenance," and send to Maria Padilla, 5700 State Highway 41, Galisteo NM 87540.

title: A Sacred Garden
body:
Women need sacred space.

I never knew that until I moved to Galisteo, New Mexico, where I kept finding myself creating sacred places. It's said the veil is thinner here. I have to agree. This part of the country is so steeped in blessedness no one thought it odd that a woman from the Northeast would create a large, sacred garden with a replica of an old stone chapel ruin as the walls.

When I bought my property, I realized the rock wall the previous owner had built around the garden was poorly constructed. I decided not to be judgmental and to regard this flaw as part of the charm of the place.

Almost the first night after I moved in, the wind gusted to nearly 75 miles per hour. (Back in Nantucket, we call "gusts" of that velocity hurricane force winds.)

However, the next morning was beautiful, and I started a ritual of taking a meditation walk at first light. My property is situated mostly on a bluff with uninterrupted views that go on for miles in all directions. As I strolled towards the garden in the dim light, I had a vague sensation that something was different. Enchanted by the distant morning light playing on the far prairies, the glow at the base of the Ortiz Mountains, I let my uneasy feeling slip away.

Soon I reached the middle of the garden. Scrutinizing the situation in the dawn's early light, I realized my funky stone wall was gone! It had blown over during the night, and I was standing in the midst of a garden of rubble.

My first thought was "Oh, goody, a real physical exercise project outside on the land. Instead of having to do 'fake' exercise and lift eight-pound weights in a gym, I'll rebuild the wall myself."

I decided to put the first few stones back in place that moment, envisioning the whole project completed in a couple of weeks. But the rock wouldn't budge. It was anchored to China. I put out the word I needed a stonemason and the synchronicity began. My new neighbor, Wendy, brought up her handyman extraordinaire, Angel, who could not only handle the stonework, but was also a carpenter, painter, contractor, and a sweet young guy who spoke only Spanish. With my two years of Spanish in high school, both of which I repeated in summer school, we somehow managed to communicate.

My "simple little project" required at least ten times more rock to complete the "chapel ruin" plan that unfolded in my mind as the work progressed. I used to think of rocks as hard dirt. Dirt's everywhere. And with that clever deduction I figured I shouldn't have to pay much more than the cost of transporting them to my property. Not so. The rocks we were matching were quality old rocks. Apparently rocks with good lineage are right up there with fine art and antiques.

We decided to make the walls look like ruins by building up the corners higher than the sides. I'd noticed on actual ruins out here that the corner joints are stronger and disintegrate last on old adobe buildings, so the walls slope down from the corners into the middle.

Instead of putting one of the original garden gates back up, I searched for double arched doors and found them at Jackalope. New from India, they're made to look like old Mexican doors painted a faded-looking light blue. What the heck - I was going for the illusion of chapel doors, not authenticity.

Inside the garden, Angel created a flagstone walk in the shape of a Celtic cross. Where the arms of the cross came together, he fashioned a circle of rose-colored stone bricks with a morning star pointing north, south, east, and west. At the end of the east arm of the cross, he made a small stone altar where I placed a bust of Buddha to honor Eastern practices. To the west we built an altar for a marble cross with carved flowers entwined, honoring Western religions.

When Angel finished the stonework many months later, he constructed an arbor with straight benches of raw wood for the middle of the garden, curved benches to go around the circle in the cross, and two large chairs with high backs for the two inside front corners. Finally it was time for the garden itself. Linda (which means beautiful), our local gardener, helped me find the plants that would thrive on my blustery sunny bluff.

One morning I carried Linda's eighteen-month-old baby girl into the sacred garden and sat in the arbor. She put her head on my shoulder and became so still and peaceful, I thought she was asleep. I sat there for quarter of an hour thinking how connected we were at that moment. A feeling like this had also washed over me the first time I'd seen her, when she had been sick and I'd given her a healing. This time, however, it seemed different and deeper than healing energies, yet still vaguely familiar. As I sat there with incredible unconditional love pouring in and out of me from this completely trusting little baby girl, I began to realize what was happening.

Sitting in the garden, we'd tapped into a connection with something ancient. This child had taken us into a calm that originated before time. And then it dawned on me, she'd linked us to a state of Grace - peace beyond belief and a connection to all that is. Her mother, always amazed at her daughter's serene behavior around me, came over and told me she was not asleep, just totally content.

The baby's name? Grace.

Excerpted from Heller's forthcoming book, If You Hear the Message Three Times, Listen.

title: 17th Annual Lamy/Galisteo Shootout
body:
We forgot to report on one major summer event in the September issue: the annual Lamy/Galisteo Challenge.

The shoot-out took place on August 26th in Lamy. Galisteo's Chris Benjamin, at 18 the youngest competitor, won the 25-pace pistol competition. (His first win was the 100-pace rifle competition in 1995, when he was only 12; his father, John Benjamin, is also a past winner, the only shooter ever to score a perfect 33 points in the pistol round, accomplished with his grandfather's World War I revolver.) Lamy's Britt Lee was high scorer in the pistol challenge and won the 1900 silver coin by being the first to hit it from 25 paces.

The 1942 maplewood 120mm artillery shell that constitutes the trophy stayed at Mark Lee's in Lamy, since this year's contest ended in a tie. The final event, when both teams laid into their side of a Chevy car hood (marked L or G) for 30 seconds with all they could muster, was also a tie. The metal was so badly riddled no one could count the holes.

title: Terrorist Within
body:
In the light of our current situation, it is not so easy to talk about personal health. Our leaders have been encouraging us to "get back to normal." While on a run this morning, I was thinking about the personal terrorists within us - from allergies to heart disease.

Our country has been reinforcing everything from airport security to immigration. In terms of our own health, this could be translated into vitamins, exercise, good sleep, and a plethora of good habits for our own security. We need to care for ourselves before we can help others. Remember that in an emergency on an airplane, we must put on our own oxygen masks first, before we put them on our children.

It seems that "normal" is not good enough.

title: WET DOWN: FIRE STATION DEDICATED
body:
Like a kid ready for his first dance, the Galisteo Fire Station was all slicked up for its gala November 10th dedication. Community members, including a lot of kids and dogs, enjoyed the warm sunny day, which got under way when Mezzo Soprano Janice Felty Griscom gave a stunning unaccompanied rendition of the Star Spangled Banner. (Not many villages have a world famous singer in residence to do the honors!) The brand new flagpole was dedicated in memory of J.C. Gregory, Philip McKee and Liz Langer, and a moment of silence was offered in memory of the World Trade Center victims, among them the brother of a GVFR auxiliary member.

The entire department had worked tirelessly for the previous week. The station's color plaster coat was completed, the entrance road was paved, a bright new sign was installed, tanks were moved, floors washed, and everything else in and out of sight was cleaned and polished and rearranged within an inch of its life. All our trucks were outside gleaming in the sun.

The event was lively and colorful, attended by a number of County fire officials in dress uniform, including County Fire chief Steve Holden. Some firefighters from a neighboring station were in bright red gear, and there was a covey of engines or trucks from Hondo, Glorieta, La Cienega, Eldorado, and Stanley. County personnel from as far away as Pojoaque attended.

The dedication ceremony proceeded inside the cleared bays of the station. Speakers were our Chief Steve Moya and County Chief Holden. Moya first acknowledged GVFR founder John Benjamin, who was present and applauded. (After a couple of false starts in the 1970s and '80s [see EL PUENTE Feb. 2000], the fire department got underway in its present, fully professional incarnation in 1991-93, when Benjamin, with early help from Dave Ahmann, petitioned the County, got State Certification, acquired the first truck, and designed the passive solar, water collecting fire station, built in part by community work parties, and completed in 1995.)

With some jocularity, County and other fire personnel - ranging from financial officers and arson investigators to the firefighters and EMTs themselves - were introduced, along with each member of the Galisteo department. (Pretty impressive: our working members were resplendent in white shirts, black pants and ties; Steve and Assistant Chief Jean Moya were in dress uniform.) No "politicals" showed up, but bouquets of flowers were given to Linda Anaya and Jean Moya for their contributions to Galisteo and their work as part-time countywide substitutes.

In an emotional moment (several current and former GVFR members being part of the immediate family) the station was dedicated to the memory of Joe Anaya, whose widow, four of their six children, and several grandchildren were also present. A red GVFR jacket was presented to Kaye Sandford of Vista Clara Spa for her extremely generous contributions to the department over the past few years. Raffle results were announced, and, appropriately, several County fire people were winners. The much coveted turquoise and silver ring donated by Scott Diffrient was won by our own Remy Chavez, who had bought the very last ticket. The money went to NYC Ladder Co. 20, which lost several members. A video "slide show" about the Galisteo Fire department (starring a lot of people you know) coordinated by Wendy Beck was shown in the station office.

Finally the long awaited "wet-down" got going - a rousing old fashioned ritual for such inaugurations. To the tune of sirens and applause, four trucks directed huge arcs of water that met over the station-white against the blue sky, echoed spectacularly by a full rainbow. (A good omen? Rain at last!)

More news from the GVFR: Congratulations to Miguel Padilla, who passed his Firefighter One tests at 17. He is the youngest full-fledged member of the department and will go to work with the others as soon as he turns 18.

When Steve and Jean Moya were in New Orleans for the International Chief's Association conference, Steve won a raffle for a $2,000 Mini warn gas sensor. No other County department has one.

We all won when, after a lot of hard work by the GVFR, our ISO went from a rating of 9 down to a 6. That means we will each save a lot on our insurance. Ranchitos (which is much further from hydrants) also improved its rating to an 8. (How about donating the difference to the GVFR ?)

title: LONG AWAITED BOSQUE SOLUTION PROPOSED
body:
For several years the Galisteo Community Association has been attempting to address the problem of who owns the land under and south of the [old] bridge on the east side of the river. In 1997 when Richard Griscom attempted to quiet title this land, the GCA intervened, funded by Moira Walden, claiming ownership of 1.1 acres leading into the bosque along the [east] bank of the river. There are no recorded deeds to this area and the community's claim was based on the historic use of this land by community members. Over the past several years there have been numerous meetings and consultations in an attempt to resolve the dispute over ownership and use of this land.

Recently the present board of the Community Association has received an offer which, in the opinions of board members, and Moira Walden, gives the community what it has desired from the outset of these proceedings: i.e. the ability to use the land as we have in the past. Richard Griscom would own the land in question. However the community would have an irrevocable easement for its use. A parking area would remain near the bridge and the path along the river would be open to use by walkers, horses and others who wish to enjoy the bosque. In order to preserve the fragile ecosystems, motorized vehicles would not be permitted beyond 120 feet south of the bridge.

This easement would be a legal attachment to any deed to this property. To our advantage, an easement would create less liability issues for the community than actual ownership. It also eliminates the possibility that, should we lose our suit for possession, we would have to enter another legal battle to establish the easement we are currently being acknowledged to possess. The funds of the GCA are not adequate for prolonged legal actions.

Before we accept any offer, however, we feel it is imperative to have input from the entire community. If anyone has objections to our accepting this proposal and its conditions, we would like to hear their specific reasons. The Board would welcome the opportunity to meet with any member of the community to discuss their concerns. Please call any of the following to set up a convenient time to discuss this issue with the Board: Joette (466-3099), Barbara Cooper (466-3827), or Barbara Holloway (466-2118). Calls must be made before November 28, 2001. If you do not call any of the above we will assume you are in agreement with accepting this proposal and we will proceed accordingly.

We have decided to communicate with you by this letter, rather than a meeting, because we would like the input of the entire community. Galisteo is your community and the GCA Board truly wishes to represent the wishes of the entire population. Thank you for your assistance in resolving this matter to everyone's satisfaction. - Joette Trofimuk, GCA president.

(Ed. note: this letter was put in all mailboxes the week of Nov. 12; the proposal would not affect those residents who haul water.)

title: IN MEMORIAM: Bennett Lawson Fisher
body:
The events of September 11 have deeply affected me and my family. My brother Bennett Lawson Fisher, 58, died in the World Trade Center. Ben was a senior vice president at Fiduciary Trust Company International. He worked on the 97th floor of the second tower and was last seen on the 44th floor, implementing the evacuation plan from 1993, when he had witnessed the first attack on the building. A profile of Ben appeared in the New York Times "Legacy" section. A memorial was held in Greenwich, Connecticut, on October 1st.

Ben was a man of great humor, a colorful raconteur. He was committed to being the best husband, father, brother, friend and co-worker possible. He is survived by his wife of 32 years, Susan Huntington Fisher, daughter Louise, and son James. He is also survived by his mother, four sisters, two brothers, and sixteen nieces and nephews.

His interests, beyond sailing, skiing, and creative use of computer technology, included lively political debate and conversation. He was instrumental in raising funds to preserve open space and historical landmarks in his community. Recently his enthusiasm focused on an effort to bring the light back to the lighthouse on Great Captain's Island in Long Island Sound. Contributions may be sent to: Let There Be Light, Inc., 21 W. Putnam Ave., Greenwich, CT. 06830. - Connie Fisher.

title: Santa Fe County Open Space Acquires Thornton Ranch Parcel
body: After much negotiation, The Santa Fe County Open Space program has acquired a second parcel on the Thornton Ranch, north and west of Cerro Lucero, which, when opened to the public, will be accessed by County Rd. 42. A management policy for the archaeological resources is being worked out. At the same time the Trust for Public Land is exploring the possibilities of a cluster development on 4,400 additional acres of the Thornton Ranch that would leave all but some 7% of the acreage for open space and a trail system. Possible land trades through the BLM will open up an even larger expanse of public domain. EL PUENTE will have more on this as decisions are made.

title: Geoff Laurence Gallery Show: "The Shape of Life"
body: Galistefio realist painter Geoff Laurence's show "The Shape of Life" will open with a reception at Linda Durham's Galisteo gallery on Saturday, Dec. 15. The centerpiece will be a large triptych titled The Faith Healer. "I think I am part of a new emotionalism which attempts to marry the intellect and the subconscious," says the artist, whose work has been shown internationally.

title: Janey Katz's Recycled Car-Metal Art
body:
Janey Katz's whimsical recycled car-metal creations ("Re in CARn ART") are featured in the December issue of New Mexico Magazine. When she moved to Galisteo in the 1980s, she started pulling junk out of the arroyos, bought a welding torch and began to make metal art (after waitressing for 5 years at Tomasita's and being voted Santa Fe's "Best Waitress.")

"I love the patina that years of sun create on painted metal," she says. "I don't paint any of my work - all of the colors you see were applied in Detroit many years ago." Her santos and angels (Our Lady of Broken Hearts and Mended Fences, Our Lady of Holding On and Letting Go) and her Critters from the Hood are sold in over 200 galleries nationwide. "Animals convey the essence of unconditional love," she told Tina Kessinger. "My wall sculptures represent hope, a reminder that all things are possible."

title: John Massee's Sculptures Featured
body: Two of John Massee's sculptures were reproduced in Pasatiempo, Sept. 14. Writer Robert Nott speculated that Massee "must have some pretty interesting dreams - or nightmares. For every fun, cartoon like figure or image you find in his work, you'll discover some unsettling imagery to make you think twice about what he's trying to convey."

title: ELDORADO MORATORIUM AMENDED
body:
After several months delay, on Oct. 22, the County Commissioners finally voted on the 3 amendments to the Eldorado Moratorium, which could have a dire effect on the water resources of the Galisteo Basin. Despite pleas from the public (speakers came from Eldorado, Galisteo, and Cerrillos), for patience and more information, the Board of County Commissioners approved two of the three amendments, which means more development in the Eldorado area (or the Simpson Ranch Contemporary Community, which includes Eldorado and all its sibling developments).

The first amendment - which would have allowed the creation of 2.5 acre lots if a hundred-year water supply could be approved - was unanimously denied. The key second amendment most opposed by the public- allows developers to transfer water rights to the EDU (Eldorado's utility company) in return for service. In the end, only Commissioner Paul Campos voted against it, though statements made by other commissioners made it appear that they too would oppose it. Chairman Paul Duran remarked at the beginning that they had spent a lot of time and energy "trying to squeeze blood out of this turnip," and noted that most solutions "are only going to intensify the problem." Despite a letter to the commissioners signed by 73 Galisteo residents, the village was never mentioned by anyone, including our commissioner, Jack Sullivan, who stated that numbers meant nothing to him.

Amendment 3, also approved unanimously, is more beneficial: it allows expansion with recycling and conservation of water.

(More on the water situation in coming issues of EL PUENTE,)

title: Hoback Horse: From Ancient Bones to the Bloodhorse
body: Hoback Horse: "Look back on our struggle for freedom! trace our present days' strength to its source/and you will find that our pathway to glory/is strewn with the bones of the horse." This anonymous poem was the inspiration for Priscilla Hoback's From Ancient Bones to the Bloodhorse, one of New Mexico's marvelous public art remuda. Her Painted Pony was sold at auction for $7,000 at the Lensic on November 6 to benefit the Santa Fe Waldorf School. The buyer was the Santa Fe Ranch. So far the Horsepower Project has raised over $500,000 for local organizations with more sales to come. (You can see them all on www gopaintedponies.com.)

title: 'TIS THE SEASON
body:
A number of clients and friends have mentioned to me that they feel a bit slow and lack some energy. After leaving the concrete jungle of New York City, I've come to appreciate the wonders of nature. Out here in beautiful Galisteo, we get the opportunity to observe the cycles of the seasons. I just finished planting about two hundred bulbs for the spring. The best time to plant trees is the fall because the roots grow best then - less activity above the ground and more energy into the heart of the plant.

After reading this, I couldn't help but think that we people put so many demands on ourselves and others. Why should we act like summer when it is fall? Maybe we should align ourselves with the seasons and allow our roots to grow so that we may bloom in the spring.

title: Tobias Anaya, Artist: From Galisteo's Roots
body:
If you're lucky, you've lived here long enough to have known Tobias Anaya, and you had the sense to buy one or more of his sculptures. A Galisteo icon and one of its greatest artists, Tobias sold his wares next to the old cemetery, where a well-tended cross and text in his memory still stands. Tobias Lane, on the Hill, is named for him.

Tobias's sculptures were assembled, or transformed, from found objects - what most people think of as junk. He scavenged the Galisteo roadsides daily, a familiar figure in his black coat, on crutches, or two canes. David van Dyk, who enjoyed his company, remembers that when the family clothesline was raided by the wind, the children's socks would turn up in Tobias's art. He displayed his works on an old bedframe, and later made a whole cage, or cerquito, for them.

Tobias was born in Galisteo in October 1909 and lived here for most of his life, dying sadly in a house fire on November 29, 1989. He was Clarita and Serapio Anaya's older brother, Michael D. Anaya's uncle, and was related to many other people still living in the village. For years he lived with and cared for his mother, Carmelita Anaya, an extraordinary woman who lived into her nineties. (See EL PUENTE #2.)

Even as a child, Clarita recalls, Tobias liked to make things. When he retired from working at various jobs - wartime service in California, harvesting in the Estancia Valley, working with Major Felton at his furniture store, and hauling water in a cart to the then-waterless Galisteo Loma (See El PUENTE #42)- he became a full-time artist. (It runs in the family; his great nephew Kenny Chavez is carrying on the tradition, exhibiting and selling his assemblages of wood, old bottles, and other finds.

Tobias Anaya was well-known outside the village, and his funeral at the Cathedral in Santa Fe was crowded. (He is buried at the National Cemetery.) His "folk art" was collected by visitors to Galisteo and art dealers in Santa Fe and occasionally it was written up - even in foreign magazines. In a 1986 feature in the New Mexican, Hollis Engley reported that Tobias began making his figures in the 1950s and his first two wooden horses were sold to buy two live horses to draw his wagon.

He also carved tree roots into violins, made many "dolls" (sculptures that didn't stand up by themselves), musical instruments, and animals-cattle, cats, a man milking a cow. Joe and Barbara Cooper have a lovely coyote, a handsome elk, and a cart made to hold flowers at their daughter's wedding; the reins are phone cords, the seat a bisected drawer. Santa Fe dealer Murdoch Finlayson says, "Tobias was really very, very good- prolific, with a great imagination." Photographer and one-time Galistean Ray Belcher took many pictures of him and his work.

Musicians, carts, and horses with riders were Tobias's favorite subjects; he also made washerwomen. A curiously "indigenous" little root figure wears a cape of leather-like rubber. The pieces are often held together with wire and the details are endlessly innovative - garden hose for arms, tire rubber for horses' ears, beer cans, eyes of cut tin, bits of cloth, matchsticks, orange bailing twine, a dog collar. You name it, he re-envisioned it. David van Dyk took some of Tobias's musicians to Africa with him, where they were much admired by the locals, who recognized their spirit and invention. He also owns Tobias's last piece, delivered the day before he died. With hindsight, it seems significant - a typical Anaya horse, but riderless.

"Anista?" said Tobias, who spoke mostly Spanish. "I've never really been called an artist. An artist must have an education. I have no education. It's a hobby, something to do." Today, his status as an artist is in no doubt.

title: Residents Request Road Surface Change
body:
On November 20, 2001, twenty three Galisteo residents, most of them living along Via La Puente, La Vega and Otra Vanda, sent a letter to Robert Martinez, Director of Public Works for Santa Fe County, requesting that the base course used in surfacing those three roads in the fall of 1998 be removed.

Based on two professional laboratory analyses of a sample of the base course (by AMEC and the UNM Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, both in Albuquerque), the letter pointed out that the sample's contents do not conform to State standards for this type of road in two respects: 1) it is too fine, as measured by the percentage of the sample that passes through a #200 sieve; 2) it contains 12% silt (state standards allow NO silt). The sample was taken according to industry standards by John Benjamin in September of this year from Via la Puente between the old bridge and the highway.

In addition, the letter pointed out, the sample contains almost 4% of particles smaller than silt. Numerous medical studies have shown the negative health effect of inhaling such small particles. One of the laboratories also tested for lead in the sample and found that it contains 27.5 parts of lead per million. This lead becomes airborne and those who live and/or walk along these three roads breathe it when vehicles pass.

On November 30, Chris Graeser, Assistant County Attorney, informed me that the County has ordered its own laboratory test of a sample of the material in question, in order to confirm (or dispute) the accuracy of the information presented in the letter. The County's response to the letter, based on its own test, will be reported in a future EL PUENTE. If anyone wants a copy of the Galisteo residents' letter and its six attachments, please contact me at 466-3996.

Ed note: A story in the Reporter (11/21) quotes Martinez as planning to add a clay mixture to lay the dust, and Benjamin warning that total removal may be the only solution.

body: The Nacha Mendez concert at the Community Center on November 17th was covered at length in the Santa Fe Reporter. It was a lovely evening, and very well-attended by a combination of community and people from Santa Fe. The stage of the Community Center became the focus of a cozy living room. The lights were low, the music, as advertised, was "sad and beautiful." Altogether this was an auspicious beginning for the Bridge Series - which refers not only to our own old puente but to outreach beyond the village, expanding our Studio Tour identity as a center for all the arts.

body: On the night of December 1, the Fire Department responded to a wreck just north of town. A car was totaled but the family in it came out relatively unscathed. They were admiring the huge moon when they went into the guard rail and ditch. Beware of star-gazing on the road!

title: Moira Walden Letter on Arsenic and Health
body: Moira Walden wrote a letter to the editor of the New Mexican November 17, reminding us that despite the naturally occurring high level of arsenic in New Mexico water, we see obituaries of "innumerable men and women with Spanish names [who] died at ages 85, 93, 97, 102, etc. - all of them born and raised in rural New Mexico. Perhaps the National Research Council should run some surveys," she continued, "and do some statistics in our Southwestern states instead of (the places) that produced such alarming rates of lung and bladder cancer. Maybe arsenic is not the cause of these cancers after all?" Hope she's right!

title: Who We Are: Profile of Richard Griscom
body:
Dick Griscom has owned a home in Galisteo for over thirty years, but he's been away from it a lot. Son of a Quaker farm family in New Jersey, he graduated with honors in economics from Wesleyan University in Connecticut and thought he was heading for a business career. But in 1958, a year as a Fulbright scholar living with a German family in Wurzburg, Germany, gave him a fresh perspective, sparking a life of intensive involvement in the world.

The following summer he led Experiment in International Living student groups to Germany and Mexico. In 1961 he earned a doctorate in law from Harvard, but international involvement proved more satisfying than law. In 1962 he became Acting Peace Corps director in Venezuela and then in El Salvador. In 1965 he went to Bolivia with former wife Chris and their baby daughter Karen Griscom (now Carrier). Their second and third children, David and Britt, were born in Paraguay. Megan was born in Galisteo, in 1972.

After the Peace Corps, Griscom worked in a range of government-funded projects including a State Department position in coordination with the UN High Commission for Refugees, when thousands of refugees were streaming into Sudan from Ethiopia and Uganda. In Papua New Guinea from 1988-90, he trained officials in a World Bank project. A stint in Panama from 1992 to 1996 had him working with two other New Mexico attorneys to improve an unwieldy legal system. His wife Janice Felty was also traveling the world for her musical engagements. Altogether, Griscom has lived and worked in Panama, Papua New Guinea, Sudan, Bolivia, Paraguay, El Salvador, Costa Rica, Colombia, Ecuador, Egypt, Peru, Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Central African Republic, Namibia, Tanzania, and Jamaica. In between, he has practiced family law in New Mexico and served as an Assistant Attorney General and General Counsel for the New Mexico Health and Human Services Department.

Griscom's boss in the Peace Corps and a consulting firm was Leveo Sanchez. They discovered belatedly that they had Galisteo in common. Leveo Sanchez is the son of Victoria Sanchez, a schoolteacher here for several years, and great grandson of Josefa Ortiz and Sylvester Davis, who lived in the hacienda.

Today Dick still consults in various countries and - continued good health permitting - he is ready to get on the road at any time for short-term overseas assignments. But he and Janice, and their daughter Hannah, are settled here in Galisteo, where Dick was the first president of the GCA in the 1970s, has often served on the Water Board, and is a member of the GVFR Auxiliary.

title: News from Nizhoni School
body:
Our highway cleaning project is underway. Starting from the Nizhoni Road north of Galisteo and going towards the church, both sides of highway 41 are being de-trashed every Tuesday morning between 11 and 12. We've been at it for three weeks and expect to continue for several more. There's a lot of litter. We'll be back after vacation.

Speaking of the holidays, we have several special events lined up for the New Year, beginning with a "meditation for the new year" running from 5PM Sunday, December 30th and continuing until 1 AM January 1st. We will also hold sweat lodges on Dec. 30-31, as well as a fire walk on December 31st. The workshop starts at 9:30PM and we walk at midnight. We warmly invite you to join us.

One of our most important efforts in recent months has been promoting peace, discussing and exploring how being peaceful can allow us to find entirely new answers to life's challenges. This effort continues. Through our students and faculty we are offering Peace Workshops around the state and Chris Griscom is traveling around the country doing the same. If you are interested in having us speak, please let us know.

Also, come January, we will be starting our Academy of Peace, offering special weekend seminars and more comprehensive courses of two weeks, four months, or one year's duration. Our curriculum is designed to teach people how to access and share the power of inner peace. We will train students to facilitate the choice of peace, to become skillful in helping others, and to find peaceful solutions to personal and global situations. For questions and information, please don't hesitate to contact us at 466-4336; e-mail nizhoni@nizhonischool.com. Our new web site is at www.nizhonischool.com. We wish you and yours a very special Christmas and a wonderful New Year.
