title: News from the County - Zoning and Water Systems
body:
A recent email from Commissioner Kathy Holian stresses the importance of the Oct. 16th meeting on zoning in the County's new Sustainable Land Development Code (see p.1): "We don't currently have real zoning in Santa Fe County. We do have density restrictions (based on geohydrologic zones), but currently we don't have zones in the sense of defining what kinds of uses are allowed. This will be a major change in the new code, so I would really urge you to attend the public meetings. There will be zoning maps (so that you can see where your house is), and there will be use tables to give you an idea of what kinds of developments could be done in your neighborhood."

Holian also alerted us that in April, the BCC adopted a resolution setting out a policy for the County to adopt rural water systems so that County funds could be used in the emergency at the Upper Cañoncito Water System, and help the system upgrade its infrastructure.

However, the resolution was quite abbreviated and did not spell out exact processes and procedures. Upon reflection, staff felt that exact procedures and the requirements for both the County as well as the local private water systems should be articulated, and a new, much more specific resolution was brought forth. (If you would like to see a full text, please contact kathleen.holian@comcast.net.)

She continues that one important part of the policy in the resolution requires that if the County is to help a private water system financially, that system must be adopted into the County water utility. Staff strongly recommends this because if the County is to commit taxpayers' resources, then it should have control over the improvements in that system. She agrees with this philosophy because "in the past, some water systems have been real sinks for funding coming from either the state or the local government." Frequently it seems that the problems never get solved, though more funding is requested year after year.

However, this provision was a sticking point with Commissioner Anaya in particular. So the BCC tabled the resolution for continuing discussion. The original resolution is still in place, and the commissioners voted unanimously to adopt the Cañoncito Mutual Domestic into the County water utility.

We look forward to hearing where the Galisteo Water Association comes down on this policy.

title: Solar Systems #5: Nancy Helle
body:
An ongoing series on solar energy systems used by Galisteo residents. E-mail the editor to participate (flip14@wildblue.net).

The 24-panel solar array erected for Nancy Helle on McKee Road was designed and built by GoSolar. Nancy wanted to reduce her electrical bill and become more sustainable (like most people in Galisteo).

The array is a 5.5 kilowatt grid-tied system that was designed to provide 100% of her electrical needs for the main house and a guest house on the property. With this system she pays only a connection fee of around $10 to PNM. All of the electrical production of the array is totaled each month and she receives a check at the rate of six cents per kilowatt hour as a Renewable Energy Credit (REC). The current system also has net metering, which means she only pays for electricity when the array cannot produce more power than she uses in a given billing period.

She was also able to take advantage of a 30% federal tax credit and a 10% state tax credit that significantly offset the cost of the solar array. The payback period for this size array at the current electrical rate and REC rate is under 10 years. As rates go up, this period will get smaller.

GoSolar works out of an office in the Agora Shopping Center in Eldorado with only four employees, all living in Eldorado. Owner Leszek ("Les") Teterycz is an electrical contractor with a BA in electrical engineering and over 10 years experience in designing and building electrical and photovoltaic systems.

Since the beginning of this year GoSolar has installed six arrays in the area and has contracts for two more. The goal of the company is to make our area an example of what a solar community should be and bring more local workers into the workforce, installing solar photovoltaic systems throughout the community.

title: Next Step on Route 41 - NMDOT Planning Update
body:
Notice was recently received from the NMDOT that plans for the Rt. 41 bridge and roadway construction had been approved by the Federal Highway Administration. As agreed at the last (and final) NMDOT public meeting with the Galisteo community, Leslie Dilworth and Roger Taylor met with a DOT representative to discuss remaining issues. They report the following highlights:

We pointed out that the well-intended safety re-design of the road's width on Clark Hill - straightening the curve and allowing for a 55 mph posting -- could encourage higher speeds and eliminate the intent of the safety design.

About five hilltops will be reduced in height by an average of 5', and a similar number of low "troughs" or "dips" will be filled and elevated about 5'. We were concerned that several of these "fills" would significantly increase storm run-off and erosion as well as blocking wildlife crossings.

We raised significant concerns about the future design of the roadway through the village -- especially the 4' shoulders on each side. Not only could this impact visual appeal for properties such as Romona Scholder's or the Gwyns' but it could also result in a retaining wall being dug out of the Hogback and/or road widening (and fill) along properties such as the Snyders' and Maria Ortiz y Pino's. For example, approaching the village from the north, there is no place for increased width except a huge amount of fill and a big wall on the Snyders' side, and a c. 12' retaining wall on the uphill side, plus removal of all the trees. That will totally change the character of that entrance to the village.

We left the meeting understanding that the NMDOT feels its plans have been completed. But we strongly stated that we continued to have objections to the design work within the village, and we wished to be included in the process as design work progresses. The good news is that construction on the bridges will not occur until early 2014, and work on Rt. 41 will not begin until 2015 or 2016. We will continue to report on this as plans evolve.

From the DOT: A copy of the environmental assessment, the public and agency comments received on it, and responses to these comments are available at: http://dot.state.nm.us/en/D5/ProjectsD5.html#NM41. Please contact NMDOT Project Development Engineer David Quintana at (505) 476-4169 if you have any questions or want additional information. The NMDOT will notify you of future updates and opportunities for public participation during final design.

title: Another Studio Tour Is History
body:
Crowds of people came to both beautiful days of the Studio Tour's 25th birthday to admire the cusp of the golden cottonwoods (they turned early this year) as well as the art and culinary offerings. Ours is one of the longest running tours in northern New Mexico -- and certainly one of the best! Word on the dirt roads is that not all of the visitors were buying. Reviews from the artists ranged from enthusiastic to disappointed, which I am told is pretty much par for the course.

Cindy Lux, one of the many dedicated organizers, writes: "I love the energy that seems to bloom here in the fall, particularly Tour weekend, which reminds me of just how lucky and talented we all are to have found this place in the sun. It takes a village to pull this off -artists, of course, but also a village of patience for the over 1000 visitors we have strolling though our beautiful streets, backyards and bosques. Signs went up, studios and homes opened, visitors came and went. We had 34 artists exhibiting, smiling, directing, cooking, chatting and surviving ... and by Sunday night next October seemed waaay toooo soon!"

We non-artists, on the other hand, have a lovely leisurely time wandering from studio to studio and next October will be welcome. Thanks to all of the exhibiting artists and the Studio Tour Committee for their hard work and enthusiasm.

title: Galisteo
body:
And as I walk outside
I am met with the soft kiss of winter
The gentle hiss of the breeze combs my hair softly
The glow of the moon floods the hills with blue
I am home
As I look at the naked branches, they blow me a soft wave
Relaxed and at ease, I gaze upon the blanketed hills
Looking past the junipers until I meet eyes of silver
This is where I come from,
This town built me
Taught me
Loved me
Galisteo

title: Early photograph of the old Galisteo Church
body: The early photograph of the old Galisteo Church on The Hill illustrated Marc Simmons' "Trail Dust" column (2/25/12). He quoted the late Mela Ortiz y Pino de Martin: "When I was young and there was a drought, my mother would wash the saints in the Galisteo Church. Then they would be carried through the town's streets, as people sang alabados - hymns of praise-and prayed for rain. The priest led the way into every part of Galisteo with the church bell clanging the entire time. Then my father [Jose Ortiz y Pino I] would take the priest out to the ranch [Vista Clara] to pray for rain there ... it always rained."

title: Helium balloons environmental concern
body: Try to avoid sending beribboned balloons out into the atmosphere. According to High Country News (8/6/12), a 16" helium-filled latex balloon can travel hundreds of miles and climb to an altitude of 25,000 feet, where it freezes, explodes, and rains down to earth as garbage. Latex balloons eventually biodegrade but the metalized nylon balloons do not. "Because they conduct electricity, they also cause hundreds of blackouts each year by short-circuiting power lines. If 'Cactus Ed' Abbey were alive today, he might enjoy the idea that the elaborate infrastructure of post-industrial capitalism can be brought down by a single, drifting, metallized Mickey Mouse."

title: Santa Fe/Espanola air quality
body: And speaking of the environment, Santa Fe/Espanola was one of 2011's "cleanest air cities" for "short-term particles." We got an A for ozone and passed the annual particle pollution category as well. One in seventeen Americans live around unhealthy levels of ozone and particles. We're lucky.

title: Water, Water ...
body:
The Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association (MDWCA) report from the NM Environment Department (as required by the EPA) dated 7/31/2011 and sent out 9/13/12, provides a "snapshot" of a year's water quality from the one groundwater well that provides our community. "Susceptibility Analysis" states that the utility is well maintained and operated, and "susceptibility" is "high." (Not clear if that's good or bad, but what water in this state isn't "susceptible"?) Copies of the source water assessment are available from andy.edmondson@state.nm.us. (Include your name, address, phone no., email address, and name of water utility.)

The report goes on to deal with "cross connection control" involving "unprotected or improper connection to a public water system that can cause contamination." You are asked to contact the GMDWCA if you have any of these devices: Boiler/radiant heater (not water heater), underground lawn sprinkler system, pool or hot tub (not whirlpool tubs), additional sources of water on the property, decorative pond, or watering trough.

There is also a caveat about elevated levels of lead which can come from service lines and home plumbing and are not the GMDWCA's responsibility. They advise that "when your water has been sitting for several hours, you can minimize potential for lead exposure by flushing your tap for 30 seconds to 2 hours" (!). To get your water tested: see www.epa.gov/safewater/lead.

A "Water Quality Data Table" listing all contaminants (including arsenic, fluoride, and radioactive Alpha emitters) found in the year 2009 is highly technical and quite confusing. But it appears that we have negligible ranges of all of these, or we did three years ago. A Galisteo-specific conclusion to these reports would be very useful. Perhaps Water Association President Rod Hall will provide one in a future issue.

An article in The New Mexican (10/10) announced "County OKs Buckman Waterline to Eldorado," where it would serve over 3000 households from Rancho Viejo to Eldorado, eventually extending to the existing Cañoncito Mutual Domestic Association. One question is whether customers outside the water district's two mile area (like Galisteo) would be served by the Eldorado District or by Santa Fe County.

Two days later, however, a letter to the paper's editor from David Chakroff, General Manager of the Eldorado Area Water and Sanitation District (EAWSD), contended that the original article was inaccurate, and that the County did not OK a Buckman waterline to Eldorado. The Board of County Commissioners approved an MOU "to serve as a framework for future discussions" about such a waterline, but no agreement has been reached. The EAWSD can make no decisions before public input has been heard.

title: Towards Community Zoning
body:
The second public input meeting on the Sustainable Land Development Code took place at the Community Center on October 16th with County Staff Robert Griego and Sarah Ijadi presiding. The focus for this meeting was zoning. The code, which has not yet been finalized or accepted by the BCC, is a voluminous 344 pages. Because it is difficult for lay people to take it all in, Sarah has kindly provided the following summary about Galisteo's future role, which includes reconstituting the long-suffering Planning Committee, or what's left of us.

The Galisteo Community Plan, adopted in February of 2012, is an amendment to the Sustainable Growth Management Plan (SGMP) and aspects of the plan related to land use and development are expected to be "codified" as a text and map amendment to the new, but not yet adopted SLDC and corresponding Zoning Map. Zoning for the Galisteo Plan Area will be established as the "Galisteo Community Overlay District" and will be closely aligned with language in the Galisteo Community Plan. (See Chapter 9 of the SLDC Public Review Draft for an outline of "community overlay districts").

The process for drafting the community overlay district will be a collaborative effort between community members and county staff. It is expected to involve several meetings with the Planning Committee, one or two community wide meetings in Galisteo and two public hearings before the BCC. The process is expected to take 3-5 months.

The most recent draft is the "SLDC Public Review Draft of Sept 2012," available on the county website, www.santafecounty.org. The Code Development Team is in the process of drafting a revised SLDC and corresponding Zoning Map based on input from public review process and a technical/legal review. Once the revised SLDC draft is complete and the adoption process is outlined, county staff will have a better handle on the scope of a "Galisteo Community Overlay District" and an appropriate adoption schedule. We'll communicate this information as soon as we have it.

On Oct. 23, a meeting was held at the Community Center for input on the nomination of Galisteo Basin sites for the National Historic Register, under the auspices of the Galisteo Basin Archaeological Sites Protection Act. Jeff Pappas, the new State Historic Preservation Officer (SHPO) attended.

The meeting livened up when Joe Miller, whose battles with the County are legendary, recommended that landowners who find artifacts "just get out there and destroy all archaeological sites." Archaeologists in the room gasped, and an interesting discussion ensued. Eric Blinman, Director of the Office of Archaeological Studies, suggested that it would depend on your values, the greater good to the community. Is it more important to preserve our past heritage or build two more houses? Miller (sort of) agreed that sites should be preserved, but demanded to know why property owners should carry the burden, paying taxes but not being allowed to develop -- which amounts to a "taking." The fact that the State can hardly afford to buy all potentially developable sites makes this a real problem, one that will be a challenge for the new Code.

title: A Big Bird
body:
When birders excitedly exclaim, "We got a REALLY BIG BIRD today", BIG refers to importance and rarity, not to size. That certainly was the case recently in Galisteo.

On October 8th, 2012, a little bird struck a window at Ramona Scholder's home and died. Ramona took the bird to Judy Tuwaletstiwa, who carefully laid out the 5 1/2 inch specimen on her studio shelf. Two weeks later I dropped by Judy's for the Studio Tour. The sight of a bird I could not identify sent me scurrying back home for my field guide. Once identified as a male Black-throated Blue Warbler, news of the little bird's appearance went out by e-mail to a network of birders around New Mexico.

Soon we were contacted by Sandy from Albuquerque, who drove to Galisteo for the "hand off" from Judy. The bird will rest in UNM's Museum of Southwestern Biology. Sandy advises, "Salvaged specimens add much to our understanding of birds. Put specimens in a Ziploc bag in freezer with information including the exact date found dead, a precise location where found, name and contact info for person who found it and circumstances of the discovery (e.g., window kill, cat caught, found dead, etc.)"

Galisteo's little warbler is an uncommon summer resident in the East from Canada to Florida and a very rare "vagrant" west of the Mississippi. Turns out, our bird is only the fourth specimen recorded in the state. The male's blue back, white belly and black throat make him a stunner and quite a nice OCTOBER SURPRISE.

Many thanks to everyone in Galisteo who has helped us with donations of time and money this past year. We are grateful, and encouraged by your enthusiasm.

title: Tacho Sandoval, 1934-2012
body:
Anastacio (Tacho) Sandoval was born in Galisteo April 16, 1934 to Frank and Lucia Sandoval, one of thirteen siblings. For 52 years he was husband to Libby Sandoval. He was father to Teresa (and husband Sam) and Frank (and wife Sadie), grandfather to Frank Jr. and Joseph, Monica, Samantha, Samone and Juan, great-grandfather to Analicia, Estevan and Juliet. He was uncle and godfather to many and friend to all.

In his 78 years, Tacho, like many of our elders, had a quite a life. He was a sheepherder in Galisteo, an Army veteran, stationed in Fort Bliss, Texas, in 1957. He was a grounds caretaker at the College of Santa Fe and worked in the cornfields irrigating for Governor Bruce King. He retired as caretaker for the King Estate. He was a member of the St. Anthony and St. Joseph Societies here in Galisteo.

Tacho was an extra in the movie Young Guns. He was also a musician who played beautifully on the accordion, and sometimes harmonica. He would play with my Dad Onesimo, Luis Chavez, Benjie Mares, and Orlando Sanchez from Lamy. He would also convince Marie Sandoval to play the accordion. Teresa and Frank remember when they would all go over to Manuel and Clarita Anaya's and then to Mela's or Mary Alice's to sing Las Maiianitas for New Years Eve.

When the children were little, the family would stop at Landon's Store in Stanley to pick up snacks, then visit with friends and family. He loved to go hunting with his brothers Fidel, Joe and George, and later with his son, Frank. He could fix just about anything people would ask him to, and now Frank does the same, as well as the grandsons.

Tacho especially loved joking with his grandchildren and great grandchildren. Family was very important to him and Libby. They were also very social, going to the Senior Centers in Santa Fe and always showing up at the GCA's Saturday Coffees.

I knew it was officially summer when Freddie and I would sit and listen outside our home at the top of the hill to Tacho playing with my Dad and Mom, or over across the bridge with Luis and Remedios, or at Tacho and Libby's house. The music and children's laughter could be heard throughout the village. Sometimes I still go out, thinking I can still hear them.

title: Who We Are: Julia Cairns and John Bulger
body:
Anyone sound like they aren't from here? You betcha! That would be our resident Brit -- Julia Cairns, and her Minnesota PhD hubby John Bulger. Two nicer folks haven't graced our little village in a long time. Alongside their two children, Robin (off on her 'gap year' this fall to Thailand and places beyond) and son Oliver, a sophomore at Desert Academy, the family is very active. Julia and John met in Botswana where John was studying baboons in the wild and Julia was on her own 'gap year' ("it never really has ended!") from Oxford, England. Years later, the family moved north from Santa Cruz, CA. to Salt Spring Island, BC, Canada. In 2008, the coast was finally clear to leave Canada (on Canada Day) and return to the U.S. on Independence Day. And now they have happily landed here in Galisteo. "We just love it here .. .it's full of interesting characters .. .it reminds me of my village in England growing up."

Julia, you may have noticed, is our local yoga instructor and a Studio Tour member for the past three years. She not only creates lovely whimsical paintings of African and East Indian subject matter but also illustrates children's books and her work is featured on quilting fabric. She is constantly creating, with shows now up in the Santa Fe restaurant 'Jambo' and in northern California galleries.

John, when not joining in the yoga classes or taking Oliver to taekwondo classes in town, works from home, consulting on many woodland/lumber ecological and environmental impact assessments that, on occasion, still take him to places far away. The baboons, "unfortunately, are a thing of the past." Robin is a fantastic fiddle player. This past summer you could usually find her at the Friday Farmers Market in Eldorado, making great music and extra money for her upcoming travels. She recently won a science award from Desert Academy for her study of packrat behavior -- a local subject we can all relate to! Oliver (a future international man-of-mystery) is taking Russian language instruction from Phil Pfeiffer in between school and contemplative wilderness strolls in his favorite bathrobe. Both kids are curious, sensitive, loving and engaging, even with us old folks.

With horse Louis ( who recently left for a new home), a now lonely goat, some ducks and chickens, dogs Gus and Puck and the mean cat Mina (not true!) the family is full and vibrant. When I asked Julia what she was most proud of she said "her children". John answered identically and then added "and my wife." Extra points for the husband!

title: A German Painter in Galisteo
body:
In 1937, painter Heinz Emil Salloch (1908-1985) was teaching art to Jewish children in Berlin and refused to use the Nazi newspaper in class. He was forced to flee persecution, going first to Cuba, and then to the U.S. Known in America as Henry, in the 1950s (according to Michael Abatemarco in Pasatiempo, 11/12), "he turned his attention to the landscapes and distinctive Pueblo style architecture of the Southwest," including New Mexico villages like Cundiyo, Cerrillos and Galisteo. An exhibition at the A Gallery in Santa Fe recently showed his watercolors and pastels. Salloch's son Roger lives in Santa Fe and writes for THE Magazine.

The two images (far more interesting in color) are dated Galisteo, 1957 and 1971. Can anyone identify the sites?

title: Galisteo Volunteer Fire & Rescue Pre-Incident Emergency Planning
body:
In January, when the fire department sends out the Galisteo phone directory, you will find enclosed new forms for pre-incident emergency planning ("pre-plans"). The GVFR's current files are aging and out of date. New houses have been built; old ones have been added onto; owners have sold, moved away, separated, or died, and new people have moved to the village. Pre-plan files help the fire department anticipate what may be encountered at an emergency, especially at night when visibility is poor. Although no one is required to submit the requested information, it can improve our services to the community and benefit everyone. These files are treated with confidentiality and are used only to help emergency responses be as efficient and timely as possible.

At the request of several people in the village who live alone, following a recent incident here, the new pre-incident form will ask that the emergency contact name be someone who is next of kin or who has power of attorney. While this is not strictly necessary for minor incidents, it is critically important if one lives alone and becomes unresponsive due to a severe injury or illness. The fire department is likely to be the first responder to a medical emergency and may be the only early resource for contact information. Because of federal privacy regulations restricting who can know about a victim's injuries or illnesses, only someone who is next of kin or has the power of attorney can talk to hospital personnel and find out what happened and take control of the patient's welfare.

The pre-incident forms will request information about building construction, location of propane tanks and electrical circuit breaker boxes, exterior hazards that can trip or entangle a firefighter and any water sources on the property, as well as a sketch of the buildings and any special conditions in approaching them. Please do your best to give your fire department the requested information. It could be a life-saver.

title: {Solar Systems #6: Your Editor}
body:
When I built my little "shack by the creek" in 1992-93, it turned out to be terribly expensive to get electricity to it. (I was then the only one between the highway and the Griscoms on the west side of Avenida Vieja.) At first I plugged the house into my car battery. A little dayglo plug hung out from under the hood and hooked up to a socket in the wall. "Is this legal?" I asked. "Oh yes, in New Mexico, it's a badge of honor. It means you're rural!" But I had to use the car every day; it wasn't the solution. My builders were from Madrid and lived off the grid, and they recommended solar. A then-boyfriend knew how to hook up a couple of solar panels, leaning against the side of the house, to golf cart batteries in the living room. When the inspector came the panels were hidden in the arroyo. "Why?" I asked. "I thought it was legal?" "Well,just to be on the safe side ... "

To make a long story short, I eventually got a solar tracker and a slightly less hokey system (though I had to crawl under my desk and breathe fumes to top up the battery water.) Finally, Positive Energy entered the picture. With them I got rid of my nasty gas ice box, and had more panels installed on the roof. It's all much more efficient, but it's also more sophisticated, i.e. computerized; I'm not always up to the maintenance. Allan Sindelar, founder of Positive Energy, has been incredibly patient about my occasional ineptitude. And I love having lights when the rest of the PNM-reliant village goes dark!

title: Talking to Doc Ferneau
body:
I met Doc (Elmer) Ferneau in early 2011, soon after Richard died. Wonderful Wendy Chase (Galisteo misses you, Wendy!) was a godsend to us toward the end of Richard's life and she mentioned that she often visited Doc. He was open to a visit from me, and we hit it off right away. We enjoy a friendship that is full of laughter and singing (hymns from my mother's Baptist hymnal and popular songs from the 1930s and '40s - he sings melody and I sing harmony). I always receive a warm, enthusiastic welcome and find him alert, engaging, thought-provoking and fun - at age 94.

When I asked Doc to tell me about his life he said, "The beginning was a long time ago". He was born on a farm in southeast Iowa on December 7 (later to become the "Day of Infamy" - Pearl Harbor Day, 1918). His grandfather was a pioneer of sorts. He plowed with four horses and used a large "breaking plow," that turned the prairie grass sod. His father was a skilled farmer, raising herds of Guernsey cattle and Duroc Jersey hogs. His mother had been a school teacher before she married. He remembers his dad getting lime from the railroad and then spreading it on the ground in the spring to de-acidify the soil, rotating his crops, and spreading manure. His dad built the house and barn, could fix anything, and put in one of the first grain storage silos in the area. In the middle of winter, there was often four feet of snow on the ground.

Doc, his parents and older brother attended a little country church, the Highland United Brethren Church, and their social life centered on the church. He attended a one-room school, kindergarten through 8th grade. He believes it was a wonderful learning environment. Because the older students shared desks with the younger ones, and were expected to help, they all learned more quickly. Fights only broke out when an older student felt his younger pal was being picked on. In those days, there was a recitation bench in front of class and each student was expected to recite what his class had been learning. This was another way the younger students learned from the older ones.

Doc skipped a grade in elementary, as was sometimes the case back then. As a result, he was always younger than most of his schoolmates, starting high school when he was 12 years old! He weighed 180 lbs and had a 17 1/2 " neck, which stood him in good stead playing football and wrestling. Later at Iowa State College, he paid $10 a quarter for tuition if he kept his grades above a C+. He worked for his board as a dishwasher and potato-masher in a fraternity house kitchen. His parents sent him $5 every 2 weeks, which paid for his room in a boarding house. Doc majored in vocational agriculture and studied soils, animal husbandry, and farm mechanics, including blacksmithing, which he especially enjoyed.

He graduated from college when he was 20, and was hired to teach vocational agriculture at a high school in Bedford, Iowa. The recruiter happened to see him applying for a job and hired him on the spot, probably convinced by his size that Doc could handle a class of unruly high school boys who had caused problems for the previous instructor. On the first day, Doc proved he could indeed handle unruly boys. It's safe to say his disciplinary techniques would never pass muster today! Three years later war broke out and Doc volunteered for service in the Navy, reporting for duty January 3, 1942.

( Part 2 of this interview will appear in a future issue.)

title: Salsa the Night Away
body:
Saturday night Feb. 16th, in the Community Center, we had one heck of a party! Valentine's Day? Mardi Gras? Salsa? Well, it all came together under Xmas lights and candles, with tons of food and drink ... and a great Cubano salsa band --Havana Son --led by Galistean tres player Fred Milder: www.havanason.com. It seemed we all needed to get out and shake our bootys 'cuz the joint was jumpin' from start to finish. There was a cake walk (music plays, music stops, and the 15 attendees who landed on the right number went home with really yummy confectionary delights). There was a photo booth and some wild costumes - a giant vulture, an alien, a king and queen of hearts.

Did we mention this was a fund raiser for La Sala de Galisteo? As La Sala moves towards some big construction this spring and summer, money is needed and welcomed. Galisteo comes through on every level, every time, and we all appreciate it. The entire Board worked hard to bring this event together, from setting up Friday afternoon thru clean-up on Sunday.

"We need to have dances more often!" was heard time after time, all night long. OK, OK! Seems a nice fit to be restoring our village dance hall by doing just that ... .. dancing!

Ed Note: My dancing pictures didn't come out, and there was a lot of flashy competition. But I'd vote for Lisa and Orlando Griego as the smoothest couple on the floor.

title: Citizen Rights in Galisteo
body:
Last summer, working at the Galisteo Community Museum Gallery, I met visitors from around the state, the country and elsewhere. I learned that most of them came specifically to enjoy the 'non-touristy' tranquil setting, see unspoiled traditional adobes and real history. During impromptu discussions on the portal, perfectly timed Alta oil tankers barreled through, shaking the ground, upsetting and startling visitors, most wondering aloud why this occurred.

I ask that myself, along with why the road in the village must be 'widened', after two years of writing letters to the department of Historical Preservation, the Highway Department, and Alta Oil Co. in Colorado -- to no avail. There is nothing like Galisteo anywhere in New Mexico, but the state will not protect it; their excuse is 'safety'. BUT no highways anywhere else in the country skim so near buildings now, let alone after widening. Safety is not the answer. Highway construction dollars and corporate oil interests are not the answer. Deadly accidents with tankers occur on the straight wide road from Clark Hill to Moriarty, and on the hill itself, not on our section of narrow hilly Highway 41.

Alta Oil Co. answered my letter truthfully about speeding trucks, an answer I already knew. Drivers will not slow down if they know nothing can be done to stop them. Period. One highway worker retiree visiting the village gave me a startlingly excellent bit of news saying "the department doesn't want you to know you can have stop signs installed at either end of town." IT IS OUR RIGHT.

Speaking of rights, Alternative Radio's David Barsamian recently broadcast a talk by Paul Cienfuegos, from Portland, Oregon, speaking at length about citizen rights to determine what is best and safest for communities if the government will not. He outlined decisions made by communities around the country to protect homes, children, air, water quality and general safety of their towns: A) Lancaster, Pennsylvania passed and enforces a law to not allow fracking within or near the town. B) The state of Montana has a constitution giving citizens the right to vote on any corporate activity deemed unfit for a community or the state to protect citizens from corporate malfeasance. C) Bellingham, Washington blocked a mining company moving coal through town at a rate of twenty open train cars daily, leaving a trail of deadly coal dust dirtying the town, endangering citizens.

Mr. Cienfuegos went into some detail about we can accomplish the same and how corporations have been setting up laws in this country over 100 years to their advantage and our detriment. Highway 285 serves extremely well as an alternate route for tankers. It is not too late to stop tankers altogether and stop the broadening of the highway in the village, and possibly the rest of the road. It is time to have by-laws for the village to protect OUR interests, including the traditional aspects of all kinds. Our buildings should not be shaken to pieces, our children, adults, horsemen, or dog walkers need not be endangered by corporate oil 'interests'. See this link: http://coal-free-bellingham.org/.

title: Notes on Buying a Used Bicycle
body:
Hi neighbors! Now that the weather may be getting nicer and you are contemplating getting a bicycle to get around the village, here are some tips for you to consider.

A good friend of mine bought a used bike at a garage sale for $50 and asked me to fix it up so that they could use it to get their mail, etc. After figuring that (for starters) it needed roughly $180 in parts (no labor) to get it operational, we agreed to give it the appropriate burial it warranted. Garage sales are famous for the bargain bike that only needs a "little work" to get it going again. If you absolutely have to get a bike at a garage sale, think of these things as you decide:

A) Consider the fit of the bike to your body. If it is too small or too big, you won't remember how cheap it was when your back and knees start aching, even if only using it to go to/from the mailboxes. Getting the right size bike is what bike shops are for.

B) In most cases, the frame will be fine. Generally bikes at garage sales aren't being used very much. The moving parts are where things go bad after sitting in a garage for any length of time.

C) Check the tires for tread wear. Are the tires pumped up? Tires are expensive and if they are flat, you will also need inner tubes and protective rim strips. That's 3 items to purchase for each wheel.

D) Squeeze the brake levers. If they are stiff or not moving, you may need new cables and housing for the front and rear brakes. If these cables are bad, chances are you will need cables and housing for the front and rear drivetrain as well. That's 4 cables and 4 separate housing, plus lubrication for all.

E) Make sure the seat tube is removable.

This is just some basic stuff to make you a more educated consumer at garage sales. Sometimes you get lucky, and sometimes a trip to a bike shop might be a better thing. They have warranties, bikes on sale, and smart people who will steer you in the right direction if they know what you want.

title: San Cristobal Ranch Wins American Quarter Horse Association Award
body:
The San Cristobal Ranch won the prestigious American Quarter Horse Association's Bayer Best Remuda Award in 2012. Grant Mitchell, SC ranch manager in 2000, took over the horse division for Singleton Ranches (30 in NM alone) in 2005. Three stallions are used to "breed for cow sense and trainability .... We raise everything here, start [the quarter horses] as 2-year-olds and then give them to cowboys to ride. Our goal is to give the cowboys a horse that lets them get the work done."

To be eligible for the Best Remuda award, applicants must breed and use five or more Quarter Horses for ranch work and be a member of the AQHA. Singleton Ranches Ranch Rodeo Team also won the New Mexico Championship Ranch Rodeo two years in a row. (Thanks to Denice Pruett for the info.)

title: Starry Starry Night
body: Humankind has long loved and celebrated the night sky. Vincent Van Gogh, Don McLean and Carl Sagan, all legendary sky watchers, implore us with their art, science and music to revere the heavenly cosmos whirling overhead. The musical sound track from my patio on this May Day is the trill of a Saye's Phoebe and the flute of a White-throated Sparrow. These and many other species found their way to Galisteo this spring by winging tirelessly through the dark sky using its billions and billions of stars and the earth's magnetic field to map-quest their journeys from latitudes as far away as 2,000 miles. By flying at night, even the tiniest sparrow travels safe from hawks and other diurnal raptors. Even so, millions of migrating birds are killed each year by windmills, cell phone towers, and high power lines. One of the biggest challenges birds face is the disorienting glare from outdoor lighting -- mine and yours. The Earth Week editorial in The New Mexican tells me that too much light at night damages humans as well as animals. More than one-fifth of humanity can no longer see the Milky Way. While the loss of inky dark nights disrupts migration and breeding cycles in wildlife, for humans it means an interruption of sleep patterns and ancient body rhythms. We need dark nights. Unnecessary night-time lighting adds to the demand on coal-burning power plants, thus contributing to air pollution and global warming. Here in the Galisteo Basin, our precious Dark Sky is fading. Light bleeds into the night from Santa Fe, Albuquerque, and our own exterior lighting to dim the once velvet dark of the night sky and pick clean the diamond-field of stars I marveled at as little as twenty years ago. Tonight, tum out the lights. Ask your neighbors to tum out theirs. Sit outside. Watch the stars wink on. Wait for the moon. Listen for the chirping of songbirds migrating safely overhead in our precious darkness.

A unanimous vote changed the requirement to 12 members for next year. Joe Cooper and Rod Hall will try to reconcile the articles of incorporation and the by-laws. Elections were held: Rod Hall remains President and Scott Diffrient Vice President; Janice Felty Griscom was elected Secretary. Wayne King (Treasurer) and Joette Trofimuk were reelected. Phillip Tuwaletstiwa was elected a new Board member (replacing Tom Morin). He joins Matthew McQueen, Richard Patton and Antonio Chavez. (Romona Scholder continues as Bookkeeper and Florence Sohn keeps the records.) Meters are read quarterly -- by Antonio until someone can be hired. Few of us are aware of, or appreciate, the incredibly complex and time-consuming job these people perform on a volunteer basis. THANKS! The old red tank (still full of water for fire department use) has been disconnected and the old silver tank has gone to the Rodeo Grounds. The current tank holds 55,000 gallons. A new tank would cost $104,000 and the Board is looking into grants. The distribution line runs under NM41 and the Board will try to tie in with the upcoming State roadwork to improve the pipe. (Thanks to former Secretary Joette Trofimuk for her minutes.)

title: Citizen Rights in Galisteo (Part II)
body: My article on Galisteo citizen rights in the previous issue of El Puente outlined what may be done to stop heavy traffic through the village. Widening shoulders will not only reduce room for people riding their horses, walking their dogs, taking their children for an outing or just living on either side. The "safety" work will promote careless drivers' false sense of security; they already pass on hills, speed, tailgate and generally risk their lives and ours. Highway 41 between Clark Hill and Moriarty, already widened and straightened for "safety," so far has suffered three fatal accidents, two involving tankers. Between Clark Hill and Lamy, several fatal accidents have occurred. Speeders heading south and hitting the north curve into Galisteo roll their vehicles. The latest serious accident was March 3. Friends coming to my home for a birthday lunch were hit through no fault of their own and almost killed. They missed County Rd. 38B (Frank Anaya Ranch Road) by a few yards, turned around, and approached going north, signal on, slowing down. A speeding driver behind them decided to "beat them," as he later said. He appeared so quickly my friends never even saw him. He hit the hinge section of the front door of their little truck, spinning them around and off the highway totaling both vehicles. The speeder was unharmed. My friends were badly hurt. One had a black eye the size of an apple and torn ligaments in her shoulder. My 82-year-old friend suffered a blow to her leg from the console of the gear shift; in a mere ten minutes, her leg was swollen to twice normal size from knee to ankle. If they had been hit directly on the door it would likely have killed them. The Galisteo Fire Department arrived within minutes and did a fine job. Thank you so much, Corey McGillicuddy and Jon Stern. Once NM41 is widened, accidents will certainly increase, as will heavy traffic through the village with no provision for real safety or patrols by the police. There is still time to gather together and deal with this in a way to protect village inhabitants and drivers on NM41 north and south of Galisteo. Once the road is widened, there will be no recourse.

title: GCA Annual Meeting
body: Twenty two people and a dog attended the annual Galisteo Community Association meeting (fulfilling the quorum, though not a great turnout for a village of 250 ... And where were all those other dogs?) Matthew McQueen reported on the Saddleback subdivision, which is being foreclosed, though if the bank sells it to another developer, nothing will change. Commonweal Conservancy has suffered from the recession and is selling more large lots from its former open space but the Preserve will remain at 3000-4000 acres. Believe it or not, the "land grab lawsuit" (led by Galistean Morgan Gafford, with Peirce Clayton) is still dragging on under its third judge. A gazebo and picnic table in the Bosque will be dedicated to Richard Griscom; timing and funding still being determined. And finally, elections: Anna Cardenas remains President, and Corinne Anaya Treasurer; Roger Taylor is Vice President; Janice Griscom will be Secretary. Thanks to departing Board members Frank Hirsch, Amber Haskell, Muriel Fariello, and Joette Trofimuk. Matthew McQueen is joined by new Board members Wayne King, Eric Thomas, and David Van Dyk, with Judy Tuwaletstiwa as Alternate. Then - a new tradition -- margaritas were served.

title: BCC Updates
body: On April 30th, after two hours of discussion and amendments on a "Resolution to Appoint a Water Policy Advisory Committee," sponsored by Kathy Holian and Robert Anaya, the Board of County Commissioners approved a panel on water and wastewater issues, a project that our own Roger Taylor, President of the Santa Fe Basin Water Association, has long been advocating. (Taylor was quoted on The New Mexican website (3/29) on evidence that suggests expanded pumping at the Santa Fe City "northwest well" could reduce the lives of local domestic wells by more than a decade.) The Committee will consist of 12 members representing mutual domestic water associations, soil and water conservation districts, acequia associations, the Estancia Basin Water Planning Committee and the Buckman Direct Diversion Board, as well as representatives from central and northern water planning areas. Five members will be selected by the commissioners. Nominations are under way and will close in two months. This citizen's committee will make recommendations to strengthen sections of the draft County Code that relate to water conservation and protection; research and recommend on a possible Regional Water Authority; and look at planned water storage and recovery efforts by the County. Joe Miller returned to the BCC on April 9th to request (and receive) final approval for his Spirit Wind West Subdivision: a "39-Lot Residential Subdivision On 133.73 Acres; Phase 1, Which Will Consist Of 16 Lots. The Property Is Located South Of Eldorado, On The East Side Of US 85, Off Old Lamy Trail (County Road 33)" -- at the curve by the railroad tracks. Recently Miller told a community meeting that he was moving ahead with his developments before the new County Code takes effect so that he can put in modular homes (not mobile homes, but "stick houses") and avoid open space and trails provisions, as well as placing different sized and priced homes on different sized lots. The County also compromised on the affordable housing requirement. Other developers are using the same strategies and getting three-year extensions so they will be grandfathered into the old code. If they all succeed, the area will resemble a congested Albuquerque or Phoenix suburb. And the water will come from where? In response, a "285 South Sustainability Alliance" is being formed to protect the area from over-development, with a steering committee of representatives from Eldorado, Lamy, Galisteo and several subdivisions. Roger Taylor will represent Galisteo. Asking for "no growth" is apparently illegal, but asking for "sustainability" isn't ... yet.

title: Goat Grazing for Fire Prevention
body: The January 2003 cover of El Puente showed a mob of the 200 goats grazing Galisteo fields under the auspices of the Earth Works Institute. Now they're back (temporarily joining our permanent residents Dooley and Ted at Janice Griscom's). Jennifer Hogan and Dorothy Van Ark have hired fifty goats from Horned Locus Goat Scaping to graze on their overgrowth for three days. They note it's a good way to safeguard our properties from potential fires in this terrible drought. If you are interested, call Amanita Thorp at 505-917-9885 to get prices and schedule grazing, or call Jennifer at 466-1518 for more information.

title: Coal Train Derailment in Lamy
body: Several cars of a coal train on a side track derailed in Lamy, dumping mounds of coal on the main rail line and causing long delays for Amtrak passengers. Steel rails were ripped from the ground and warped; wooden ties were crushed and strewn about the scene. The cause had not been determined when this was published in The New Mexican on May 1, 1988.

body: Two TV pilots are being filmed at Cerro Pelon Ranch in April and May.

title: La Sala Renovation Work
body: La Sala renovation work is moving along: major work on corner wall replacement will commence soon. There was a good work day a few weeks ago for grounds clean-up, re-set of nail heads in floor boards, and a second exit door was installed.

title: New Book Published on Chaco World
body: The Museum of New Mexico Press just published Time and Time Again: History, Rephotography and Preservation in the Chaco World by photographer Peter Goin and writer Lucy R. Lippard. There will be a signing (6/20) at Collected Works.

title: Spring Cleaning: Village Yard Sale
body: Garages and storage lockers and the backs of closets -- Oh My! These places seem to grow junk, so "why not clean them out once a year?" Because its a pain, that's why. But La Sala gave us all an excuse on May 4th to make it worth our while to do just that. The weather was good, considering what had blown through the week before, and the yard sale was on. Twenty nine households at fourteen stops decided to try this money-making venture and, well .... at least it gave us an excuse to get rid of stuff. The crowds were a bit thin, but most stops made a least a bit of $$. Most of us bought from each other. "One man's trash is another [wo]man's treasure" held true. A giant thank you to all who participated, and tithed to La Sala's building fund more than their meager sales would have warranted. We hope to do this again next May Day and get Santa Fe accustomed to making an annual spring trip to Galisteo.

title: {Last Stop for Legal Tender?}
body: Just as the Legal Tender restaurant is being threatened with closure over the details of an agreement with the Railroad Museum (see their website for updates), Amtrak is considering abandonment of the Lamy to Colorado line because of deteriorating maintenance. The State has dissolved its agreement with the Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railroad for this stretch, gaining millions of dollars but forfeiting a north/south connection that could prove vital in the future. The Lamy to Chicago line would not be affected.

body: Denice Pruett warns us that the County is cracking down on pet licenses and even going door to door. It's only $8 but there is some question about where they are getting their database; veterinarians will not give out clients' information. Call Denice - 466-3601-- if you get a notice in the mail. It will be interesting to see how far they will go with this.

title: THE (ONGOING) SAGA OF BOB THE COP
body:
Our small village has recently come up with its own solution to those speeding 18-wheeler oil rigs and Walmart delivery trucks that roar through our quietness to save 40 miles connecting with the Interstate ... and those late-to-State workers zipping by at 85mph to get to Santa Fe on time .

Enter a used Santa Fe County Sheriff car donated to our fire department, parked on Hiway 41 and moved daily. At first this worked as "slow down ... cop car ahead!" But it wasn't until Bob arrived that things got interesting. He's a John Nissen dummy (mannequin) imported from Berlin, Germany. The fire department dressed him in uniform and aviator glasses and gave him an old hand radio phone.

One day, an unknowing Santa Fe County beat officer stopped, thinking Bob was a "real" cop who'd had a heart attack or stroke in the heat of the day, He called 911. Our fire chief heard the dispatcher say, "There's an officer down in Galisteo, I think he's had a heart attack." Jean said it was the best laugh she has had on her birthday, ever!

One recent afternoon, Bob was cited for being "one of the rudest cops in America," for not responding to an elderly Sikh trnck driver from New York who had just driven across the U.S. and had stopped to ask Bob for directions. He told the adobe workforce at La Sala: "I knocked on da window twice and he didn't even bother to open his damn winda, he was too busy on his hand radio, you guys should report dat cop!" He drove away, leaving the gang rolling on the ground with laughter.

Some have suggested that Bob needs an attitude adjustment class. Others think he should learn to speak English (since he's a Dutch/Geiman dummy). Others have said he needs coffee and a donut. Yet Bob has definitely filled his monthly quota of fun (revenge) with the truck drivers. He has them slowing down, turning heads and turbans,

So when you drive by Bob on his regular beat, give him the thumbs up. He may not respond, but he'll appreciate your driving 35mph through the heart of our village.

title: PUT YOUR SKILLS TO WORK
body:
Do you like to get muddy? Can you swing a hammer? Do you grocery shop? Well. . .it just so happens all these skills are coming in very handy this summer at La Sala!

Have you noticed the new adobe mud on the south wall? It's the result of partnering with Cornerstones' restoration experts. All summer long (Fridays and Saturdays, 9am to 3pm) our local young interns -- John Garcia, Joseph Garcia, Ruben Anaya, Joseph Sandoval, Oliver Bulger, and Emily Montoya- will be helping this new look extend around the building.

On the vacant lot next to La Sala, thanks to Jose Ortiz y Pino, we now have an adobe "factory" where we make bricks and mud to restore and re-plaster our 100-year-old dance hall. Antonio Chavez donated the professional grade adobe forms. Jim Sloan and Phillip Tuwaletstiwa provided and operated the earth moving equipment to clear the property and dig for good adobe clay. Water was trucked in by the GVFR and generous Galisteans are pitching in with additional brawn. As part of this restoration, we will also continue refurbishing the ten windows. Help is needed for this project as well -nice indoor work on these upcoming hot summer days .... It's very cool inside.

Or you can just drop off bottled water or soft drinks for all these hot volunteers. So it's EZ to help on many levels! Stop by over the summer and see how far the village has come with this restoration. While you are there, come on inside and see the interior bracing system and ... We have really neat T-shirts and hats for sale too.

And word is spreading. Tour groups from Michigan and Wisconsin are coming to help mud plaster La Sala's walls!

title: GCA REPORT ON NM 41, BRIDGES
body:
According to the DOT, an RFP for the two bridges will go out to bid in August, and will be awarded in November. Work on both bridges will begin March or April, 2014. Truck detour signs will be placed at the junctions of both 285/41 and 40/41. Construction will take c. 6 months, with one lane open on each bridge for through-traffic while the other sides are being re-built.

The Galisteo Creek Bridge will have casings drilled to bedrock at 30' for metal and concrete pilings, with a normal noise factor. However, the San Cristobal Bridge will need to have a hydraulic hammer pound steel piles down 100', and this will be noisy. Vibration monitoring will be performed for the duration.

The design for the bridges is close to the existing appearance, slightly wider, with guardrails, and an elevated pedestrian walkway on one side only. Cyclists will use the paved shoulder.

Funding for re-paving NM 41 (with 12' lanes and 6' paved shoulders/bicycle paths) has been delayed. The new target dates are: San Cristobal Bridge to Clark Hill, Spring 2017-2018; Goose Downs Farm to Rte 285, 2019-20. Work in the village center (from Goose Downs to the Galisteo Bridge) will most likely be done in 2018. There the lanes will taper from 12' to 11' (current width) with a 4' shoulder. NMDOT will look into the possibility of a natural/tan coloring for the shoulder in the village center. Surprisingly, there is some paved shoulder there already, just hidden under accumulated dirt and gravel.

There will be medians between lanes by Goose Downs and the Galisteo Bridge, to slow down traffic. Each median (planted with native drought-tolerant vegetation) will be 17' wide, tapering down to c. 600'. Roger and Wayne will continue to represent the GCA in meetings with NMDOT. Next update, Fall 2013.

title: WHY SO MANY WESTERN TANAGERS?
body:
So many Galisteans reported mobs of stunning Western Tanagers at their suet feeders this May that I felt duty-bound to search out an explanation for this unprecedented concentration of what I consider the most beautiful bird in the world.

Here's what I found out.

In her Wild Birds Unlimited column in The New Mexican, Anne Schmauss explained the phenomenon this way: "Yes, the deep drought has compressed the corridor of migration so that birds are more dependent on backyard feeders and birdbaths. With no rain, few leaves, and fewer insects, birds that don't normally frequent our feeders for seeds are finding that suet cakes are just the ticket for desperately needed nourishment."

In addition to the drought, strong weather systems stalled over southern Colorado caused birds to stay put in New Mexico. Not unlike people caught in an airport when outgoing flights are cancelled, birds began to "stack up" and "pile up" in the same fast food lines in an avian holding pattern. Backyard bird feeders were never so vital.

May 2013 brought the most amazing birding I have ever experienced. The Galisteo Bosque, a well-known hot spot, got even hotter as it provided shelter to many exquisite rare species such as Painted and American Redstarts; Scarlet, Summer and Hepatic Tanagers; Lazuli Buntings; a pair of Blue-winged Teal, an Eastern Blue Jay and an Eastern Towhee, to mention a few.

As a result, the Bosque was a daily scene of fired-up birders flitting about attached to binoculars, camera, IPods, bird guides and smart phones in a desperate effort to get the low-down and a "good look" at the rare species of the day. It was wild. It was wonderful. Feed the birds.

title: Bearing Down
body: Thanks to the drought and absence of fruit in orchards this year, Black Bears looking to beef up for hibernation are in bad straits. They have been coming down arroyos from the mountains and the Galisteo Bosque is one of their refuges. In the last few weeks, reports of a young male bear and a mother with two cubs have flooded the village airwaves. Seen on both sides of the creek and all over Ranchitos, bears are after garbage, birdfood, grease on grills, compost heaps, and at my house, a bag of appropriately-named Yum Yum. The friend staying here reported two visits that had my dog going ballistic. A souvenir remains -- a huge muddy pawprint on a window which was not even washed off by the rains. When Janice Griscom heard a rumpus around her goat pen, she got in her car and drove back there. The mother stood up to full height, ready to protect her cubs. Margaret Wrinkle has also had a dramatic encounter, as presumably others have too. Sightings have now diminished. As of this writing it seems the poor bears may have wandered off to more fertile feeding grounds. Lemon berries could be ripening in the mountains, providing some food for desperate creatures. In August, High Country News reported that New Mexico activists were trying to get the state to "implement an emergency 'diversionary' feeding program to feed bears in the backcountry" to reduce human confrontations, but not everyone agrees this is a good idea.

title: Bear Medicine
body:
When my father retired, he directed some of his time towards genealogy. Not too far in, he learned, to everyone's surprise, that his lineage included Native American ancestors.
I found this fascinating and delightful. I had always been interested in Native American traditions--attending sweat lodges and the occasional ceremonial dance. After my father's discovery, I began learning and integrating Animal Medicine into my life.
With beautiful, curious bears honoring us with their presence, it is interesting to look at the Animal Medicine, or message, that Bear is bringing.
In many Native American traditions, "medicine" refers to anything that improves one's connection to all oflife. This would include the healing of body, mind, and spirit.
This medicine is also anything that brings personal power, strength, and understanding. Native American Medicine is all encompassing as it involves being on the earth in perlect harmony with the Universe or "Great Mystery."
Native American Animal Medicine teaches that our fellow creatures exhibit habits that can relay messages and lessons for healing to anyone through sightings, observation, or resonance with a particular animal. Each animal is assigned a lesson based on a specific concept for the sake of simplicity. This is free, precious medicine.
"The strength of Bear Medicine is the power of introspection. Bear seeks honey, or the sweetness of truth, within the hollow of an old tree. Bear enters the womb-cave-Great Void to hibernate and digest the year's experience.
"To accomplish the goals and dreams that we carry, the art of introspection is necessary.
"The Great Void is the place where all solutions and answers live in harmony with the questions that fill our realities. If we choose to believe that there are many questions to life, we must also believe that the answers to these questions reside within us. Each and every being has the capacity to quiet the mind, enter the silence, and know.
"Bear invites us to go within .... so that our dreams become concrete harmonious realities." (Jamie Sams and David Carson Medicine Cards: the Discovery of Power through the Ways of Animals, Santa Fe: Bear & Company, 1988.)

title: Gold in Them Thar Hills
body:
The price of gold rose to $1,420 an ounce at the end of August, and industry pressure is mounting to permit Santa Fe Gold's new $2 billion mine project off NM 14 in earache and Lukas Canyons. It would be near Lone Mountain (the volcanic peak many of us see from our windows), where there is also an abundance of copper to be extracted . (The Martinez administration has gutted the pit rule protecting ground water at copper mines.) The company has sent out thousands of glossy brochures asking for support, which they are unlikely to get from most locals.
Among the opposition are archaeologists, Pueblo tribes protesting the impact on many ancient and sacred sites, wildlife advocates, residents worried about machinery and dust, destruction of the landscape, tourism, trucks on the Scenic Byway, expansion of mining in the Ortiz, and the 200 acre feet of water they would need for ten years, although the Madrid well, originating in the Ortiz, has been dropping 15 feet a year.
SF Gold ( affiliated with an infamous Australian corporation) claims it will use a new environmentally friendlier technology instead of cyanide leaching (though not for the copper), but they will reportedly level two hills in the canyons in an open pit operation. This is happening just as the gold scar from an earlier mine on the eastern slope of the Ortiz mountains (see p.4) is beginning to grow over, In the mid-1980s, a citizen's group successfully sued LAC Minerals over water contamination from that mine. Looks like it's time to rev up again. See Stop Santa Fe Gold on Facebook.

title: {Bob: The Backstory}
body:
Bob is part of Eric's dummy collection (last count thirteen -- from his past doing visual display work at Macy's). Bob was bought on German Ebay two years ago for $25. The seller in Berlin said anybody who can" get this thing out of my apartment today can have it." It belonged to her former boyfriend and she had Bob posed on a couch with a top hat, a necktie and a wine bottle. He looked homeless and hated. But as John Nissen is a top mannequin model, Eric had my nephew in Dusseldorl call a friend in Berlin and hand the lady the twenty five bucks the same day. (How about that for global transaction!) Then Bob was packed and UPSed ($225) and arrived in Galisteo with the usual delivery sarcasm: "Got another body here for Eric Thomas!"
Bob got a new set of blue glass eyes, and sat around here up on the Hill, clothesless, scaring unsuspecting souls who responded with "that's creepy" and mostly "Eric does what?!" So, when Jean Moya was talking at a La Sala meeting about how the lurking squad car would be better with a cop in it, Bob's services were offered and he got the job -- legless, with a wig.

title: Stalking Bob
body:
Bob was in the Rodeo parade, "incognito" ( cowboy hat with mirror sunglasses) on La Sala's float. He had such a good time with the candy-throwing kids that he lost his donut on the parade route. On Monday morning, Jean Moya left a message: "I'm looking for Bob! He's late to work!" Obviously, he'd had a good time at the rodeo and was hung over on the Hill.
One day Jean, our fire chief, got a visit from the police chief. She was afraid she was in trouble, but he said he wanted to see for himself if a dummy cop worked. He spent over a half an hour watching the traffic and concluded that "Bob works!"
The latest is that one morning at the beginning of August, when Jean brought Bob "down to his job," a dark car followed her from the bridge and stopped to watch as she set Bob up south of the church. As she was struggling to get Bob's arm up on the steering wheel, a well-dressed woman approached and knocked on the squad car window. Jean rolled down the window, apprehensively, and the woman said she'd come by the other morning on her way to NM 14 and had stopped to ask Bob for directions. When he didn't respond, she went around the back of the car. When she realized Bob was a mannequin, she said she laughed and thought, "Oh, am I the dummy!"
So, the reason she was stalking Bob (and Jean) was that she was building a house off NM14, was brand new to the area, and wanted to photograph Bob for her Christmas card! She told Jean that Bob was the "most ingenious" thing she had found all around Santa Fe.
So now Bob is getting smart (and smug) and considering a Santa suit to make some extra cash for the holidays. We may even see him as a poseur during the upcoming Galisteo Studio Tour!

title: Thinking Ahead: Studio Tour 2014
body:
The 26th Annual Studio Tour is now history. There were 31 artists at 24 sites and 3 food stops, beautiful weather, and a gorgeous poster by Vonnie Cameron to lure visitors.

Most of you know that the tour is always the third weekend in October. The committee that organizes and follows up on this event changes over the years as interested parties come and go, move in and out, or just plain don't have the time to give from one year to the next.

Now that this season's tour has ended, some of us will pass on our duties after years of contribution. The committee will need 3 or 4 fresh faces and hands to help next year. Members do various jobs with help from tour participants on outside assignments. Nothing is too difficult or too large! The schedule is easy: Spring and Fall meetings with email follow-ups to participants and sponsors. The only requirement is an email account you know how to use. title: {Money for Bosque}
body:
The GCA has obtained partial funding for restoration work on the Galisteo Creek, and is working on obtaining the remainder of the funding for future work. This is tentatively scheduled to begin in the spring of 2014, and will focus on a 1/2 mile stretch on either side of the old wooden bridge. The work will include some removal of sediment/mud build-up in the creek bed, clean-up of collapsed banks, and removal of invasive species such as salt cedar. Some of these issues are normal "wear & tear", some are due to the flooding from the intense rains this past September, and others result from recreational vehicle use. More details will be forthcoming in a few months, however prior to any work being done there will be consultations with adjacent property owners as well as community meetings to obtain community input.

In the meantime, the GCA has installed cable and bollard fencing to prevent further erosion from recreational vehicles. There is still easy access for walkers, hikers, horseback riders etc. but vehicle use of any kind is significantly restricted.

title: New Life for Former Galisteo Inn
body:
Jeff Ruzich and Scott Canning from the Bronx (N.Y.) have just purchased the former Galisteo Inn. Scott was the director of horticulture at Wave Hill in Riverdale-- a unique combination of contemporary art museum and botanical garden. Jeff is an emergency room physician. While serving in the Air Force, he was stationed in Albuquerque and fell in love with New Mexico, often visiting a photographer friend -- Jerry Ackerman -- in Galisteo: "I would look at the Galisteo Inn and imagine that someday I would return to New Mexico and find a place like it."

"When I found myself 18 months ago relocating here, friends told me that of course I had to buy the Inn. Knowing the amount of work involved, I clearly did not need it! But a property like this has spoken to Scott and me before, and we are aware of the work - and even more the potential. We bought an old farm on the Hudson River near Rhinebeck, N. Y. and spent 15 years restoring that. We understand the Inn's meaning to the community. We want to respect its history as the Juan Ortiz homestead. Our aspirations are to restore the farming element of the property." We wish Jeff and Scott joy in hard work.

title: Yoga for Your Health
body:
When people who have not tried it think of yoga, they tend to imagine some extremely flexible person getting into positions that would be worthy of a circus act and definitely not something they could ever do. Well, I am here to tell you that yoga is for every body, and every age. It is in fact a gift for older people. Those who study yoga in later life not only gain health but also a freshness of mind and a happy outlook on life. With yoga comes a rebirth, teaching one to face the rest of one's life happily, peacefully, and courageously.

There are many different kinds of yoga but most of them tie into the classical Hatha Yoga that has been practiced in India for hundreds of years. Yoga is really all about balance; we are balancing the mental and the physical through breath and movement. On a physical level, as in life, being 'off balance' doesn't feel good, and as we age we lose not only our ability to balance but also our flexibility, strength, and focus. Yoga teaches us to slow down, breathe, and move with awareness at our own pace. It is not about keeping up with others in a class; we are all at different stages in our lives and therefore in yoga practice.

When you begin a yoga class it may feel intimidating at first but through gentle practice (twice a week is good) you will find that you not only feel better in your body but also more relaxed and open to whatever life brings. It is not a purely physical practice but affects our whole being. Some people complain that they injured themselves whilst practicing yoga and so had to stop. They hurt themselves by not practicing correctly, so it is important to find a teacher who takes time to explain poses and assist when necessary.

There is no magic pill that will give you better posture, strength, energy, balance or inner joy, but with the regular practice of yoga all these benefits can be yours. Give this gift to your body and your whole being will benefit. If you would like to try a class right here in Galisteo, come to my house at 5687 Hwy 41 on Monday or Thursday morning (8:30am - 9:45). I teach all levels, and welcome beginners. For more information: 466-1935 or Julia.c.cairns@gmail.com.

Ruby Renshaw is also a yoga instructor living in the village and offers classes throughout the week. To see her schedule, visit www.integrativeyoga.net.

title: Gold Mine Update
body:
The New Mexican (10/6) reports that Mary Lloyd Estrin and her husband/ranch manager Robert Estrin of Lone Mountain Ranch have filed a lawsuit against Santa Fe Gold Corp., Emily W. Potter, and Ortiz Mines. The Lloyd family has owned the 27,545 acre ranch since 1965 and has been fighting mining for decades. The Potter family of Missouri owns the mineral rights beneath the entire ranch and in 1992 sued the Estrins for "discouraging" mining operations. It was settled out of court. Now the Estrins are suing for their First Amendment rights to participate in the process without being sued again for doing so.

Residents of the area fear noise and light pollution, environmental and wildlife destruction, traffic on NM 14 (designated a "scenic byway" thanks to local activism), water contamination and the 70 million gallons of water required annually for ore processing. Rumor (unsubstantiated) has it that Santa Fe Gold has failed to pay for the environmental impact study and scientists have been pulled off the property, which would be good news ....

There will eventually be public meetings on the proposal. Opposition to the mine is being led by Turquoise Trail Preservation Trust with legal support from the New Mexico Environmental Law Center. See TTPT's website for updates and info. DONATE to support preservation of our cultural landscape. More in the December issue of El Puente.

title: {GCA Update}
body:
The Draft Sustainable Land Development Code has held 5 public hearings around the County, and a number of organizations have been highlighting errors, corrections, improvements, etc. Final formal public hearings will be held on Nov. 19 at 6:30PM and on Dec 3 (time tbd) at the County Commissioners' hearing room. The BCC will vote on Dec 10. Although it still has flaws, overall this is a good document and worth approving.

Our 100-year-old dance hall is embracing the digital era. The new website--Lasaladegalisteo.org -- is loaded with photos and information. You can help by buying a very cool t-shirt or hat on line or make a simple donation. We are also writing grant applications for continued funding.

Restoration work on La Sala has stopped for the winter, and we met all the construction goals we had set! The majority of the heavy construction has been completed, and next spring we can begin work on internal cosmetics such as replastering the walls and fixing the bancos.

title: Los Pastores in Galisteo's Past
body:
The performance of Los Pastores at Nuestra Señora de los Remedios on December 15th was the first time it has taken place in Galisteo since 1964. The December 1997 issue of EL PUENTE ran a photograph of the Galisteo version around 1940, with Chavez, Sena, Anaya, and Sandoval elders participating. Mela Montoya wrote a reminiscence. At age eleven or so, and for many years afterwards, she was "the Gila," accompanying the pastores (shepherds). Rehearsals were overseen by the Sena family, who also stored the costumes. In 1964, Mela's oldest daughter Geraldine played Gila, and Rudy Sena was Lucifer.

Los Pastores - a drama about shepherds' search for the newborn Christ Child -- originated in 16th century Spain, one of a series of autos sacramentales illustrating lessons in faith in the days when few could read. It was traditionally preceded (in Galisteo as well) by Las Posadas -Mary and Joseph going from house to house seeking shelter; each household would hand out treats or money. Though fading, these traditions are still maintained in New Mexico. If you missed the event in Galisteo, there is one on Dec. 20th at St. Anne's Catholic Church in Santa Fe. Call 575-758-4020 for other venues.
