title: Griego Fallout
body: For the second time in a year Governor Martinez has replaced an elected Democrat with a Republican to represent us in the Legislature. Galisteo Democrat Matthew McQueen won back Stephen Easley's seat from Martinez appointee Vicki Perea in the Nov. 2014 election. But Republican Ted Barela, the former Estancia Mayor appointed to fill Phil Griego's seat, will now serve as our Senator for District 39 until November 2016, when he intends to run in the general election. Former State Senator Phil Griego did us no favors by resigning during the recent 60-day legislative session under a cloud of ethics violations surrounding a real estate deal, as his colleagues threatened to expel him. He had served since 1996. His business dealings were exposed in a series of investigative reports in the Santa Fe Reporter last summer. (See SFR 3/18/15 for details). Santa Fe County Commissioner Liz Stefanics, who was nominated by three counties (but as a Democrat had no chance of being appointed), also plans to run for the Senate seat in 2016. So does Galisteo Mike Anaya, who preceded his brother Robert as County Commissioner and worked at the State Land Office until Commissioner Ray Powell lost to Aubrey Dunn in November. Anaya withdrew his name when it was clear that Stefanics had more popular support. We are hoping that Griego's departure will not affect the funds he had allotted for work on the Galisteo Bosque. Also during the legislative session, The House passed a memorial introduced by Rep. McQueen calling on four state agencies to study whether setting a floor price on alcohol would reduce its consumption.

title: More on Land and Lives in Galisteo
body: Not much news from Galisteo this last month so here's more history, excerpted from the rough draft of an unfinished book on the village. It picks up where the December/January issue of El Puente left off, around 1880. From around 1850, the Southwestern cattle industry was extremely profitable. Millions of pounds of beef were shipped out as far as Europe. A rancher or speculator had only to secure title to the water supply to control land for surrounding miles. In the 1860s and '70s there was "an almost complete encirclement of the Hispano domain of New Mexico" by Anglo cattlemen. It soon became clear that the Homestead Act's 160 acres was not enough to support a family in arid New Mexico. In 1877 the Desert Lands Act was passed. It required no residence and became another abused source of free land for the powerful. Now 640 acres could be acquired, but that was too small for stock range and too large for a small farmer to irrigate. One settler could apply for a whole township and not even settle on it. In 1878, the first steps were made toward a geological survey of New Mexico. The same year, John Wesley Powell, in his Report on the Arid Regions of the United States, made an impassioned and prescient plea for bioregional boundaries in the arid west, which unfortunately went unheeded. With the current water crises, this would still be a great idea, though unlikely to be implemented. By 1885, however, overgrazing and crowding was taking its toll on the cattle industry and by the early 1890s much ranchland was overstocked, overgrazed, and subject to growing competition from farmers. In 1886-87 blizzards in the Northern Plains caused huge cattle losses, but New Mexico got off relatively easily. The cattle depression here came later, due to droughts, overstocking, and low prices. Demetrio Leyba, described in 1884 as a "well-known citizen of Galisteo" was in Santa Fe trying to sell wool, found no buyers, and was "compelled to go to Las Vegas to sell." Despite all the land available, there was a national distrust of New Mexico land titles that discouraged rapid settlement. (The U.S. Congress could also take up to 36 years to clarify land titles.) Surveyor General Henry M. Atkinson, who supervised most of the New Mexico land transactions from 1876, turned a blind eye to irregular practices. There was a general feeling among Anglos that most of this land was unusable (in this "low culture" of snakes, Mexicans, and Indians), so carelessness didn't matter. Moreover, the pay was inadequate for good survey work. Low settlement and racism in turn retarded statehood. Nicolas Pino is listed in 1870 as a wealthy "farmer" with real estate worth $1500 and other assets of $1500. He owned a flour mill in Galisteo (location unknown) and from 1866-70 he was also postmaster of the Juana Lopez Grant in the western Galisteo Basin, where the Pinos owned land. In 1872 he claimed seventeen strips in the Cadial grant east of the village and a large piece of land at Stinking Springs (Ojo Hedionda) in the southeastern Galisteo Basin. Nicolas had been a State Senator and President of the Territorial Senate. In his old age, he sported a voluminous patriarchal white beard. He died in Galisteo in 1896 at age 77, of Parkinson's disease. He and his wife Juana have been said to be buried beneath the oratorio in the old Galisteo cemetery, in unmarked graves. Nicolas' brothers Miguel Estanislao and Jose Facundo Pino also settled in Galisteo or were landowners in the Galisteo Basin. So was his cousin Ambrocio Pino (referred to at the time as "Honorable"), who in 1870, aged 32, was even richer than Nicolas, with a combined $1500 and $2500. In 1884, there is a reference to his "herd of 100 brood mares." In 1876, Ambrocio "staked two flocks of sheep and a herd of cattle in a bet against Santiago Baca of Pecos on a rooster pull," and won. In the 1890s he often stayed at the Bon Ton, an upscale hotel in Santa Fe. At one point Ambrocio defended the character of Jose Luiz, "the Portugese merchant," whose wife had died of epilepsy; he was accused of beating her, but she had fallen.

title: Public Protection Classification - Galisteo Fire District
body: During the month of November 2014, the Galisteo Fire District met with the Insurance Service Office, Inc. (ISO) to complete the Public Protection Classification survey for our community. Our preparation was extensive and the resulting classification improved our rating from a 6/8B to a 5/5Y effective May 1, 2015. ISO's Public Protection Classification Program (PPC) plays an important role in the underwriting process at insurance companies. In fact, most U.S. insurers, including the largest ones, use PPC information as part of their decision-making when deciding what business to write, coverages to offer, or prices to charge for personal and commercial property insurance. PPC is important to communities and fire departments creating guidelines for enhancing fire suppression services. Communities whose PPC improves may get lower insurance prices depending on the type of construction, the hazards of occupancy and other factors. Please contact your insurance agent to determine the effect these changes in classification might have on your policy. Sincerely, Jan Anaya Moya, Chief, Galisteo Volunteer Fire District

title: Evelyne Franceschi
body:
Evelyne Franceschi
Sept. 10, 1963 - May 11, 2015

Evelyne made a graceful, peaceful exit at home, after a long and courageous battle with cancer, during which she kept up the spirits of others with her Joie de vivre. Born in Frejus, France, she was very proud of her Corsican heritage, which bore some resemblance to that of New Mexicans. She studied art at Studio Bercot and her talent soon garnered jobs in the fashion industry, for which she traveled all over the world, where she was always greeted with great affection and respect. When young she wanted to be a painter and continued to paint and draw until her death. She rejected offers to be in the movies.
Evelyne met Bernard Pomerance, her husband-to-be, in 2005, in Eldorado, where she was visiting friends. On moving to Galisteo she immediately became involved with the church, made many friends, and began to create her remarkable film animations (www.evelynefranceschi.com). They star an elegant, long-legged protagonist - very stylish, very French. Evelyne was also a superb chocolatier, participating in the Galisteo Studio Tour. Survived by Bernard, their dog Lily, and her brother Gilbert, Evelyne will be remembered as a bright light that flashed through Galisteo for too short a time.
A prayer service for Evelyne will be held at Nuestra Senora de los Remedios after Mass on May 24th. At 2:15 PM, all are invited to a potluck and celebration of her life at the Community Center.

title: Paved with 6000 Intentions or the Road to Ruin?
body:
Roads in and out of Galisteo and environs have been rough over the last year or so. On April 22, the Santa Fe County Public Works Department closed County Road 42 (aka Camino de los Abuelos) to all traffic for over a week for emergency road reconstruction to restore the portion damaged by large gravel trucks, some headed for the reconstruction of the Galisteo bridges. CR 42 was not built with that kind of heavy traffic in mind, but ironically it was not included in the proposed weight limit ordinance (see below). Why not? Where was our County Commissioner?
The affected portion of CR 42 was about 5 miles east of NM 14. Motorists and bicyclists had to "seek an alternate route ... and allow additional time to negotiate this work zone." Residents to the west of the construction area were forced to utilize NM 14 for access and residents to the east were told to use NM 41. The good news is that large trucks are still barred from crossing to NM 14 this way, and hopefully that will last. (For further information or to put in your 2 cents worth, contact Diego Gomez, Santa Fe County Roads Maintenance Manager at 992-3025).
And at last, on April 28, after a unanimous 5-0 vote, the Board of County Commissioners approved the long awaited ordinance establishing weight limits on four County-maintained paved roads, including CR 33 to Lamy. Robert Martinez of the Public Works Department opened the final hearing with a brief overview of the ordinance and explained staff-recommended changes. (View the final draft at the County website: santefecountynm.gov.)
Over a year of citizen activism, led by NOCoil, has succeeded in vanquishing plans for crude oil transfers at the Lamy railway station and the birth of this significant ordinance. Can it eventually be applied to CR 42?
Finally (or never say finally in this saga), the endless work on the two bridges south of the village is purportedly winding down, though you'd never know it from the gigantic machines, mountains of dirt, and constant racket I see out my window as I write this. Habib Abi-Khalil, Assistant District Engineer, NMDOT District Five, tells El Puente:
"The bridge project is nearing completion. We anticipate that the contractor will complete the paving by the end of next week (May 29). We also need to apply the friction layer on top of the paving and we need to overlay the bridge decks with an epoxy material and gravel. Seeding and permanent signing will follow these operations. I anticipate that we will be done with all the project items by the end of June. We have the walkways across the bridges blocked off because we are still missing some of the inserts for the pedestrian railing. The inserts should be delivered and installed this week. Once installed we will make sure all the features are in place to safely open the walkways. We appreciate your patience during the construction of this project. As far as any work through the village, the NMDOT has no plans at this time."
Mr. Abi-Khalil has been consistently courteous and prompt to answer complaints and requests for information. But rumor also has it that while the heavy rains should have interrupted construction, it went ahead, perhaps for the Century bicycle race on May 17th, or because the contractor was losing money. The soil on the east side of the creek is apparently difficult to pave over and rain should have made it inadvisable.

title: Water Association Meets
body:
On April 23rd, the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association held its annual meeting, with a quorum, presided over by Treasurer Wayne King in the absence of President Rod Hall. Along with maintenance and improvement of the system, issues under discussion included more frequent meetings of the Board and term limits for officers.
Rod Hall, who lives here in the winter, is the longtime President. Like him, other generous souls have been on the Board for many years. "Not that we want to!" said Vice President Scott Diffrient, who has served for 26 years. "Stay too long and you deserve what you get!" said Richard Patton, another lifer, who is the Licensed Operator of the water system. (This demanding job is required of every system and involves taking courses to be certified, and then "continuing education.") It was decided that these Board members had to stay on, since their knowledge, experience, and contacts with the County are invaluable, but that the officers should rotate.
Janice Griscom, Matthew McQueen, and Joette Trofimuk (yet another longtime member) have all resigned. Diffrient's, King's, and Phillip Tuwaletstiwa's terms were up. All were re-elected. Hall and Foreman Antonio Chavez are in the middle of their terms. King was reelected as Treasurer. Patton became Secretary (he voted against himself, but no luck). New Board members are Anna Cardenas, Michael Golino, and Lucy Lippard.
Also discussed was some form of compensation for archivist Florence Sohn and bookkeeper Romona Scholder, who do a tremendous amount of work but don't want to be on the formal Board. The result of the term limits discussion was Diffrient's resignation as Vice President and his replacement by Tuwaletstiwa, giving Scott a well-deserved rest (sort of) but no escape.
Only two members of the Water Association are in significant arrears as of mid April; turnoff threats tend to bring in the payments. Future discussions may look at the success of phased pricing for greater levels of use, as in Santa Fe, which attracted national news coverage recently. Ranchitos also does this.
Maintenance consists primarily of broken and leaking pipes. But in 1997, the Water Association was misled by engineers and the 2" ID (Inside Diameter) of the feedline pipe running under the highway is too small. It must be replaced by a 4" pipe, which should serve for any foreseeable future. At an emergency meeting of the Board on May 18th, a contract with utility contractor BET, LLC was approved. Excavation will begin as soon as permits are acquired, probably in mid-summer. It will take place around the old mailboxes next to the church.
Readers please note that Water Board meetings are open to the entire membership and are posted on the mailbox bulletin board; non-members are also welcome, though they cannot vote.

title: Broadband in Our Future?
body:
Over the years, Liz Rose has been trying to establish Broadband Internet service in the Galisteo area via the LCWA (La Canada Wireless Association). Dana Simmons, New Member Orientation and Training Coordinator, writes:
"We are an all volunteer organization. Over the last few years, we have not been able to offer our Internet service to the Galisteo area as we have no volunteers there. We are seeking a year-round Galisteo based volunteer" who would work with other LCWA volunteers in the Eldorado and Lamy areas managing the new Galisteo area members.
"Most of the LCWA volunteers have some technical orientation (comfortable with computers, their home router, interested in learning more about wireless networks, capable of installing a rooftop antenna and the necessary cabling to an inside router). Any skill lacking will be taught by the other more experienced volunteers. If you are interested in joining LCWA and being the Galisteo go-to person, please contact me." (danagsimmons@gmail.com, 505-216-6161.)
As a member of the GCA Board, Michael Golino is leading the investigation into wireless possibilities for Galisteo. He may meet with LCWA, but has some other suggestions as well. "From what I understand," he writes, LCWA "is a WISP system (wireless internet service provider) much like Higher Speed Internet and will have a lot of the same issues: service capacity, need for line of sight between transmitters and receivers (a real problem in Galisteo because of hills and trees), reliance on relays (which tends to be the problem with Higher Speed's system)."
Right now Golino is looking at two other possibilities for Galisteo: 1) A system that uses TV White Space which could deliver up to 100Mbs up and down (this system does not require line of sight). 2) Fiber optics which could deliver Gigabit service to Galisteo residents curbside (no antennas). "Both of these directions would have reasonable costs, professional service (not volunteers) and capacity which will allow for almost unlimited uses by all Galisteo users." Golino will report with more information to the next GCA Board meeting.

title: {History Tidbit}
body: The population of Galisteo in the 1890s remained around 700; "some residents of Galisteo took advantage of the nearby public domain and filed homestead claims where they then grazed their livestock." Villagers raised sheep, cattle, horses, corn, pinto beans, and probably a few other crops. "The country is settling up considerably," reported the newspaper. "A half dozen families from Fort Worth, Texas located near Galisteo this month, and others are en route. They appear to be thrifty people with good range stock. The citizens are glad to welcome them." (What became of them?) The article went on to mention Ambrocio Pino's herd of one hundred brood mares foaling well; "losses by loco weed were none, whereas in the last five years, many died." One A. Kirschner had 75-100 horses on the Galisteo range and two unnamed Portuguese brothers had started a chicken ranch. Even the fruit crop was "bountiful," doubling the ordinary yield.

title: Community Plan On Last Stretch?
body: When a few Galisteans suggested creating a Community Plan in Summer 1998 (see El Puente #16), when after a few years of work we were given the go-ahead by the County in 2005, and when the completed plan was approved by the BCC in February, 2012 .... who knew that it would still be requiring revisions and meetings in 2015? A small committee has been meeting with County staff for the last five months to work out endless details and ensure that our plan adheres to the County's Sustainable Growth Management Code. We have been going over design and land use standards in the "use tables" for the Galisteo District Overlay and tailoring them to our community. Categories (each with numerous subheads) are: Residential; Hotels, motels or other accommodation services; Commercial; Industrial, manufacturing and wholesale trade; Public assembly structures; Arts, entertainment and recreation; Institutional or community facilities; Transportation-related facilities; Utility; Agriculture, forestry, and conservation/open space; and Mining and extraction establishments. We could permit, deny, or allow consideration of various options, with the Residential and Commercial sections receiving the most scrutiny. Meanwhile, another group (some of the same people) was meeting with the Frontiers Initiative to create a "Village of Galisteo Revitalization Plan" that will be incorporated into the County Plan. The final document proposes "Pedestrian Pathways" at the crossroads, welcoming signs at each end of the village, a "Cultural Plaza" on the vacant lot next to La Sala, and an "Artists' Cooperative/Incubator" on the south side of the church. Various events and strategies to support economic development in the village will be announced. Two public meetings are required to approve the Planning Committee's work on the Overlay and zoning. An announcement for the first Open House on June 11th went out very late but the few alert attendees approved of the revisions. The second meeting is on the evening of June 25th. (El Puente will be in press). Then the plan and proposed zoning will be presented to the Board of County Commissioners at two public hearings, to be considered for adoption. Finally the Galisteo Community District Overlay will provide a guide for future development, land use, community facilities, projects, and programs.

title: No End to Clayton's Schemes
body: On June 16th two process servers working for a private investigator hired by the Bank of Oklahoma tried to serve the Galisteo Community Corporation with a lawsuit in the amount of $190,000. It seems that in 2009, landgrabber Peirce Clayton and his wife (see El Puente, March 2015) obtained a loan from the Bank of Oklahoma in this amount and gave them a trust deed for the Community Center (building and land) as collateral. (Morgan Gafford, Clayton's partner in the attempted land scheme, knew nothing of this scam.) Anna Cardenas and Roger Taylor met with the process servers and explained that this individual had never been a resident of the Village, owned property here, or had any authority to take a loan against the building and land. The lawsuit notification was refused, and the process servers were advised to track him down by his social security number and to check with the Texas and California Real Estate Boards to see if he was working in those states. (He taught school in Eldorado too.)

title: Jeanette Anaya case review requested
body: The steadfast Teresa Anaya and other relatives of Jeanette Anaya asked the New Mexico Law Enforcement Board to order a new review of a dashboard camera video of her daughter's death in 2013, when police fired 16 shots into her car. A grand jury incredibly found the killing justified. The Anayas were joined by the mothers of other children slain by officers. A letter to the editor of The New Mexican (5/22) from the Anaya family lamented the fact that the case had been closed and that Officer Wilson has gotten away with murder: "Our lives will never be the same. No one should be above the law, certainly not God's law."

This was the site of La Mancha, a restaurant run by Yolanda and Jose Ortiz y Pino, and the former Linda Durham Gallery. Galisteo's art creds were rolled out, with mentions of Agnes Martin, Fritz Scholder, Bernard Pomerance, Susan Rothenberg, Bruce Nauman, and Woody Gwyn. The asking price is $1,588 million.

title: High-speed Internet access for rural New Mexicans
body: The issue of high-speed Internet access for rural New Mexicans is ramping up. (See El Puente, May 2015.) The New Mexican published a feature ("Who says you get what you pay for?") on May 31st. Galisteo is shown on a map as having "fixed wireless 3Mbps $98," compared with 6Mbps in Santa Fe and Eldorado for $49.95 from Comcast. Michael Golino (who "runs a photo identification software company in Galisteo and has team members all over the world") joked with the reporter that their Internet phone call via Higher-Speed Internet in Moriarty can be affected by bad weather and might disconnect at any moment. After the big storm of June 16th, several of Century Link's village phones went out. Wayne King reports that his rain gauge had 1.2" in it and we're already over 10" for this year. (May the downpours continue!)

title: Break-in attempts in Ranchitos
body: There were break-in attempts in Ranchitos at several different houses a couple of weeks ago. The perps are two tall, well-dressed men in their early 20's driving a late model grey extended cab pickup, with a strip on the side rear and a tarp covering the back. (They also drive a blue Toyota 4 Runner.) These men drive around affluent, somewhat isolated communities looking for "for sale" signs and break down the front door. It doesn't matter if someone is living there or not. The police have been chasing these men for awhile now. Call the Sheriff's Department immediately if you see either of these vehicles. For those selling a home, you may want to require your realtor NOT to post a sign outside. Most potential buyers do not cruise around looking for homes for sale; they use online and press listings.

title: Orange barrels: construction and development updates
body: More orange barrels: Construction of the Galisteo Water Association's improved water line under Highway 41 has begun on Via La Puente and will progress to the old mailboxes. A huge two-story garage is going up on Beau LeBeau's property on La Otra Vanda, and there is now a little village of three portable buildings on the Bohn/Godman property on Avenida Vieja. A couple of weeks ago, the delivery of one of these didn't go so well; it slipped off the flatbed truck onto the road near the Moyas'. title: History Tidbits
body: 1890s Galisteo was described as "a delightful overnight stop" in the "Sunshine State," as New Mexico had been dubbed by Governor Bradford Prince. Around that time, a rosy picture of a "prosperous" Galisteo was painted by Nicolas Pino, quoted by a local reporter: "Grass is abundant and cattle of all kinds are rolling fat. Lambing season closed most satisfactorily. The wool clips are all that could be expected. Several thousand head of cattle and sheep are fattening on adjacent ranges. Nine thousand pounds of wool were shipped from Galisteo this week." Pino's own Galisteo mill was "a five horsepower, water powered, rimstone machine" with which in one ten-month period he milled "47 barrels of flour, 2400 lbs. shorts, 3600 lbs. bran and 6500 lbs. of corn." Said to be "by the bridge," the mill's exact location is unclear, as is how it managed to be water powered on a creek as small as the Galisteo. In 1873, Juan Ortiz II had married Concepcion (Conchita), the second daughter of Nicolas Pino and Juana Rascon. Nicolas died around 1897 and Juana preceded him by four or five years. When Concepcion (b. 1852) died at age 42 in 1894, Juan married her older sister Margarita. Trinidad Pino (1828-1924), the widow of Nicolas's cousin Ambrocio Pino, also lived with them. According to Ortiz family oral history (via Marion Steele), Juan Ortiz II became a trader like his father, Juan Grande, traveling as far as Durango, Mexico and St. Louis, Missouri in his ox-drawn wagons to obtain and sell goods. In 1881 he also established a mercantile (store) in the building that was the Galisteo Inn. The late Tony Anaya (1916-1997), a lifelong Galisteño, recalled buying candy from Juan's store; its concrete loading dock could still be seen in the 1980s, when Steele was writing his unpublished manuscript on the village. Throughout this era the wealthier citizens of the village would go up to Santa Fe and The New Mexican recorded their visits. Among those registered at the Bon Ton Hotel in 1893 was Ascencion Chavez, and in 1894, F. Chavez de Montoya and Apolonio Chavez. M. Pino and Demetrio Leyba stayed at the Palace Hotel, as did Sylvester Davis at various times. (In 1908 Jose Ortiz y Pino registered at the Claire). Among the Galisteo houses apparently built in the 1890s were the Panteleon Montoya house on Avenida Vieja (now a rental), the Cayetano Chavez house (former Light Institute, now Duran), and the Frank Sandoval house at 6 Marcellina Lane. Bluebell and Ramon Hurtado's little home is a ruin on La Vega. Around the turn of the century, Justiniano and Demetrio Leyba ran saloons in Galisteo (on Montoya land on CR. 42) and at the railroad stop at Kennedy.

title: Ed Epping Named Galisteo's Newest Firefighter One
body:
Ed Epping survived 17 weeks of grueling trainings and two final exams (skills and written) to become Galisteo's newest Firefighter One on June 2911, at the Santa Fe County Fire Department's 1011, Volunteer Cadet Graduation, held at the Institute of American Indian Arts. Several members of the GVFR were there to cheer him on. 

Galisteo may be a small department but Galisteans bookended the ceremony. Assistant County Chief Steve Moya, master of ceremonies for the evening, spoke first and Fire Chiefs Association President Jean Moya (proudly introduced as "my wife of 34 years") made the closing remarks. 

Chief Fire Officer Sheila Beuler of the Santa Fe Fire Department gave the keynote address and County Chief Dave Sperling and Captains Mike Jaffa, Mike Mestas, and Assistant Chief Charlie Velarde were among the speakers. County Clerk Geraldine Salazar delivered the Oath of Office to the recruits. 

The sole woman graduate, Raylynn Trujillo, carried her infant child through the receiving line. Fathers, mothers, parents and colleagues did the honors of pinning on the badges. "Don't hurt me!" said Ed as Peggy struggled to pin his shiny new badge onto his blue firefighter cadet shirt.

title: La Sala de San Jose de Galisteo Added to Historic Santa Fe Foundation Registry

body: On July 3, Christine Mackenzie gave a reading from her science fiction novel - Lisa Bennett Visits Utopia -- at Madrid's Engine House Theater.

title: Judy Tuwaletstiwa Exhibits in Axle Contemporary Mobile Gallery
body: Judy Tuwaletstiwa was in a four-person show in the Axle Contemporary Mobile Gallery in August. She exhibited panels from her new series where does art come from? made of clay, thread, wool, porcupine quills, and glass. "The act of creation," she says, "becomes more mysterious the more I do it. Maybe I haven't lived long enough to decipher its meaning. Living as an artist means being part of the flow."

title: Historical Note: Antonio Ortiz y Pino Death (August 1915)
body: From The Santa Fe New Mexican, August 26, 1915: "News was received in the city today that Antonio Ortiz y Pino, the seven-months old son of Jose Ortiz y Pino, Chairman of the Board of County Commissioners, died of whooping cough yesterday afternoon at his father's home in Galisteo .... Mr. Ortiz did everything in his power to effect a cure, summoning numerous physicians and lavishing the best attention on the infant. The funeral took place this afternoon from the Catholic Church, where services were held. Interment was in the Ortiz family plot in the Catholic cemetery."

body: In 1938 the Reina de la Fiesta de Santa Fe was Reynalda Ortiz y Pino Dinkel, from the Galisteo family.

title: Wildlife Sightings: Bobcat Kittens in Bosque, No Bears This Summer
body: No bears sighted this summer that we've heard about, but a bobcat and her kittens are thought to be living in the Bosque. Their voices sound something like coyotes, but with a different ending to the wail. Bears, in fact, like cougars and coyotes, are on the run as an increased number can now be legally killed.

title: Sina Brush Letter on Disease-Carrying Rodents
body: Sina Brush's letter to The New Mexican's editor (8/26) was brief and to the point: "Disease-carrying rodents are rain's downside. That's a very good reason to leave coyotes alone and let them do their crucial work."

title: {Coyote Management and Protection Strategies}
body: Domestic dogs are far more aggressive than coyotes. From the other side of the fence comes an article by Judy Paulsen in The Bosque Beast (June/July) offering ways to keep coyotes and dogs out of your yard and away from your pets with commercial roller bars on fence tops. They can be homemade with PVC pipes or ordered from coloradocoyoterollers.com. She notes that killing resident coyotes only leaves a void for unpredictable transients. Coyotes are wily, indeed. They know that mice can be roused from their holes by loud noises, so they hang out by railroad tracks or fields being mowed. They are omnivorous and will eat anything from juniper berries to horse manure, although given the number of rabbits racing around Galisteo, they seem to favor a bunnie-low diet. They also like grasshoppers, which are everywhere, so for the time being, your pets may be safer.

title: County Mining Ordinance Approved
body:
On August 11 111, in response to the uproar around the application to strip-mine basalt at La Bajada mesa, Santa Fe County Commissioners approved tougher rules for sand and gravel mining operations and other developments considered to have countywide impact (DCI), such as landfills and junkyards. (The vote was 4-0; our commissioner, Robert Anaya, was absent.) 

An earlier version of the DCI Ordinance was reviewed and discussed in a meeting at the Galisteo Community Center on July 6t11, attended by about twenty community and citizen action group members from Galisteo, Lamy, Eldorado, Cerrillos and Madrid. The result was a prioritized list, and many of the comments and suggestions from the Galisteo meeting were incorporated into the next revision. Other communities in the County also had input meetings. 

Nearly two dozen people spoke during the August public hearing. Our own Roger Taylor said the Ordinance had improved: "The language is a lot stronger than it has been, so each reiteration seems to have gotten us into a much more positive place." The final Ordinance was months in the making, ending a one-year moratorium on new mining permits from September 2014. At that time the County was updating Ordinances as part of the new land-use code. But the La Bajada applicants, Buena Vista Estates and Rockology Limited sued the county, claiming the moratorium unlawfully singled out their project. The lawsuit is still pending in federal court, with a hearing scheduled for November 2.

title: Water Policy Ordinance Passed
body: From Roger Taylor: "Another important ordinance passed this month was one I worked on with Charlie Nylander (head of the County Water Policy Advisory Committee) and Adam Leigland (Director of County Public Works). It establishes a detailed, fair, transparent policy and evaluation process for assistance from the County to mutual domestic water consumers associations or private water groups. It also provides credits for assets, absorbs liabilities/debt, and provides for a transition and oversight role for the Board operators of the mutual domestic associations. It was passed unanimously by the BCC, replacing a much more unfriendly policy which took the assets but not liabilities or debts, provided no transparent evaluation process, and excluded the mutual domestic water operators. I presented a summary of its value after Director Leigland explained the actual policy. In addition to the points I've already mentioned: most of the 30+ mutual domestic water associations are operated by individuals 60-80 years of age, and a number of them are also confronting issues with natural contamination from elements in the soil such as arsenic, radium, and uranium."

title: News from the Galisteo Basin Preserve
body:
Good news for the entire Galisteo Basin is that the Santa Fe Conservation Trust has announced a 318-acre conservation easement, preserving scenic open space, wildlife habitat, public recreation and historic and cultural resources. This brings the number of conservation agreements held by SFCT to 82. The new easement is located within the western border of the Galisteo Basin Preserve, where a rich variety of flora and fauna inhabits the property, contributing to the larger migratory corridor that stretches from Alaska to Mexico as part of the Western Wild way Network. 

The easement includes a well-preserved section of the bed of the Santa Fe Central Railway (locally known as El Central, the Kennedy Line, or the Chili and/or Bean Line) which ran from 1903 to 1929 and was an important connection between Torrance County and Santa Fe. The Kennedy Depot, where many Galisteans found work, was located just southwest of the property where the railway bed intersects the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway. It was something of a flourishing community for a few years and foundations of several buildings remain visible. The rail bed area on the easement, bisecting the property north-south, is to be developed as part of a larger regional trail system for hiking, bicycling, equestrian, and other non-motorized uses, preserving the historic rail corridor and opening the area to recreational users. 

And those of us who hike the Preserve will be happy to hear that Commonweal Conservancy recently received a $7,500 grant from REI to enhance and expand the Galisteo Basin Preserve trail network, repair sections damaged by storm flows, improve the parking area at the Cowboy Shack Trailhead, and fund new signage at key intersections. This summer Commonweal has been working with archaeologists, professional trail builders, and local volunteers to design segments of a multi-use trail that will expand the network in the Preserve's "central basin region." REI's grant will fund the first phase of this 3.14-mile stretch linking the Cowboy Shack and Cottonwood trailheads. The new trail will significantly extend the loop routes available for hiking, horseback riding, and mountain biking. 

Complementing REI's funding commitment, Reineke Construction has offered to make a generous in-kind donation to partially defray the design and construction cost of the new trail segments. The Galisteo Basin Preserve website (www.galisteobasinpreserve.com) has been updated to include a map of the trail network currently open to the public.

title: Infrastructure Update: Route 41 Road Construction on Hold
body: According to the DOT no major road construction is planned for Rte. 41 from Galisteo up Clark Hill. Design work is being developed but won't be implemented for several years and no funding has been approved. There is neither funding nor design for Rte. 41 through the village center. So that's the end of construction for a while? We'll see what's coming down the pike, so to speak.

title: Rodeo Grounds Back in Use
body: The Rodeo Grounds are back on track. On August 29, a Democratic Party Fundraiser was held there, promising "horses and carnival games and food on a stick in gorgeous Galisteo." It was "fun, but sparsely attended," according to one attendee.

title: Solar Installation at Ed Epping and Peggy Diggs Home
body: The latest solar array to be installed in Galisteo (by Positive Energy) is at the home of Ed Epping and Peggy Diggs on Avenida Vieja. The valuable federal and state income tax credits for solar systems are available only for another 18 months. They reduce the cost of installation by 40%. Solar prices have come down over 60% in the last five years, so it's actually possible to use solar for no more than you're currently paying PNM. Now's the time to Light Up!

title: Bosque Restoration Project Moving Forward
body: Potential work on the Bosque is moving along, but slowly. The funds have been released, but since there are five agencies involved, the contracts took some negotiating. They are now in final stages. Work should commence by the end of the year or early 2016. The bulk of the clearing will take only four weeks, and completion date is still targeted for early April 2016. We have also applied for a Round 2 of funding in 2016 from the Governors Water Conservation & Restoration Program.

title: Bank Claim Against GCA
body:
On September 25th the GCA was notified that a notice was being posted in the ABQ Journal North regarding an action being taken by the Bank of Oklahoma as Plaintiff, against Defendants Peirce Clayton (a local realtor) and the GCA. The Bank is claiming it cannot locate Mr. Clayton (who now resides in CA); notice in a local newspaper serves in place of personal service to him.

The GCA has retained the firm of Graeser & McQueen to examine the issue and to represent the GCA as needed. Matthew McQueen has examined the Court complaint and it appears to be a foreclosure action on Peirce's house in Eldorado. It is unclear why the GCA is named. Matthew has filed for a copy of a "Transcript of Judgment", and is in discussion with the Bank's attorney. More on this as it develops.

title: Commonweal Master Plan Amendment
body:
Commonweal Conservancy has submitted a Master Plan Amendment to reduce the Planning Envelope for Trenza from 10,360 acres to 2,502 acres; to reduce the development size from 965 dwelling units to 275 units, and from 150,000 sq ft of commercial & civic use to 71,000 sq ft. This also includes a green cemetery and a 60 seat outdoor amphitheater, all of this to take place in 7 phases (in place of the original 5 phases) over 10 years. Originally it was anticipated that water consumption would be@ 195 ac/ft annually; with the reduction in size it would be @ 65 ac/ft annually.

The reduction in the Planning Envelope removes 7,860 acres from the original build-out. About 4,000 acres is under an agreement to purchase from the Thornton Ranch, but is not yet purchased; and of the remaining 4,000 acres (which has already been purchased), about 2400 acres has conservation easements. This leaves 1600 acres that could potentially be built upon.

Commonweal intends to obtain conservation easements for the 1600 acres also, but should financial pressures arise the property could be marketed as building lots. It will be important for this property to be zoned "Agricultural/Ranch", which would limit any lot in the 1600 acres to 160 acres in size, so making 10 lots. Should Commonweal market this property in the future, it would have to file a Master Plan and hold a public Hearing. If you have concerns about this, you may wish to contact your Commissioner about zoning this property "Ag/Ranch".

Although Commonweal also has an agreement to purchase water rights from the Thornton Ranch, that purchase has not proceeded.

A public hearing will be held before the CDRC (County Development Review Committee) on Oct 15 at 4pm in the County Commission Chambers on the corner of Grant & Palace Avenues. The CDRC will then make a recommendation, and a final hearing will take place at the County Commissioner meeting on November 10, at 5pm.

We all know the Galisteo Volunteer Fire Department needs volunteers, and many of us suppose they need fire fighters. But as the majority of the calls they receive are for emergency medical help, Chief Jean Anaya Moya says that now they really need EMT personnel. As it turns out, Santa Fe Community College's Emergency Medical Services Institute offers a one-year course in Basic EMT Training. As the SFCC website says (www.sfcc.edu/programs/emergency_medical_services), "You can earn Emergency Medical Technician certification and state licensure at the Basic, Intermediate and Paramedic levels. The Institute also offers certification in CPR/First Aid and post licensure certification courses in Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS), Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS), Advanced Medical Life Support (AMLS), and Pre-Hospital Trauma Life Support (PHTLS). Once you're licensed, you're eligible to work in a variety of rural and urban emergency settings."

title: Chile and Margarita Cook-Off
body:
The "Chile and Margarita Cook-Off" on September 22 brought out many fine cooks, one fine margarita maker, and a large number of eager consumers. Side dishes were donated by attendees as well, and it seemed a good time was had by all.

The event began with live music by Julian Prada. Along with the tunes, there were appetizers and drinks, with margaritas concocted by Roger Taylor. A cook-off requires judges who compare the submitted chiles and margaritas, and then award prizes in various categories. Our judges were Jean Moya, Philip Tuwaletstiwa and Matthew McQueen. And the winners: For traditional chile, First Prize went to David Maestas; Second Prize to Bobby Anaya; and Third Prize to Susie Shanklin. There was a category for non-traditional chile: First Prize went to Stanley Perdue; Second Prize to Richard Fenker. Finally, for margaritas: First, Second and Third Prizes went to Roger Taylor, partly because his were the only margaritas submitted, and partly because they were that good.

Finally, just for coming, each attendee received a ticket, and door prizes were awarded. Prizes included a Fritz Scholder limited edition poster, a photograph by Barbara Seigel, a photograph and notecards by Judy Tuwaletstiwa, a ceramic bowl by Barbara King, a ceramic container by Frank Lux, a gift certificate for chile to be made by Cindy Lux, and 3 gift certificates for Santa Fe establishments donated by Corinne Anaya. All of these generous donors we heartily thank.

title: Update on Broadband Quest
body:
Last month Michael Golino, Stanley Perdue and Roger Taylor had a discussion with Johnny Montoya of Century Link about the possibility of Century Link using CAF II money to do a project in Galisteo. CAF II is "Connect America Funds" given out by the FEDS to bring broadband to rural areas. Century Link has accepted $66 million of CAF II funds over 10 years. It is not clear to Century Link if Galisteo will qualify. CAF II has a complex formula based on Census Blocks. CenturyLink needs additional time to do engineering studies to determine what, if anything, they can do.

The TV White Space (TVWS) project Golino has been pursuing has taken a turn as the Canadian company has decide to launch its first project in SE New Mexico next year, more economically feasible than in our area. The Canadian company continues to work with the economic development agencies in NM to find ways to bring their technology to our area.

And finally, on November 4th there will be a hearing at the PRC offices to get public input on redirecting funds (up to $5 million) to form programs dealing with Plain Old Telephone Service (POTS) to Broadband. This date is not firm and will be finalized in October.

title: The Wild West Fest
body:
The Wild West Fest in Old Galisteo took place Saturday, August 29. Although it was sited on the rodeo grounds, many Galisteans didn't know it was happening until the week before. They began selling tickets online, and the very small type at the bottom indicated the following: "New Mexico law requires that we disclose occupation information for donors contributing $250 or more in an election cycle. Individuals, corporations, and labor may contribute to the 6 County PAC. The 6 County PAC does not coordinate with any candidate or campaign committee. Contributions are not tax-deductible. If you have any questions, contact the 6 County PAC at info@6countypac.org". Other beneficiaries included Watermelon Mountain Ranch and Horsin' Around Therapeutic Riding Center.

The event, presented by Lisa McWhorter, included live music, with performances by Half Broke Horses and others, barrel races, carnival games, auctions, food/beverages, and celebrity guests, including Cassidy Freeman, star of Smallville and Longmire. The big draw, however, seemed to have been a last-minute casting call for extras for the locally-filmed new production of The Magnificent Seven. To be considered, people had to arrive in full western wear, with "western skills a major plus". Did any Galisteans make the cut?

title: Profile Galisteo: Stella Maestas
body:
Stella Maestas describes herself as "an old member of the town, maybe not the oldest, but ..." She's from generations of family on both her parents' sides who were rooted here in Galisteo. Her family of 14 provided constant work for her mother, while her dad, Frank Sandoval, ran the store, bar and gas station at the crossroads opposite the church. She remembers her dad being deeply involved in Los Pastores, the Christmas Eve play about the shepherds keeping watch on the night of Jesus' birth. She also tells of the Christmas Eve Day performance, La Posada. A mobile play no longer performed, it was a re-enactment of the wandering of Joseph with Mary searching for a place to stay. The performers wandered around Galisteo, sometimes on an actual burro, and sang for entry at various people's doors; they were always told no. Of course it was only when Mary and Joseph sang for a place to stay at La Sala that they were admitted, and the whole Galisteo village welcomed them with the bounty they'd provided.

When she was growing up in Galisteo, Stella said supernatural stories about "occurrences" in the village were well loved and passed around. And they are tales that contribute to the sense of the place. One story told to her was about The Old Bridge crossing Galisteo Creek. She heard that long ago, a young woman had been courted by two men, and she chose one of them to marry. After their wedding in the church, they walked across the bridge to the wedding reception at the bride's home. But the rejected man appeared at the bridge and, angry and jealous, shot them both dead. So it is said that the bride can be seen on the night of her anniversary on the bridge where she was killed. Truth or myth? Stella asks.

Stella has worked as assistant chef at the former Galisteo Inn, but then decided to go to Santa Fe Community College's Early Childhood Center for training. Working with very young children turned out to be her calling. Although recently retired, she speaks with sincerity of her fascination with the thinking and learning processes of young children.

Asked what she'd like Galisteo folks to know about her, she replied candidly: "I'd like them to think I'm someone they can depend on. I'd do the best I could possibly do to care for" a person or a situation that needed her.

title: Profile Galisteo: Diana Gaston
body:
Diana Gaston is so new to Galisteo that she's not even fully moved in. She is finishing up her current job as Lead Curator of Fidelity Investments' Corporate Art Collection in Boston. With branches throughout the country, the company displays the vast majority of its art holdings for associates and clients visiting its offices.

But as of January 1, 2016, Diana begins her new position as Director of Tamarind Institute in Albuquerque, currently part of UNM. An art print facility, Tamarind helped to introduce to the American public in the 1960s the new enterprise of producing lithographic limited-edition prints done by contemporary painters and sculptors. In this way collectors could own artworks by artists whose work in other media normally would cost five to ten times what a lithograph would cost.

Diana has wanted to return to NM since the early nineties. She had been the Curator of Prints and Photographs at UNM at that time, and was permanently struck by the power of this state, this place. Her partner, our own Michael Golino, took the first leap, bought a house in Galisteo 2 years ago, and Diana found work to bring her out here too.

Asked what has surprised her most about moving to Galisteo, she reports that it's more magical than she expected. For example, she spoke of Christmas Eve in 2014 when she was visiting Michael. Late at night they walked towards the church, both moved by the lit luminarias lining La Puente. It was midnight and there was no one on the street, just them and the lights.

Diana is also a writer. Someone who writes professionally about art for magazines and catalogues, she also writes a food blog (pleasurebelly.com). She began the blog while traveling extensively for Fidelity, often eating out alone, and wanting to keep engaged with the world. So she began writing about what and where she ate. She's intrigued to see what moving to NM is going to do to and for the blog.

title: Sighting: A ring-tailed cat?
body: A ring-tailed cat? A civet, perhaps? Heavier, taller than a cat, ear tufts, long thick bushy ringed tail, dark coat the color of volcanic rock, round eyes in a broad cat face. About 7am last week [now longer ago], I watched a creature slink along the perimeter of a hedge, stop and sit staring in my direction. Seated, his ears reached just below the 2'3" fence bar. A neighbor recognized the description as the ring-tailed animal she'd seen last January in Ranchitos late one night. Has anyone else seen him?

title: The Galisteo Studio Art Tour 2015
body: Below is a series of reflections on this year's studio tour written by some of the participating artists. Inside this edition is the first ever color coverage of the participating artists in their studios. Enjoy!

title: Studio Tour Reflection by Judy Tuwaletstiwa
body:
Studio Tour was a great experience. People looked closely at the work, asked intelligent questions, discussed ideas. Those who bought my work responded to it from their heart. Yes, I was tired at the end of each day, but that was totally outweighed by how wonderful it felt to open my studio in the middle of Galisteo and to be part of a dialogue about art. And to be surprised.

The funniest incident: A man walked into my studio on Sunday and blared, in a Brooklyn accented voice, "So, what's dis? A synagogue?" I responded, "In a sense: it is my sacred space." He continued with New York Jewish humor, "That's a good answer. How long you been dovening here?" I said, "You know only men doven [ rock while praying] but I've been working here for ten years." He looked around. "Hey, this is pretty good," he said. Pointing to a particular piece, he shouted, "How many scheckels for that?" When I told him the price, he said, "Either you're famous or you think you're famous." I almost fell on the floor laughing. When he left, I felt my studio had been blessed by a humor I recognized from my childhood.

title: {Studio Tour Reflection by Kenny Chavez}
body: My 2nd year as an honorary artist in the tour was, as last year, a wonderful experience. So many friends and family members from Galisteo came by to see me and my wonderful world of recycled folk art. Thanks for the opportunity.

title: {Studio Tour Reflection by Ruby Renshaw}
body: I had a wonderful experience my first tour --the creative journey was amazing!

title: Studio Tour Reflection by Amy Sealove Lynn
body: I am proud to have been the chairman of the 2015 Galisteo Studio Tour. With the help of Barbara Seiler and the committees led by Cindy Lux, Anna Cardenas, Barbara King, Barbara Holloway and Judy Tuwaletstiwa, we had a great tour. Special thanks to: Ed Epping for his help with our brochure, Janet Pfeiffer for help with our bookkeeping, and our new neighbor, Estelle Berger, who guided us in getting our 501 c3 status. And a special thanks to our generous anonymous donor who provided the funds. I'm looking forward to next year and another great studio tour.

title: Studio Tour Reflection by Anna Cardenas
body: The best part of Studio Tour is meeting people who lived in Galisteo years ago or whose family did. This year we met up with two couples, and Freddie got to talking to one gentleman about their old neighborhoods in Santa Fe. His wife had family that used to live in Galisteo. It turns out I had already met Lorraine Sandoval a couple years ago on her visit to Galisteo trying to get into the old cemetery to look up relatives. I was telling her about Stella Maestas' "truth or myth" story published in El Puente recently and Lorraine said, "Oh, I've heard that one, but it wasn't a wedding". She told me her version, and gave me the phone number for Fannie Montoya, who knew personally the people involved in the incident. Her mother, Lucia Madril (married to Thomas Montoya) had an aunt named Lola Madril (a teenager then) who refused to dance with a young man with last name of Mora. She couldn't recall his first name. The next day Lola and her sister Sillo (Rosario) were walking to school and met up with the young man. He shot Lola and then turned the gun on himself. Sillo witnessed the whole thing. This was a tragic incident, and a corrido (a ballad) was written because of it. Fanny promised to mail me a copy of it with her translation. Although usually corridos state the day and year an event happened, she didn't know who wrote it or when. More to come!

title: {Joseph Morgan Cooper Jr. (1933-2015)}
body:
On October 15th, I lost my best friend of almost 70 years. It was a peaceful, quiet ending, for which I am grateful. Joe grew up in Syracuse, NY, spending many happy summers at his family retreat-The Pines, in Skaneateles, NY. He was a proud graduate of Phillips Exeter Academy and Yale University, and had a long career in corporate advertizing with Procter and Gamble, Eastern Airlines, Pan Am, and Xerox.

Joe and I met as children in ballroom dancing classes and we had a magic marriage of 58 years. In the early 1960s we moved with four children under the age of seven to Manila, the Philippines, where our fifth child was born. Five years later we all moved to Mexico City. Our life was full of discovery, adventure, and travel.

Twenty eight years ago, Joe chose early retirement and we bought the Lucas Anaya house on The Hill in Galisteo. After renovations, we moved in on June 1, 1987. At the time there were only 110 hardy souls in the village. When we arrived, Manuel Anaya, next door, welcomed Joe over the fence: "I understand that you are buena gente." And this we have always tried to be.

Joe worked for many years on the Water Board with Rod, Scott, and Anton, who became like sons to him. He was instrumental in the endless Lamy Well lawsuits. We were founding members of the Studio Tour and took part annually for 18 years. We also helped Lucy to found El Puente, now a beloved institution.

Joe was an artist, a reader, a bird lover, and a gentle and caring friend. His delicious sense of humor, his sonorous voice, deep laugh, and endless curiosity endeared him to (almost) everyone he met. As a close friend said, "There was always an element of surprise with Joe." To me he was a fun-loving and funny companion as we explored the world together. He often said, "We have gambled with our lives." And that we did together, loving each discovery of the new, the different, the interesting.

Joe lived a full life, adoring his five children, their spouses, his eleven grandchildren and two great grandchildren. He has bequeathed to us all a gentle affirmation of life in its fullness and an optimistic, happy view of the world he knew for 82 years. We miss his bright spirit. Galisteo and our caring friends and neighbors have filled our lives with joy and now bring me great comfort. I am full of gratitude, and cannot grieve.

title: County Code/Zoning, Imperfect ... But Approved at Last
body:
Both the SLDC (Sustainable Land Development Code) and Zoning Ordinance were approved during a packed marathon 7-hour session of the BCC (Board of County Commissioners) on December 8th. A number of personal and philosophical issues were presented by the public, and two in particular were raised by representatives of Galisteo, the Turquoise Trail Preservation Trust, and the Rural Conservation Alliance.

The first concerned setbacks for sand and gravel operations of 10 acres or less. The Ordinance includes a provision mandating that operations must be 200 feet from a roadway or property line. A number of people presented concerns that 200 feet provided insufficient protection from dust, noise, and traffic. At least 500 to 1,000 feet was recommended. The Commissioners did not address this except for one suggestion to possibly revisit the issue in July 2016, when the SLDC is open for review and revision.

[This comes up as the County faces three lawsuits by Albuquerque-based Buena Vista Estates, Inc. which had applied to blast, mine and crush basalt for construction on 50 acres the company owns on La Bajada Mesa. Under widespread public pressure, the BCC rejected its contract in order to protect the iconic southern entrance to Santa Fe.]

The second issue raised on Dec. 8 was a last-minute amendment presented by Commissioner Robert Anaya allowing family sub-division transfers of 40 acres within Agriculture/Ranch properties (which are zoned at 160 acres per dwelling). This could potentially be used to evade Master Planning requirements, opening a back door to developers. The purpose of the amendment was not well explained, and public discussion was limited. Yet it was approved by four Commissioners, with only Kathy Holian strongly opposed [as is El Puente.] (Thanks to Roger Taylor for this report.)

title: Craig Moya's New Mexico Hard Cider Taproom
body:
Jean and Steve's son Craig Moya, with his wife Heather, has received a good dose of publicity for their New Mexico Hard Cider Taproom, which opened recently at the Luna Center (505 Cerrillos Rd.). A feature in The New Mexican (12/2) reports that Craig resigned from the Santa Fe County Fire Department to open his first bar. Apples first came from his uncle's 200-tree orchard in Villanueva, one of five orchards in Chimayo and Southern Colorado now sourced by the business. The ciders have catchy names -- Doña Tules, Bruja's Apple Pie, Manzana Muerte, and Dry Mariachi (which took the gold medal at this year's State Fair).

The SF Reporter (11/25) devoted its weekly "3 Questions" to Craig, who ascribes the popularity of cider to its wide range of possibilities. Local ciders are less sweet than commercial ones, with no artificial flavors or colors. The taproom also has 15 beers on tap and Moya specializes in "small batch" offerings. Food can be ordered from next door at the Talin Market's noodle bar and from Bang Bite food truck. Plans are to show sporting events and "have lots of music." The bar is open Mon.-Thurs., 3-11PM, and 11AM-11PM Fri., Sat. and Sun. Support a born-and-raised Galistefios's startup!

title: Historical News Item: Antonio Ortiz y Pino, 1915
body: From The Santa Fe New Mexican for Aug. 26, 1915: "News was received in the city today that Antonio Ortiz y Pino, the seven-months old son of Jose Ortiz y Pino, chairman of the board of county commissioners, died of whooping cough yesterday afternoon at his father's home in Galisteo. For months the baby had suffered with whooping cough ... Mr. Ortiz did everything in his power to effect a cure, summoning numerous physicians and lavishing the best attention on the infant. The funeral took place this afternoon from the Catholic church, where services were held. Interment was in the Ortiz family plot in the Catholic cemetery."

body: And in Nov. 21, 1965, The New Mexican reported a theatrical squabble between the Santa Fe Community Theatre and the Pink Garter Blackouts at the Lamy saloon later called the Legal Tender when both groups performed George Bernard Shaw's Mesalliance at the same time.

title: Stray Dog in Southern Galisteo
body: Some of us in SoGal have been worrying about a shy but friendly dog who appears to be a stray in this harsh weather. title: Bosque Restoration Project
body:
You may have noticed a cluster of vehicles by the old wooden bridge, and several men walking and placing flagged stakes along the Bosque. Thus began Phase 2 of the Galisteo River Restoration Project, involving survey work along the 25-acre project area (from the northern hogback to the Galisteo bridge on NM 41). A map of the actual work to be done along the route is being drawn up. It includes removals of invasive species such as Russian Olives and Salt Cedar (Tamarisk), and plantings of native species, such as grape vine, willow and other saplings.

At times surveyors may need to access the top of the higher banks along the Bosque in order to take sightings and readings.

Phase 1 of the project involved negotiations and contracting of all parties involved: 3 State agencies (Dept. of Fish/Game/Wildlife; Dept. of the Environment; State Engineers Office), 5 subcontractors for surveys, permitting, and the actual removal and planting work; and 18 Landowner Agreements with those who have property along the Bosque banks. Although only 17 Landowners signed the Agreements, we managed to get a special exception from the State Engineers Office to continue. Without that exception, the grant funds would have had to be returned and the project would have been cancelled.

Phase 3 will most likely begin in January. The completed survey will be used to obtain final permits to conduct the work (probably in February). Once the surveys are completed, Roger Taylor (acting as Project Manager on behalf of the UCA) will discuss the more specific plans with each Landowner.

If you have any questions or concerns during this project, please contact Roger (505-466-3469 or clearskynm@gmail.com.)

A December 10th statement from Fire Chief Jean Anaya Moya emphasizes the importance of the Bosque project for our communal safety. In the past few years, The GVFR has been concerned about several issues: "an explosive growth of underbrush and invasive species in the Bosque, heightening the fire danger threat. Flooding that is eroding the banks of the Galisteo River and causing silt build-up in the Bosque. Mosquito infestations that reduce our summer outdoor enjoyment."

title: Fire Department Elections and News
body:
Elections by acclamation for officers in the GVFR were confirmed at the last business meeting over yet another scrumptious meal provided by Cindy Lux. The results: Chief, Jean Moya; Assistant Chief, Jon Stern; Fire Captain, Jay Hetler; Secretaries, Barbara King and Janice Wall; Emergency Recorder, Wayne King; Treasurer, Frank Lux (who is also President of the 501C3 Friends of GVFR with Janice Wall as Vice-President). Congratulations and thanks to all for keeping us safe.

Holiday baskets will be distributed by GVFR members to elders in the village. During the Light Up A Life event in the Santa Fe Plaza on New Years Eve, there will farolitos lit in honor of villagers who passed away in 2015: Will Mares, Evelyne Franceschi, and Joe Cooper.

The phone book will be out around the first of the year. Donations of $75 or more will receive a cool (or hot) T-shirt. Recipes are welcome for the GVFR Cookbook.

Welcome to new member Joshway Short. And remember, volunteers (especially those interested in EMT training) are drastically needed.

title: Development Updates: Commonweal
body: Commonweal: The Commonweal Master Plan Amendment (Galisteo Basin Preserve) has been approved to downsize the proposed development from 10,360 acres to 2,502 acres, as reported in the October issue of El Puente. The village of Galisteo notified the County of its concern on the zoning for the 8000 acres removed from the building plan which was still designated as "Planned Development District" (one dwelling per acre.) Commonweal director Ted Harrison approved this and the Saddleback changes.

title: Serapio J. Anaya (1925-2016)
body:
Serapio Anaya passed away on January 5th and a Rosario and funeral mass were held at Nuestra Senora de los Remedios on January 11-12th. He was buried at the National Cemetery. A reception was held afterwards at the Nancy Rodriguez Center. The following account is adapted from his granddaughter Linda Anaya Gomez's eulogy, read at the mass by her cousin Carrie Montoya Pegg.

Serapio was born in Galisteo on December 5th, 1925, the youngest son of Carmelita and Serapio Anaya Sr. He never forgot where he came from and his memories tell us about how hard times were, and how different his life was from a child's today. In a 2004 interview in El Puente, he spoke about being pulled out of school and having to work as a sheepherder: "It was hard, I was too young, you know, fourteen years old. I could see my house from up there on Cerro Pelon, so far away. Sometimes I used to cry." But he always found humor, even when talking about the hard times: "I tell people my first automobile was a donkey .... I didn't have to put gas."

At about the age of sixteen, Serapio's father passed away and he started working on the railroad at the Lamy stockyard, then in Colorado, which, he said, "was hard, but better than sheepherding." He then came back and worked in Santa Fe as a laborer, and then he was off to the Army in 1944, serving his country as a medic at the Panama Canal. He was a Guard Patrolman 522 and Sharp Shooter Rifleman, traveling on the train from New York all the way to California as a guard for the wounded. He was honorably discharged in 1946 and made his way back home.

Among the great moments in his life, Serapio said "when I came back from the Army, I was looking for girlfriends. Finally, I met someone." He and Julia ironically met on Galisteo Street in Santa Fe, and that is why they married and moved to Galisteo at the age of 21! They raised their eight children in Galisteo: Rudy, Billy, Velma, Alex, Jeana, Michael, Sylvia, and Daniel. Serapio worked as a truck driver and Julia stayed home to take care of their children. After the children grew up, they continued their lives with one another in Galisteo.

Serapio's children and grandchildren have many memories, such as riding with him in his company truck, going for firewood, making adobes, listening to Antonio Aguilar on the record player, Serapio and Julia talking and laughing while the kids played in their little home. They were married for 67 years.

He loved going hunting and drinking beer with his sons and grandsons, riding his bike and taking walks in Galisteo, singing Spanish songs outside under the tree with his son in law as he played the guitar. Many of us will remember him when we hear the songs he used to sing-- You Are My Sunshine, Oh My Darling Clementine, and Three Little Indians ... Julia remembers getting up early in the morning and going to the casino with him. On their way home they would stop and eat at McDonald's: he sure did love his McDonald's. Then they would go home and watch the Wheel of Fortune.

We all remember what a hard worker he was; and how he was a firm believer in good work ethics, and being part of the working class. He was very proud of his children, and glad that they were hard workers like him. Serapio had a generous kind heart, and would go out of his way to help anyone if he could. He once drove from Galisteo to Pojoaque just to lend his daughter and son in law five bucks, because they were broke. He would pick up his youngest daughter at 1:00 in the morning when she worked at the Legal Tender in Lamy, with a blanket and pillow so she could get some sleep on the way home, to be ready for school the next morning. He took orange juice and Tylenol to his daughter in law when she was sick, because everyone else was afraid to catch what she had. These 90 years of the life that Serapio lived were a blessing from God for him, and for all of us.

title: Galisteo 1977-1984
body:
The first of two excerpts from Agnes Martin and Me (Brooklyn: Lyon Artbooks, 2016) by photographer Donald Woodman about his years as amanuensis to Agnes Martin in Galisteo, 1977-1984. Agnes "voices" had told her she could not own land, so she commandeered Donald and his newly acquired property in Galisteo, having decided that it was "an innocuous location where we could live and just the right size to build her studio."

We soon arrived in Galisteo, which is a beautiful area. At an elevation of 6,000 feet, it is dotted with pinon and juniper trees. Galisteo Creek winds its way through the town with huge old cottonwood trees lining its banks. In 1977, Galisteo was considerably different from the fashionable artists' enclave it has become; then, it was a sleepy little Hispanic town with fewer than fifty families. Imagine a time before the proliferation of cell phones, instant messaging, e-mail, and the Internet. The closest pay phone was the one outside the Santa Fe Railroad train station in Lamy, eight miles north. If you wanted a telephone in your home, it would have to be a party line, which meant that a line might not be available when you most needed it.

The village center boasted a small variety store in the front room of one family's old adobe home; a Catholic church, and a historical museum/herb store run by Jose Ortiz y Pino III, the curandero .... Based on his long family legacy, Jose had appointed himself 'patron' of the community. I was purchasing my land from him on a real estate contract whereby the mortgage is carried by the seller.

At that time, the only art world luminaries living in Galisteo were Fritz and Romona Scholder, whose historic adobe hacienda was situated across the highway just south of my property. Fritz was a well-known Native American artist who had come to local prominence in the 1960s. He taught at the Institute of American Indian Arts in Santa Fe and influenced a whole generation of native artists. His wife had the reputation of being the consummate artist's wife because it was she who had propelled his career in the Santa Fe art scene.

The three acres of land I owned were on the north side of town, bordered by Highway 41 to the west and Galisteo Creek on the east and north. The property was at the end of an unnamed dirt road [now Marcellina Lane], which it shared with five other parcels. Agnes never mentioned whether she had visited Galisteo before so I gave her a tour of the town, stopping to introduce her to Jose and showing her where the Scholders lived. As we drove onto my property, I pointed out the pile of vigas I had been collecting for use in building my studio. I parked her SUV and continued to describe the boundaries of the property. We then walked down the steep drop-off to the creek. ...

Agnes must have been pleased by my tour because she smacked her lips with great satisfaction and announced we would go to Santa Fe for dinner at a place called the Pink something.

title: {A Dog's Life}
body: The brindle dog who has been wandering Galisteo for a couple of months now was briefly named Bobo and taken in by Rudy Sena. But proximity to the highway was too threatening and he is now Soya (a Hopi word related to Winter Solstice) in the home of Phil and Judy Tuwaletstiwa. Each morning, though, when let out, he still runs off for about an hour, perhaps because some good people were feeding him while he was a stray. Now this is a habit that needs to be broken. Evelyn Gregory is helping to train him to stay on the property; you can help by not feeding him. If you find him wandering near your home, please call 466-1060.

body: Galisteo rep Matthew McQueen, our rep to the State Legislature (which takes up cudgels on Jan. 19 for 30 days) was quoted in The New Mexican as appreciating the passion of supporters of Bernie Sanders and Hillary Clinton but said he'd heard fellow Democrats threaten not to support the winner if their candidate loses in the Democratic primaries. "That just sends chills down my spine," he said. "We lost the 2014 secretary of state race because of low turnout [and we all know how that turned out!]. body: 2015 was the fifth wettest year in recorded New Mexico history, c.137% of "normal" -- whatever that is. Wayne King has been measuring the moisture and came up with a final figure of 29 inches for Galisteo (SoGal). This is more than the neighboring rain stations like Las Vegas and Santa Fe. He says he "used 0.10 inches of water for 1.0 inch of snow, which I was able to correlate a couple of ways."

title: Plague Warning
body: Cases of the plague have been confirmed in some pets in Santa Fe and the SFPD warns that there may have been exposure at the Frank Ortiz Dog Park and La Tierra Trails. Plague can be fatal to both pets and humans if not properly diagnosed and treated. It can be spread through fleas and contact with infected animals such as rodents, rabbits and cats. Symptoms include fever, chills, headache, muscle pain, weakness and sometimes tender and swollen lymph nodes in the groin, armpit or neck. And a serious dog flu has been detected in other states but not yet in New Mexico, though some veterinarians are recommending shots now. If you go to the Eldorado Animal Clinic, keep an eye on their website.
