title: Agnes's Swimming Pool .... and More
body:
"In the early summer of 1982, Agnes [Martin] decided to install an outdoor swimming pool. When she was a young woman in Canada, she had been an Olympic-class swimmer. Her Galisteo pool was to be of a pretty good size: approximately twenty feet by forty feet. Without consulting me, she hired a pool constructor. He arrived unannounced one day with a backhoe and promptly dug the hole. Then a crew came to put in the steel reinforcing, applying Gunite ... to create the surface shell. The work was very noisy and disrupted our quiet life. Although I was somewhat stunned by all the activity, I didn't object, remembering that I had agreed that Agnes could build whatever she wanted. She chose to leave the pool in a raw, unfinished state, never painting or embellishing it in any way except for installing a diving board. The pool's top edge was raised several inches above the ground and consisted of a concrete lip wide enough to walk on, beyond which was a scrabble of desert grasses. For some reason, Agnes did not have the customary pump and filter system installed to keep it clean. Instead she threw a generous quantity of chlorine pellets into the water on a daily basis.

"At the end of the hot summer days, she seemed to derive great joy from donning a one-piece black swimsuit and diving into the cool water. Watching her swiftly moving up and down the length of the pool, it was obvious that she was still a talented swimmer ... She also enjoyed lazily floating on her back out in the center of the water while staring at the luminous New Mexico sky.

"During this period, none of the few dirt roads that traversed the village of Galisteo had names. One day Agnes pointed out to me two signs proclaiming EASY STREET, which she had installed at the beginning and end of the dirt road that served our property. She showed it off with exuberant pride, saying "You see: I've made it so that everyone that lives on our street now lives on Easy Street." When village patron Jose Ortiz y Pino saw one of the signs, which he had to pass going to and from his hacienda, he was furious and had both of them removed, declaring with the absolute authority he assumed for all affairs in town that there would be no street names in Galisteo, adding that if streets were ever to be named, he would be the only one to choose those names." (Excerpted from Donald Woodman, Agnes Martin and Me (Brooklyn: Lyon Artbooks, 2016). [When street names became required so the fire departments could find their ways, Moira Walden did most of the choosing, along with John Benjamin.]

In early 1983, after being hospitalized in Colorado Springs for a mental breakdown, Martin was told by her therapist to move out of the camper in which she had been living on Woodman's land, and to build a house, which he proceeded to construct from rammed earth. The design was a simple rectangle, 16 x 48 ', and Martin moved in by early summer. The house has since been remodeled by successive owners and the adobe-clad camper was dismantled. (Ed note: some of the adobes ended up as a low wall in my back yard.)

The pool was purportedly built for local children but when it was vandalized, Martin filled it in. At some point in the mid to late 1980s, she also took it upon herself to alter the course of the Rio Galisteo, which was eating into the cliffs on which her house was built. Disdaining the Army Corps of Engineers, she had a huge earth berm built to redirect the waters to the east.

For those interested in more on this important artist and former Galistena, see Nancy Princenthal's excellent book: Agnes Martin: Her Life and Art (New York: Thames and Hudson).

title: Galisteo Solar Heating Up
body:
There are wackos out there who claim that solar panels "suck up the sunlight" and will leave us in the dark, cutting off photosynthesis and killing all plants! OMG! (Ed note: I've been off the grid on solar for two decades. Sorry about what that's doing to your gardens ...)

As renewable energy gets increasingly affordable, Galisteo's solar presence becomes more visible. Over the years, El Puente has tried to cover each addition so you know who to contact if you're considering solar. Let us know if you should be added to the sunny news.

On Avenida Vieja, two additions: Matthew McQueen and Caroline Seigel just added a dual system on their carport roof: both solar electric (photovoltaic), and solar thermal (hot water). The installation was done by AMENERGY, a locally owned company. Matthew reports that he's not "off the grid; I'm still grid tied but get a little check from PNM every few weeks for the excess energy we generate. Plus, the house is nice and toasty."

Ed Epping and Peggy Diggs have a ground-mounted, 20-panel solar array; it's also grid-tied -- a 6.54 kilowatt, batteryless electric system, installed by local powerhouse, Positive Energy. The panels and inverter are made by Sunpower, guaranteed for 25 years. (The "25-year cumulative return is $98,684"!) "Positive Energy also smoothly coordinated various inspections that we needed to have at various points throughout the readying and installation process," says Peggy, "and provided the forms necessary to apply for the New Mexico Solar Tax Credit and the Federal Solar Tax Credit."

title: Water Board Meets
body:
The Board of the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumer's Association met on February 8th to discuss several pressing issues. A lawyer is being consulted about updating our bylaws and a committee was formed (Anna Cardenas, Mike Golino, Lucy Lippard) to scrutinize the current bylaws for needed changes and report back to the Board. Among them are the fees for overuse, the Board's liability for damages, the number of hookups one household can have, and the definition of a "household" or "single family dwelling." Any recommended changes to the bylaws will then be put before the entire membership.

There are also complicated decisions to be made about how to connect a new hookup to an older one in SoGal and other infrastructure limitations to the current system, such as the way pumping water uphill burns out pumps, persistent leaks, and the need for new pumps and wellhouse. President Rod Hall says that the association needs to get out of the zoning business and just deliver water. Galisteo members still get a bargain even though monthly bills have been raised (since 1962) from $5 to $15 to $30. ANNUAL MEMBERSHIP MEETING, MARCH 24, time TBA.

title: La Bajada Monument
body:
At their last meeting, the BCC voted to table the Resolution in Support of a La Bajada National Monument for four months in order to allow more community discussion to occur. There was a good turn out at the hearing from people on both sides of the issue. In addition to many supporters who spoke in favor, representatives from the villages of La Cienega, La Cieneguilla, and La Bajada also attended and spoke eloquently about their concerns and need for more assurances before they can get behind this effort.

With few exceptions, the "opposition" speakers voiced support for the continued protection of these lands, but expressed concerns over continued access to the land for traditional uses and more inclusion in the process. Resolution leaders were heartened by the civility of the discussion and believe that common ground can be found to bring everyone behind this effort.

The stated intent of the Monument includes continued support for traditional uses, including grazing, wood and piñon gathering, as well as recreation. With the appropriate safeguards and assurances that these protected uses will remain intact once the Monument is established, supporters believe everyone will come to see it as a good neighbor, an asset to Santa Fe's tourism and recreation offerings, and the best way to ensure long-term protection. Resolution leaders wish to express their thanks to all who supported the measure and ask for their continued support of efforts to protect the greater La Bajada area. Please watch for updates on future developments.

title: Sina Brush Op-Ed on Bundys
body: Sina Brush contributed a My View to the New Mexican on Jan. 31st: "The Bundy Boys: Another B Movie." It begins: "I have lived in the Southwest all my life, worked as caretaker on ranches and know cowboys pretty well. They tend to keep a low profile, have great respect for the government, and are too busy making a living to play at being what they already are — men doing dirty, hard, often aggravating work that leaves no time or interest for pretending or pretension."

title: Jose Ortiz y Pino III (1932-2016)
body:
Jose Ortiz y Pino III, descendant of a well-known New Mexican family dating back to the early 1600s, passed away on January 17, 2016 at the age of 83, after a long illness. He was preceded in death by his father and mother, Frank and Mary Ortiz y Davis, his brothers, John and Frank Jr. and his sister Margaret Truscott. He is survived by Yolanda, his wife of 64 years, his son Jose Ortiz y Pino IV and wife Lori, his daughter Maria Ortiz y Pino, his sister Maria O. Catanach, grandchildren Miguel and Estevan Padilla and Theodore Ortiz y Pino, as well as many nieces and nephews.

Jose was born and spent most of his childhood in Santa Fe, where he attended St. Michaels School, later moving to the New Mexico Military Institute in Roswell, and to NMSU, where he received his BA degree. He was commissioned a Second Lieutenant in the U.S. Army, serving for two years in Munich, Germany, and was honorably discharged as First Lieutenant. He came home to Galisteo to ranch with his father and enter the field of politics, a longstanding tradition in his family. Jose was a Santa Fe County Commissioner for two terms (1958-62), a State Senator (1964-66), a member of the Education and Judiciary Commission, Chairman of the State Parks Commission and Special Assistant to Governor David F. Cargo (1968-70). He introduced and passed the first anti-billboard law in the U.S. and was instrumental in building the Villanueva State Park in San Miguel County.

While Jose was performing all his political duties, he and Yolanda owned and operated the famous La Mancha Restaurant on La Vega in Galisteo (1959-71) as well as a general store and bar in the Ortiz "hacienda," where he also created the Galisteo Historical Museum. He finally retired to do what he liked best - write, and enjoy nature in his beloved Galisteo. He was the author of several books, including Don Jose: The Last Patron, The Herbs of Galisteo and Their Power, and Curandero: A Cuento. He also owned the Remedios y Yerbas shop which he enjoyed very much. He was a loving, caring son, husband, father, grandfather, and friend. He will always be remembered and hold a special place in our hearts till we are all together again as a family with our Lord God.

Special thanks and our gratitude to the Northridge staff and Ambercare Hospice staff for their very special care given to Jose for his time spent there during his illness. A rosary will be recited Friday April 15, at 6:30p.m.at Nuestra Senora de los Remedios in Galisteo. The funeral Mass will be on April 16, at 10:30 a.m. followed by interment at the Galisteo Catholic Cemetery and a reception at the Galisteo Community Center.

title: Libby Baca Sandoval (1934-2016)
body:
On February 23, 2016, The Lord took his servant Libby's hand, and said, "Come Let's Walk with Me." We will miss her. At least once in our lifetime, we are fortunate enough to walk with an angel. I feel that I am one of these chosen individuals. Libby was my sister-in-law, but I always felt that she was more like my sister.

She was born in Tapia, New Mexico, to Pedro and Lucy Baca on April 17, 1934. Libby was the third child in a family of ten siblings. Her early years of education were spent in a small school in Tapia. Later, her family moved to Santa Fe, where she attended St. Anne's Catholic School. Libby joined our family when she married my brother Anastacio Sandoval. They settled in Galisteo, and raised their family here. Libby was devoted to her children, Theresa and Frank, to their spouses, six grandchildren, and five great grandchildren.

I am grateful for the moments I spent talking with Libby and learning from her. I know some of her wisdom and knowledge has influenced my life, as I am sure it did others. Her religion was a big part of her life; she devoted a great deal of time to prayer, and passed on her religious beliefs to her family. She was also a member in good standing of Our Sacred Heart of Jesus Society. Although many other activities were part of her daily life, she always found time to study her books on herbs and remedies. Very often, Libby shared her remedies for whatever was ailing friends and relatives. She was also a creative cook; her dishes were quite amazing, but she would only share some of her recipes, which is quite all right. (Some cooks don't reveal their secrets.) Libby also cultivated her own garden, so a large part of her recipes included home grown vegetables. I can still remember when she made a variety of goatsmilk cheeses. Some were plain for those who didn't care for added ingredients, and some were quite tasty with different herbs and spices.

Libby was an individual with many talents, and if you were lucky she might have given you one of her lovingly created pieces of jewelry. When her husband was alive, and they were both healthy, Galisteo enjoyed them playing their instruments at parties -- Tacho on the accordion, and Libby with her tambourine. On New Year's Eve, they would join friends to go out and serenade las Manueles, a treasured tradition that has long since been forgotten in our culture.

As some of our residents might have observed, Libby enjoyed her morning walks. She knew how important it was to exercise for her health, so she made it a daily regimen, although when she became less able to walk long distances, she limited her walks to her daughter's home which was closer to her residence. We of Libby's family are very grateful to the citizens of this town who looked after her on her daily walks. Thank you for keeping her out of harm's way, and for all your comforting words, donations, and prayers we received during this difficult time. To Libby, I want to say, "Watch over us from that special place where you reside now, Help us to find the strength, and the will to take it from here."

title: GCA Annual Elections
body:
On March 5th, the annual Galisteo Community Association was called to order after a good crowd enjoyed a scrumptious breakfast. Elections were held with the following results, all by unanimous votes. Acting President Wayne King became the real President. Secretary: Judy Tuwaletstiwa; Treasurer: Estelle Berger, who was first elected to serve on the Board, as were Stella Maestas and Susie Shanklin.

Michael Golino reported on the internet possibilities. Century Link now has government money and Michael has urged them to spend some on fiber optics here, but they didn't want to discuss it when he, Roger Taylor and Stanley Purdue met with them. New Mexico Surf is line-of sight Internet. If you can see the Ortiz Mountains from your home, you can get it. Terra Stream, which broadcasts between television interspaces, is not based on line of sight. They are working in Roswell but having some issues and might be five months out.

Shirley Hirsch reported on the renovation of the Community Center kitchen. Thanks to a large donation from Bernard Pomerance for a memorial plaque in the Reading Room dedicated to his late wife Evelyne, there was also funding for a new sink, faucet, and countertop, to paint cabinets and create an island on casters. Thanks to committee members Peggy Diggs, Barbara Seiler and Hirsch, as well as to helpers Roger Taylor, Muriel Fariello, Antonio Chavez, Phillip Tuwaletstiwa and Michael Golino.

Anna Cardenas spoke on the community breakfasts. The April breakfast will be held in conjunction with the Community Cleanup on April 23. May 7 and June 4 have been signed up. July 9, August 6, and September-November are open. (Ed note: Hey, these gourmet breakfasts/book exchanges are fun! Sign up!)

Roger Taylor reported on several ongoing programs, including the Bosque Restoration (see p.3), and the Frontiers initiative to revitalize downtown Galisteo, which is focusing on efforts to bring in a coffee shop, a convenience store (not a 7-11 !) and/or a restaurant, and rest room. Another project, which will probably be covered by the $2000 "placemaking" grant we have received, is to highlight the original plaza (before NM 41) with historical plaques and a timeline. More discussions with the NMDOT are in order about traffic calming. The Frontiers committee (Roger Taylor, Michael Golino, Leslie Dilworth, Anna Cardenas, Frank Hirsch and Lucy Lippard) will continue to meet with representatives from County and State.

The GCA and the Water Associations of both the village and Ranchitos continue to work on registering as COs and ROs (see El Puente last issue).

La Sala will be open Fridays through Sundays all summer, beginning May 13th. Barbara King is heading a gallery committee. Internet service and a satellite dish will be installed in mid March and an Ipad with Swipe capability is being purchased. Window and door restoration is the spring/summer focus. A training workshop will be held on Wed., 4/27, 9:30-12:30. It would be helpful to have some mallets, chisels, scrapers, routers; table and coping saws, etc.(Contact Roger Taylor for details.)

Happy Birthday was sung to Janet Pfeiffer and the meeting adjourned after 41 minutes. Wasting no time, a meeting of the new GCA Board then convened in the Reading Room.

(Thanks to Judy Tuwaletstiwa's detailed minutes.)

title: {Update: Bosque Reclamation Project}
body:
The target start date is Monday 3/21, but no later than 3/28, dependent on reception of the final permit from the County. Work will begin at the southern end near the NM 41 bridge and proceed northwards, continuing for four weeks, Monday through Friday, 8:30AM - 5:00PM.

At the February 18th meeting with Bosque landowners, some community members voiced concerns about whether this work would interfere with bird mating and nesting. This question was brought to the Santa Fe Raptor Center, to an ornithologist at the National Audubon Society, and to NM Fish/Game/Wildlife. All replied that while birds are nesting earlier due to the changing climate, the majority wait until early-to-mid April. However, in New Mexico, the Great Horned Owl mates and produces 3-5 eggs in January; it takes 3-5 weeks for the eggs to gestate and hatch; fledglings usually come forth in mid-to-later February and begin to fly around mid-to-later March.

The hoots and other noises you may be hearing right now are territorial warnings. A pair of Horned Owls usually mate for life. Full courting and mating diminishes after the first year. This pair have been together here for several years now. They usually nest high up (50-75' above ground), often in hollows of cottonwoods or stolen nests built by other birds; they don't build their own. Owls are not fond of nesting in Russian Olives, Junipers, or Pinons. If there are no Cottonwoods, they make do with an Elm.

We also have Barn Owls, which prefer human-made structures like bridges and barns, and Western Screech Owls, which prefer more open areas. Both nest in late Spring. Our sources reassured us that noise, and in particular the Bosque work, will not drive them away or force them to abandon the nest. If anything, these specialists were more concerned that workers could be attacked if they got too close to the nest. The Bald Eagle is about the only bird that equals the Horned Owl in ferocity.

In any case, we have arranged for a Fish/Game/Wildlife specialist to walk the bosque before work begins in order to identify any nesting sites, so that we can minimize disturbance. A crew of up to eight members of the Navajo Nation will be doing much of the heavy work, and will be living in self-contained campers on the GCC parking lot. They understand that loud music, trash, and running generators are not acceptable. If neighbors have any concerns during this time, contact Roger.

title: Mike Anaya Launches Campaign
body:
The launch of Mike Anaya's campaign for State Senator on February 20th at the Community Center was "exciting and spirited," in the words of one attendee. Former Attorney General Gary King and former Land Commissioner Ray Powell were there to endorse him. District 39 covers parts of six counties, and is a primarily rural population. Anaya welcomed the crowd, many in cowboy hats:

"Many people have asked me, 'Why you want to be a Senator? Why and how can you do a job without pay? Is it worth it?' My answer is simple, I have lived my life to help people and now more than ever, people, especially people in District 39, need help. Every time we turn on the radio, the TV or the computer, we look and we hear from someone, usually not from New Mexico, about what we need to do to save us from ourselves .... My motto is simple: 'Common sense solutions, Less Talk, More Action.' My dad used to say, 'Don't talk about it, do it first, then talk about it.'"

Wouldn't it be something if Mike won and Matthew were re-elected? Tiny Galisteo would be home to both our legislators!

title: Marc Simmons Column on Historic Galisteo and Salt Harvests
body: In The New Mexican (3/12) Marc Simmons' (reprinted) column featured a 1880 photograph of Galisteo from somewhere south/west of the church (on the cover of the bicentennial booklet). The column was about Galisteo as the meeting and departure point for annual expeditions to the Salinas, or Salt Lakes in the 18th century and later. There was often a "wild fandango" the night before the group set out on the cosecha de sal (salt harvest) on a 3-day march to Laguna del Perro, the largest lake. The wagons were often accompanied by soldiers with a small cannon since the lakes were in Apache country. Each family that sent a representative for the hard work of extracting the salt received a share of the harvest. Simmons quoted an older resident of Galisteo telling him years ago "that her grandfather had been conned into buying the lakes for a princely sum .... This was not uncommon. In those days purchasing the New Mexican salt lakes was equivalent to a New York visitor buying the Brooklyn Bridge."

title: Liz Rose Publishes Two Books
body: Liz Rose (E.P. Rose) recently published two books: a delightful illustrated children's book in Spanish and English: Ditty Dotty Ditties, written on a Mexican beach, and dedicated "to all grandchildren - especially mine"; and the paperback edition of Poet Under a Soldier's Hat, a fascinating account of her family over the last century of the British Raj in India, based on her father's autobiographical notes. Liz born by lamplight on a dining room table in the Himalayan foothills-was a "Raj orphan," shipped to England at age seven, "roaming the moors of an English children's home, feral, her imagination developed unschooled and uncensored." She has run wild in Galisteo since 1986.

title: Micaela Theresa Griego (1990-2016)
body: Micaela Griego was born July 8, 1990 and passed away in a tragic automobile accident near Galisteo on April 2. For 25 years, she lived in Galisteo with her parents, Orlando and Lisa Griego, and her brother Timo, near grandparents and many aunts, uncles and cousins. Micaela loved family. She was a loving and caring person who would help everybody. It didn't matter who it was, if they needed her, she was right there for them. She loved spending time in the outdoors camping or fishing. She loved sunsets while driving to and from work. This beautiful girl will be missed dearly. The Griego family would like to thank all their family, friends, and the community for all the thoughts, prayers and gifts that have helped us get through this terrible tragedy. We would like to thank our nephew Carlos Montoya for making the cross placed on Highway 41 going towards Santa Fe, where everyone can say good morning and goodnight to Micaela. She will be the community's guardian angel, as the cross faces towards Galisteo.

title: Bosque Reclamation Project Under Way
body:
Several work days were lost, thanks to the difficulty of obtaining the County permissions, but workers and some huge machines have been hard at it in the Bosque for over a week, cutting down the Russian Olives and dead Willows, chipping them and spreading the chips over the ground to keep the soil moist now that the canopy is more open. Three large metal water troughs filled with native saplings (Cottonwood, Willow, Grape vine, etc.) to replace the Russian Olives will be at the basketball court.

At this writing the place looks like a war zone, and it will get worse as the stumps are removed, using chains and a root borer. Eventually, however, the new plantings will take hold and the Cottonwoods will be flourishing, though this will take at least a couple of years. I miss the buffer between my house and the noise and sight of the highway, but I am reassured that this is really good for the creek, and the openness is already appealing. (LRL)

title: What Does the GCA Do?
body:
The Galisteo Community Association (GCA) is an incorporated, non-profit organization governed by a Board of Directors from our community. Membership includes all residents of Galisteo who are 18 years or older and have lived here for at least 18 months. The GCA does four major things for the Galisteo community:

First, it owns, cares for, and rents out the Community Center on Avenida Vieja. The Center is a passive-solar hall that everyone may use. Daily rent for Galisteo residents is $75 and for non-residents, $150. Rent is free for memorial services for a local person. Events have included monthly coffees and book exchanges, memorial receptions, birthday parties, wedding receptions, baptism celebrations, going-away parties, Los Pastores, voting, state and county governmental meetings and corporate workshops. (Contact me at 466-3219 to find out if a date is open and to reserve it for your event.)

Most of the GCA's annual expenses are associated with operating and maintaining the Community Center. The largest expenses are for fire and liability insurance. Others include electricity, cleaning and building maintenance. Income is from rentals, donations and movie companies filming on the Cerro Pelon Ranch.

Recently, generous donations were used to upgrade the kitchen, including modifying the electrical system so that several crockpots and cookers can be plugged in simultaneously without popping the circuit breakers. As money accumulates, the Board will apply it to refurbishing the window sealants and exposed wood at the front of the building, grading and graveling the parking lot, repairing the basketball court and playground equipment, repainting the interior walls, and cleaning and polishing the floor. Volunteers take care of minor repairs and maintenance.

Second, GCA sponsors annual events in the community, including the Spring Clean-Up in April and the Chile and Margarita Festival in August or September. Donations usually cover the expenses.

Third, GCA sponsors one-time special projects that benefit the community, guided by one or more Board members. Current projects include: Neighbors Helping Neighbors; bringing high-speed internet to the community and creating a GCA-Galisteo web page; the Bosque Reclamation Project; and preparing a master plan for the revitalization of "Downtown Galisteo." These projects are made possible with volunteer labor and/or grants.

Fourth, GCA represents the community before governmental bodies. It is concerned about water resources, land-use planning and zoning, and traffic control. In the past, it was up to the GCA or individual members to find out about issues that would adversely impact Galisteo and then to lobby appropriate officials or agencies or go to court to get a hearing. Such issues included proposed fracking in the Galisteo Basin, the proposed oil depot in Lamy, and ongoing proposals for real estate developments. Now, as a Community Organization (CO) recognized by the county, GCA can assess development proposals when initially raised to the County Planning Department and present our concerns to the appropriate officials. Our CO status is brand new and we'll see how it works in practice.

title: Coming Soon: La Sala Gallery Shop
body:
From mid-May through August (Friday and Saturday 10am to 6pm, Sunday Noon to 4pm), you will have an opportunity to sell your artwork, books, or CDs and benefit La Sala. With a standard 50/50 gallery split, La Sala's portion will go toward the $6,000 we still need for interior finishes and lighting for future shows.

The Gallery Shop will be set up in the front half of the building while window restoration is underway in the back. There will be temporary work space for the artists volunteering and Internet access will also be available. We hope to fill the five four-hour gallery sitting shifts by recruiting five people each week (along with some alternates). These volunteers can catch up on reading and computer work or art projects, and will have the option of receiving 100% of their sales. The Gallery Shop is a community opportunity to transition into full use of the building while allowing visitors to see and contribute toward the restoration work being done.

Please let us know if you're available to sit for any amount of time so that we can send more detailed information and forms for submitting artwork to interested artists. We hope you'll join us this summer. Questions? Email us at: galisteo.lasala@gmail.com

title: {Coming Down the Pike}
body:
At an Eldorado neighborhood meeting on March 10, Joe Miller and his partners unveiled the Cimarron Village Subdivision -- a major new "high density" development for US 285, stretching from the existing gas station at Colina Road north towards Old Las Vegas Highway. The initial proposal encompasses 96 residential detached and attached town homes; a 96,000 sq ft (approved for up to 300,000 sq ft) mixed commercial/retail area of shops, offices, grocery, drug store, restaurant(s), coffee shop, a 13-space RV park, a possible motel complex, as well as the existing storage units and Country Store (being marketed for commercial office space or a restaurant), a plaza, open space, and possible gallery spaces, and a six-building senior housing/assisted living complex.

Development rights and 20.25 acre feet of water rights were approved in 2007 as part of a legal settlement among the County, Joe Miller, and five other developers in the 285 Corridor. In 2008 Miller transferred a high-volume production well to the Eldorado Water District (which has been using that water ever since) and signed a contract with them to supply the water needs to this proposed development.

This was an informal meeting of local residents. A second review of a revised proposal will be held April 14th at the old Country Store off US 285. The Galisteo community email will keep you informed.

On March 18th a major new organization was launched with a full page ad in The Santa Fe New Mexican. The Turquoise Trail Regional Alliance is sponsored by the Turquoise Trail Preservation Trust, which was founded in 2007 to develop a vision and long-term planning strategies for one of New Mexico's eight National Scenic Byways and its surrounding region, including the area east of the Sandia Mountains, roughly bounded by I-25, I-40, Hwy 285 and NM 41. The Alliance will serve as an umbrella organization for grassroots and community organizations in the area to leverage our collective strength. The goal is to support and preserve the intrinsic beauty of our natural scenic landscape, cultural and historic qualities, archaeological sites, local businesses, and an ecological habitat recognized as a critical wildlife corridor. The Galisteo Community Association is a member. (See www.turquoisetrailra.org.). (Thanks to Roger Taylor.)

There is a movement under way to pass a Santa Fe County Ordinance to end chaining or tethering of dogs outside. (I would add "for long periods of time.") Not only is it cruel and inhuman to leave a dog on a chain 24/7, it is also a public safety concern, since dogs left on chains out in the cold become isolated and aggressive. The CDC says chained animals are three times more likely to bite and the victims are usually children. If you support this, send an email to your commissioner (ranaya@ santafecountymn.gov) or to all the commissioners.

title: Annual Water Association Meeting
body:
The annual meeting of the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association was on March 26. A quorum was met (barely); only four members attended, plus the Board of Directors (Rod Hall, Phil Tuwaletstiwa, who held a proxy for Richard Patton, Wayne King, Antonio Chavez, Michael Golino, Lucy Lippard, Anna Cardenas, and Scott Diffrient). The Treasurer's Report and Financial Report were approved. Arrears were around $1,040. One member, who had been in arrears for over a year, was sent a certified letter requesting payment in full or membership would be terminated. Reinstatement would cost $10,000. A check was promptly received.

The Board is mindful of the fact that there are members of the community who own land in Galisteo, but are unable to build or bring in mobile homes because the current $10,000 for a water hookup is just too high. We do not want to become a community where only the rich can afford to live. Under discussion are ways to pay in installments or by financed payment plans, or to lower the price of a hook up. (Ranchitos charges $15,000 and Eldorado $20,000.) One suggestion is to use an Ombudsman to hear complaints from membership.

An application to form a formal R.O. (Registered Organization) has been submitted to Santa Fe County along with the Ranchitos Water Association to keep both up to date on proposed land and water use in our area. Quotes for a new building for the Pump Station near the current tanks are being obtained, and there are future plans for the second well located on GCA's ten acres on NM 41, and possibly a second tank. The problem of sulphur-smelling water seems to be solved.

A Board committee is working with a lawyer on updating the current By-Laws. By-Laws determine how the Association governs itself. The Board decides how much water members can use depending on whether we are going through a drought or whether our system can handle any more hookups at any given time. The Water Association owns 42.56 acre feet.

Rod Hall stepped down as President, having been on the Board for some 35 years. He was asked to remain as a consultant and thanked for his long service. Michael Golino was elected to take his place. Antonio Chavez will stay on as Foreman and Richard Patton as Secretary. Florence Sohn was elected as a new Board member. (She has been helping out with paperwork and logistics for years.) Rod moved to thank past members who also contributed their time to the Water Association, such as Joe Anaya, Sarapio Montoya, Joe Cooper, and Roman Attenberger, all of whom are deceased. The next Board meeting is June 27, 2016, 7:00pm at the Community Center. (Thanks to Anna Cardenas for her thorough minutes.)

title: The Bosque Transformed
body:
The Galisteo River Bosque project was completed the evening of May 3rd, with 95% of our goals reached. The area from the old bridge south to the NM 41 bridge was completed, however there are still some dead fall willow clumpings we would like to remove. The area north of El Puente was completed up to 800 feet beyond the stream curve, about 2000 feet short of our goal to reach the Ortiz y Pino/Singleton Ranch fenceline. This was due to a combination of the County permit delays and weather.

Hundreds of invasive trees were eliminated (mostly Russian Olives); over a dozen truckloads of root balls and stumps were trucked out; about ten cords of firewood were distributed to the community, as well as truckloads of wood chips; machinery ruts were raked out and covered with chips; over 600 cottonwood saplings, native willow, grape vine, plum and currant bushes were planted. There remain some small areas that we were unable to plant, due to lack of funds. We have applied to the Governor's River Stewardship Program for a second round of funding to complete the work: we hope to hear by mid-June. Come on down and perambulate a bit - you'll be surprised at the open, airy, restored ecosystem!

title: Jan Willem Jansens on Bosque Reclamation Project
body:
Seventeen years ago Jan Willem Jansens, who was then a contractor for Earth Works Institute, launched the Galisteo Watershed Association and Galisteo Watershed Restoration Project and soon began to think of plans to reclaim the Bosque in Galisteo. El Puente reported in December, 1999, that in the previous spring and summer, Jansens and interns had staked out the creek between the two bridges to measure the rate of erosion, and Eldorado schoolchildren had planted seedballs on the newly graded banks that replaced growing gullies. Since then, he has often met with the community and initiated other work in the creek. This time around, through Ecotone, his own company, Jansens as Project Director has been instrumental in the reclamation process that finally came to fruition.

Because of his long history with the Bosque, El Puente asked him a few questions in early May, when the work was almost finished.

Anything more you want to add about the history of this project?

I have always seen the Galisteo Bosque as an unusual place with its somewhat hidden, sunken location, its flaming yellow color in the fall -- visible from many miles away, its permanent flow of water, and its unusual spread and continuity of Cottonwoods and Willows, which is quite rare in the Galisteo Basin. Later I discovered many more peculiarities which made it speak to me even more as a place to take care of somehow. Yet it has been a very difficult and long process. Some may remember that Earth Works Institute made a first attempt, with the help of many landowners and the GVFR, to remove Russian Olives and Tamarisks on the wetland on the west side of the highway bridge, in 2004-2005.

When in 2006 we learned more about the Galisteo Bosque and discovered that it is part of the largest continuous wetland area in the Galisteo Basin, stretching to the La Jara Ranch irrigation dam on Cerro Pelon Ranch, and perhaps beyond, we proposed that it be placed on a list of priority wetlands meriting ecological restoration and protection. Yet the last ten years have been a huge administrative struggle to implement some of the proposed work. Legal battles, financing puzzles, regulatory limitations, costly surveying and permitting procedures sent us back to the drawing board numerous times, and this spring almost prevented the project from going ahead again. At the eleventh hour, as if squeezed through a key hole of time and funding limitations, we made it work.

You've heard the story about how the Cottonwoods got planted in a then pretty bare Bosque?

Yes, I heard that in the 1950s, Mrs. Philip McKee wanted to create a park-like environment along the Galisteo Creek between El Puente and the NM 41 bridge. I suspect that in those days, there was mostly a poorly vegetated gully bottom, at best with some grassy vegetation, willows and other shrubs, and a few clumps of cottonwoods (for example those at Harmony Hammond's and the Griscoms'). The arroyo was probably also a few feet deeper than it is now, because we have seen considerable build-up of sediment in the last two decades. People have recalled that in the 1950s much more of the abutments of El Puente were visible.

With the Russian Olives and Tamarisk (and some dead Cottonwoods) gone, what's the future of the surviving Cottonwoods?

The Cottonwoods that are there now will experience less competition for water, light and space from other vegetation. This should give them a boost in vitality. I expect that with many trees gone, high water will have an easier time flowing all across the bosque, smoothing out the soil disturbances, and irrigating the arroyo floor. Occasionally, perhaps once a decade, events in nature are so aligned that high water while the Cottonwoods are blooming will spread their seeds all over the Bosque. The seeds root in late May and sink their rootlets to the pace of the retreating water table. In that case, we will see the sprouting of thousands of young Cottonwoods, producing a new generation of future big trees. I expect also that grasses and the Willow population will grow back and fill open spaces within a few years. In a year the Bosque will be teeming again with birds. Larger wildlife will still pass through silently in the early morning hours -- more visible, but also more able to spot threats from a distance. We'll place wildlife cameras to document their presence.

A lot of the Willows look pretty done in. Will they survive?

Willows are very flexible and resilient. They bend and are sometimes mangled in a high flow. But they rebound. They grow and regenerate by roots, seeds, and by stakes cuttings that root when stuck in moist soil. A fair number of the willows in the Bosque were dead. Now they will have more space and water to grow back more vigorously.

Are the Russian Olives gone for good? What's the citric acid application for?

Russian Olives are also very resilient and grow from seed, roots, and cut stumps. To prevent them from growing back it was essential to remove their roots and stumps as much as we were able. It was impossible to remove a small number of stumps without causing great damage to the Cottonwoods and Willows, or the stream banks. The cut stumps that were not removed were brushed with an organic herbicide composed of a 21% vinegar and citric acid solution in water, with molasses as an emulsifier and sticking agent. Its effectiveness is limited, and some stumps may still need to be cut and treated again. I hope that landowners are willing to continue as good stewards of the place and take a saw to hand once or twice a year to cut off any resprouts. If that is done diligently, the roots will be starved of the necessary nutrients and wither after several years.

Where do all those huge piles of wood and roots end up? Why weren't they chipped too? Will the chips encourage grass to grow?

The piles of roots and root wads were taken to transfer stations; some were brought to Eldorado, but most had to be hauled to the Buckman Transfer Station in Santa Fe to prevent them from sprouting again when left on site. Some wood has been left on site for local use. The thinner branches - up to about 2" diameter -- were chipped and placed on bare areas as mulch. Chipping bigger logs and stumps requires a huge machine, which would have been cost prohibitive, dangerous, and wasteful. The chips will be spread and raked. If they are concentrated in mats of an inch thick or more, grass growth will be smothered. Again, it would be great if landowners could help to spread the mulch out as much as possible; people are also free to pick some of it up for use around their homes.

title: {GVFR Badly Needs Volunteer Firefighters, EMTs (... and a grill)}
body:
80% of our Fire Department's calls are medical and with the loss of Jon Stern, who is moving into town, we have only one EMT. If you are interested in helping your community, contact Chief Jean Moya for details by July. Emergency Medical Services classes (for State certification) start in August at the Santa Fe Community College. The Fire Academy begins in September. Volunteerism is going down across the County. Wouldn't it be terrible to imagine Galisteo without a Fire Department again?

Also, from the sublime to the delicious, the GVFR would welcome the donation of a Charcoal Weber Grill so that on the hot summer nights of our monthly business meetings, the station's meeting room is kept cooler while we enjoy great food from our resident chef, Cindy Lux. title: Mailing List Notice and Wildlife Sightings Request
body: NOTICE: If you didn't receive last month's El Puente it's because the Post Office has a new machine that is very fussy on address details. I think we've got our mailinglist (which worked fine until the machines took over) up to snuff now. Let El Puente (flip14@wildblue.net) know about wildlife sightings over the summer? We should know our often invisible neighbors. Your editor and her dog spotted two bounding mule deer off Avenida Vieja the other day. One night there was a sad, single coyote howling and yipping ... but there was no answer.

title: GVFR to the Rescue: Cerro Pelon Fire
body: In the early afternoon of June 7th, GVFR member Corey McGillicuddy noticed a small plume of smoke on the west side of Cerro Pelon. Firefighter Gwen Feisst was first to respond, with the brush truck, and she alerted the Cerro Pelon Ranch manager. Ed Epping and Steve Moya followed, along with the County Wildland Fire Crew and Med 80. Soon there were nine personnel on site. "The wind picked up and that puppy started to run," says Epping. The lightning-caused fire quickly jumped from a half acre to four acres. Then, miraculously, the winds slowed and humidity increased. It was totally controlled by the time all but the wildland crew left around 8PM. Ranch manager Jeff Hilliard said that a major lightning storm the previous night had fried a gate and burned fence posts. Keep your eyes on Cerro Pelon, the Bosque, and our whole environment during the very hot summer to come. Call 911 if you see smoke or flames.

title: Joshway Short Achieves EMT Certification
body: Joshway Short passed his EMT Basic and will be licensed after the National Registry Test. Wheh! Another Emergency Medical Technician for Galisteo.

title: More Good News for the Bosque: Governor's River Reclamation Fund Award
body: The Governor's River Reclamation Fund has awarded $170,000 for Round 2 of the Galisteo River Project. Work will focus on more plantings of native species, removal of Russian Olives between El Puente and the boundary with San Cristobal Ranch, and stream correction so it stops undermining the high clay embankment in the same area. Work could begin any time between early March and December, 2017. A project plan will be shared with the community and landowners for input.

title: The Rio Galisteo Over Time: Interview with Jan Willem Jansens
body:
Part II: Interview with Jan Willem Jansens
[Bracketed interruptions from El Puente]

You've talked about how mobile the Rio Galisteo has been even in its recent history.

Landscape features around the village and upstream seem to suggest that the Galisteo Creek was a narrow, gently meandering stream through grasslands, which must have been at the level of the older houses bordering the creek. I imagine that there were clumps of Willows, here and there a single Cottonwood, some Box elder, and perhaps a few clumps of young Junipers. There may also have been some patches of raw sand and clay and some old abandoned channels. All these features describe a landscape of an alluvial fan, an ever-changing, large sediment plume that spilled out below the [northern] "hogback" and was bounded by the rises in the landscape on the east and west until it merged with the sediment bed of the San Cristobal Creek south of the village.

[The diary of] C.E. Pancoast [who was on his way to the Gold Rush in 1849, describes how] he crossed the Galisteo Creek on a single plank; there was no "arroyo," meaning that the creek was free flowing and not down cut as it is today. Other documents describe how the creek fed acequias that irrigated fields until the early 20th century. [Joe Anaya, now in his nineties, recalls that an acequia ran along what is now NM 41 past La Sala and the church and the Sandovals' homes, and then, according to John Benjamin, wound around the hills below John Young's home and to the west. Laterals may have fed south along the narrow fields allotted in the Galisteo Grant. David Kammer, who wrote the nomination for the State Register of Historical Properties, states that this acequia "and small reservoir .... ceased to operate in 1926." Another ditch on the east side of the creek feeding the Cadial is less well documented. Research continues .... ]

Between 1880 and 1892, some cataclysmic event drastically changed the creek's course and shape. Between documents, stories, some old maps, and what I know about that period of time, I pieced together that in or shortly after 1880 one of several heavy floods hammered the creek, probably exacerbated by the narrowing of the creek bed and floodplain resulting from the construction of the railroad grade in and along the flood plain, upstream between Glorieta and Lamy in 1879-1880. In any case, there is evidence that in 1892, farmers [in the pasture called the Cadial on the village's eastern boundary] no longer repaired their irrigation dams because the stream had cut too deep to feed the acequias.

It is my understanding -- from old meander patterns upstream and an old map -- that the creek moved from an alignment just east of where State Road 41 is now to the current location further east of the village. [This must have been before the late 18th century, since the barracks and later the Davis y Ortiz hacienda would have been underwater.] In a few decades, it dug itself into its own old sediments. Over time, floods widened the trench it was in and created the current 100-yard wide arroyo floor which was probably entirely barren, full of sand and clay, with some patches of grass, an occasional clump of Willows and a grove of Cottonwoods between what is now Harmony Hammond's and Janice Griscom's properties. [Photos from the early 1950s and earlier show a barren arroyo.] That led to the construction of El Puente, the old bridge [which was preceded by a steel truss bridge that washed out at an unknown date, perhaps the 1920s].

I believe that all this started to change in the 1950s, when more Cottonwoods were planted [by Phil McKee's mother-in-law]. Sand started to pile up behind the trees and the bridge pillars and the highway bridge [constructed in 1936]. As more sediment accumulated on the floodplain, more terrain along the creek became too high and dry to sustain Willows, and in the last three decades, more drought-tolerant Tamarisk and later Russian Olives invaded the Willows and Cottonwoods.

And so the Bosque changed once again, becoming in many places a dense mass of spiny brush. Many Willows and some of the Cottonwoods died in the competition for water, light, and nutrients with Russian Olives, causing a partly dead thicket that increased the risk of wildfire and reduced the habitat quality for wildlife. Parts of the channel dug themselves into the sand and the water flowed fairly rapidly through the bosque, with only large floods spreading all across the valley floor. That's the situation I found in 1998 when I first started working in Galisteo.

Back to the present. Are there still plans for an improved trail in the Bosque?

I am not aware of any plans for an improved trail. It is beneficial for birds and wildlife that the current path remains simple and unimproved (unpaved). The bosque is not a park; it is still a pretty wild piece of nature: a wetland. We should anticipate that bank-to-bank flooding will continue yearly, slightly eased by the removal of so many trees. And ecologically that is good. We may also see some sediment moving from the upper to the lower parts of the bosque, which is also just fine in the bigger picture. The trail, if left in the same location, will continue to be inundated and covered with mud in floods. It would be costly to help it withstand either sedimentation or the eroding and undermining effects of flooding. Only if the trail is brought to somewhat higher ground can it be kept drier and somewhat less susceptible to flood impacts.

For me it comes down to the character of the bosque and a sense of balance with nature; I think a good trail in this place is one that blends in, the product of benign neglect. If it washes out a bit, that can be fixed with ease.

title: Conscious Solutions
body: "Global warming is a challenge to the consciousness of all humanity; not only as a technological or scientific dilemma, but also as a matter of planetary survival and being conscious of our human responsibility to life on earth. The solutions to global warming will be found not only in what we must stop doing, but what we must do on entirely new levels of consciousness." -- Chris Griscom. She is initiating a global call for a Conscious Solutions Initiative to reverse and balance the "greenhouse effect" through de-manifestation. She calls for "a new, specifically designed Conscious Technology," sponsored by The Light Institute and The Nizhoni Institute for Global Consciousness. For information, go to Eco SOS.

title: Michael D. Anaya State Senate Campaign
body: Michael D. Anaya came in second to Liz Stefanics in the race for the Democratic candidate for State Senate District 39, beating the other two contenders, including Hugh Ley, the Santa Fe New Mexican's choice. Mike made a good run, and in a campaign letter he quoted his late father, Joe M. Anaya: "There are people in this world that make things happen, people that watch things happen, and people that wonder what just happened."

title: Marco Serna District Attorney Nomination
body: Marco Serna, who won the Democratic nomination for District Attorney in the First District, was a student of Jan Saunders at St. Michaels.

title: Janine Stern Gallery Expansion
body: Janine Stern's gallery Janine Contemporary Industri has moved into a large new space at 328 S. Guadalupe in the Railyard. After a hiatus for remodeling, she is opening on July 2, 5-7, with an exhibition on "New Identity," featuring 22 local and national artists, until Aug.20.

title: Dave Montoya's Daughter Emily Graduates from Marine Boot Camp
body: Dave Montoya's family traveled to Chicago to see daughter Emily graduate from Marine boot camp. She is now stationed in San Antonio.

title: KSFR Radio Cafe Discussion on Bosque Remediation
body: Roger Taylor, Jan Willem Jansens, and Jim Matison from WildEarth Guardians were on KSFR's Radio Cafe on May 13th talking about the Bosque remediation. It was an illuminating discussion, especially in terms of the bureaucratic hoops everyone had to jump through to complete the project. A lesser team would have given up in disgust. (The program may still be available as a podcast on KSFR's website.)

title: Harmony Hammond Solo Exhibition in New York
body: Harmony Hammond's solo show at the Alexander Gray Gallery in New York has been well received and reviewed. An interview with her appeared in the on-line journal Hyperallergic.

title: Ray Belcher Photography Featured in El Palacio
body: Ray Belcher's lovely photograph of the gate to the old Galisteo cemetery with the church spire in the background was featured in El Palacio, Summer, 2016.

title: The Legal Tender in Lamy Reopens
body: The Legal Tender in Lamy has been re-opened by the owner of the Swiss Bakery in Santa Fe, and is awaiting its wine/beer license. Word on the street is that it has some kinks to work out but should be on track soon.

title: Caroline Hinkley Berlin Foto Biennale
body: Caroline Hinkley will show her work from Iceland in the Berlin Foto Biennale 2016.

title: Catherine Ferguson Exhibition at El Museo Cultural
body: Catherine Ferguson is showing her paintings and an installation at El Museo Cultural in the Railyard. Daughter of Rooms (including Susan Ferguson's Mexico years) opens July 8 (1-3, with Videopoems) and on July 16 is a Poetry Reading.

title: Bill Mitchell Installations at Currents New Media Festival
body: Former resident and current GVFR member Bill Mitchell is showing two installations (one of which includes the Galisteo Rodeo grounds) at the 2016 Currents New Media Festival at El Museo Cultural through June 26.

title: Cerro Pelon Ranch for Sale
body: The recent issue of the glossy realtors' magazine Leading Estates of the World announces that the Cerro Pelon Ranch -- "a sparkling sanctuary in the vast American Southwest... with the allure of ancient petroglyphs, pottery shards and Pueblo ruins juxtaposed with Tadao Ando's dramatic contemporary compound" (see above) -- is for sale, price on request. At some 20,000 acres (32 square miles), it is "among the largest properties in Santa Fe County and is home to the iconic western movie town originally built for the film Silverado.... Meandering through the northern boundary of the ranch, the Galisteo Creek provides scenic vistas from open waterways to picturesque canopies of shady cottonwoods. The land and water have been conscientiously managed to provide beautiful grazing pastures within a productive cattle ranch." More in the next issue on the possible ramifications of this sale for our community.

title: Lucy Tafoya Memorial Cross and Accident Prevention
body: For many years there has been a cross at the intersection of NM 41 and US285, in memory of Lucy Tafoya. (Was she a Galisteña?) Another descanso was recently avoided when a drunk driver crashed through the same barricade. His vehicle hung up on the guard rail and he survived.

title: Vista Clara Ranch/Spa Sale to Chi Center
body: The Vista Clara Ranch/Spa was foreclosed, and has been sold to The Chi Center for the ancient Chinese practice called Chi Gong (Qigong), or "life energy work."

title: Orenda Healing International Four Winds Journal Call for Submissions
body: In 1992, former resident Valentine McKay-Riddell founded Orenda Healing International (OHI), a nonprofit organization that originally focused on arts-based community service programs in New Mexico, Northern California, and Oregon. Its mission has expanded to support research in the field of alternative healing. Until 6/30, its online publication Four Winds Journal is accepting submissions of art, writing essays, poems and visual art on the theme "Winds of Change" for the Fall issue. OHI also welcomes research proposals, online courses, tutorials, and webinars. To join the email list, go to orenda@orenda-arts.org.

body: IF YOU HAVE NEVER SPONSORED AN ISSUE OF EL PUENTE (AND IF YOU HAVE), PLEASE CONSIDER DOING SO (AGAIN) TO KEEP US GOING AS WE COMPLETE OUR 20m YEAR OF PUBLICATION: $80, check made out to GCA with "newsletter" in memo line; send to El Puente, 14 Avenida Vieja, Galisteo, 87540.

title: Movies Galore
body: Irritating as it is to have cars speeding down Avenida Vieja and parking across driveways to make "important" phone calls, it's always kind of fun to have movies filming in Galisteo. This month has been an extravaganza, with La Sala and Priscilla Hoback's property as locations, as well as sets and base camps on Cerro Pelon Ranch and on San Cristobal Ranch. For a couple of days the Netflix movie Godless (a title which almost lost them access to church parking) crammed downtown Galisteo with gigantic trucks, an outdoor cafeteria, buggies and buckboards, and a kind of 19111-century farmer's market on Via La Puente. I was offered some chile peppers as they dismantled, but the other baskets of produce were headed for another (11011-southwestern?) set. The typo-ridden "film notice" left at residences for Woman Walks Ahead, on San Cristobal, said filming would continue in September-October, 7AM-6PM, with access on Avenida Vieja, La Vega, and La Otra Vanda, so watch your dogs on the roads, especially in SoGal. The film is an independent feature, an 1890s drama starring Jessica Chastain, Sam Rockwell, and Michael Greyeyes. Netflix gave a very generous donation to La Sala and another is expected for the GCA. Woman Walks Ahead will pay $100 per day to the GCA for access through the village.

title: Goodbye to Nancy Helle
body: Goodbye to Nancy Helle, who has graced Galisteo for decades and had to move to the west coast for health reasons. We miss her already.

title: Hello to Catherine Rose McQueen
body: And Hello to Galisteo's newest citizen, who was born on August 4th to Caroline Seigel and Matthew McQueen. Catherine Rose McQueen, with her brother Jack, resides on Avenida Vieja, turning it into Avenida Joven (or Mozo). Daddy, of course, is running for re-election as our State Representative for District 50. You can donate to his campaign at his website: www.mcqueenfornm.com.

title: Muriel Fariello's My View in The New Mexican
body: On August 12th, The New Mexican published "Village of Galisteo is a happening place" -- a "My View" by Muriel Fariello, who should now be appointed our Chamber of Commerce. "The village of Galisteo," she writes, "epitomizes a melting pot of wonderful people who care about their neighbors. Many residents are writers, artists, poets, movie directors, fashion designers, doctors, professors, financial consultants and elected officials, some of whom are well-known around the world. In addition, there are dedicated activists who, over the years, have joined other communities to keep oil companies from drilling in Santa Fe County. We have also prevented development that would have a negative impact on our resources.... People here are from all walks of life with a common goal of caring for their neighbors ... We are close enough to enjoy the activities of Santa Fe yet far enough away to have that small town feel." And she goes on to praise the GCA, La Sala, and the Bosque restoration project. (Hey, what about the Fire Department and the newsletter?) She ended with a plug for the Studio Tour. Let's see if this sells some of our empty houses.

title: Bruce Nauman Profiled in The New York Times
body: In early September, The New York Times ran a lengthy feature: "Bruce Nauman, Art Provocateur, Returns. Are You Ready?" The writer visited him in Galisteo, described as "far from Santa Fe, half an hour out on the sparsely inhabited high desert," where he and Susan Rothenburg have lived since 1989 in a "humble and plain ... middle-class American" home. Nauman's latest videos (developed with local artist Bruce Hamilton) take off from his 1968 classic, Walking with Contrapposto. Also mentioned was the 1987 video Clown Torture; the actor was sometime Galisteo resident Walt Stevens. This fall Nauman's Contrapposto Studies, i-vii will be shown at Sperone Westwater in New York and the Philadelphia Museum.

title: Peggy Diggs in National Exhibition
body: This summer Peggy Diggs showed work in "Of the People," a national exhibition at Smack Mellon Gallery in Brooklyn reflecting "of-the-moment political opinions shaping the 2016 presidential race." Her piece, Heirloom, considered the fairness (or not) of ballot design with a handcrafted "cozy."

title: Woody Gwyn's American Vista Exhibition
body: A show of Woody Gwyn's virtuoso realist paintings titled "American Vista" was at the LewAllen Galleries until Sept. 5th. In the catalogue Kenneth R. Marvel calls Gwyn "this extraordinary interpreter of the poetic possibilities of landscape" who "transcends mere description" to take us into "the realm of meditative imagining."

title: Judy Tuwaletstiwa's Glass Show
body: Judy Tuwaletstiwa's glass show at the William Siegal Gallery in August was reportedly the usual hit.

title: Harmony Hammond at Georgia O'Keeffe Museum Symposium
body: Harmony Hammond was interviewed at length in The Brooklyn Rail (July-Aug.). On Sept. 15th, she and Lucy Lippard (old feminist activist pals since the early 1970s) spoke together on artist's archives at a Georgia O'Keeffe Museum symposium.

title: Arthur Lynn Wins Knife Show Awards
body: Arthur Lynn won two First Place awards at the Denver Custom Knife Show: Best Damascus Knife and Best Hand-forged Primitive Knife.

title: Jose Ortiz y Pino Political Note from 1966
body: From the New Mexican, August 31, 1966: "Senator Jose Ortiz y Pino to the [Republican] David Cargo for Governor camp" after being defeated in the Democratic Primary for re-election to his State Senate seat.

title: Nocturnal Animals Premieres at Venice Film Festival
body: Nocturnal Animals, Tom Ford's new film, "an art world thriller" starring Amy Adams, premiered at the Venice Film Festival.

title: Galisteo Basin Preserve Completes New Trail
body: The Galisteo Basin Preserve is just completing a new mile-long, multi-use trail linking the Cowboy Shack trail with Leona's Loop and Glenn's Way, forming a continuous 7-mile loop.

title: Matthew McQueen Quoted on State Employee Turnover
body: State Rep Matthew McQueen was quoted in The New Mexican, as being worried about the revolving door between public servants and industry (since Environment Secretary Flynn quit to join the fossil fuel industry). He said the turnover of top state workers is "certainly not good for the health of the agency, but if you have professional state employees who are allowed to do their jobs, then the impacts should be muted." However, he added, "whether or not they have been allowed to under past leadership [at the Environment Dept.] is up for question."

title: Eric Thomas's Native American Scout Figure Accepted to Indian Market
body: Eric Thomas, a Rhode Island Narragansett, and ten-year Galisteo resident, had "a dream come true" when his figure of a Native American scout (c.1870's), complete with Union army coat, rifle and guns, beaded moccasins, and fringe leggings, was accepted by SWAIA for a juried contemporary show in the Santa Fe Convention Center in the August Indian Market. All the costumes and accessories for this 20" ball-jointed figure with resin cast head were made from scratch. His work is said to defy categories of traditional doll making and modern sculpture.

title: Opening of Qigong Center
body:
The Center for Wisdom Healing Qigong has a new home. Internationally recognized teacher and healer Master Mingtong Gu purchased the magnificent Vista Clara Ranch and Spa in Galisteo this past spring and will be opening the new center on October 1. A manifestation of Master Gu's long-held dream, this new qigong retreat center will be a place where people from around the world gather to awaken and heal body, mind, and heart. It is a continuation and expansion of the world's largest medicine-less qigong center, the venerable Huaxia Zhineng Qigong Training and Recovery Center in China.

Situated on seventy-nine acres with ancient cottonwood trees, a fishpond, labyrinths, and a striking circular building set into the earth, reminiscent of sacred underground ceremonial kivas, this healing center will be a powerful energetic gateway to health, promoting peace, harmony and love for generations to come.

Master Gu fell in love with New Mexico during his first trip here in 2013. He explained his life-changing decision to buy Vista Clara: "New Mexico is still a relatively new experience for me. From my very first trip here, I felt the magic of the high desert. The historical energy of Native American and Spanish cultures are very much alive on this property, and it fills me with awe. The union of heaven and earth is tangible, there is a deep primal life force at work here. This is the ideal place to honor ourselves, our community, our ancestors, and our kinship with the Earth. The kiva and land in Galisteo connect us with the reciprocity of the natural world, and is a gift for everyone's benefit."

Inaugural Grand Opening festivities begin with An Evening of Wisdom Healing Qigong with Master Gu on Friday, September 30, at the Santa Fe Community College. The Grand Opening Ceremony takes place the next day, Saturday, October 1, followed by a community potluck, world kirtan music by the Bhakti Boogie Band, and Dances of Universal Peace. Completing the weekend on Sunday, October 2, Master Gu will be teaching an all-day qigong workshop at the new center: "It will serve as a physical portal for connecting people locally, and globally, to the self-healing and self-empowering approach of Wisdom Healing Qigong. The center will energetically support the expansion and integration of all wisdom traditions and wellness modalities."

Restoring wholeness in ourselves and our world is the vision Master Gu is holding for us all.

Information on Grand Opening weekend festivities: 707-347-6489. ChiCenter.com. Questions: admin@chicenter.com.

Thanks to Debra Rosenman for this contribution, edited by El Puente.

title: {Lights Out: GVFR to the Rescue}
body: On Tuesday, Sept. 6th, when GVFR members are usually settling in for the monthly business meeting and a Cindy Lux Special, half the department was missing. A branch on a tree by Priscilla Hoback's studio had fallen (not for the first time) on electric wires. We were all blacked out for several hours, except of course, those of us basking in the light off the grid. The GVFR meeting was held by romantic flashlight and the tree limb has been punished.

title: Galisteo Connected
body:
From July to September of 2016, Ranchitos and the village of Galisteo got another choice for Internet connectivity. Over the summer Century Link rolled out DSL service that offers real broadband internet with speeds up to 40 mbps (mega bits per second) download and 5mbps upload. Unlike satellite service like Wild Blue and Exede there are no data caps. Galistefios can now surf the web and download movies just like the rest of the civilized world.

The process that led up to this started when the GCA asked one of its board members to make getting better internet services a priority for the community. Over the course of almost two years the GCA, as part of the State Broadband Task Force, was represented at PRC meetings and relentlessly hounded Century Link State Government Relations Director Johnny Montoya.

In August of 2015 we learned that Century Link had applied for and would receive CAFII (Connect America Fund) money to the tune of $66 million. The GCA agitated, with the help of George Clarke (New Mexico Department of Information Technology), David Griscom (Santa Fe County Department of Economic Development), and Sean Moody (City of Santa Fe Department of Economic Development), to be one of the communities to benefit from the CAFII monies. We were successful and most of the community has taken advantage and benefited from this new service.

For more information about setting up an account please contact Jared I. Roybal, Retail Manager: 1 Montgomery Plaza, 4411 San Mateo Blvd NE, Suite E6, Albuquerque, NM 87109; Cell (505) 228-3467; jared.roybal@centurylink.com.

(In case you hadn't guessed, the GCA Board member who did all this work and got us Broadband was the author. Thanks, Michael!)

title: {Mark Edward Benigno (1960-2016)}
body: Mark passed away suddenly of a heart attack on Sept.261" at the age of 56. He was born in New Orleans and raised in Houston and Dallas. Having played baseball in high school, he continued his excellent pitching at Texas A&M. After graduation he opened a successful marketing company in Dallas. Years later he moved to Galisteo and worked on nearby ranches. When in the village, he statied eve1y day with cups of coffee with neighbors and was always ready to help anyone with any project any time. He appreciated a shot of Bourbon, a Cuban cigar, and a good laugh. Mark gave of himself tirelessly to make others' lives better. He delivered meals for Seniors in the Galisteo and El Dorado area. He and Sherry divided their time between Galisteo and Pennsylvania and traveled extensively. He loved adventure and created memorable moments whereever he found himself. On frequent travels to Guatemala, he took hungry children out to eat, bought clothes and school supplies for the needy. Mark is mourned by his beloved partner Sherry Kerstetter and his many friends here. At a memorial at Priscilla Hoback's on Oct. 23,ct, his humor and generosity was recalled and his friends made it clear they felt lucky to have known him. Mark is survived by Sherry, his mother, five brothers and sisters, and nieces and nephews. (Thanks to Sherry Kerstetta)

title: Galisteo Village Center Revitalization Action Plan Update
body: Following the County approval of the Galisteo Community Plan & Zoning in 2012, the Planning Committee (Roger Taylor, Anna Cardenas, Leslie Dilworth, Michael Golino, Frank Hirsch, Lucy Lippard) began working with the NM Frontiers Program to develop plans for limited growth and revitalization in Galisteo along NM 41 -- to respond to the loss of businesses since the financial crash of 2008. When a draft plan was submitted, we were considered to have successfully completed the Frontiers program -- the first community in the County to do so! The County decided to sponsor this effort, and contributed $20K to hire consultants to assist us with the Galisteo Village Center Revitalization Action Plan. The revised plan will be presented at the Nov. 121" breakfast meeting (seep. I). The community will 1) review the prior planning efforts in Galisteo; 2) gather ideas and input on the village center; and 3) amend and prioritize Revitalization Actions to launch implementation.

title: Thornton Ranch Open Space Master Plan
body: Santa Fe County held a public informational meeting at the Community Center on October 20th to discuss the Thornton Ranch Open Space Master Plan. A draft master plan of 4-5 proposed public access trails totaling c. 7 miles, with parking areas and historical display panels, situated on 2,440-acres of County-owned land across the railroad tracks to the south of County Rd 42. The presentation attracted a large audience of area residents, hikers, equestrians, and bicyclists. The county has made this a high priority project, and funds are to be provided through the Open Space/Trails Bond issue on the November ballot. Once funding has been approved, before the trails will be open to the public, it will take about four years of additional planning, construction, and sign-offs from various County, State and Federal Departments, as well as from eight to ten Pueblos whose ancestors lived in the Galisteo Basin.

title: La Sala Progress Update
body: La Sala made great strides to completion this year. The interior walls were covered with off-white American Clay, and the bancos and trim boards were painted with a gray-green popular in the late 1800's (thanks to the Netflix film production crew.) A grant paid for materials & equipment for the 2-coat final mud plastering on all the exterior walls, and community volunteers, interns and a crew from Castleton University in Vermont provided the labor. A second grant helped pay for two of the most damaged windows to be repaired, sealed and painted (thanks to volunteers Ed Epping and Charlie Holloway). The Board and Gallery Committee did a remarkable job opening the gallery this year to successful sales, a busy Studio Tour artists preview and info center, and the recent Salsa dance. More to come in 2017 !

body: On Saturday, July 91\ the GCA hosted a Saturday Coffee & Breakfast in the bosque. After delicious offerings from Cafe Fina kicked in, groups formed to do follow-up maintenance work from the bosque restoration in March/ April this year. Blockages in the stream bed were removed and dead willows were piled higher up on the embankments. (BTW, dried willow wood makes excellent kindling - bums hot! Anyone is welcome to haul some away.) Russian Olive shoots were pruned and bagged and a citric acid solution was applied to the stumps. Alas, it didn't help. This fall hundreds of stubborn shoots are flourishing again. More work to do.

title: Letter to Galistenos - Ten In November Fund Raiser
body: For over 40 years the Galisteo Community Association has worked hard to preserve the charm and beauty of our village, helping to keep our community vibrant and viable. This work takes money: It takes money to maintain and repair our wonderful community center, sustain the bosque, work to calm traffic, and meet with the county to guarantee that planning and zoning ordinances make sense and benefit us. It takes money to protect our Galisteo Basin from the encroachment of gas and oil and other destructive commercial developments. The work the GCA does is for all of us: It means having a community center available for weddings and other events. It increases the value of our properties. It protects and enriches our community. To continue this important work, we are reaching out to you, friends and neighbors, in a new way as we enter the 21s1 century: Please, join us in our first Ten In November fund raiser. Ten In November enables us, the residents of Ranchitos and Galisteo Village, to calculate a fair and equitable donation to the GCA: we suggest each household gives an amount equal to 10% of the yearly property tax bill that comes in November. For example: If your property tax is $2150, you would donate $215 for the year. If your property tax is $532, you would donate $53. We already have commitments from twenty households. We invite you to join us. Thank you, The GCA Board
