title: Overlay: Community Revitalization
body:
The November 17th community meeting with County Planning staff member Lucy Foma and consultant David Breecker provoked a lively conversation on possible improvements through a "Community Overlay" on the Traditional Community Plan. The purpose was to define a few less restrictive, "conditional" commercial uses outside the zoned commercial corridor designated by the Planning Committee for the Sustainable Land Development Code.

Parking for La Sala, Studio Tour, movies, and possible new enterprises was a big issue. A parking lot on community-owned property along NM41? Or dispersed on smaller lots? Suggested changes included community identified design standards -- for commercial structures only. Jim Sloan warned against a "boutique business vision." The long-desired coffee shop at the old Tienda Anaya is no closer to fruition, although the 2010 permits are still valid under the old code. Scott Canning brought up the possibility of a lavender farm on the former Galisteo Inn property.

Priscilla Hoback argued that all these plans were "putting the cart before the horse"; first it is up to the community to make Galisteo "more interesting so people want to come here." Anna Cardenas advocated participation by the young people (though none attended the meeting). Liz Rose suggested a free library, and Denise Lynch a little museum for the tribes in the area and more "real industry" (like a woodworking shop), not just tourism. Other proposals were signage, maps, horse and buggy tours, a convenience store, more emphasis on the healing community (massage, yoga, Qijong). Residents expressed reservations about signage, colored crossways and paths at the "Plaza Nueva," and the advent of trucks making deliveries, lights, and other annoyances that would come with increased activity. The point was made that at least a couple of businesses are necessary to support each other. On the wish list were public restrooms (for La Sala and Studio Tour), parking, music, coffee shop, slower traffic, and less dust.

It was proposed that the section of the current Overlay draft on "Permitted Uses" should be amended to read: Offices, small-scale shops, restaurants, tap and tasting rooms, exhibitions and galleries, community centers, porous or permeable surface parking, and welcome centers. (Highway rest stops was deleted.) Under "Conditional Uses," there is some overlap with permitted uses: An office or store with residence, covered atriums and public enclosures, bed and breakfast inns, retreats, theater/dance/music establishments, exhibitions and art galleries, performing arts and supporting establishments, permanent outdoor stages or similar structures. It was agreed that the limitation to 2,500 sq. ft. should be changed to 5,000 sq. ft. (the old Inn was 10,000 sq. ft.).

Roger Taylor is working with the County Film Dept. on regulations for movie uses. Michael Golino will work on the website, which exists but needs work. El Puente would post old issues.

This is not the first time Galisteo has re-invented itself as a tourist destination, as Maria Ortiz y Pino noted at the meeting. In 1959 Mary Branham reported in New Mexico Magazine that the new people restoring old adobes were bringing commerce to the once destitute village, despite the loss of both the school and the Post Office by the end of the decade. In the 1960s, Galisteo was not the quiet, quaint residential community it is today. It was home to a number of younger families. Children attended school in Stanley. (Anna Cardenas recalls the school bus leaving at 5:30 AM.) Village phone numbers were "Galisteo 1, Galisteo 2, Galisteo 3 .... "

On the façade of the former Ortiz hacienda (Gwyn home) was a sign reading "Historical Trading Post Frank Ortiz y Davis and Sons." It boasted a "museum" and a popular bar, and the nearby La Mancha restaurant. Anglo businesses had also sprung up, operating out of La Sala de San Jose. These included "Spanish and Mexican Imports, Gay and Glittering Gifts, Elita Wilson's Southwest Dresses," as well as La Vela -- "Candles, Ceramics, Baskets, Gifts" run by Jeannie McKee and her mother Helen Hover. "Hacienda de San Francisco" was southwestern painter Maria Salazar's studio, and the Blue Bulto -- "Something Old, Something New" -- was run by Henry and Virginia Wicks. Next door was Major Felten's Galisteo Craftsmen, offering "the most beautiful custom-made furniture in the Southwest."

All this was part of a major push to "revitalize" the village, but a 1962 Westways article warned "Business is rotten in Galisteo." Lamy was recommended as another stop for "Wild West atmosphere," thanks to the reconstruction of the Legal Tender bar and restaurant (owned by oil magnate Robert Anderson and featuring the beautiful, grandiose bar that dates from the days when it was called The Pink Garter).

An undated report (probably from the 1960s) in the State Library calls on the State to establish a visitor center to the Galisteo Basin in the village and to acquire "certain points of interest such as the Galisteo Pueblo, the San Cristobal ruins, petroglyph sites, picnic and rest areas, along with reconstructed hotels, craft shops, horseback riding facilities, and similar establishments .... "

title: Frank M. Sandoval II (1937-2016)
body:
On November 7, 2016, Frank was called away from this earth to be with our father in heaven.

What a multitude of people accompanied my brother Frank, for his services on Saturday, Nov. 12th at Nuestra Senora de los Remedios in Galisteo. The turnout of family, friends, and acquaintances overflowed our little church. It was obvious that Frank had made a lasting impression on so many people.

Frank was the fourth child, born Feb. 9, 1937, of Frank C. Sandoval and Lucia A. Mora, and would one day have thirteen siblings. He grew up in Galisteo, attended elementary school here, then later in Stanley. On May 17, 1958 he married Doris Baca, the love of his life. Together they raised three wonderful boys -- Ernie, Leroy, and Jerome -- and one lovely young lady, Mary Louise. They are all grown up now and have blessed him and Doris with thirteen grandchildren, and five great grandchildren. Frank lived a very full life with his family closely around him in Stanley, where he worked for the King Brothers Ranch. He was a lifelong member of Nuestra Senora de los Remedios Parish, and belonged to the St. Joseph's Society.

I will always remember my brother Frank for his gentleness and patience in every situation. He had a wonderful singing voice, and could whistle a tune that would cheer people up if they were having a bad day. One of my fondest memories is of the days when my brothers would go out singing Las Mananitas for New Years Eve. I can still hear that amazing voice that blessed my brother Frank. We are left with many wonderful memories of him that will comfort us as we carry on, and live each day as he would have done. All his family and friends will miss him dearly. - Stella Maestas

"I shared all my woes with him and he grinned and said his cover technology could take them all away .... Nobody else in the US has a system quite like Grow Y'Own, with summer and winter covers working in tandem during the coldest times of the year." After eight years of business, Kuhne, a former custom home builder, has his hooped, raised, and covered beds in 30 states and Canada. title: Plague Strikes
body:
In mid-December, John Watson-Jones, a retired zookeeper who lives on Avenida Vieja, notified the community that his 70-pound dog, Otis, who has been known to chase down and kill a jackrabbit, turned up positive for plague. He started limping on one leg, then within a day became very reluctant to move at all, went off food and water, and developed a fever of 104.5 degrees within 2 days. An antibiotic by IV and then pills cleared up his signs within a day, and the blood test later confirmed the suspicion. He had not been out of Galisteo during the previous week. John and Angie's other dog, Pearl, was not infected.

John warns us that biting or being bitten by a rodent (not just by fleas) is the most common way dogs get the plague. Two to seven days can elapse before there are any signs. It's also possible for pets to transmit the plague to people. As some of us may remember, there was a case several years ago, when a couple from Eldorado got the plague from a dog's flea bite and were in New York City when it hit. Doctors there didn't even consider the possibility until they contacted Dr. Louise Abel in Santa Fe. Both victims were seriously ill and one lost a leg.

John adds that although such cases are rare, at this time of year rodents come in closer to human habitations, and plague is carried by fleas on rabbits, ground squirrels, pack-rats, prairie dogs and gophers. We've also had an increase in bosque sightings of deer, raccoons, and bobcats, often associated with rodents. It would be a good idea to keep a close eye on your animals while out walking and also to watch for changes in behaviors.

The Eldorado Animal Clinic recommends that we treat our pets with Frontline (or other brands) year round.

title: Film Production Guidelines and Protocols for Galisteo
body:
Following the big Fall season of filming here in Galisteo, several members of the community and the GCA Board met with representatives of the Santa Fe Film Office (SFFO). We reviewed what worked well and those activities that caused issues and complaints. A work group was formed to study the process by which permits are obtained, locations identified, and film sets organized. We came up with a list of suggested protocols for future filming in Galisteo. The goal is to encourage filming, as overall it was a positive experience for many in the community, but also to control aspects that were not so positive.

The following draft film protocols are being further refined through ongoing discussions with the SFFO Board. If you have questions or comments, please direct them to Judy Tuwaletstiwa, Roger Taylor, or Michael Golino.

Notification: The SFFO notifies the Galisteo Community Association Board contact when a production company identifies our village as a potential site. The pre-production team location manager, a SFFO representative and one to three GCA Board members will then meet to discuss these points:

Overview: Where will filming take place? Duration? Number of people involved, etc.?

Location Selections: If needed, work with the production team to identify locations and connect with the owners of those sites.

Traffic: What are the expectations of traffic volume and flow? Will there be peak times during the on-site filming? How is it controlled? How is it routed? Should it have a monitor? Can it be reduced by shuttling?

Dust: How do we minimize or mitigate dust? Signs? Water truck?

Noise: How do we minimize noise? Identify generators and other equipment that might run continuously and suggest best placement for them.

[El Puente suggests the addition here of Lights.]

Equipment Drop Off: Identify times and places with the least possible impact in terms of noise and disruption.

Equipment Staging: Where will trucks, catering vans and other equipment be located to minimize impact on the community?

Schedule Changes: Identify a contact list of point people (names, phone numbers, emails). Develop a process for significant schedule changes during the production (Who contacts who, how and when info gets out to the community).

Complaints and issues: Set up a process similar to that of schedule changes.

Production Wrap: Define process to address damage, remediation, etc.

Remuneration: Agree on donation amount to the GCA. (We are discussing various approaches: a sliding scale based on duration; a multiplier based on numbers of people, vehicles and disruption).

The meeting between the community and the SFFO will result in a written description of the project and the production, addressing activities in or around Galisteo. The one-page document will be a combination of short paragraphs and concise bullet points. To communicate timely, accurate information, we would use, as appropriate, our community blog, community email, bulletin board posting, sandwich board posting, El Puente article, or, if needed, individual mailers.

title: Santa Fe County: Culture and Water
body:
It is always important for small communities like ours to be represented on County committees to be sure our issues are considered. While application deadlines have passed (they were announced on the Community Email), these opportunities seem worth reporting for future reference, or in the unlikely event that deadlines are extended.

First, coinciding with Galisteo's ongoing "revitalization" efforts, the County was looking for candidates for the Arts, Culture, Cultural Tourism (ACCT) Committee, established in 2014 "to provide guidance to the Santa Fe Board of County Commissioners on specific policies, projects, and other related items that would enhance and expand the arts, culture, and cultural tourism industries in Santa Fe County." Committee members, appointed by the BCC, would represent the following sectors: the crafts cottage industry; the cultural tourism industry (could include heritage tourism, ecotourism, and/or agritourism); general arts organizations; the film/digital media industry; and organizations for economic development.

The second bulletin called for interested citizens to serve on the twelve-member Water Policy Advisory Committee (WPAC), which advises the Board of County Commissioners on county-wide water policy on a variety of topics, including water rates, water and wastewater system acquisitions, water and wastewater utility growth, back-up water supply, the concept of regional water authorities, the County's 40-year Water Plan, water conservation, and the conjunctive use of surface and groundwater.

Hopefully, some Galisteans responded to these calls? If so, El Puente would like to hear from them. If not, please consider serving the next time around.

title: Water System Modernized
body:
On December 3rct, the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association (GMDWCA) replaced the old manually-read water meters with new radio-read meters -- tiny radio transmitters that send encoded information to a special receiver, which then records the current water use. This procedure is faster, less labor intensive, and is not affected by weather. (No more looking for meters buried in snow.) Our new Certified Operator, Rudy Martinez, can read the meters from his vehicle while driving past, since the information is legible within several yards.
The GMDWCA has implemented this change in order to read our meters more often ( every month now) and more accurately. Why more often? Because these meters can also detect leaks, which means we can help our members be more efficient with their water use, and be warned of intermittent leaks (like toilets running) so they can be fixed sooner.
Starting in March of 2017, we will implement a new tiered pricing system. The new rate structure was included in members' February water bill. The Board will be happy to answer any questions.

title: {Return of the D.O.T.}
body:
As the Galisteo liaison with the County and State, I have been notified that NMDOT plans to begin road construction on Highway 41 in mid-to-late July 2017, continuing through late Fall of 2018. They will release a Request for Bids to contractors later this month. I met with the Project Manager for a three-hour deep dive, and can confirm that the plan will follow the agreement reached with our community almost five years ago. Here are the key components:
Re-construction of NM41 will start from the far side of the bridge over the San Cristobal Arroyo, this side of the Rodeo grounds, and extend 9-10 miles to the top of Clark Hill.
The high points of hilltop rises will be "sectioned," meaning that they will be lowered by several feet. The fill removed will be used to increase the heights of the dips in the road. The road will not be a flat highway ( one of the original proposals we opposed years ago); it will still be a rolling road, just with less highs and lows. The lanes will remain 12-feet wide, but 6-foot shoulders will be added on either side.
Several sections of roadway will be under reconstruction at any one time with one-lane access, and each section will have signalized traffic stops; in some areas there may be traffic lead cars.
For the duration of construction, "Closed to Truck Traffic" signs will be posted at the intersections of NM41/I-285, NM4I/I-40, County Roads 14/42. When re-construction is complete, the current posted speed limit of 55 MPH will remain the same.
At my request they will direct the winning contractor(s) to bring equipment, asphalt, etc. from Moriarty and restrict use ofCR42 and NM41 for this purpose. During the timeline of this project, the Project Manager will remain in contact with me to notify us of any changes, and I will be the contact with him about any issues that may arise in the village. I will also keep Representative Matthew McQueen and Senator Liz Stefanics informed. Our County Commissioner Robert Anaya is apparently already in the loop.

title: Memories
body:
Some people spend a lifetime searching for treasures. They don't realize that the memories stored in their minds are treasures. I feel that each day we take away a memory from our existence in this world. I am very fortunate to have been blessed with a family that shared a mutual love, kindness, and respect.
Growing up in a household of fourteen, we learned to live within our means, and considered ourselves lucky to have the necessities provided for us by our parents. My mother and father both worked very hard to take care ofus. My mother made mounds of tortillas, and provided a comfortable home, and my father worked outside to buy food and keep a roof over our heads. Sometimes I wonder if I thanked them enough for their efforts. I'm positive they are both still watching over us.
My early years in school were spent in a classroom that was heated with coal. The heater stood in the center of a large room with wood floors, and very old-fashioned desks. I remember taking lunch to school on days that were so cold that my parents did not want us to be walking home. Our lunches consisted of a mason jar of oatmeal with milk and sugar. I still remember how good that tasted. Or my mother would fry eggs with potatoes, and make us sandwiches on homemade tortillas. Some of the other children made fun of us because we didn't have a sandwich on bread with lunch meat in it. When my older son was in school, his classmates wanted to trade him for his homemade breakfast burrito. Now, burritos are a way of life.
Wow, how times have changed. Life was so simple then, and we were content. Today, there is so much, and yet we take it for granted. As children, when the holidays approached at school, we sang all sorts of festive holiday songs. One in particular made an impression on me -- "Over the River and through the Woods." Now I don't know exactly why, but songs that talked about turkey and all the fixings made me wonder what having these foods at our table would be like. We never had a turkey until much later in my life. Today it seems to rain turkeys from the sky. Now here is another way in which we are truly blessed these days. Oh, we had plenty of food for the holidays, just not these traditional foods. Fortunately my brothers were great deer hunters ( during deer hunting season, of course), so we always had venison.
My fondest memories of those days were when my grandfather Epifano Mora came to visit with us on Christmas Eve, when everyone gathered for Los Pastores. He brought us Christmas candy, peanuts, and walnuts. It was wonderful to have him come to spend the holidays with us. The younger children in our family were very early to rise on Christmas morning. Like all the other children, we would go out to friends' and neighbors' homes to ask for Christmas candy. Our flour sacks would get generously filled with goodies. (I ate only small amounts of mine so it would last longer.) This was another one of the traditions in our culture, kind of like "trick or treat."
Those were only some of the days that I hold dear to my heart, and these are only a few bits and pieces of my treasured memories. Hopefully I have shared my philosophy with you. I know that God has blessed me abundantly with my family, and all that I need to be comfortable. Until next time, I leave you with these words: "We have all been given a gift, let us grasp it, and be grateful."

body: Patrick McFarlin's exhibition-Fresh Oil, Crazy Quilt Paintings, Word Pictures -- is up and running at Phil Space, 1410 Second St, Santa Fe, 12-5, M-F. It was pictured in Pasatiempo and featured in the SF Reporter, which noted that some of the colorful work evokes mortality, given that McFarlin is recovering from tonsil cancer. "It wasn't a Beach Boys summer," he told Jordan Eddy, but one large new painting shows the artist hopefully headed off our planet to a smaller one, where he is greeted by a child: "That's the new world, I guess."

title: Brides Come Home
body: After months of searching for the right wedding venue in their former hometown of Chicago, Estelle Berger and Marcy Hintz looked at each other and said, "Galisteo is our home. Let's have the wedding here." And so they did. On September 17, 2016, Estelle and Marcy were married in the Galisteo Community Center, surrounded by family, friends, and Pippin the dog. The brides exchanged rings designed and made by Scott Diffrient. Artwork on loan from Amy Lynn, Barbara Seiler, Florence Sohn, and Muriel Fariello put the warm colors of the Galisteo Basin on the walls. Several Galistefios opened their casitas and studios to out-of-town guests. And the wedding dinner, provided by Walter Burke Catering, was topped offby a quickly devoured chocolate cake from Roger Taylor. Both brides remark that there's no place like home . . .in Galisteo.

title: 25 Years of the GVFR
body: Mark your calendars! Galisteo's beloved (and beleaguered) Fire Department will celebrate its 25111 year with a breakfast at the Station on April 29111. Bids will soon go out for the construction of the new truck bay (hopefully to be completed by August), and the whole building will be reroofed and re-stuccoed. Because the village is so small (and careful?) Galisteo has the lowest number of calls in the County, just below Stanley, which does not mean that it is any less necessary for our safety and those of other towns where the GVFR often performs mutual aid. The County's almost 8,000 annual calls (including false alarms) are primarily medical emergencies, with only 452 fires last year.

title: Local Democrats Hold Elections
body:
On February 2011, registered Democrats from Ward 3D gathered at the Galisteo Community Center to elect a Chair, Vice Chair and Delegates to the Santa Fe County convention. Ward 3D includes Cerrillos, Golden, Madrid, Galisteo, and parts of Lamy. Estelle Berger and Roger Taylor of Galisteo were elected as Ward Chair and Vice Chair. Both have a long history of activist engagement in the village and beyond, and are committed to supporting our local communities.
Seven Delegates were also elected to the County Central Committee: From Galisteo: Anna Cardenas, Ed Epping, Leslie Dilworth, and Rachel Darnell; from Golden, Karen Yank; from Madrid, Emily Graeser; and from Cerrillos, Eric Tysson. All will vote for Santa Fe County Democratic Party leadership later in March.

title: THE (DIFFICULT) BIRTH OF THE GALISTEO COMMUNITY CENTER
body: In 1973, the nascent Galisteo Community Association received a $25,000 grant to build a community center on donated land on Avenida Vieja. Dick Griscom, with former residents Rosie Rosenwald, and a retired general named Jackson contacted an architectural draftsman living in the village. After blowing some $4,000, he came up with plans that would cost $85,000. This was out of the question, and the County wanted their money back. Rod Hall (who moved here in late 1972) stepped in. Hall designed a simple passive solar building, produced hand-drawn blueprints, and spent about $10,000 digging the foundation and getting concrete blocks. The County reconsidered and CETA provided seventeen workers (derelicts and ex-cons with no construction experience whatsoever) for 12-18 months. Rudy Sena was hired as foreman. Little was accomplished over the winter aside from building fires and wind blinds to stay warm. Finally, with a few people from the village joining in, they found cheap untreated lumber, got the blocks laid and filled, bermed the north side, set the vigas, got the glass in and plastered the interior. All this for the c. $21,000 that was left of the original grant. (Kitchen and bathrooms came later.) Rod then got a lot of keys made and handed them out to villagers. Some wild parties ensued (Boy George's brother showed up at one of them) until vandalism forced the center to be locked up except for events. Rod is amazed that the back walls didn't crack and that the place is still standing! And it is. Many thanks to Rod and Rudy and the motley crew. But this story makes a good case for some repairs, after forty plus years .…

title: THE MEETINGS OF THE BOARDS
body:
March is election time in Galisteo, with the Boards of Directors of the Galisteo Community Association, the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association, and La Sala de Galisteo all choosing up. Here are the results:

The GCA's Annual meeting was held with a breakfast at the Community Center, on March 11. County staff were present to answer questions on the revitalization plans added to the Community Plan. New Board members were elected by acclaim: Richard Fenker and Jane Perry (Alternate). Continuing Board members: Stella Maestas, Philip Pfeiffer, Shirley Hirsch, and Janet Pfeiffer. Officers were elected following the general meeting: President, Roger Taylor; Vice President, Barbara Seiler; Secretary, Judy Tuwaletstiwa; Treasurer, Estelle Berger. Thanks were extended to Wayne King for leading the prior board, to Barbara Seiler for acting as interim President, and retiring member Peggy Diggs for her contributions.

Estelle Berger and Marcy Hintz are resurrecting the Neighbors Helping Neighbors initiative with the GVFR as advisors. The new contact for Community Center reservations is Suzie Shanklin: suzieingalisteo@icloud.com or 466-2412.

The Water Association met March 21st with more than the required quorum, including several proxies. Ana Berry, our new bookkeeper, was present to answer questions. The revised Bylaws were adopted by a vote of 25 to 1. Given comments that came in too late to be considered, modifications will be considered and presented at the 2018 meeting.

Meters are read between the first and third of each month. Phil Tuwaletstiwa acknowledged that there were still glitches in the new tiered system: "Don't get excited if you think it doesn't reflect your usage," just contact the Board. The old bills were flat fees and they are now based on usage. The first 1000 gallons are almost free (c. $1).

Some underground leaks are totally invisible. "We give you reasonable time to fix the leak before you are initially charged for it." Hardship cases will be addressed by the Board: "We are a community volunteer organization and I hope we have a soul. We have liberalized the rules, but we can't be a mom and pop organization any more. Our fees are consistent with, or lower than other similar systems." Steve Moya raised the issue of stand-by fees (c. $3.50 a month?), instead of charging the base fee of $22 for those who are not using their hookups yet.

New houses on one lot will have to apply for an additional hookup (at $10,000, which makes it difficult for villagers' children to establish a home here). Residents in the north of the village would like to join the system but the big expense of adding that much new line is dependent on our receiving a large grant; Michael Golino is applying for us.

Tuwaletstiwa praised all the hard work of past boards from the beginnings of the Water Association in 1961, when it was instigated by Joe M. Anaya and others. Past mayordomos (foremen) were Felipe Chavez y Chavez (Antonio's grandfather), Serapio Montoya (Anna's uncle), and Roman Attenberger (Romona's father).

Officers were elected at a Board meeting a few days later: President, Phillip Tuwaletstiwa; Vice President, Richard Patton; Secretary/Treasurer, Wayne King. Board members: Foreman Antonio Chavez, Lucy Lippard, and newly elected members Steve Moya and John Watson-Jones.

La Sala held elections on March 6: President, Ed Epping; Vice-President, Jean Anaya Moya; Secretary, Barbara King; Treasurer, Anna Cardenas. Board members: Roger Taylor, Shaun Gilmore, Gwen Feisst, Janice Wall, and Rachel Darnell-Heath. Roger Taylor was thanked for his leadership as President for several years; he will remain on the Board to focus on continued restoration efforts.

Congratulations to all, and many thanks to those who keep our community chugging along.

title: {LA SALA'S SUMMER PLANS}
body:
We are pleased to report that we made great strides toward restoration completion in 2016. The interior walls were covered with off-white American Clay, and the bancos and trim boards with a grey-green color popular in the late 1800's (many thanks to the Netflix film production crew!) A grant paid for materials and equipment for the 2-coat final mud plastering on all the exterior walls, and community volunteers, interns, and a crew from Castleton University of Vermont provided the labor. A second grant helped pay for two of the most damaged windows to be repaired, sealed and painted (thanks to village volunteers Ed Epping and Charlie Holloway).

The Board and the Gallery Committee did a remarkable job opening this year to successful sales, a busy Studio Tour artists' preview and info center, a Salsa dance, and most recently the Los Pastores pageant. All funds raised go towards restoration costs.

Our 2017 goals are to complete the restoration of the remaining windows and the front doors and hopefully raise enough funds to install a heating and cooling system (similar to the one in the Church) as well as a gallery lighting system.

Starting on Memorial Day weekend (May 26-29), La Sala will open an exhibition and shop where community members can sell their art - two or three dimensional, crafts, authors' books, musicians' CDs. Coffee, cold drinks and snacks will also be for sale. Changing exhibitions will continue into the Fall, with a standard 50/50 with the artists to cover our expenses. We have Internet service, new wall finishes, and will shortly install gallery lighting.

We propose to open our doors Friday and Saturday, noon to 6, and Sunday, noon to 4, with modifications for special events. This will require five 3-hour shifts per week, totally dependent on volunteers. Anyone can do it, and it's a great way to catch up on reading and computer work. Please let Barb King know by May 1st when you are available: barbaraking3219@gmail.com. or 466-3219. Artworks should be delivered on May 5th - 6th for the first show. Single works may not exceed 24"; you may show a grouping of your art. Please respond with the type of work so we can anticipate display areas.

title: BOSQUE PROJECT: ROUND TWO
body:
A meeting was held in March for landowners along the bosque with an update on the latest Bosque Project, to continue restoration of water quality and riparian vegetation along the Rio Galisteo. This time it is funded even more generously than the last round: $169,000 -- all from New Mexico Environmental Department, which means that the debilitating interdepartmental process won't slow things down this time.

Objectives include: reducing wildfire hazard; reducing non-native invasive plant species and replacing them with native riparian species; reducing water temperature; maintaining permanent flow and enhancing overbank flow opportunities; preventing stream channel degradation; increasing overbank flows and improving wetland conditions where appropriate in the floodplain; and increasing visual quality, view lines, and access for visitors. The project will contribute to healthy water systems across the State of New Mexico, benefitting all of us.

title: A SIGHTING OF FERRUGINOUS HAWKS
body:
Ed. Note: Walking in the field along the San Cristobal fenceline last month, I was startled to see in a distant tree a very large bird with a solid white breast; later in the week there was a pair. Not being a birder, I contacted our longtime columnist to find out what I had seen, even though shes now an expatriate. So, over to Jan Saunders, in Arizona, just north of the Mexican border.

The long arm of El Puente reaches me by e-mail from our ever-vigilant editor. Even from this distance I can't resist delving into my memory banks and The Sibley Field Guide to Birds to write a few words about my most favorite hawk. A single Ferruginous is always a wonder; two-at-a-time is a gift.

Our largest -- and to my eyes the most beautiful -- hawk, the Ferruginous is right at home in the arid grasslands of the Galisteo Basin. Not "rare," but certainly rarely seen in Galisteo, this large, broad-headed, big-billed, mostly white-breasted, white-winged elegant raptor hunts the basin for small mammals from a perch like a telephone pole, by kiting (hanging in the air), or sitting on the ground. Unlike the more common Red-tailed Hawk, the "Ferrug" wears feathered leggings down to its talons. Juveniles' leggings are white; adults wear the signature ferrous or rust color. Male and female are alike. I'm depending on you, reader, to determine the ages of our two visitors as you scan the skies.

It has been said that if Ferruginous Hawks were a European species they would be called eagles, as they are so large and impressively elegant. The genus and species name says it all: Buteo regalis, regal hawk.

They are primarily a western species, year-round residents of our area, although individual birds may move around in winter and summer. (Other Galisteo residents -- Cory McGillicuddy, Catherine Ferguson, Kevan Saunders -- have reported Ferruginous sightings over recent years.) Since this is spring migration time for many birds, these two could just be passing through. I certainly hope they turn out to be permanent nesting mates who find abundant prairie dogs, their favorite food.

title: El Davez to the Rescue
body: Dave Montoya has run his Galisteo auto body/repair/welding business (El Davez on Chevy Lane offCR42) for thirty seven years. He started out working construction for his Dad, Onesimo Montoya. They built his body shop and he started his own business when he was 24. First he just did mechanics in Galisteo (John Massee was his first steady customer). Now he does body work and repairs and is known for his paint jobs on hot rods and other vehicles. His reputation has spread, and he gets commissions from all over, even painting some Harley Davidsons for people from New York who were visiting New Mexico and saw his work. Dave is passionate about car shows (remember the one at the Galisteo Bicentennial celebration in 2014?). His Northern New Mexico Junkyard Classics Club -- covers Galisteo to El Duende/Espanola. On June 10th they will celebrate their seventh annual show, at the Camel Rock Casino. People bring their cars in and prizes are awarded and car freaks hang out. Outside of the house he shares with Veronica, his wife of some 40 years (and their now grown children and around ten visiting grandchildren and dogs, including a teacup Chihuahua named Chevy), is a rusting vintage vehicle they proudly call their "landscaping." Dave has many times over been a godsend for your editor and others in the village and Ranchitos. Once he and a friend had to drive my car into town, ducking down in embanassment so nobody would identify them with my bumper stickers -- "Uppity Women Unite!" "Wild Women Don't Get the Blues," and so forth. Thanks, Dave, for coming to the rescue so often. And Dave, in tum, says "I just thank all the people in Galisteo who keep coming back!" (We do that because he's good at what he does. Keep his number in your car: 501-1991.)

title: Neighbors Helping Neighbors
body: Two years ago a committee comprised of Roger Taylor, Judy Tuwaletstiwa, Julia Moore, Janice Wall, and Scott Canning drafted a plan for facilitating community assistance in times of need -- i.e.: Neighbors Helping Neighbors. This short-tenn relief might include general handyman tasks (like heavy snow removal), meals, e1rnnds, transpmtation, caregiver relief, or pet care. (See below for specifics.) The idea isn't to set up a system of pennanent help, but to have assistance available in emergencies. Estelle Berger and Marcy Hintz have agreed to coordinate and would like fo know if you're interested in participating. Several Galistefios added their names to the initial list of volunteers two years ago. If you are one of these, Marcy and Estelle will be contacting you to see if you're still able to paiticipate. If you're new to the neighborhood or to this idea and would like to add your name, please write or call Estelle and Marcy (marcyhintz@gmail.com; 466-1870). We're looking forward to supporting our wonderful community with you. More details will follow in upcoming issues of El Puente and at Saturday breakfasts. A fuller description of assistance categories: General Handyman Services: Light and battery replacements, opening/closing problems with windows/doors, blown fuses or outlets, minor carpentry repairs, things you don't know how to do. Speciality Assistance: with medical forms, completing reimbursement forms. Food: light meal preparation or meal service for up to several days, either in the home or by drop-off for times of infirmity or primary home caregiver relief. The requestor should be prepared to identify dietary needs, food allergies or foods/meals to avoid. Errands: Light shopping for household items, groceries, library books, dry cleaning, prescriptions, etc. If possible, please give helpers several days' notice beforehand; be ready to draw up a list or give the helper a list; agree on a means of payment for items bought. Helper should provide receipts for all expenses and requestor should be prepared to make payment upon delive1y. Transportation: Short trips to local appointments: doctor, dentist, library, supennarket, etc. Please give helpers several days' notice beforehand. Caregiver relief /visits: To allow the primary home caregiver up to several hours of personal time: light house cleaning, laund1y, sitting with/reading to an infinn individual, or just being in the home while the caregiver takes care of personal needs. This is not meant to substitute for more dedicated medical or nursing needs provided by a healthcare specialist. The primary home caregiver should provide emergency contact info during such a visit if the caregiver is absent; should review with the helper any pertinent medical information and care (medications and schedules, etc.); and should a deterioration of condition occur the helper should be prepared to call 911. Pet Care: Emergency care for up to several days which may involve feeding, walking, ensuring safety of pets, etc. This may involve a sudden trip of an emergency nature, or relief to a home caregiver experiencing an increase in home care demand. The requestor should be prepared to identify pet schedules, feeding times and foods, contact info for the veterinarian, and any other information needed. This is not a substitute for ordinary paid pet care while you are on vacation.

title: Architect Douglas Atwill in Galisteo
body: The book Douglas Atwill Houses (Santa Fe: Boxwood Press, 2016) includes several Galisteo houses and a number of near misses. Atwill lived in the village for three months in the mid 1980s, having designed what is now Deborah Madison's and Patrick McFarlin's home. Betty Stewait built it for him (and designed and built the now Hinkley/Beauchamp house next door). He loved it but after a huge snow storm decided it was too inaccessible. Atwill's first Galisteo house was Wendy Lynn's on Marcellina Lane, which he had hoped to make into a little neighborhood placita, though that never happened: "It seems such a natural, economic way to group several houses together, a common center garden with separate residences along each side. The Pueblos managed that - why it is so hard today?" Atwill also remodeled what is now Mike Golino's (home once owned by painter David McIntosh and gallerist Laura Carpenter and previously used to house equipment for the Galisteo fire department). He found the house "dark" and "dreary" but kept its "natural quality." Chris Griseom offered to "cleanse the house of the many bad spirits she felt were living there. I declined." Atwill bought Agnes Martin's house when she left for Taos. He described it as "a pinched, spare property ... Despite Agnes Martin's renowned ability as a painter, she had an odd eye for houses .... This Galisteo house and studio showed itself as little more than a shelter from the weather and a place to work. So I sold it and moved on." (He notes her trailer covered with adobe bricks, some of which are now a low wall in your editor's yard.) His most recent Galisteo building was Nancy Holt's in Ranchitos, where Atwill much taken with the moonlight views -- learned that "most people do not want to walk outside to reach their bedroom, even ifit is across a covered portal." Before Holt bought it, he gave in and enclosed the portal, which became her dining room. Holt converted the existing garage to a studio and added a new garage and a sauna room, but he notes that "from the road it looks very much like it did when we finished."

title: Marcelina Mares (1920-2017)
body:
Marcelina Mares died on May 29th at the age of 97. She was born in Moriarty, one of nine children of Isabellita Baca and Luis Montoya. The family lived in Moriarty, Lamy, and Madrid before settling in Galisteo, eventually making their home on Marcellina Lane (which, by the way, is misspelled on the sign). She is survived by four of her children: Modesta Presley, George B. Mares, Barbara Marshall, Beatrice Myers (and Patrick Ortiz whom she helped raise); grandchildren James Myers, Nathaniel Presley III, Cassie Marshall, Linda, Michelle, Nicole and Augustine Mares, and godchild Vincent Ortiz, plus great grandchildren.

Marcelina was a well-known enjaradora (mud plasterer) in her day, and she and her late son Will Mares plastered and built the gates and brickwork at Major Felten's (now Romona Scholder's). She loved to cook, working at the Ortiz y Pinos' La Mancha restaurant, and catering parties for Santa Fe galleries, individuals, and at the Loretto Chapel. She sewed new dresses for her daughters for school, and was skilled at various crafts. "Mom was an amazing person, headstrong, no budging. Her knowledge was never ending." She is remembered for her independent spirit.

(El Puente thanks Modesta Presley and Bea Myers for their memories. Photo: Marcelina and her beloved dog Pancho)

title: Richardson Dilworth (1938-2017)
body:
Richardson Dilworth died May 25th at the home he and his wife Leslie designed and built 14 years ago in Ranchitos de Galisteo. He was diagnosed with Alzheimers disease 6 years ago. Dick and Leslie first came to Galisteo to stay at the Galisteo Inn in the mid 1980s, returning every year through 2003. It was on their first trip to Galisteo that they were driving on CR 42 and saw the view of the Galisteo Basin. With the intention of eventually living in New Mexico, each year they explored different locations throughout the state. But each year they became more attached to the Galisteo Basin and the village of Galisteo, and the views from Ranchitos. Finally, in May 1990, while on their honeymoon following a rafting trip in Utah, they met by chance the owner of their favorite lot in Ranchitos. They purchased it that very day.

A native Philadelphian and long-time Philadelphia resident, Dick Dilworth was the youngest of eight children of Richardson and Ann Dilworth. His father served as the city's respected and idolized mayor, treasurer, district attorney, school board president, all of which gave Dick a longstanding fascination (and disdain) for politics. He attended Saint Mark's School and Yale University, and served for three years as an officer and tank commander in the U.S. Marine Corps, then established the real estate firm Lexton and Dilworth in Philadelphia.

An avid hiker and camper, Dilworth had a deep affection for the Southwest his entire life. His first trip to Chaco Canyon, in 1958, was with his Yale roommate -- Santa Fean David Grant Noble. In 2002 he finally left Philadelphia to live full time in Galisteo with his wife, architect Leslie Gallery-Dilworth. He enjoyed the contemporary house they designed, as well as his friendships here. And he delighted in living in the beautiful Galisteo Basin, looking at its clouds and brilliant blue sky.

Dick's life goals were reading history and fiction, learning, reading and watching shows about nature, especially animal behavior, and working in his shop designing and building creative and unusual structures. He definitely lived his entire life on his terms. Friends enjoyed his razor sharp wit, his sense of humor, his kindness and keen intelligence. They were amused by his irreverent postcard collection, and his collection of Hawaiian style shirts and outrageous T-shirts.

Dilworth is survived by Leslie, his wife and companion of 34 years; by his son, Richardson Dilworth III of Philadelphia, chairman of the political science department at Drexel University; by his step-sons who adored him, Wyatt Gallery of New York City, and Andrew Gallery of Los Angeles, and by his two young grandchildren, Sam and Nina Dilworth. Also three cats: Nina, Sam, and the very shy Miss Congeniality.

(El Puente thanks Leslie Gallery-Dilworth for this remembrance.)

title: Looking Back
body:
How lovely the world is in the spring. All vegetation seems to be in bloom. Little tiny leaves are cropping up everywhere, and even the New Mexico cactus is budding. I can't wait to see what colors they will be. The anticipation of fruit on our trees, and the wonderful essence of Lilacs in the air seem to make everyone cheerful. I know for me the promise of fresh fruit on our trees takes me back to the days when my grandfather -- Epifanio Mora-- harvested all sorts of fruits in the orchard. He lived in Galisteo, and owned a big home with a great orchard. I remember my grandfather bringing wheelbarrows full of peaches over to our house for my mother to can and make preserves. We certainly had our work cut out for us with all those peaches. We peeled them until our hands were stiff from holding a paring knife.

The rewards were wonderful when we were allowed to open a jar of those sweet tasting peaches. However, little did we know that our older brothers had enjoyed them before any of the younger members of the family. My brothers had their room separate from the main house, and it was also where my mother would store the jars of fruit and jams. When we went to their room to clean and, make beds, we discovered empty jars and spoons under their beds. Of course my mother would never scold them because her sons could do no wrong. Isn't that just like a mom?

We were all pretty special to our parents. My father spoiled the girls, we were gentle people, and so we were assigned the easier chores. When my parents could afford to buy a toy for us, we took good care of it because those times were rare. My father bought me a "Little Red Riding Hood" doll. Needless to say this was my most treasured possession. I took good care of it ... until my brother George got mad at me and threw her in the well. That is a memory I keep alive by reminding him every time I see him that he owes me a doll. In those days we had to bring up the water in a bucket with a rope; this was another job for George. He would also chop wood, and the younger children brought it in the house along with kindling for the evening use.

My brother George and I were closest in age so we worked together, shared chores, and played games. Sometimes he helped me with my homework. George was resourceful and creative. He made little cars with a spool of thread, a match stick, and rubber bands. Those were fun, and the stilts he built were so tall that we stood on top of the roof to get on them. Back in those days we entertained ourselves with simple games and homemade toys. We played with marbles, walked on stilts, climbed trees, and occasionally went to the stream under the bridge, where we walked in the water. I loved to jump rope, and play with jacks, but George wouldn't play those with me because they were girl games. Those were the days of a simple, uncomplicated life. If not for them my past would be empty. Everyone has something that makes them chuckle when they look back .... and remember.

"She taught us, people only die when no one tells their story any longer." -- Patricia Marina Trujillo on her Gramita.

title: Safety Tips: Cougar Encounter
body: And here's some advice on what to do when encountering a cougar: Face the cougar, remain upright and look large by raising arms and coat. Pick up children and stay calm. Do not run, talk to it firmly and try to back away slowly. If cougar advances, threaten it with walking stick or by throwing rocks or sticks. Make it think you are dominant. Fight back if necessary, stay standing. (Good luck!)

title: Part II: Architect Doug Atwill's Galisteo Projects
body:
Atwill's "near misses," as he puts it, are as interesting as the projects he finally built. For example: "Sara Melton showed this house to Betty Stewart and me. It had lots of authenticity, a few adobe and stone rubble rooms left from what had been a grand family home. There were traces of a small placita where the original house had circled about. I think only three rooms were left, little trace of the other twenty or so rooms. It was twenty five thousand dollars with a good sized piece of village land. The urge to bring it all back as a family hacienda around a newly planted placita was strong, but we both chose to walk away. Lucky us." (Atwill told El Puente that this is David van Dyk's house on the Hill, which was originally part of a string of houses reaching south to Rod Hall's.)

Here's another "near miss," apparently Vista Clara/Qigong Center: "House and Acreage Along the Galisteo River: This property always caught my eye as I passed by on my trips .... It must have had twenty or so acres surrounding a comely adobe house nestled in a grove of giant cottonwoods. The Galisteo River was nearby and water was just under the surface. The south border of the property went right up onto the Creston, a long volcanic escarpment, with several spreads of petroglyphs. If I was to have a home farm in New Mexico, this could be it. Laura Carpenter owned it and did some demolition work in advance of a more extensive renovation." Instead, she sold it and "some other people proceeded with an immensely ugly building project there, completely destroying whatever lure this had for me. At least the cottonwoods are still there, unharmed, and presumably the petroglyphs."

Atwill also recounts buying with his brother Jim "four acres to the right of the road as you came into the village." Well drillers found only "nasty yellow clay, indicating no water," and they decided to sell rather than build. "This was about the time that a small girl had fallen into a well in Midland, Texas, to much media coverage. Jim had an awful dream about our open well, so I went out with a large flagstone to cover up the exposed hole."

title: Movie Nights at La Sala
body:
La Sala hosted its first two Movie Nights on May 18 and 25. Angie Beauchamp -- a Galisteo resident who teaches Cinematic Arts at UNM -- selected and presented two Billy Wilder films, Ace in the Hole and Sunset Boulevard. Ace in the Hole, starring Kirk Douglas as a heartless journalist, was particularly interesting for its location in New Mexico, featuring an Albuquerque newspaper office, an accidental tourist attraction, and a "400 year old Indian ruin." (If it had been real it would have been considerably older.)

Both movies were categorized as film noir -- a cinematographic style or genre characterized by a mood of pessimism, fatalism, and menace. The term was originally applied by a group of French critics to American thriller or detective films made in the period 1944-54, and to the work of directors such as Orson Welles, Fritz Lang, and Wilder.

The movies and popcorn were free but the audience was encouraged to make a donation for La Sala's restoration project. Attendance for both evenings was encouraging (20-25 film buffs each night). So the Board is exploring the presentation of more films. When finalized, these plans will be announced on the Community Bulletin Board, Community Association email and signage at La Sala.

La Sala is also looking for sponsors or donations to help restore and electrify four old gas lights found in the former dance hall during restoration. The cost is estimated at $300-400.

title: Bernard Pomerance (1940-2017)
body:
Bernard Kline Pomerance, resident of Galisteo for thirty years, died at his home August 26th of complications from lung cancer. He was 76. In the community of Galisteo, this wry and enigmatic man was a somewhat reclusive but always supportive presence. (An unpublished collection of short sketches called Dreamshouters was fondly based on the village.)

Born in Brooklyn on September 23rd, 1940, Pomerance graduated from the University of Chicago in 1962 and moved to London in 1968 where he began to write plays and co-founded the Foco Novo theatre company. With his first wife, Sally Belfrage, he had two children, Moby and Eve, who survive him, along with their spouses and two grandsons. As everyone in Galisteo remembers, his marriage to artist Evelyne Franceschi sadly ended with her death in 2015.

Pomerance was the author of the Tony-Award-winning play, The Elephant Man. First staged in London, then in a New York church, it moved to Broadway and became a huge success. Since then it has been revived twice on Broadway, starring Billy Crudup in 2002 and Bradley Cooper in 2014. (The 1980 David Lynch film of the same name was unrelated to the play; Pomerance and his producers sued and won a settlement over the title.) In 1979, The New York Times drama critic said that his tale of a man viewed as a "freak" actually "lofted on poetic wings and nested in the human heart." One of the most innovative aspects of the play was the lack of makeup or mask to define the severely deformed protagonist. "The most important element in theatre is the audience's imagination," the author explained.

Among Pomerance's other dramas were Foco Novo, High in Vietnam, Hot Damn, Hospital, Thanksgiving Before Detroit, and Quantrill in Lawrence. He often wrote unsentimentally, with humor and empathy, about Native American history and issues. Melons starred Ben Kingsley as a wise Native chief. A book-length epic poem, We Need to Dream All This Again: An Account of Crazy Horse, Custer, and the Battle for the Black Hills, was published in 1987. Pomerance was close to many in the New Mexico Native community and collected contemporary Native art. Among his closest friends was the acclaimed Kiowa writer N. Scott Momaday (who talked him into moving to Galisteo).

title: Frank Sandoval Jr. (1994-2017)
body:
July 28, 2017 was a day that brought pain and sorrow to our family. Our Frankie went to be with our maker in heaven. Although he has found peace and happiness in the arms of our Lord, we have been left with a hole in our hearts. We may never understand the reasons for our loss, but we find comfort in the memories he has left for us to hold dear.

Our Frankie was born on June 19th, 1994, and is survived by his parents, Frank Sr. and Sadie Sandoval, and his brother Joseph, with whom he had a special sibling relationship. They were very close and always looked out for each other. Frankie also had many relatives and friends who will miss him greatly. Each one of us has some special moments that we spent with him, and these memories will stay with us forever. Our Frankie had such a wonderful smile that always seemed to change the mood in every room he entered. David and I were honored to be Frankie's Godparents; He was an infant when he was dunked in the holy water at Santa Maria de la Paz. Ever since he could talk, he always called us Nino and Nina. I like to think we had a very special bond with him. When he was with his friends, he always took the time to come to us and say hello. It is a rare trait for a young person to possess these days, but then my Frankie was a special young man. He had a big heart, and was always ready to help anyone who needed assistance. He never turned me down when I wanted his help. I will always be grateful to God for allowing him to be with us, even though he was here for such a short time.

In this life Frankie worked alongside his Dad and his brother in the garage repairing and rebuilding engines. Working on cars was his passion. It seemed that he was always tinkering with something that needed fixing. He had a natural talent for this sort of work. Most recently, Frankie was working for the King Brothers Ranch in Stanley. Wherever he worked, he did not shy away from hard labor, and he had so much knowledge that he knew how to do just about any task he was presented with.

Frankie had many interests; among them were hunting with his Dad and brother. He often spent time at their ranch in Gonzales. He loved to venture out on the four-wheeler, and to go mud bogging. Frank was a free spirit, and an outdoors man, camping and fishing. We will miss him so very much. It will be a long time for our hearts to heal, if they ever do. We laid our lovely young man to rest in a beautiful church yard alongside his maternal grandparents. I still think it is a bad dream we will all wake up from, but in reality, Jesus took my Frankie to sit beside him in heaven. I believe we must have needed an angel to take our hand, and look out for us.

title: GVFR and GCA Updates
body:
Attendees at GCA social functions (the Chile/Margarita Cook off and the "monthly" breakfast/book exchanges, etc.) are invited to bring one canned or packaged non-perishable food item which will then be collected and distributed by the GVFR to local families. The Food Depot's Neighbor to Neighbor Food Drive in our area is Sept. 11-16. Items including non-perishable food, pet food, baby food, and personal hygiene products can be dropped off at the hardware store in La Tienda, the market or pet store in the Agora, or at the Eldorado Community Center and Library. Or mail a check to the Food Depot, 1222 A Siler Rd., SF 87507 and write "285ALL" in the memo line.

From the GVFR: The department heartily welcomes three new (and badly needed) members: Steve Beecraft, Chris Powell, and Janet Pfeiffer. (Janet, whose dad Philip is already in the auxiliary, tells a moving account of being helped by the GVFR and realizing she wanted to give back by becoming an EMT.)

As we all watch Hurricanes Harvey's and Irma's devastation and feel for the months and possibly years of strife for the unfortunate people suffering through the power of Mother Nature, the GVFR (in addition to our own donation), will write a check for 100% of all donations received until the end of September. Thanks in advance for whatever you can afford to give. You will receive a 501c3 tax-deductible thank-you letter.

From the GCA: The GCA and The Light Institute co-sponsored a Community Flea Market/Yard Sale on August 26-27. About fifteen residents participated. Sales were moderate and the GCA cleared c. $250 from sales of donated items, table rentals, food and drink.

body:
The exhibition committee of La Sala de Galisteo is asking Galisteo artists to contact them to express interest in participating in the May through September 2018 theme exhibition on the concept of The Chair. title: High and Low: More Changes for NM 41
body:
Our very rural highway is getting a lot of (too much?) attention. The New Mexican ran a front-page story on August 3rd headlined "State to Improve a Long and Winding Road," noting that "some in Galisteo worry about increased traffic." An understatement.

From the San Cristobal bridge to Clark Hill, the NMDOT, citing "an inordinate number of crashes," will resurface, add 6-foot shoulders on either side, and smooth out some of the steepest dips over twelve miles. At least more grandiose plans for a wider, flatter road gave way to something more moderate over the years of negotiations.

Work on the culverts has already begun and construction will continue through November, take a break for winter, and resume in March, Monday–Friday, 6AM-5PM. It is expected to last 350 days (with possible delays taking it into 2019), and to cost c. $22 million. Signs on truck restrictions will be posted at I-40, 285, NM 41 and 14 when work is in progress (but not during winter breaks). Work areas will have one open lane and a pilot car. Expect delays of ten minutes or more. Here we go again.

Roger Taylor was quoted as saying "No one is fighting the road. It's the outcome that concerns us." While cyclists will be safer, the improvements may bring faster traffic and more trucks. At the community meeting with DOT officials, Rep. Matthew McQueen contended that the DOT was "putting out the welcome mat," while on the other hand, truckers are reported to be worried that residents will try to ban all commercial traffic - something the community has been attempting for years with no luck.

And then, sometime in the future, the last phase will remodel NM41 north of Galisteo to US 285. In a nation where so much infrastructure is going to hell, I guess we should be pleased at the attention.

title: Rural Commercial Overlay Open House
body: On September 7th an open house concerning the Rural Commercial Overlay was held at the Community Center. Although it had already been presented at two meetings last fall and approved by the community as part of the Community Plan, it was overlooked and omitted during the approval process for the County Code. In order to amend the County Code this additional public meeting was required as a formality. Nothing new is being added to the overlay. It establishes a narrow area on both sides of NM 41 from the Hogback on one end to the Galisteo Bridge on the other that allows for very limited non-residential development. This could include small unpaved parking areas, shops and restaurants, and a welcome center. Any questions please call County Planning Manager Robert Griego 505-986-6215 or GCA President Roger Taylor 505-466-3469.

title: Stanley Cyclone Center Opens
body: A lengthy feature in The New Mexican (June 11) on the Stanley Cyclone Center, an equestrian arena planned to "breathe new life into the dusty town on NM41," reported that it had been in the works for almost a decade, "a vision of Mike Anaya, a Santa Fe County commissioner from 2003 to 2011." Mike lobbied for funding; his successor on the BCC -- his brother Robert Anaya-- presided over the ribbon-cutting. The Center is described as "a multipurpose facility for anybody in the region," offering a place for kids in 4-H, rodeos, and other events. It is called the Cyclone Center because of Stanley's trademark dust devils. Residents hope that it marks the town's revival.

title: {STORMY WEATHER}
body:
A "tomadic" thunderstorm event hit the Galisteo area on October 4th, bringing flooding and destruction in its path. Roger Taylor measured 6" of rain in 20 minutes when it was at full force. Judy Tuwaletstiwa reports there was a "strange fierce wind from the west, driving golf-ball sized hail around 6:30 PM." Power went out around 7:06 and residents gathered at El Puente to watch the creek rise over 6' high and 60' wide. PNM worked all night to make a temporary line to restore power on the east side. The bridge was closed to traffic, and so were portions of CR 42. A chunk of the creek's east bank collapsed. Vultures were staggering around on the ground until their rain-heavy wings dried enough to fly again. Galisteans suffered hail damage to vehicles and many broken skylights.
Downstream, the reporting gauge c. 5 miles north west of Cerrillos peaked around 5AM but water levels to the Galisteo Dam didn't subside until mid-morning. Of course it couldn't have anything to do with climate change ...
(Photo: John Watson-Jones)

title: PERFECT PITCH
body:
On a whim, Angie Beauchamp entered a Pepsi/Aquafina text-to-win contest, and as one of four winners was selected to throw out the first pitch at an Albuquerque Isotopes game on August 27th. Back in the day, she had been a softball catcher, never a pitcher, and never overhand with an actual baseball. The day before, she practiced by herself against the coyote fence in her Galisteo backyard. On the big day, she threw it overhand right into the strike zone!
Peggy Diggs and Ed Epping accompanied her to the park for the event, which included an air-conditioned suite and catered meal while watching the game with the other finalists and their families. At the end of the game, everyone went down on the field for a final selection of an oversized check. Angie's intuitive pick revealed a $1000 win, while the three others won $250. Her partner Caroline Hinkley missed all of this while photographing in Iceland, but Peggy and Ed scored a photo opp with Orbit, the Isotopes mascot. (Photo: Ed Epping)

title: IMPORTANT NOTICES FROM GVFR
body:

Complete one Medication List + Emergency Contact Information form for each person in your household; place them in separate Red Alert Bags with their name on the bag and then place the bags in your refrigerator freezer. title: Jean Anaya Moya featured in Spanish Market edition
body: Jean Anaya Moya was featured in the Spanish Market edition of The New Mexican in July. It mentioned that five generations of her family have lived in her house in Galisteo, going back to the land grant given her great-great grandfather. She chose the often-neglected medium of straw applique to honor her cultural heritage and religion. Her De Colores was also included in an exhibition on Frida Kahlo at the Spanish Colonial Art Museum. (Craig Moya also participated in the prestigious market.)

title: Peggy Diggs presents Money Stamping Project
body: Peggy Diggs had a booth at the aha art fair in Santa Fe in September for her popular Money Stamping Project in which she stamped people's currency with provocative questions, such as: "In What Ways Has Money Hurt You?" and "What If You Only Had What You Needed?" Some of the bills she was proffered were $100; the art was free.

title: Craig Moya's New Mexico Hard Cider featured
body: Advising us to "put down the craft beer and try a hard cider at one of these chill taprooms," an on-line feature (Sept. 28) headlined "Five Cider Taprooms to Try This Fall," selected from across the nation, included Craig Moya's New Mexico Hard Cider in Santa Fe: "This desert dive features a long bar, plenty of two-tops, and taps of hard cider made from apples sourced in-state and brewed locally. Cider flavors cover the fruity rainbow: strawberry, blueberry, mango, raspberry, cranberry, and apricot. Its flagship cider, the Doña Tules Semi Sweet, is lightly carbonated with a crisp, clean finish. The most exotic cider flavor here has to be the Purple Bunny, an earthy mixture of sweetened apple cider and purple carrot wine. Tacos, quesadillas, and (yes!) Frito Pie round out the Southwestern-inspired food menu."

title: Greg O'Byrne featured in Wine & Chile Fiesta article
body: Greg O'Byrne enjoyed his annual moment of fame as Executive Director of the always successful Wine & Chile Fiesta. He was quoted in The New Mexican's feature (Sept 23) that "people like what's new and interesting," and they often choose authenticity over price.

title: WATER BOARD'S DILEMMA
body:
The Board of the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association is struggling with the contradictions between unavoidable State legal regulations and being responsible and compassionate members of a small community. We are bound by law to collect payments, and several villagers are in arrears.
As unpaid bills stack up, members have several options: Come and talk to the Board about your concerns at the next meeting; pay in full; send one half the owed amount with a letter to the Board; initiate a hardship claim by contacting any Board member. (The Board will respect your privacy but will need some proof of your financial situation.) The monthly $22 membership fee (plus tax) is due even if your service is shut down and we have to charge $25 to turn it back on. A meaningful community dialogue around these issues will benefit us all.
