title: Mysterious Lamy Ruin
body: The pictured "old Spanish Convent" was founded by Archbishop Jean Baptiste Lamy, who arrived in New Mexico in 1851. The back of the postcard reads:" The town of Lamy, between Las Vegas and Albuquerque, was named for the good Archbishop who founded nearby a convent, the walls of which are still standing, and who also once taught the Indians in a little adobe schoolhouse. At the time of the founding of this convent he was a missionary priest, but afterwards became Archbishop Lamy of Santa Fe." Lamy was French and strenuously disapproved of the "Mexican" church that ruled in the state, conducting a famous feud with the (married) Padre Martinez of Taos. At some point, perhaps in the late 1850s, this "church" or convent was erected on the Bishop Lamy land grant, east of the present day village, which did not exist at the time, although there were settlers in the Ojo de la Vaca/ Cañoncito area. Lamy was founded in 1880 when the Atchison Topeka and Santa Fe Railroad came roaring down Apache Canyon. It was initially, and briefly, called Galisteo Junction. Little seems to be known about this structure, though the fact that it is often called a "convent" suggests that it might have been an early home for the Sisters of Loretto, brought to New Mexico by Lamy in 1852. The impressive ruins remain (see 2017 picture lower right), still isolated on a small hill on a patch of privately owned grazing land above the Galisteo Creek. At least a decade later, Lamy bought and built the "Villa Pintoresca," now the Bishop's Lodge resort in Tesuque. The postcard (above right) was sold at El Ortiz, the elegant Fred Harvey hotel next to the Depot in Lamy, that was constructed in1908, closed in 1940, and dismantled a few years later. I've been told that its original name was to be Los Pinos, but the name badly pronounced in English too closely resembled male anatomy, and it was changed to El Ortiz, both names honoring the Galisteo family.

title: Los Pastores Presentation and Potluck
body: Los Pastores will be presented Saturday, Dec 9, 1:00 PM at La Sala, sponsored by La Sala de Galisteo and the GCA. A traditional New Mexican potluck lunch at the Community Center will follow and we welcome contributions of a side dish or salad. Suggested donation is $5 and a non-perishable food item (including dog and cat food) to help local families. For info, Anna: 466-8967 ;galigirl312@centurylink.net.

title: Farewell But Not Goodbye
body: A sad farewell to Barbara and Wayne King, who are leaving us for the bright lights of Santa Fe. They bought their home on Avenida Vieja in 1998 and moved here full time in 2006, having added a barn and a studio. Between them they have put an immense amount of energy into the community's organizations - the GVFR, GCA, La Sala, Studio Tour, and the Water Board. They have been model neighbors and members of our community and they will be sorely missed. But Santa Fe is not exactly Timbuktu, so we certainly haven't seen the last of them.

title: Galisteo Shares a Living Treasure
body: Priscilla Hoback was honored as one of three Santa Fe Living Treasures at the Unitarian Church in Santa Fe on October 15th. Here are excerpts from the anonymous nomination text: "A trne woman of the west. A person of the earth. A native Santa Fean. Priscilla Hoback epitomizes the essence of New Mexico through her art and her lifestyle. Her expressions manifest in diversity as a clay artist, writer, storyteller, teacher, businesswoman, horse whisperer, master gardener, community member and beloved mother. "Priscilla comes from a prominent New Mexico family. She spent many hours in and out of the landmark Pink Adobe restaurant, which her mother opened in the 60s. . .. She owned and ran the Pot Shop, her home/studio/gallery on Canyon Road before moving to the village of Galisteo ..... She creates ceramic relief murals inspired by prehistoric cave paintings, depicting the animals she knows and loves here at home .... Her book Living Clay, published in 2000, details her artistic journey and another book in progress shares vignettes about life in Galisteo and New Mexico .... Anyone who experiences her art glimpses a vision of the southwest that few are lucky to know." In an interview in The New Mexican (10/15) Priscilla said she grew up on Canyon Road, "in every sense of the word," but almost forty years ago she moved to Galisteo, where she has more space for studio, horses, and organic gardens. She also digs her clay south of the village to "reflect the very energy and spirit" of the Galisteo Basin.

title: GVFR Station Construction
body: Chief Jean Moya announces that after several years of paperwork, construction has finally begun on a new bay at the GVFR station, to accommodate our growing fleet of trucks. It began on October 31 and is expected to be completed on March 29, 2018. Workers will use NM 41 to Avenida Vieja to access the station. Chief Moya has advised them to drive slowly, but walkers and especially dog walkers should keep an eye out for speeding vehicles, daily from 7:00 AM to 5:30 PM.

title: GVFR HazMat Course Passed
body: Also from the GVFR: Christopher Powell and Steve Beecraft passed the dreaded HazMat course. Now if a WIPP truck implodes on 285 we can send them out to save us.

title: Eldorado Middle School Bosque Field Trip
body: A group of some fifty or sixty 8th graders from the Eldorado Middle School (chaperoned by teachers and parents) visited the Galisteo Bosque on a nature field trip for 5 hours on October 26th. The trip was coordinated with Rich Schrader, of River Source, by Roger Taylor and Matthew McQueen, focusing on ecology, wildlife, and river habitat. Roger was with them all morning and Lucy Lippard came later to speak about local history and the cultural landscape. The group parked at the Community Center, and signed liability waivers.

title: Andy Peña Obituary
body: Back in April (apologies for the delay), Andy Peña passed away at the age of 78. He was born in Galisteo, son of Pedro and Ursula Peña, brother of Clyde Peña.

title: Frank Hirsch Elected President of Santa Fe Symphony
body: Last July, Frank Hirsch was elected President of the Santa Fe Symphony Orchestra and Chorus.

title: La Sala Lectures Fundraising
body: Audiences for the lectures at La Sala in November varied, but $500 was raised for continued renovation.

title: Sustainable Land Development Code Petition
body: According to The New Mexican (11/1) "Dozens of Santa Fe County residents submitted a scathing petition to County Commissioners seeking changes to the Sustainable Land Development Code," claiming that it is an economic hindrance causing significant delays in the processing of applications due to a "regulatory morass." Commissioner Anna Hansen defended the Code on grounds of its commitment to sustainability. Changes to the Galisteo section of the Code are being considered and will be proposed to the Community in a public meeting soon.

title: Voting Center Consolidation Reconsidered
body: A divided Board of Santa Fe County Commissioners has approved the consolidation of voting centers for next year's elections. The original plan cut the number of voting sites from 51 to 24 and Galisteo's Community Center was among the casualties. Our commissioner, Robert Anaya, objected to the cuts, and Anna Hamilton wondered if the consolidation represented "a trend towards disenfranchisement." Amid such concerns, the BCC has reconsidered, and when six sites were reinstated, Galisteo was one of the winners.

title: More Storm Stories
body: During the recent apocalyptic storm, the Arroyo on McKee Road was roaring as Evelyn Gregory had never seen it in thirty years and locals hadn't seen it in a lifetime. Evelyn was forced to spend the night with a neighbor. The next morning, worried about her five dogs, she tried (at the fearless age of ninety), to plow "Buttercup" -- her yellow SUV-- through the gigantic sand dune the flood had deposited in the Arroyo: "I thought I'd get stuck," (she did), "but decided to give it a shot." And she began to walk up the road with Janet Pfeiffer, who had also been stranded. They looked back to see Michael D. Anaya and Chris Watts coming to their rescue. They became the heroes of the day. "If it hadn't been for them we'd still be stuck there," says Evelyn. The dune was too much for Mike's little tractor, but County equipment was right there on Camino Los Abuelos, as was our Commissioner Robert Anaya. But despite pleas for help for the elderly people cut off across the arroyo, they refused. Chris and Mike finally got Evelyn's car out and the McKee Road residents hired someone to move sand to clear the road through the arroyo. Despite Evelyn's many calls to the County, none were returned. Elsewhere, one Ranchitos resident received an insurance estimate of around $10,000 worth of damage to skylights and stucco walls. Another had some thirty damaged skylights. At least one other family home was flooded. Your editor got off easy with huge hail holes in one window screen and inexplicably nowhere else on that side of the house.

title: Mail Call: Collect It or Lose It?
body: Mailbox thieves have been targeting the area and residents are urged to collect their mail daily and to report suspicious activity. Criminal investigators from the Santa Fe County Sheriff's Department are looking into various incidents of theft focused on locked cluster units, which offer multiple mailboxes to steal from. Thieves are looking for documents like bank account statements and mortgage and credit card bills that provide them with personal information, including social security numbers, account numbers and addresses, allowing them to steal the victim's information and illegally access bank accounts or open fraudulent accounts. If you have had your mailbox broken into or witnessed suspicious activity, you are encouraged to immediately call 505-428-3720 to notify law enforcement. The Sheriff's Office also encourages residents to establish a Neighborhood Watch group if one does not already exist.

title: Glorious New Open Space and Trails
body: A management plan for 2500 acres on what is being called the Thornton Ranch Open Space across the Railroad tracks on the south side of CR 42 has been approved by the BCC, which also authorized an interpretive plan for the Galisteo Basin. The open space is centered on a double hill that is sacred to several local Native tribes and will be off limits to visitors, but at least twelve miles of multi-use trails will eventually be connected to the extensive network in the Galisteo Basin Preserve. Some 400 acres are State and BLM lands, but most of the property was acquired by the County in 2016, thanks to a voter-approved general obligation bond for capital improvements. The area's ecology, and its ranching and railroad histories will be included in proposed interpretive and educational programs and exhibits. Early Galisteo residents should figure prominently. Much of the area was owned by Jose Antonio Anaya, ancestor of many Anaya and Montoya descendants living in the village today. One of them -- Commissioner Robert Anaya-noted the threats to public lands posed by current Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke, declaring that "what we need is to continue to have projects like this."

Heartfelt thanks to all those who have participated, providing literary, moral, and financial support in the past year."

title: La Gran Pastorela de Belen
body:
La Gran Pastorela de Belen took place again at La Sala de San Jose on December 9th, with an overflow crowd and delicious potluck at the Community Center afterwards, thanks to organizers Anna and Freddie Cardenas. A handsome booklet was distributed detailing the history, synopsis, and song sheet for the traditional Christmas play about the annunciation of the birth of Christ to the shepherds by San Miguel, who must fend off Demonio (the Devil) who is trying to distract them. Finally each shepherd brings a gift to the Holy Child, including water, diaper, sheets, blankets, a rooster, and empanaditas.

Los Pastores originated in Spain centuries ago and was once common in New Mexico, although only a few villages (and the city of Santa Fe) still perform it. This version was resurrected three decades ago by Filomena Baca of Belen's Nuestra Señora church, and she was present to accept our thanks, along with other dedicated volunteers in the chorus and in the band of shepherds who provided the event's lively music. A clever expandable backdrop changed the scenery and the Devil and drunken shepherd Bartolo offered dashes of contemporary humor. (A "My View" in The New Mexican (1/14), written by a former Demonio, cited Galisteo as a source for the figure's validity.) Nine-year-olds Jason Montoya and Savanna Gallegos were Mary and Joseph this year.

In the audience were several Galisteans who had participated in Galisteo's own version before 1964, including Rudy Sena (whose father Natividad began the play in Galisteo), Martha Delgado (whose parents also contributed), and many from the Montoya family. Inez Sena Montoya, once the keeper of the play's costumes, recalls that each actor had to bring a piece of wood for the stove to keep the room warm during rehearsals.

title: County Commissioner Candidacy
body: No one has yet announced their candidacy for our district's County Commissioner, and Robert Anaya is termed out. The primary is in March. Step up Galisteans!!!

title: Matthew McQueen's Bump Stock Ban Proposal
body: Matthew McQueen made the front page of The New Mexican (12/16) for proposing a bill that would ban bump stocks -- the devices that turn semi-automatic weapons into rapid-fire guns and were responsible for the high fatality rate at the Las Vegas mass shooting. And Matthew has a potential challenger in the 2018 election, one Jarratt Applewhite, an Independent and "self-described high-school dropout" from Lamy.

title: Zorro Ranch Legal Issues
body: Also in the news is our neighbor to the south -- Zorro Ranch owner Jeffrey Epstein. A civil suit has been filed against him by three teenage girls. Steve Terrell (in The New Mexican 12/10) noted that the opposing lawyer has agreed not to refer to Epstein as a "billionaire pedophile" or "convicted child molester" and assumes that he will also refrain from calling Epstein "a creepy scumbag" or "despicable perv."

title: Sina Brush Book Signing for 'Working with Laura Gilpin, Photographer'
body: On Dec. 10th, Priscilla Hoback held a reception and book signing for Sina Brush, who after working on it for some three decades, has published her lavishly illustrated book Working with Laura Gilpin, Photographer; an intimate portrait of the 1970s when Brush worked at the Museum of Fine Arts and gave birth to her daughter Aissa, long before she settled in the Galisteo Basin. She describes her first view of the village in a visit to Romona Scholder, who had asked Laura Gilpin to come to Galisteo to make a portrait of her then husband, the artist Fritz Scholder: "Galisteo was very traditional in those days, a Spanish community of adobe homes hundreds of years old, enormous cottonwoods shading portales ... orchards of ancient Spanish fruit trees and native grass yards tall green corn stalks rose grandly over adobe walls, wild gourd vines with long narrow pointed grey-green leaves spread over road shoulders, knobby green and yellow striped baseball-sized gourds scattered among the leaves .... 'Scholder' in script, flowed across a wall near the gate fabricated in wrought iron letters several inches high ..... A few moments later Mrs. Scholder appeared, dressed in a flared calf-length knit skirt and three/quarter length sleeve top, all black, including black high heels and stockings, an elegant picture .... "

title: Jean Anaya Moya at 'Chispa!' Exhibition
body: Jean Anaya Moya took part in "Chispa!", a one-day exhibition at La Fonda on Dec 19th.

title: Charlie P. Anaya Obituary
body: Charlie P. Anaya (1928-2018), uncle of Robert and Mike Anaya and Jean Moya, brother of their father Joe M. Anaya, and son of Miguelita and Basilio Anaya of Galisteo, passed away on January 8.

title: Peggy Diggs Anti-Racist Work
body: Peggy Diggs' anti-racist work on "whiteness" was featured in The Santa Fe Reporter's coverage of presentations by the Santa Fe Art Institute's Equal Justice Residents in November. She also participated in a performance there, handing out fortune cookies with pointed messages.

title: The Return of Corey's Sunday Supper and Soup Stop
body: January 28: Comfort Buffet from 5-7 at the Community Center. A selection of soups will also be available for purchase. February 4, Super Bowl Sunday: soups and snacks to enjoy in front of the TV will be pick-up only from 3-5. Featured will be my salmon chowder - a prizewinner at the 2007 Santa Fe "Souper Bowl." February 18: Chinese New Year's Buffet. Menu details and more dates to follow. Please call Corey at 466-1831 with any questions. Reservations helpful but not necessary.

title: Judy Tuwaletstiwa's Paintings Featured
body: Pasatiempo (12/15) reproduced an installation of Judy Tuwaletstiwa's paintings. She is also represented in the New Mexico Museum of Art's 100-year anniversary exhibition.

title: {Liz Massey's Health Challenge}
body: Sadly Liz Massey, who, with her husband Paul, has long been our newspaper delivery team, has been diagnosed with a severe illness. They have sent the community their thanks and the reprint of a delightful newspaper column by Liz. The community has reciprocated.

title: Galisteans Speak Out: Letters to the Editor
body: Galisteans speak out: Letters to the editor of The New Mexican by Sina Brush, Barbara Holloway, and Joette O'Conor (Trofimuk) over the last month or so covered (respectively) DWI offenses, local gun control, and pro-Israeli government comments.

title: Catherine Ferguson's New Book Launch
body: Catherine Ferguson launched her new book I Thought You Would be Shelter: Men Poems at two events in December, one at Teatro Paraguas in Santa Fe, along with James McGrath's A Festival of Birds.

title: Deborah Samuel's Photography
body: Deborah Samuel's photography was shown at the Webster Collection in Santa Fe and reproduced in Pasatiempo.

title: Deborah Madison's New Cookbook and Recognition
body: Deborah Madison's new book In My Kitchen: A Collection of New and Favorite Vegetarian Recipes (Ten Speed Press) was featured in The New Mexican's 2017 Winter Guide with a portrait including some greenery and her sweet dog Dante. Among the advice offered cooks: "Don't apologize. Your food may not taste as good to you as it does to those to whom you are serving it. If so, it's most likely because you've been inhaling it for a while so its flavors are no longer vivid and new. But that doesn't mean that others are faking their praise!" Madison was also honored by the Santa Fe Farmers Market Institute's Fall Fiesta for her 40 years of work in the "food world" (27 of them in New Mexico).

title: Galisteo Volunteer Fire and Rescue Leadership
body: The Galisteo Volunteer Fire and Rescue unanimously and enthusiastically re-elected Jean Moya as Chief. Janice Wall will continue as Secretary despite the lamented departure of her co-conspirator, Barbara King. New member Alice Kruse, an RN, is training for EMT. Ed Epping, John Watson-Jones and Steve Beecraft are stepping up to fill Wayne King's shoes. The Friends of GVFR 501.c3 officers remain Frank Lux and Janice Wall and everyone else in the department are Board members.

title: La Sala Restoration Project
body: The double front doors and transom window of La Sala have been removed and replaced by plywood while restoration work on these items begins. The process of paint removal, sanding, wood repair, sealing and re-painting, and hardware replacement will take about 4-6 weeks and cost @ $3,000. Donations towards the expense are very welcome!

title: Craig Moya's Desert Dogs Brewery and Cidery
body: Craig Moya is now the co-proprietor of Desert Dogs Brewery and Cidery on San Francisco St., featured in The New Mexican (1/9). He's quoted as saying: "I feel like in Santa Fe you have one shot. If people talk bad about you, nobody comes in." Given the ongoing success of his other cidery, we trust his jitters are unfounded.

title: Galisteo Planning Committee Recommendation on Commercial Uses
body: As you know with an eye to the future, continuing to encourage a vibrant, mixed use community -- the Galisteo Planning Committee has been working with County planners for well over a decade on the Galisteo Community Plan. After innumerable meetings and public presentations, a proposed amendment to the County Sustainable Land Development Code to allow additional commercial uses in the Traditional Community was presented to the community at a well-attended September 2017 meeting in the Community Center. Several residents inquired about additions to the proposed (very limited) Commercial Corridor along Highway 41. Subsequent to this meeting, the Galisteo Planning Committee reviewed the potential implications of this designated Commercial Corridor. After much deliberation, the committee recommended that the best way forward will be to give equal opportunity for limited commercial proposals to every landowner in the Galisteo Community District.* All property owners have the ability to apply to the County for uses identified in the Galisteo Community District in the Sustainable Land Development Code. This means that each application will be considered individually on its merits and impact on the village and on private properties. This democratic process will involve far less bureaucracy and far more fairness. *Excluding Ranchitos which has its own covenants. The Use Table below should answer basic questions, but the County planning staff is available to answer any further questions: Robert Griego, AICP, Planning Manager (505) 986-6215, rgriego@santafecountynm.gov; Lucy G. title: Loose Animals
body:
Now and then El Puente receives complaints about unaccompanied loose dogs annoying or frightening people or fenced-in critters. Some of us walk our dogs off leash, but do it with care, for the dog's safety as well as that of others. Just so you know, here are some excerpts from the Santa Fe Sheriff's Office Animal Control Division Ordinance, courtesy of Evelyn Gregory:

Restraint of Animals: "All persons owning or having charge, custody, or control of any animal shall keep such animal restrained to prevent damage or harm to people and property .... When a dog is off its owner's premises, it must be under leash or control by owner .... The owner shall not allow it to run at large or create a nuisance on another's property, be it public or private". [Pooping is defined as a "nuisance."]

Dogs Running at Large (under Prohibited Activities): "It is unlawful for any dog owner to allow or permit any dog to run at large. Any dog permitted to run at large in violation of this Section is declared to be a nuisance, a menace to public health and safety, and may be taken up and impounded .... "

Fines for dogs running at large range from $25 for first offense in a calendar year to $60 to $100 for the third offense. And there are also draconian laws and fines for cruelty to animals.

title: Native Response to Manifest Destiny Comments
body: After the state Public Education Secretary Christopher Ruszkowski praised Manifest Destiny as a "fundamental principle" of this country, Native responses were quick and angry. Among them was Phillip Tuwaletstiwa's "An Ignorant View About Native People," in The New Mexican (12/31/17): "My first thought was that Ruszkowski, under the cover of darkness, should crawl out from under his rock, slink back in his car, and reverse the Western movement of Manifest Destiny by driving back to Delaware ... he has no business educating any of New Mexico's children. There is an alternative: Take a month, without pay ... and visit every reservation in New Mexico. Let us Indians give you a real education about our people and the genocide we suffered under Manifest Destiny."

title: Bosque Clearance Continues
body:
Scott Canning, Galisteo resident and director of horticulture for the Botanical Gardens in Santa Fe, was quoted in a Green Fire Times article (12/6/17) on removal of invasive species in local wetlands: "Cienegas are one of the rarest kinds of landscapes in New Mexico," and they are disappearing all over the state as city and agricultural wells drain the aquifers that supply their springs, "so we're doing everything we can to save [them] .... When the trees leaf out, the water level drops four feet."

Of course Galisteo's own ongoing clearance of Russian Olives in the Bosque is exemplary. For almost ten years now, under the direction of Roger Taylor and Jan Willem Jansens of Ecotone, the bosque south of El Puente has undergone a transformation from a sometimes impassable jungle of invasive Russian Olives and Tamarisks to the park-like expanse we now enjoy. (Jan Willem and your editor celebrated twenty years of village cooperation on watershed protection with a hug.)

In November 2017 we commenced the latest stage of work with two weeks of Russian Olive removal on the north side of the bridge. On Feb. 10th, community volunteers, with students from the UNM Environmental Studies program, worked hard to clean up and make piles of the debris. On Feb. 13th, with a permit for remedial burning, the Galisteo Volunteer Fire and Rescue, with the help of the Black Canyon Hand Crew (a County wildlands group described by a participant as "a really nice group of young people, fit, healthy, and friendly") completed an all-day marathon. The weather, for once, cooperated, winds subsided, and so did the six-foot-high piles of brush.

San Isidro Permaculture will begin the next stage of work north to south, planting loads of willows that have already arrived. It will take some 3-4 weeks, starting from the northern end with the removal of a berm illegally constructed to reroute the river away from Agnes Martin's former home. They will work southward, ending at the NM 41 bridge to deal with remediation/ replanting of a poorly planned NM DOT project, the week of March 5. WildEarth Guardians will also be on site during this time. The noise and bustle of work crews will be completed by March 16th.

Grants for this project total $170,000, in addition to the $130,000 already received for the south end of the bosque, as well as $15,000 from the NMDOT for the bridge area. Thanks to Roger, Jan Willem and the powers that be!

Photos left: Willows delivered; brush piles; (photos: Roger Taylor). Christopher Powell tests a hose before the big burn (Corey McGillicuddy). Below: After the burn.

title: Mike Anaya Running for County Commission
body:
Michael D. Anaya, born and raised in Galisteo and on the family's Stanley ranch, served two terms (2003-2011) as County Commissioner for our District 3, and was succeeded by his brother Robert Anaya, who also served two tenns. "I feel that in the years I had there [ on the Commission] I learned a lot," he says. This year he is running again as an Independent.

Commissioners are limited to two consecutive four-year terms but can run again after a break. According to Secretary of State spokesperson Joey Keefe, by June 28th, Independents need to file a number of nominating signatures equal to 3 percent of the total votes for governor in District 3 in the 2014 general election. If Anaya makes the general election ballot, he'll face a Democrat. Three Democratic candidates are running in the June primary in District 3: Santa Fe School Board member Rudy Garcia; Filandro Anaya, a general construction contractor in Edgewood (not related to our Anayas); and Santa Fe County Legislative Liaison/Project Manager Donald Reece, also listed as a board member on the County's Health Policy and Planning Commission.

Mike spoke on Wakeup Call on KSFR on March 16th, emphasizing that he would like to cut down the bureaucracy and red tape involved in building a home or starting a small business.

title: Last Word on the Bosque
body:
The bosque continues to be transformed. Much ofit looks like a highway at the moment, but all those willows and some cottonwoods planted near the highway bridge bode well for Spring and Summer. The long timbers, sawed off to points and placed vertically deep into the ground, often backed up by huge gray rocks, are forming a barricade to the rerouted creek north of El Puente, keeping it away from the eroding cliffs and eventually forming a natural wall of sediment.

The surprise for workers was that the weather at the end of February resembled that of the end of April, thanks to climate change. The water table was higher than expected, vastly complicating the process. Mud made it difficult for the big equipment, though easier for the plantings. The only downer at the moment is that the walking paths have disappeared, but plans for remediation are in the works.

Here is a detailed account of the project from Jan Willem-Jansens of Ecotone:

The Galisteo bosque restoration project is drawing to a close. In the last few weeks, San Isidro Permaculture (SIP) completed the removal of part of the berm on the n01ihem end of the project area, and WildEarth Guardians (WEG) planted willows and cottonwoods along the creek in the old oxbow wetland behind the be1m and down to the northern end of the "S-curve" area, north of El Puente. SIP re-meandered the stream there to improve its hydrology and ecology and to reduce erosion of the steep bank on the east side. This ended up being a very difficult task because of the high water table and muddy work conditions. WEG will return in the next few weeks to complete plantings in that area.

SIP also built three post-and-willow wicker weirs (see above right) in the creek channel, about 80-90' apart. These structures serve as leaky dams that slow the flow and accumulate sediment. They also cause higher flows to spread out over the banks more easily, and altogether create an ecology emulating the work of beavers. (During a recent visit, the Environment Department Project Officer remarked to her surprise, "hey, these structures are in fact beaver-dam-analogs!")

WEG has already planted some willows, cottonwood poles and berry trees in the area between El Puente and the highway bridge, but they will return to plant more, especially irt the recently disturbed areas. Finally, they will work with SIP to redo mitigation work in the NMDOT Right of Way of the Highway 41 bridge. They have transplanted fourteen poorly placed and partly bent cottonwoods and will return to complete willow planting there. SIP built a set of three post-and-willow wicker weirs, a rock rundown, and rock bowls to stop erosion at the confluence of a side channel joining the main channel beneath the bridge.

In the next month, Ecotone will work with the Galisteo Community Association to organize a community work event to celebrate the completion of the project, sow native grass seed across the disturbed areas, and remove woody debris and any remaining Russian olive sprouts. After that, the area will be left to the healing powers of Nature to green up and let the waters flow and do their work. If you have any questions, please contact jwjansens@gmail.com.

Once they take off, showing off their signature V-shaped wingspan, they circle slowly, catching waim air that lifts them higher and higher until they are almost invisible.

title: Save the Galisteo Basin Preserve!
body:
By now we all know that the Commonweal Conservancy's Galisteo Basin Preserve (and Trenza village proposal) are in financial trouble and may soon be foreclosed. The 9,500-acre open space (3,500 acres of which are cun-ently at risk) is the only area where we can legally walk into our views.

The debt to the Los Alamos National Bank and two other financial institutions is around $10 million. A group consisting of deep-pocket donors, Land Trust, and County representatives are discussing ways to address preservation of the Preserve, which is the major recreation amenity in the eastern Galisteo Basin. Its 28 miles of trails connect to the 15-mile Santa Fe Rail Trail. Another section of the Thornton Ranch off CR 42 is County Open Space and is in the management stage of planning, dealing with limited access in order to protect Native American sacred sites.

The Galisteo Basin Preserve also provides a crucial migration corridor for wildlife, while development could threaten local water sources. Least known, and least visible, is the archaeological and historical significance of the Preserve. While there are no major pueblos, the remnants of pre-European gardens, campsites, seasonal dwellings, and other scattered traces show that this landscape holds important evidence for reconstructing some 7,000 years of Pueblo history, according to archaeologists Eric Blinman and Cherie Scheicl<, both of whom have worked in the Galisteo Basin for decades.

Agreements may be dependent on dropping the conservation village plan. There are patches of state and federal land inside the Preserve's borders, which could help future planning. Ifit is foreclosed, it will surely be developed. Public access to some 40% of the trails could be cut off. "Instead of being in a natural, wild place, the way it is now, you'd be walking past a neighborhood," warned Ted Han-ison, Commonweal director, who has spent some twenty years on this conservation project, only to be defeated by the 2008 recession and water woes (as well as some local opposition to the high density town plan). Parts of the property have been sold to private owners in order to finance the larger proposal, but private sales did not meet expectations.

"When wild land is developed, people generally don't take good care of it," said Jan-Willem Jansens in an extensive front-page article in The New Mexican (2/20). The newspaper also devoted an entire editorial (2/22) to the Preserve, entreating local groups to save it. As Jessica Brown, of Lamy, wrote in a letter to the editor (2/24): "Let's get on it, New Mexico. Save this. Or, what the heck, let's just drill oil there, put up a bunch of plywood adobes and look at nature online."

title: Getting Your Goat (Cheese)
body:
Mix a thwarted yearning for a pet goat and herb-marinated feta samples at the farmers' market and you get...a job at a dairy goat farm! Estelle Berger and Marcy Hintz started volunteering at Dream Catcher Ranchi to after meeting owner Mary Ann Andrews at the Santa Fe Farmers' Market and tasting her delicious wares. In between mouthfuls, they asked ifMary Ann needed volunteer help at her farm. Why, yes she did! So Estelle and Marcy started trundling out on chilly, still-dark mornings to feed and milk the goats, including bottle-feeding fuzzy newborn kids. Estelle recently began apprenticing as a cheesemaker and has thus far helped make chevre, feta, and mozzarella.

Dream Catcher sells goat milk, buttermilk, and yoghmi in addition to a variety of cheeses. Contact Mary Ann at 505-699-3080 or find her booth at the farmers' market if you're interested in trying these wonderful local dairy products for yourself. A Galistefia might have helped make them!

title: Fire Alert
body: On April 10th, given extreme drought and hazardous conditions, Santa Fe County has imposed Emergency Fire Restrictions, prohibiting all open fires and campfires for the next 90 days. Also prohibited are smoking and the use of off-road vehicles and motorbikes within County parks, campgrounds and wildland areas, as well as littering on public roadways with cigarette butts or other "ignited smoking materials." Violators face up to 90 days in jail and a $300 fine. Please remember: when pulling to the side of the road to text or speak on a cellphone, make sure there is no dry grass nearby; a hot exhaust pipe can quickly start a fire in these extremely dry conditions.

title: The 6000 Things
body: "We get used to the good very quickly." ( "A lo bueno se pone uno muy pronto. ") These are words I remember my mom saying to us often. Situations presented themselves to which the phrase certainly applied. We were raised in a loving home with the basics for a comfortable living. I have mentioned before that my parents both worked very hard to provide for the family, and when the day arrived that we were finally able to drill a well, it was a miracle. We did not have to bring the water up in a bucket any longer. I got used to turning on the faucet very quickly. We still had little money, but somehow we made do. I remember my father taking two of us at a time to buy shoes at the general store. It seemed that he wasn't done replenishing the money from that purchase when it was time to buy two more pairs of shoes for the other children. You would never hear him complain about it though. In school there were those children who destroyed their shoes on purpose just so their parents would buy them another pair. I was horrified when I saw that. When I wanted twenty five cents for something, I shifted from one foot to the other before I found the courage to ask my father for money because I knew how hard he worked for the little we had. He never turned me down even if it was his last twenty-five cents. Parents are wonderful, we are so lucky to have had them, and those of us who still have them please let them know everyday how much they mean to you. My mother worked equally hard at home. In those days the comforts of home didn't come from a store. I remember in the spring it was time to wash the mattresses, and I mean that literally. We had to take them apart, take out the inside filling, and wash them in big tubs with soap and water. After we wrung out the cotton, it was laid out on a tarp to dry in the sun. Meanwhile the mattress covers were also washed thoroughly. Once they were all dry, we had to remake those mattresses - an exhausting process for both our mother, and the girls of the family. Today this is unheard of, and everyone has a pillow-top mattress or some fancy kind of bed. I am one of these people, and I have gotten used to the good things like my mother said, but I did learn to appreciate what it took to get here. I don't think anyone wants to return to those days because of the hard work involved, but the lessons learned are always with us. The time spent with our loved ones is something to treasure. Not a day goes by that I don't remember something I've taken away from my early years. I owe it all to my parents, and the knowledge they passed on to me. Sometimes I'm asked, "why do you prick the biscuits with a fork like that?" or "why do you prefer to wait until daylight to do that job?" The first answer is because my mother always did it that way. The second is because if you do a task at night, you will be able to tell in the morning that it was done with little light: "Lo que de noche se hace, de dia parece." Until next time, my friends: enjoy the modern conveniences. Let's not forget that we contributed our hard work, and played an important part in progress.

title: La Sala Events
body: May 10th at La Sala, 7PM: Sixty-Six Mile Radius, a film starring three artists living within that radius of the Tamarind Institute at UNM -- Nina Elder, Tom Miller, and Galistean Judy Tuwaletstiwa. La Sala's regular season begins May 26th with the opening (4-7PM) of the exhibition Best Seats in the House: over 30 New Mexico artists interpret the chair in various media, examining functional and non-functional appearances both seriously and playfully. (Show is up until September 16th; open Saturdays and Sundays, 11-5, and it's free.) Also on view is Honoring Our Community: "The Board of La Sala honors members of our community who have generously contributed to the needs of our village, our state's heritage, and our nation's cultural achievements. These 2018 Honorees will be the first in a multi-year program to recognize the remarkable people who live and have lived in our village. We thank them for their accomplishments and successes."

title: Annual Water Association Meeting
body: On March 22nd, the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association (GMDWCA) held its annual meeting at the Community Center, led by Board President Phil Tuwaletstiwa. Attendance was sparse, but the required quorum (10% of membership) was met. Treasurer John Watson-Jones reported on the last fiscal year and projections for this fiscal year. There were some questions about $4,600 spent for the archaeology report mandated for the new line along La Otra Vanda, which will be paid back when we receive the state loan. We were assured that we got a very good deal; archeologist Mike Marshall had professional ties to some village residents. Currently we have only one well and one tank operating. If anything goes wrong with one little part, we have no water. Michael Golino was paid c. $850 per month to successfully see the complex project of a major state loan through the bureaucratic hoops. The loan is in part a grant. (We get c. $450,000 and pay back c. $130,000.) It will cover a much-needed, updated dual system, and requests for several new lines are in the works. Many extant lines that should be 6" or 8" pipes are only 2". Freddie Cardenas asked the board to consider lower rates instead of the tier system now in place. He suggested that the Board was acting like a corporation -which, in fact it is, by law-- and urged more grant applications, perhaps through our State Representative Matthew McQueen, who is a Water Association member. The Board responded that the tiers ( the more water you use, the more you pay) encourage water conservation. We will take a close look to see if we can lower rates, but we have to cover expenses: there were six pipe breaks this year and a $1,000 debt was excused in a hardship case. Board member Richard Patton and former Board member Scott Diffrient will draft a proposal suggesting reforms for the Board's consideration. There was discussion around the high cost of a new hookup ($10,000). Neither Eldorado nor Santa Fe answered requests for their rates, which are reportedly less. It was noted that rules prohibited speculators and that the fee can be paid in installments, or an interest free loan, over "a reasonable length of time." Installation costs vary; there are easy installations and difficult ones depending on terrain, distance, etc. Board member Steve Moya remarked that our ISO ratings (how much insurance we pay depending on firefighting resource availability) can go down. Ideally there would be a hydrant every 500 feet, but the loan can't pay for hydrants and neither can the GVFR. Liability insurance covers the board but not property and "unowned [private] vehicles." There were some comments on the new billing system. Our accountant, Ana Berry, said she would add dates and notices of meetings to the bills, and thanked previous volunteer accountants -- especially Romona Scholder (who did the billing for 18 years) -- for a "fantastic job" which makes her own job much easier. At the time of the meeting no member was in arears, thanks to a good deal of interaction between the Board and members when problems arise; a couple of members are behind a month or so but nothing to worry about. Board Members Richard Patton and Lucy Lippard will work with former Board Member Anna Cardenas to figure out how to manage a community fund for those who need help paying their water bills. No one at the meeting volunteered to fill the vacant spot for one new Board member, so Michael D. Anaya was proposed and approved in absentia. (Luckily, he has accepted.)

title: GCA Breakfast/Annual Meeting
body: On March 24th a gala breakfast at the Community Center was presented by Susie Shanklin, Wayland Wong, and Greg Salustro to accompany the annual GCA elections meeting. Evelyn Gregory, Phil Pfeiffer and Jane Perry were thanked as they completed their terms. Estelle Berger and Barbara Seiler were re-elected by acclamation. Anna Cardenas is the new alternate, and new neighbor Kevin Smith recently volunteered to become the second alternate. President Roger Taylor introduced new residents (Kevin and Cecille 'Cissy' Smith, Deirdre Africa) and announced a new fundraising campaign to be launched in late Summer. The Community Center, which is aging (along with too many villagers) needs a roof fix and new stucco. Someone noted that the bats were returning but bat houses now cost from $400-700 -- which sounds kind of batty. The County will plant 150 bundles of willows and clean up the bosque trails after work is done. Apparently our beloved bosque is the third most significant wildlife migration corridor in this part of the U.S. Who knows who's passing through in the night ...

title: Tom and Betty Jean Shinas Wedding Anniversary
body: In May, The New Mexican published a long account of the son, wedding anniversary of Tom and Betty Jean Shinas. The bride was the daughter of Galisteans Manuel Sosa Almeida (1914-1982) and Reynalda Chavez Anaya (1920-2000). When they were married at Cristo Rey in Santa Fe, the bride's grandmother, Carmelita Chavez Anaya (1884-1981) "gave her blessings while the couple kneeled before her." Carmelita was the mother of Clarita, Serapio, Nick, and Johnny Anaya, all of whom settled in Galisteo. Nick is the survivor of that generation in the village.

title: Ted Harrison and Commonweal Conservancy
body: This month The New Mexican also featured Ted Harrison, whom we know as the founder and president of Commonweal Conservancy (and former president and CEO of the New Mexico Community Foundation) who brought us the wonderful (and endangered) Galisteo Basin Preserve. His latest project, the restoration of a historic building on Guadalupe Street in Santa Fe, will become Common Ground -- a communal workspace, cafe, and yoga center.

title: Margaret Wrinkle on NPR Discussing Lynching Memorial
body: Margaret Wrinkle was on NPR (4/28) being interviewed about the opening of the Lynching memorial in Montgomery, Alabama. The memorial, she said "exposes the hidden narrative of the South." Lynching was a form of economic terrorism. As a generations-deep southerner, she noted that hers was the first generation to be taught that we are all equal.

title: John Watson-Jones Letter to The New Mexican
body: John Watson-Jones wrote a clever letter to the editor of The New Mexican, noting that the state's new award-winning license plates bear the names of three nations: "count 'em USA Mexico, and Chile."

title: La Sala's New Doors to Open
body: About a month ago the Board of La Sala hired Galisteo master carpenter Ted Montoya to restore the front doors and overhead window at La Sala. Now the doors and an opening transom window are installed and they are looking and working beautifully. A big thank you to Ted, and to Anna Cardenas, who was very helpful in consulting and researching hardware to create a mix of original and reproduction. This was not an easy project: filler for the cracks, replacing some wood pieces in the doors, filling and sealing the holes made over the years for locks and door knobs, sanding, multiple coats of primer and finish paint. etc. was very uneven and crumbly and the doors themselves were warped; it took some careful planing to make it fit tightly. The new threshold works great with a nice tight seal (no more wind or bugs coming through!) All this highlights the next sorely needed repair -- restoring the windows and framing on the sides and overhead. We would like to have this done in time for the late May opening, but we need funds to do so. La Sala always appreciates donors!

title: {GVFR: The Cost of Excellence}
body: Cindy and Frank Lux report that some Galisteans believe that members of the Fire department are paid! Would that it were true. Everyone works hard. No one has a salary. Chief Jean Moya sets the record straight: "Back in September of 2007 the Board of County Commissioners adopted a resolution on the Volunteer recruitment and retention incentive program to reimburse certified EMT's and certified Firefighters for expenses. As Chiefs, we receive no more compensation than any other member of the department. The program initially paid $6 for every emergency response and $2 for every approved training. These fees have since been increased to $11 and $8. This is staggering given the number of hours spent. Budgeted funds were made available from the Emergency Medical Service Gross Receipts tax voted in by the public. "Our goal as volunteers," says Moya, "remains the same, to provide quality, professional, emergency service to the people and visitors of Santa Fe County."

title: {April 21 Village Cleanup}
body: A good crowd turned out to tidy up the village's already surprisingly clean thoroughfares. The incentive was a delicious breakfast donated as usual by John and Tanya Young.

title: Lamy Dining Car Closed Down
body: The state Regulation and Licensing Department has closed the doors of the freestanding Club Car 1158 in Lamy that has been open on weekends for food and drink. It was determined that their license -- originally intended for the summer trips between Santa Fe and Lamy, halted in 2013 -- only applied to servicing passengers on moving vehicles and does not apply to stationary cars off the tracks. Owner Karl Ziebarth hopes to restart some kind of food service this summer. An "independent transportation consultant," he was involved in the attempt in 2013 to allow trucks to off-load crude oil onto trains in Lamy. It was vigorously opposed and stopped in its tracks by area residents.

title: {To Pave or Not to Pave? That Is the Question}
body:
alas poor Galisteo I see thee still,
thy land bare to the New Mexican sky
thy dust upon which coyote's padding tread marks his trail
alas poor Galisteo I knew her well
throne to Jack Rabbit
she has borne me on her back a thousand times
welcomed the scratch of quail
rain's gentle shower and pounding hail
the burning sun
how abhorred in my imagination it is the black river
of death
foreseen by the ancient guardians of this world
my gorge rises at it
I will tie black ribbon about my arm to speak my mourning
to your eternal entombment

title: {Songs of the Times}
body:
Picture this; I'm sitting on bleachers in anticipation of what I am about to witness. The stage is dark, and suddenly there is smoke coming up from it. Then very bright lights shine on four individuals wearing costumes of some kind. The smoke disappears, and very loud music pierces my ears. A young man sitting directly in front of me is moving his head forward so fast to keep in sync with the beat that I'm wondering how his neck will feel tomorrow. He seems to be feeling no pain right now. Meanwhile, my sons are sitting on either side of me, and I'm getting a little peeved at them because they keep moving me from one place to another. Finally, I ask, "why are you guys moving me? I can't see the show." They tell me those guys are blazing, and we don't want you to get a contact high. Now, being naïve about all of this, I'm wondering what a "contact high" means. I'm finally allowed to stay in one spot and enjoy the music. There is quite a bit I don't know about these concerts and what goes on there. For the most part, it was alright. It's certainly not what I was accustomed to listening to, but for one evening it was entertainment. The crowd was eager to please their entertainers too. When the camera light shone on different areas of the audience, some girls were lifting up their shirts, and creating a show of their own.

It certainly was a night to remember. Imagine me, someone who is used to music from the Big Band Era, and New Mexico Spanish, sitting in the audience of a heavy metal concert and listening to "Motley Crue." This experience takes me back to the time I took an English class with a room full of youngsters. The instructor requested that we write a paper on something we really loved and enjoyed in life. Well, that was an easy subject for me. I've always loved music, and I can get lost listening to Glen Miller, and all those Big Bands, so my paper was on my passion for music from the old time bands.

It was interesting when we read our papers in class, because the only one who knew about the Big Band Era was the instructor. I had to explain to all the young people that another time existed, and other music was made for listening, dancing, and just plain enjoying the sounds.

title: {Conserve Water, In These Dry Times}
body:
The average U.S. household of four uses approximately 400 gallons of water per day, but Santa Fe County has reduced this to 200 gallons. Small changes can make a big difference, becoming second nature. Here are some tips from the State EPA:

Short showers: 5 minutes uses four to five gallons compared to up to 50 gallons for a bath. Rinse and shut-off, lather, rinse.

Shut off water while brushing your teeth, washing your hair and shaving and save up to 500 gallons a month.

Water-efficient showerheads are inexpensive, easy to install, and can save up to 750 gallons a month.

Run clothes washer and dishwasher only when full, and save up to 1,000 gallons a month.

Water plants before 10 or after 6, 3 times a week max, slowly, so soil can absorb it. Check drip system for disconnected heads, which can leak lots of water; set auto controls for early morning hours before the heat rises; use lots of mulch.

Fix leaky toilets and faucets. Use low-flow toilets. Faucet washers are inexpensive and take a few minutes to replace. To check your toilet for a leak, place a few drops of food coloring in the tank and wait. If it seeps into the toilet bowl without flushing, you have a leak. Fixing it or replacing it with a new, more efficient model can save up to 1,000 gallons a month.

Teach your kids about water conservation to ensure a future generation that uses water wisely. Make it a family effort to reduce next month's water bill! See www.epa.gov/watersense for more information.

title: Update on Spirit Wind Development
body:
Daniel Martinez, an associate of notorious developer Joe Miller, led a public hearing at the former Country Store in Eldorado on June 22 to inform Lamy and other nearby communities about the Spirit Wind West Subdivision -- planned (and permitted) just south of the Railway tracks on US 285. The plan has been in the works since 1994, so it proceeds under the old County Code, as a result of a settlement with the County. Water rights (7.9 acre feet) have been procured through Eldorado Water, and an archeological survey has been completed.

Barker Realty is handling the 39 lots (3 acres with water hookup included = $89,000 each). Buyers can build their own homes or take the developer's. Covenants were amended to allow horses, barns and fencing. Much of the discussion focused on the maximum of 12 "modular" homes (that apparently meet affordable housing requirements); the rest are "stick-built." Martinez insisted that "modular" (i.e. prefabricated) homes placed on permanent cement foundations are not "manufactured" homes. Despite a one-story limit, two stories may be allowed given the right topography. Walking, biking and equestrian trails will connect to the Basin Preserve and Lamy open space/park.

The 285 ALL Steering Committee will review the proposed covenants. Still under revision is Miller's Cimarron Shopping Mall up past the gas station. It will be publicly presented in July. (Like we need another mall?)

title: Sina Brush Letter on Bear Invasion
body: Sina Brush wrote a letter to the editor of The New Mexican (6/4) on the potential bear invasion due to drought and lack of forage in the mountains. She notes that every day less than perfect vegetables and fruit are discarded by grocery stores: "Why can't that food be dropped from helicopters to draw those animals back where they belong and save them from certain death? ...It's a human relatively simple solution."

title: Watch Out for Bears in Dry Summer
body: Bears were also the subject of a feature in The New Mexican (5/26) headlined "Watch Out for Bears in Dry Summer." The reporter, Andy Stiny, lists the following precautions: Don't leave food or pet dishes out at night; Don't put sweet-smelling or meat scraps in compost; clean and store outdoor grills after use; pick fruit from trees when ripe and don't leave it to rot on the ground; remove bird feeders. If you encounter a bear: give it plenty of room to escape and pick up small children; make yourself larger by holding out your jacket. If attacked fight back with anything at hand and aim for nose and eyes; if the bear hasn't seen you, stay calm and move slowly away, making noise so it knows you are there. Most important: Never get between a bear and her cubs. (Camping instructions are even more complicated.)

title: Kim Sorvig on Mora County Cracking Controversies
body: Our activist neighbor to the west, UNM professor Kim Sorvig, wrote a letter to The New Mexican (6/5) on Mora County's Cracking controversies, noting that Santa Fe County did it right when they protected the Galisteo Basin from drilling in 2008 (in which many Galisteans were actively involved): "The ordinance we passed has become a national model and is the basis of Mora's current efforts. It holds industry responsible, up-front, for costs it usually expects taxpayers to subsidize." It remains to be seen how the bills proposed by NM Rep. Steve Pearce to undermine any environmental concerns and encourage fossil fuel extraction will affect the Santa Fe ordinance.

title: Manuel Romero Chavez Obituary
body: Manuel Romero Chavez passed away at age 91 on June 14. Born to Faustin and Juanita (Romero) Chavez in the Ortiz mountains, he was raised in Galisteo. One of his surviving children is the artist Kenny Chavez, who sent El Puente this picture of his father, age 15, on the steps of the family home facing the church (now Lopez-Watermann). He wanted to be buried with all his family's generations in the Galisteo cemetery.

title: Help for the Old Cemetery
body:
For the last month or so, Michael Moquin has been working to restore and mud-plaster the front of the gates and the oratorio (chapel) in the old cemetery on The Hill. Nuestra Senora de Los Remedios is now under the aegis of Santa Maria de La Paz, and Fr. Daniel Balizan has permitted the project. Moquin was hoping for some volunteers -- but so far no one has stepped up.

Around the first of June, some people knocked over and broke in half some ten or twelve headstones, some of which had been repaired the last time we did restoration and maintenance. It has been reported to the police.

In order to continue with the restoration process, rebuild some of the wall on the north and south sides, put new beams on the chapel, cap the whole wall, fill caved-in graves, and fix the broken headstones, we will need volunteers. Mr. Moquin will train them to mix the mud and apply it to the walls. The pastoral and finance council has approved a set amount for another 60 hours of work for the worst parts of the chapel. That will be it, until we can collect enough to continue. Your generous donations will preserve this historical cemetery. Make out your checks to: Galisteo Cemetery, PO Box 98, Cerrillos, NM, 87010.

title: Elmer (Doc) Ferneau Memorial
body:
A memorial was held on Sept. 2 at the Community Center for Doc Ferneau, who died in his Galisteo home a few months short of 100 years old. He loved music, and the hospice nurse said he was singing on the morning he died. Featured at the memorial was a brief video of him singing with the "Docettes": Lorraine Weiss, Julia Moore, and Lesley Dyer, who came on Sundays and sang with the still strong tenor, a tradition initiated several years ago by Janice Felty Griscom. (Doc would accompany the hymn "I'll Fly Away" by flapping his arms like wings.)
Ferneau was born in Tama, Iowa, and served in the Navy in WWII. He met Marie Humphrey, the sister of a friend, while on a leave and liked to tell the story about how she had a date the night they met and canceled it to go out with him. They married in 1942 and had a son, Brett, who predeceased him. Doc earned a PhD from the University of Chicago and became head of the Education Department at the University of Tulsa, from which he retired in 1972. When he and Marie moved to Santa Fe, Doc worked as a security officer at La Tierra Nueva, where he met Wendy Chase. Later both moved to Galisteo, the Ferneaus having transported an old yellow Depot building from Lamy to just south of town. A toast from Wendy was read at the memorial, citing the good times they had had together over almost thirty years, along with "Jack D. and George D., the Whiskey Brothers." She also praised Doc's loving care of Marie during the several years after she suffered a stroke: "with never one word of complaint," setting "a standard for those of us who complain daily about minor inconveniences."
After Marie's death, Doc insisted that he was ready too, but he lived for many more years. Although confined to a wheelchair, he continued to sing, tell stories, and keep up with current events. His devoted caretakers, Frank and Darlyn Corriz of All You Need is Us, have adopted his cat Rosie. Olivia Ogorek, who helped him with bookkeeping, arranged the memorial with Brett's partner LeAnn Knudsen. Thanks to Corey McGillicuddy for the excellent breakfast and Angie Beauchamp for setting up the video.

title: Priscilla Hoback Memorial
body:
A memorial will be held at Quartermill Farm on the Fall Equinox, Saturday, Sept. 22, 2-5 PM. In lieu of flowers please donate to Horses for Heroes - New Mexico, Inc. P.O. Box 1882, Santa Fe, NM, 87504.
Galisteo will not seem the same with Priscilla Hoback gone. Since moving to Quartermill Farm (named after the price she paid for it in 1978), and resurrecting the home of Don Jose Ortiz y Pino, she has been a generous and forceful member of the community. Hoback co-founded the Galisteo Studio Tour and partially restored the claypit near Pueblo Blanco. She raised and trained Arabian horses, and for over half a century she worked as an artist in New Mexico.
A native Santa Fean, daughter of Rosaleña Murphy of Pink Adobe fame, Priscilla was married three times - to Joe Lynch, father of her children, then Frank Hoback, a well-known pilot, and Peter Gould, a furniture maker. Hoback had The Pot Shop on Canyon Road before moving to Galisteo. She used the wild clays and natural pigments from around her to create pottery and stoneware murals inspired by her garden, horses, and the wilderness around her home. "For a time, the studio may be full of white deer," she wrote in her book Living Clay (2000) "and then those fade out. As work on another idea begins, I am in a land of herons or antelope, thinking their thoughts." When named a Santa Fe Living Treasure in 2017, Priscilla was described as "a true woman of the West, a person of the earth, the essence of New Mexico."
Priscilla is survived by her daughter Denise Lynch and grandson Sean Sohn of Galisteo, and by her son, Joseph Hoback, and his two children. Her work and presence is on display in Galisteo and at the Nedra Matteucci Gallery in Santa Fe.

title: {Froggy Went A Courting}
body:
What a divine thing is curiosity. In the evening during monsoons when the toady chorus begins, I go absolutely nuts trying to locate the culprits, the actual perpetrators of the deep, thrumming mating calls of male Spade-foot Toads. Weary of standing out in the rain trying to pinpoint the source, I get in my car and drive back roads and the highway near the Galisteo Creek, to no avail. The sound seems close only to move away when I get near, like trying to catch a spider's silk floating on the breeze.
That frogs somehow generated, quite spontaneously, from mud was a well-established notion in Aristotle's time. Well, I know a thing or two about natural history, enough to agree that the toads had to be calling from a pond, or a tank, or standing water somewhere. But where?
Wary of snakes and worried by mosquitos, I set out on foot down a dusty path bordered by Four-wing saltbush. The call of a Common Raven mocks me into thinking this is a really dumb idea and wondering what the heck I am doing out here in the heat of the day when I almost walk right into WATER!
Clearly, I'm late to the party. The bacchanal breeding frenzy that took place here is played out, and the toads have spade-footed their way backwards deep into the earth. What I see is a small, scooped-out catchment tank of muddy water teeming with the flipping, churning bodies of hundreds of big-headed tadpoles—the last stop on the metamorphosis express. What I witness is the struggle for survival.
Time is flying and the shallow pond is vanishing. Desiccation equals death and, trust me, survival is a rush job for the 1% that actually reach the finish line. In an explosion of cell growth, the fastest of any amphibian, the transformation from egg to tadpole to Spade-foot Toad needs only 14 days. The challenge is intensified by the presence of predators—snake, hawk, owl, skunk, raccoon, coyote and bobcat—that will not miss this exciting opportunity, beginning even as the males call the females to their pond to lay thousands of blobby, gelatinous eggs.
My curiosity made me pursue this mystery. Given enough time, I'm sure Aristotle would have puzzled it out for himself.
"A careful observation of Nature will disclose pleasantries of superb irony. She has for instance placed Toads close to flowers." - Honore de Balzac
* The Spade-foot Toad, found in all 33 counties, is the New Mexico State Amphibian.

title: Tarantula Mating Season Safety Advisory
body: Into November, it's mating season for big hairy male tarantulas, on the prowl on Santa Fe County highways (one was spotted on NM 41). The eight-legged arachnids are about the size of a fat doughnut and have a leg span of 4 or 5". They may look scary, but are pretty harmless and won't attack unless you corner them. And their bite is no worse than a bee sting, if you're not allergic. They are voracious insect eaters, so keep an eye on the roads and allow them safe passage.

title: {Election Day Is Coming Up}
body:
Galisteo has been well served by our neighbor, Matthew McQueen, as our District 50 representative to the State Legislature, and I suspect that few of us want to see any change. He is a leader in important committees: Chair of the Energy, Environment & Natural Resources Committee; Co-Chair of the Water & Natural Resources Committee. He knows how the Legislature works, and has established strong working relationships with its leaders. Matthew will be well-positioned to help New Mexico turn around in the next several years, especially if there is a new Democrat governor (a plug for Michelle Lujan-Grisham...)
The Democrat vote for our County Commissioner in November is split between Rudy Garcia, who won the primary in June, and our own Mike Anaya, who successfully gathered signatures to run as an Independent. Garcia has worked for the County for 27 years and is a member of the Santa Fe Public Schools Board. An editorial in The New Mexican urged him to give that up if he becomes our commissioner, given inevitable conflicts of time and commitment to two such important posts. Independents are hoping for a strong showing in November, given that almost a quarter of New Mexico voters are not registered with a major party. Another Independent, Jarratt Applewhite from Lamy—a self-described "true fiscal conservative," gun owner, and high school dropout—is running against McQueen, which means Matthew needs our support. A fundraiser is being held at the home of Leslie Gallery Dilworth in Galisteo, on Sept. 13. Contributions to: Committee to Elect Matthew McQueen, 7 Avenida Vista Grande B7-120 Santa Fe, NM 87508 www.mcqueenfornm.com

title: Robert Anaya Endorses His Brother Mike
body:
It has been an honor and a privilege to serve as the District 3 County Commissioner for two terms. I strongly believe, as does my brother Mike, "to lead is to listen, learn and then act in the common interests of the people." I am writing to express my full support for my brother Mike Dale Anaya and his desire to serve the residents of District 3. Mike grew up in Galisteo and Stanley and understands what it takes to get things done, and help others. During his two terms on the County Commission, among many other Countywide projects, Mike supported the adoption of the Code of the West, and served as President of the NM Association of Counties. He was Assistant Land Commissioner under Ray Powell. He is a Doer, Not a Talker.
In the village, Mike co-founded the GVFR, was President of the GCA, is a past and present member of the Water Board, and a longtime member of the St. Joseph's Society. [Ed. note: He was also an early supporter of El Puente, and suggested the sponsorship process.] He worked with the community to improve the old Galisteo Bridge and the Galisteo Community Park, to pave CR 42 and support open space at Thornton Ranch and the Cerrillos Hills State Park.

title: Community Center Needs Our Help
body:
Our Galisteo Community Association Board launched a fund drive this September because we urgently need funds to repair our Community Center. Although we have kept up with immediate maintenance, our long put-off big $$ projects have come due: the external stucco must be replaced; the Board Room plaster is deteriorated; the outside bancos are deteriorating. On our wish list is the addition of a heating/cooling system and upgrading the bathrooms to be ADA compliant. We also need money for monthly maintenance, utilities and insurance.

We're working with the USDA to secure a two-part grant to cover the majority of the repair expenses. If awarded, we would still have to raise at least $ I 0,000 as our share of the $40,000 first phase and a similar amount in 2019 for our wish list items. So, neighbors, watch for our "Ten in November" letter in the mail. We look forward to your contribution to our community.

A public meeting on our USDA grant application was held on Thursday Oct 4th. Under discussion were an Oct I, 20 I 8 "equipment" grant/loan application: to purchase & install a heating/cooling system; trenching & cabling for internet connectivity; adding playground infrastructure & landscaping. Also an April I, 2019 grant application for payment of engineering and architectural design work. Finally, an Oct I, 2019 "structural" grant/loan application: stucco coat for the entire building; bathroom upgrade; adding storage.

Judges at the September Chile & Margarita Cookoff: David Maestas, Mare Tomaski, Stella Mastas, Mary Alice Anaya, Cindy and Frank Lux. Winners will appear belatedly in the next issue.

title: David Burk (1940-2018)
body:
David Burk (MD, child psychiatrist), passed away peacefully on September 13th after a twenty-five year battle against Parkinson's Disease. Known in the village during the '70s as the doctor on the hill, David moved to the teachers' house behind the cemetery and water tower ( only one back then) with an expansive village dump across the road. He had one condition-to be given exclusive use of one ofthe eight precious village telephone lines. Called out during a snowstorm in the early hours one night, he delivered a neighbor's baby daughter.

"My days as the village and rodeo doc are over," he admitted ruefully when half a dozen healers raced with him onto the Rodeo parade ground to tend a fallen cowboy ... one with a crystal, one with a pendulum, and ... "I get the picture," he said.

At his shoes-off house, David put in a polished oak floor and threw wild dance parties. He painted soft abstract watercolors while listening to East Indian ragas and daily walked the empty desert that is now Ranchitos. He built an indoor conservatory famed for its year-round pink bougainvillea blossoms and giant tomato plants. He planted an orchard, and a field of corn each spring.

He strung up a hammock and introduced me into a world of desert moonrises, shooting stars, and silence I could never have imagined. "God's picture show," he called it, as we huddled together in the frozen snow, wrapped in a duvet. "Listen," he'd hush me. "Count how many dogs we can set off barking. Ahooow ... " he'd howl, laughing. And sure enough, first one ... two other dogs took up the chorus till very soon we'd hear seven or more.

Unwinding on the drive home of an evening after a day's work in Santa Fe, he was often greeted by the sweet notes of an accordion and the friendly sight of Tacho Sandoval, among other villagers, gathered on a portal strumming Spanish songs. More horses than cars traveled NM41 in those days when Galisteo, a peaceful, friendly village, was still largely Hispanic. On weekends the community could devour home-made tamales sitting on the picnic bench outside the Tienda Anaya.

Commonly, David would discover a $5 dollar bill and scribbled thank-you-for-the-beers-doc note on his fridge after a thirsty neighbor had crawled through his oversize dog door into the laundry room and helped himself. Yes, those were neighborly days ...

A conscientious and empathetic doctor, one of the psychiatrists on call the night of the prison's deadly riot, during which 31 people were killed, David saw and heard such terrible things, he closed his office and went walkabout for two years before returning to work.

Though the heavy burden of the disease gradually eroded his body and mind, it never dampened his love of adventure. David enjoyed life to the last. On his to-do-before-I-die list was this past summer's six-week trip to the mountains of France where friends and my family met for a four-day reunion cum-birthday party. He walked, picnicked in the high meadows and drove the tunnel with us to lunch in Italy. We flew to Spain to spend our second honeymoon sipping wine on a favorite beach. Included in every activity, David stayed fully engaged.

What to say about a beautiful being but that he was beautiful. We who knew and loved David already miss the intelligent and lovely, gentle being ofhim. I am oh so thankful for the thirty-five happy years we shared.

To honor David's memory and in celebration of a wonderful life, an informal wake will be held at our home on Sunday, November 18th, from 12.30; those of you who knew him are welcome. RSVP please, at 466-6003 or galisteoliz@gmail.com. For a formal obituary listing his academic and professional achievements see www.berardinellifuneralhome.com

title: Petals and Feathers
body:
What a divine thing is curiosity. A while back I VvTote about our fall grasses, identified with Catherine's help. I wish I could find that article again to help me remember all those long-forgotten wonderfully grassy names.

Now, gloriously, it is fall again and what troubles my curiosity are wildflowers. The high desert air and the angle of the sun bring out each bloom's vibrant attempt to be noticed. I admit to feding guilty that I call birds by their proper names but describe wild flowers as those "little yellow mound-y thingies." Roadside celebrations of tall sunflowers and low spreading mounds of purple sand verbena (Lucy's favorite) I can identify through my windshield at 55 mph. But the passing of summer's heat brings cooler edges to the day allowing smaller more fragile wildflowers to flourish. These little description-defying blooms become my daily focus.

The end of summer finds me, an admittedly frustrated naturalist, surrounded by wildflower books, cell phone 1D apps, and random flower specimens pressed between newspaper sheets weighed down with bricks. I am guilty of playing the loser's game of "look at the bloom, ID the flower." lt doesn't work with birds and it won't work with flowers. Kindly ornithologists and botanists worked out systems designed to ease our frustrated attempts to match names with petals and feathers.

With birds the key to identification lies not so much in a field guide's color plates but in the grouping ofrelated families sharing discernable characteristics. Simply put, a beginning birder learns to distinguish a hawk from a duck and a finch from a flycatcher based on clues of size, shape, general impression, habitat, feeding strategy and range maps. And so it is with wildflowers. Field guides show us how to find our way to the names of wildflowers by keying out families based on details of petal and leaf size, shape and arrangement, location and color.

Considering all this, I weigh my options and decide, basically, to chuck it and live with my limited knowledge of botanicals. In the soft light of fall, I decide not to be so serious about identifying every wildflower but to be very serious about enjoying their amazing diversity and ability to please and surprise me. I know a few names now and enjoy long friendships with favorites.

I choose as my favorites the chocolate flower and wild four o'clock because year after year they choose to colonize around my front patio gate. How lucky am I? Each spring the mouth-watering aroma of dark chocolate catches me by surprise as the morning sun heats the flagstones. Through the hot summer I wait and watch for the return appearance of the large leafy mound of four o 'clocks that open their lavender tubular blooms in the co.ol of fall evenings. And along with the fall, they appear as if by magic, uncultivated but quietly bidden by my anticipation.

"When you take a flower in your hand and really look at it, it's your world for the moment." - Georgia O 'Keefe.

title: Water Association Board Meets
body: The Board of the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association met on Sept. 25th. Aside from the usual discussions of billing issues, undetected leaks, and bureaucratic requirements from the State, we also received Michael Golino's update on the loan process: The archeological work to date has found nothing of concern. We are about half or more of the way through the design process. Our entire system will be pressurized, possibly by variable pumps. Power to the new site will be (hopefully) single phase (we will buy the transformer) and branch off from the church as a 7000-volt line. There will be a new pump house; some old leaky pipes will be replaced, a 4" line will come from the well. A new tank allowing redundancy, greatly encouraged by the State, will be placed next to the current tank. Design may be finished by the end of October, followed by a 1/2 month bidding process. Ground breaking could be in March, 2019, subject to weather.

Attendance at La Sala was tracked this year for the first time and nearly 650 people came through La Sala alone -- not a full measure, as not everyone stops there.
