title: The Galisteo Bosque ... Once More
body:
"What is that bird? Did you see those bear prints? ls that scat from a coyote or a bear? And what about these tracks, are those from a raccoon? Where are the Great Homed Owls?" The bosque is buzzing again with questions from Galistefios, visitors, students, and stream stewards. Because once more they can see the forest for the trees.

With a great sense of relief, gratitude, and satisfaction, many involved in the bosque restoration effmis of the last few years can now take a breather. The work has been substantially completed. Hundreds of Russian Olive trees, Tamarisks, and Elms were removed between March 2016 and December 2017, more than a dozen piles of driftwood were stacked and burned in early 2018. Nearly a thousand feet of the Galisteo Creek channel and banks have been reshaped to improve overbank flows, and thousands of willow seedlings, cottonwood saplings, and berry shrubs were planted in March 2018 to rebuild the native ecosystem.

Many volunteers helped pull and cut back hundreds of Russian Olive seedlings that rose again in the last half year. This all seemed to have pleased Mother Nature because despite a dry first half of the year, she supported a profuse reestablishment of willows, horsetail, cattails, sedges, rushes, and grasses of many kinds. All this allowed the floods between July and October to spread at least three times all over the bottom of the bosque, evening out the elevation differences on the bosque floor and irrigating even the farthest corners and forming new channels and wet spots. The bosque got so wet that it did its own job in eradicating the Russian olives by drowning them. And that's just what the restoration design intended to do.

The restoration structures perfo1med exactly as designed and were not affected by the power of the floods. They have begun blending into the landscape and over time will likely become barely visible. They accumulated sediment, bringing the channel bottom up by 18 inches in some locations. The flows also effectively recreated an acre of new wetland in an old oxbow below the fonner Agnes Martin house, and supported a beautiful new willow wetland at the "S-curve" behind the former Galisteo Inn. The old channels on the west side of the bosque downstream from El Puente once more carried water and helped irrigate the cottonwoods there that were planted upon the initiative of Mrs. Helen Hover in the 1950s.

Few residents may realize that this work was about 20 years in the making. The first steps to bosque restoration took place 1998 to 2005. Based on an assessment of wetlands throughout the Galisteo Basin in 2006-2007, and successive funding opportunities, the final push for the work restarted in 2012 with renewed funding requests to State and Federal agencies. After funding was secured, surveys, planning and design started in late 2014, leading to permits in late 2015, prompting the final implementation phase in early 2016.

State and US Army Corps oversight requires further monitoring and after-care until June 2020. Please be on the lookout for ongoing community volunteer maintenance events in the spring and fall. In the meantime, on behalf of the planning team and the Galisteo Community Association, our heartfelt thanks for your support, encouragement, and appreciation.

Note: On December I I, Jan-Willem Jans ens of Ecotone gave a presentation about the prqject for the New Mexico Wetlands Roundtable.

title: Progress, and Modern-Day Families
body:
Progress is wonderful, I think we all like the modern-day comforts of living, including me. Together with progress, the way in which we discipline and rear our children has changed. Youngsters today are different from when I was growing up. They are much more independent, and have more control over their own lives. This brings me to the way my parents brought us up, and how we were content with the worldly goods we possessed.

My parents were very strict. My father was especially protective of his daughters. They were the most likely to need adult supervision for school functions, parties, field trips, and dances. There was one field trip in particular that our school sponsored, to the State Fair in Albuquerque. If I remember correctly, I was in the sixth grade, and my brother George was two grades ahead of me. My father was not going to allow me to go, but since my brother George's class was going, my father agreed. George had to take care ofme while we were on this trip. He did not like that. His fun day came to a screeching halt when my father told him to take care ofme. George did look after me, but he did go off with his friends at some point and enjoy from the State Fair's games, food, and rides. George deserved a little time to himself

I guess money went a longer way in those days because my father gave us each five dollars for spending on our field trip, and I still came home with a few cents to my name. I remember a student on our bus asking me how much money I had for the trip. She laughed when I told her, and said I would not be able to have any fun with so little money. On the contrary, I came home with a big stuffed animal that I had won on a Spin the Arrow game. I think I spent a dime to win the prize. I guess a little money did go a long way for me that day. I don't think the gal who was skeptical of my finances brought anything back to speak of from the state fair. I felt sorry for her because she didn't seem to get any enjoyment from the field trip.

Thinking back on those days, we didn't worry about the way the world was, who was the president in charge of our country, and the value of money. We only w01Tied about learning our time tables, and being able to stand up in front of the class to read our book rep01i. I always had stage fright when it was my tum to read. Today, young people have to do research papers that are time consuming, and I'm sure create a great deal of stress for them. This is where progress comes in to alleviate the stress. Thank goodness for modern technology. The younger generation is more confident, and capable, because of progress both in their homes, and in their learning. The value of money is not as important as the value of love, and parents still know how to love their children.

title: {EDITORIAL: COMMON GROUND}
body:
The late Santa Clara Pueblo scholar Rina Swentzell defined community as "something you can't walk away from." The new year seems a good moment to consider again what community means in Galisteo, what our individual responsibilities are to the village and to each other. Perhaps you feel that this does not apply to you. Perhaps you think your home is your castle and it's well fortified. You're not on the water system, you don't expect to have an accident or have your house catch on fire. You don't care what is built where, or how Galisteo changes, as long as it's out of sight. You're too busy with your own life to bother with what goes on around you. If so, that's a pity. It's even dangerous. Not just for you, but for all of us.
A place where a few do the work and many contribute nothing is only real estate, not a community. To have no opinion, to put in no time, is to be powerless. We often don't realize how many dedicated people it takes to keep Galisteo healthy as we see it today. Some of them are virtually invisible and ask for no credit. They work for love of the village. Those of us who are new here don't always know who has done a lot of work in the past. We need others to step into their shoes when they get tired. You know who you are, whether you contribute or not.
Change is not bad, but not all change is progress. It has to be thoughtful change, agreed upon by at least a majority of those whom it affects. A few hours a month seems a small price in exchange for the beauty of this place. Consider joining the hardworking Fire Department, Water Association, GCA or La Sala boards [and, yes, contribute to the newsletter; as I sticker, stamp and label each month, I can't help but notice that some have been receiving the newsletter for most of its 22 years, but have never sponsored an issue. Time to step up?].
In El Puente's first issue, one of its founders, Barbara Cooper, wrote: "Community is a powerful thing. It enfolds us in tradition, making us an important part of history, and urgently involves us in planning for a future we will be proud to pass along to the next generation .... May we all benefit from the new energy of others who have lost their hearts to Galisteo, and from the advice and council of those who have spent a lifetime here."

title: RUDY J. SENA
body:
Rudy Sena, founder in 1970 (and President until 2014) of the Rodeo de Galisteo, died in Albuquerque in December. A lifelong resident of Galisteo, he was the son of Natividad Sena and Sara Peña Sena, and had four sisters and seven brothers, two of whom--Leo Sena and Helen Angel--survive him, along with his five children: Kenneth Carrillo, Audra Baca, Amy Gallegos, Clint Sena and Michael Sena, four granddaughters (Callie Rogers, Sierra Baca, Shelby Baca, and Sydney Baca), and Bebe Givaudon, his best friend for thirty years. His first wife, Rosemary Romero, survives him. His second wife, Candy Turner, predeceased him.
Rudy was raised in the (now Griscom) house on the east side of the old bridge; his family farmed the strip of former Ortiz y Pino land that is now occupied by McQueen, Epping/Diggs, Yeats, and Lippard. Rudy called himself a jack of all trades, having worked construction, run his own business building power lines, been a large equipment operator for King Bros., a mechanic, a truckdriver, and a wrangler and extra for many western movies filmed in the area. In the late 1980s, he began to lead trail rides for Santa Fe Detours, which he did for two decades. People from all over the world rode through Galisteo on Rudy's handsome steeds. Around 1961, Rudy began to build a rodeo ground on the land south of the village that he inherited from his uncle and grandfather. The rodeo started slow, gained momentum, and became a popular summer event. When Rudy was interviewed in El Puente #6 (Summer 1997), he said the worst he could remember was the year when the arena was a foot deep in mud. Cars got stuck and people were losing their shoes. When, for many reasons, the Rodeo de Galisteo closed down in 2016, Rudy was dismayed. But it had a really good gallop for over forty years. Thank you, Rudy!
The date for a Spring celebration of Rudy's life at the Rodeo Grounds will be announced later.

title: THE JACK AND THE JAY
body:
When the stiff iron gates of winter shut nature in, my memory returns to a warmer time...It's late summer. I hang a swing under our south-facing portal with a view toward Cerro Pelon, and take advantage of this perfect wildlife-watching perch. The meditative motion lulls both me and critters into calmness. They become accustomed to my being there. A Black-tailed Jack Rabbit nibbling shrubs and a Western Scrub Jay gathering piñon nuts are regular visitors.
The Jack, his long legs stretching out low to the ground, crouches apologetically into view as he searches through my tall grasses. Ears flatten along his back when he hears a distant noise. Round, glassy eyes stare into the middle distance. He allows I am here but does not acknowledge me. I swing and he munches.
The Jay, squawking out his arrival, bursts onto the scene diving into the piñon tree just over my left shoulder. Black eyes snapping in a cocked head demand I acknowledge, up close, his brash self. As we stare, I feel his presence as well as see it. Time suspends. The air pressure changes. His energy field is huge. It covers both me and the Jack. The boundary between us falls away. I change the way I breathe. He pulls me into his world as he takes his possession of my tree. We are exchanging. What? I am not sure. I emerge as if from a trance with the understanding that this Jay intends to lay claim to my tree and all the piñon nuts in it regardless of what my land deed may proclaim.
The difference between the two creatures and how I relate to their "otherness" intrigues me. I observe the Jack but I interact with the Jay. What a divine thing is curiosity. (To be Continued)

title: REMEMBERING TOBIAS ANAYA
body:
A few months ago Ronny Chavez Anaya sent El Puente some materials about his great uncle Tobias Anaya (1908-1988), the self-taught artist who was featured in another old issue (#50, 2001) of El Puente. Ronny was an enthusiastic collector of Tobias's art. "Thinking back on my childhood," he writes, "I do not remember Tobias's interest in art. It was in the 1980s that I remember him creating art for his outdoor gallery which was set up between the two cemeteries in Galisteo. I slowly started buying his sculptures. $2.00, $5.00, $15.00. 'No Tio, here's more money,' I pushed. He always felt guilty selling his pieces to me. I'm excited to share that I now have twelve in my collection."
In 1987 a piece of Tobias's was donated to the Smithsonian. It was titled "Man on a Horse with Tethered Animal," but Ronny notes that Tobias never titled his sculptures, and if he had, it would have been in Spanish. As a child, Ronny was a constant visitor to his grandparents' home and "a visit next door to Carmelita Anaya (great grandmother) and her son Tobias was routine.... Even though there was a language barrier our connection was through almafamilia (family soul)."
A feature article on Tobias in The New Mexican (11/3/85) noted that he had been making his art for thirty years. He carved tree limbs into violins for the fiestas at "the old Galisteo cantina." He told the reporter that he couldn't be an artist because artists "must have an education. I have no education It's a hobby, something to do."
Tobias died tragically in a house fire. One D. Padilla wrote a poem for him that reads, in part: "Tobias, get out!/The house is on fire!/His dead mother cried over and over again./Tobias get out!/Huddled in the corner/Working by moon light,/Tobias was finishing up the Christmas/Present he had promised her./A stick figure playing a guitar/Made from apple branches/Dried blossoms he called kisses/Cling to the figure's arms./Broken blue glass beads for eyes./Twig fingers scratching the guitar/Colored fishline strings./How do you tune a guitar/for your mother who lives in heaven?/Tobias asked himself over and over again./No need to worry he thought./He was sure an angel would come down/And whisper the answer in his ear./Tobias hijo the house is on fire, get out!?Tobias could no longer hear his mother's voice./ An angel was whispering in his ear."

title: Bruce Nauman Exhibition at MoMA and PS 1
body: Bruce Nauman's huge exhibition Disappearing Acts at the Museum of Modern Art and PS 1 in New York includes Contraposto Studies, a seven-channel video "that lines a gallery's wall like a moving frieze (above)" writes critic Andrew Goldstein. "Nauman walks through his studio with his hand above his head, swiveling out his hips as he walks to create the s-shape of the contrapposto figure in classical art. It's both essentially simple and profoundly complex ... It's Nauman's latest masterpiece, and one of his greatest."

title: The Jack
body:
The Jackrabbit is not a rabbit at all. He is a Hare, born "bright-eyed," long eared, and fully furred with long, strong back legs that propel him at speeds of 40 mph while scoring 10-foot-long hops and 20-foot-high leaps. Mark Twain popularized the name "Jackass Rabbit" (later shortened to Jackrabbit) because of the long donkey-like ears.

Our Black-tailed Jackrabbit is the most common Hare of the American Southwest. And, trust me, this Jack is no Bunny. An adult Jack easily holds his own against larger predators thanks to his excellent hearing, and built-in ability to hop, leap, and zig-zag his way out of most trouble. However, the fact that there are many more Hares (on the lower level of the food pyramid) than Coyotes, Cougars, or Eagles (at the top), is a dead giveaway to the reality that our Jack is an important food source for many apex predators.

The key to understanding any critter is often a little research into its natural history. Here are the "hare" facts:

Weight: 3-9 lbs. The doe is larger than the buck.
Life span: 1-5 years in the wild.
Gestation: c. 50 days. Babies, called leverets, average 4 to a litter. Doe does not stay with new born leverets. Returns only to nurse once a day.
Vocalizations: Nose clicks, teeth grinding, pleasure squeals, "death cry."
Range: Do not migrate nor hibernate.
Food: Mix of shrubs, grass, forbs, wildflowers, sage and cactus.
Activity: Mostly nocturnal. They sleep during the day.
Behavior: Recognize their own kind, form social communities.
Diseases: Carriers of ectoparasites (new word for me) like fleas, ticks, lice, and mites. Susceptible to Tularemia which is quickly fatal. Warning: wear gloves when handling carcasses. Keep pets away.
Sub species: White-tailed and Antelope* Jacks, larger than Black-tailed.

I can't leave the page without mentioning another important Jackrabbit feature, the eyes. Placed strategically far back and to the sides of the head, these large, expressionless globes are alert to predators approaching from all directions. Their purpose, not to focus but to pick up motion, explains the "glassy stare". Some people see Jacks as vermin infested pests and shoot them for sport. The other side of the argument may speak to their importance in the food web as a primary food source to avian and mammalian icons of the West we all feel lucky to see.

*Antelope Jacks are found in Southern Arizona. Not to be confused with Jackalopes found locally on Cerrillos Road.

title: In Our Backyards
body:
"The National Wildlife Federation (NWF), America's largest wildlife conservation and education organization, is pleased that Deirdre Africa at Rancho Bueno in Galisteo, New Mexico has successfully created a Certified Wildlife Habitat® through its Garden for Wildlife™ program. NWF celebrates this effort to create a garden that supports birds, butterflies, bees, and other local wildlife (lizards!).

"Every Certified Wildlife Habitat garden provides natural sources of food, water, cover and places to raise young and is maintained in a sustainable way that incorporates native plants, conserves water and doesn't use pesticides. Every Certified Wildlife Habitat garden is now also part of the Million Pollinator Garden Challenge, a national effort to create a million gardens that provide habitat for declining pollinator insects such butterflies and bees."

And in a related story, Trump's EPA is threatening to allow use of even more bee-killing pesticides on our farmlands. Chemical giant Dow has requested permission to ramp up use of these toxic chemicals. If the EPA grants Dow's wish, the impact on bees and other pollinators could be devastating. All the more reason for each of us to do what we can.

According to Cool Green Science (courtesy of Frank Lux), more frequent sightings of both Cooper's and Sharp-shinned hawks are being reported across the United States. These two similar-looking hawk species (genus Accipiter) have increasingly colonized urban areas. "The 'return of the raptors' is a trend reported (often via citizen science) around the country. And a big part of it is the bird feeder in your backyard.... More than 40 percent of U.S. households feed their backyard birds.

"By the mid-20th century, many raptor species, including Cooper's and sharp-shinned hawks, had declined precipitously. Direct persecution and pesticides had taken a heavy toll. Decades of protection have caused populations to rebound, leading raptors to reclaim habitat. But as the birds spread, they found a new world: one of growing cities. One might initially conclude that predators would not find this new world to their liking, as it was covered in concrete and buildings instead of forests. And that's certainly true for many wildlife species.

title: Donkey Mom
body:
For some time now, Angie Heath has been working as a foster mother with The Longears Safehouse, a unique organization based in Edgewood, founded by former philosophy professors Dorothy Lotter and Andrew Cross. Its mission is "... to make the world a better place for donkeys and related long ears such as mules and hinnies. TLS provides education about the mental and physical needs of long ears, their nature, training and care, rescues donkeys in need, rehabilitates and rehomes them, and helps long ears in times of crisis or emergency situations."

TLS subscribes to the 5 Freedoms of Animal Welfare, which are internationally recognized as the "gold standard" both in agricultural contexts and in those of animal rescue and rehabilitation: Freedom from Hunger and Thirst; Freedom from Discomfort; Freedom from Pain, Injury or Disease; Freedom to Express Normal Behavior; and Freedom from Fear and Distress.

You may have seen Angie and John walking around the village with the previous couple, Emma and Valentine, who were 25 and 35 years old and have since found a forever home. (The critters are only fostered and adopted in pairs.) However, Rachel and Rebecca (c. 8 and 6 years old) balked at crossing the bridge or the creek, and mostly luxuriate in their big fenced field behind the Watson-Jones home. Angie notes that donkeys "can be very hard headed when spooked by the unfamiliar, which is a survival mechanism." Due to a complicated adoption policy, she has chosen to continue to foster long ears (bunnies and jacks excluded), and wants the word to get out that since the Safe House has no physical location, temporary foster homes for these loveable critters are always needed. See their website or contact Angie for further information.

Happy Valentine's Day again; may the comets collide!

title: La Sala is "Under the Influences"
body:
Artists from across New Mexico are invited to submit work for consideration to be included in La Sala de Galisteo's upcoming summer show entitled "Under the Influences," from May 25 to September 17. Each artist should consider the influence of others on their work and how that may or may not be self-evident to the viewer. The forces of influence can range from single works to an individual's entire career. ideas or images fused across disciplines, e.g. jazz musicians, poets, visual artists, philosophers, writers, etc. and how these contributed to your process. The influences need not be all affirming, as there may be ideas or works that you strongly rejected as a means of defining the nature of your work.

Deadline for submissions is April 15. Please forward up to three images of your work, along with a short statement concerning your interpretation of our theme and a one-page resume. Send to Shaun Gilmore, shaungilmorestudio@gmail.com or to Cindy Lux, forbeslux@aol.com. La Sala's board will curate submissions and inform artists by April 30. Delivery to La Sala will be scheduled for the weekend of May 18-19. Any questions can be directed to Cindy or Shaun. Thank you. We look forward to your work!

title: {Coyotes and Bears, Oh My!}
body:
Although this winter has felt overly long, cold, and windy, Spring is here at last. Coyotes that have hunted alone for food begin forming groups in mid-winter, and mating begins in early February. One mated and monogamous pair, also known as the alpha pair, forms the nucleus of each pack of 3-8 critters, and is the only pair to breed. Pups are born after 60-63 days, in late April to early May. Coyotes in our bosque may be more aggressive than at other times of the year. Be cautious when walking there, especially with small dogs; keep pets in sight when they are out of the house.

We've got Bears too. Males and young independent bears emerge from hibernation right now and begin foraging and staking out territory. Sows with cubs follow in May; the cubs will be setting out on their own, while the mother bear will be looking to breed again. Last summer we had a sow and two cubs as neighbors.

If you encounter coyotes or a bear: Stop where you are, be still for a moment or so, look as big as you can, then calmly and slowly move away. Do not tum your back or run. Keep the animal in your line of sight, make noise as you move away (sing, talk loudly). Give the animal plenty ofroom to escape so it doesn't feel threatened or trapped. If attacked, use whatever you can to fight back, and always aim for the nose and eye area.

Some things to be aware of: Never leave fruit from trees and bushes to rot on the ground as it is a powerful attractant to bears and other wildlife. Never put meat or sweet-smelling food scraps such as melon in your compost pile. Don't leave pet food or food dishes outdoors at night. Clean and store outdoor grills after use. Bears can smell sweet barbecue sauce and grease for miles.

title: The Jay
body:
What a divine thing is curiosity.

Our Woodhouse's Scrub-Jay* is a year-round native to the pifion/juniper montane scrub lands that surround Galisteo. This slender blue and gray bird uses its strong, pointed bill to pry nuts from pifion cones in the fall and feed on insects, fruit, lizards, eggs and nestling birds in spring and summer. The Scrub-jay is a loner, choosing to forage unaccompanied through a Pifion Pine or hitting your feeder where sunflower seeds and peanuts are favorites. Watch for noisy flocks of bright blue Pifion Jays in the fall flying in for bumper crops of pifion nuts.

All Jay species are animated birds that move through trees in bold hops and lunges, squawking loudly, cocking their heads to look this way and that in a playful vocal manner. Jays have a mischievous streak and are not above the outright theft of another bird's seed cache. Well known among animal behaviorists for their foraging behavior, cognitive abilities, and spatial memory skills, Jay's talent for locating and selecting food sources is impressive.

In other words, our Jay is SMART. As a member of the Corvidae Family (Crows, Ravens, Magpies), Jays are members of the avian intellectual elite. Curious opportunists with keen observation skills, Jays can solve problems. They use a sophisticated method of triangulation to locate seeds and nuts for winter feasting more than five months after they hid them--during which time I lose my car keys at least twice.

When I first began writing about The Jack and The Jay, my curiosity about what I sensed to be different energy fields of the two animals led me to investigate innate versus learned behavior. It seems our Jack is born with innate/instinctual behaviors hardwired into its DNA that support all life activities with "knee-jerk" responses. Because The Jack is prey to so many other animals, there's no time to think; instantaneous reaction is survival. The Jay, also born with innate behavior reactions, possesses higher cognitive skills that enable it to learn new behaviors from observation, trial and error. So, while The Jack gets through his day mostly on "auto-pilot," The Jay spends his day observing, questioning, and honing his survival skills. While I find it easy to call The Jay smart, I will never call The Jack a "Dumb Bunny".

(Final in a three-part series; See El Puente, Jan. and Feb.)

*The Western Scrub-jay became the Woodhouse's Scrub-jay in 2016 when it was declared a separate species from the California Scrub-jay. Another common Jay species in Galisteo is the Pifion Jay. To our delight, every now and then an Eastern Blue-jay wanders over from Texas or a stunning Steller's Jay drops in from higher elevations.

title: River Rises
body:
For the last couple of weeks the mighty Rio Galisteo has been bubbling and roaring with muddy runoff through the bosque. It's early for snowpack melt, but nothing is normal these days. (The vultures are just filtering back into town.) Laura Paskus points out in The New Mexico Environmental Report that some streams, rivers and wetlands that are "non-navigable," or don't flow year-round were protected under the Clean Water Rule, but "the Trump administration's version would no longer protect ephemeral streams, nor play as or waterways within closed basins, which include about one-fifth ofNew Mexico's landmass. It also proposes to remove protections from intermittent streams. Most of New Mexico's wetlands .... wouldn't be protected.

"The lack of protections leaves waterways vulnerable to all sorts of threats, including mining waste, produced water from drilling, gravel operations and landfills, as well as pollution from military bases, federal facilities like nuclear weapons labs, wastewater treatment plants and others ... New Mexicans have relied upon tiny springs and streams for centuries. They gave us drinking water. And a sense of home." Temporary waterways like our creek empty into larger rivers, like the Rio Grande, but they support local ecosystems and wildlife.

title: Annual Meeting of the Water Association
body:
From minutes by Secretary Richard Patton
The Annual meeting of the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association (MDWCA) took place at the Community Center on March 27 with a (minimal) quorum of members and the sitting Board. Two technical resolutions were approved by the Board and Accountant Ana Berry reported that only one hookup is in arrears and is not expected to be a concern.
Michael Golino, hired by the Board to assist with managing execution of the building project/ loan/grant, has resigned. The total loan was for c. $430,000, of which $120,000 must be repaid at 0.25% interest over twenty years. MDWCA President Phillip Tuwaletstiwa had met with Morey Walker, the engineer on the project, and presented to the membership an overview of the project, including the blueprints of the entire design, which are available for anyone to review.
The project has three parts: A pump installed on our second well will be brought on line; a new pump house will be built, along with pressurizing of the entire system; some lines will be extended, bringing access to more of the community. It will greatly improve our system's capacity, reliability and redundancy. Bids will be made once state approval is in hand and once they are out for thirty days, we can begin the selection process. We will probably be in a position to break ground by mid-June. Phillip and Ana Berry will oversee this project with Morey Walker.
This new loan specifically excludes any money for fire protection and hydrants, so Steve Moya has arranged for us to receive an $86,000 grant from the State for water system improvement, which would enable fire hydrant installation. We cannot access this money until our new system project is finished, but planning can begin now. Ana Berry has already received paperwork for this grant. The board will send letters of appreciation to those responsible (e.g., Carlos Sisneros.)
During the community comment period, Freddie Cardenas said that village water is too expensive and asked that the tier system of charges be abolished because it punishes not only those who overuse water, but also those with large families. [However, it is, in fact, cheaper than other similar systems and a flat fee would be more expensive for all users.]
An election was held to add one member to the Board. Denise Lynch, Craig Fulmer, and Ed Epping were nominated. A closed ballot determined that Epping had won. Tuwaletstiwa announced that although he had planned to resign as President, he was willing to continue in order to complete the grant project. Mike Anaya was nominated but declined. Phillip was then unanimously approved. John Watson-Jones was re-elected as Treasurer and Richard Patton will continue as Secretary. Other members of the Board whose terms continue are Steve Moya, Mike Anaya, Lucy Lippard, and Antonio Chavez (Foreman).

title: Tom Morin (1944-2019)
body:
Former Galistefio Tom Morin died on April 18. He was born February 21, 1944 in Fulton, N.Y., the son of Tom and Mary Morin. He graduated from Syracuse University in 1966 with a BA in graphic design and received his MA from Yale. He was an accomplished graphic designer,. college. professor,. author, businessman, mentor, friend, film buff, music lover, world traveler and jazzed kid.
In 2000 Tom built what is now the Diggs/Epping home on Avenida Vieja, designed by Beverley Spears, and moved to Galisteo, where he was active in the community as a founding member of the Planning Committee, President of the GCA, and co-founder of the annual Chile Margarita Cookoff. After suffering a stroke in Fall 2012, he was forced to move to a Santa Fe retirement home. He leaves behind former wives Joan Morin and Daphne Geismar, sister Martha, son Joshua Morin, daughter Ana Geismar, granddaughter Savannah Morin, and former partner Isabella Gonzales, who shared his Galisteo years.

title: Grappa's Way
body:
Jan Saunders, drawing by Catherine Ferguson (lower left)
Grappa, my 5-month-old Aussie pup, refuses to walk away from the house down our trails in Ranchitos. Heaven knows we need the exercise, so I drive us both down to the Village, where he is fine and so am I, as soon as I hear the spring birds singing from the Fremont Cottonwoods along the road and the willows on the sandy river banks.
Of course, I have birds at my feeder in Ranchitos: Scores of blushing-red House Finches, my friend the Woodhouse's Jay, six Pine Siskins, flocks of Bush Tits and Western and Mountain Bluebirds, a noisy six-pack of Crows, a Robin or two, and the occasional Ladder-backed Woodpecker. In this still-cold-not-quite-spring weather the wind seems to tamp down our desire to walk as well as the bird's urge to sing.
But the Village is alive with bird song and there is shelter from the wind. Birds, like any animal, have simple needs: shelter, water, and food. As I walk along Grappa's Way, starting at Marcellina Lane along dusty roads, over the bridge, and along open meadows, it feels and sounds like spring. My favorites, Red-winged Blackbirds, are rejoicing from the tops of the huge cottonwoods on the old Galisteo Inn property. I stop to search for Yellow-headed Blackbirds hidden among the black flocks. To see red wings and yellow heads on shiny black birds flying together is visual candy.
Walking past a rail fence I spot a little White-breasted Nuthatch searching for insects under the bark of the wood railings and hear the chatter of a Juniper Titmouse somewhere deep in the Four-winged Salt Bush nearby. A Mountain Bluebird carrying the sky on his wings dips low in front of us as it flies across the road. From high in the clear sky overhead I hear the trumpeting calls of a skein of Sandhill Cranes leaving the Rio Grande Valley and winging their way north to breed and raise their long-legged chicks.
We cross El Puente on the high side. Grappa stops to look down into the river where he loves to splash as I search and listen for the birds that I know will arrive soon, like the Downy and Hairy Woodpeckers and Ash-throated Flycatchers. Today we avoid the river and the mud from recent snow melt. Once on La Otra Vanda, I listen for Western Meadowlarks that will soon be calling from the grasslands above the river banks. Around the curve toward the Community Center, White-crowned Sparrows are announcing in song that "Poor-Joe-Joe-missed-his-bus."
It's not all about birds. Grappa, not wanting to miss a scent, walks a zig-zag pattern across trail and road. We meet up with several dogs, some barking warnings and others testing the strength of their owner's grip in an effort to approach Grappa for a romp. But he is young and the other dogs are strangers, so we stick to the business of walking on down the road.
When it's time to turn back toward home, I glance at the bare, empty branches of the Cottonwoods bordering the east side of the river, waiting for the Turkey Vultures that will return to roost high in these trees until fall's chill calls them south again. Grappa and I will be standing here to watch "the black-watchers" dropping in to roost. (We spotted the first Vulture over Galisteo on March 27.)

title: The Red Clay Gang
body:
Ring! Ring! That's the last bell of the school year. It's summer vacation. Yea! My sister Terry and I are going to spend two weeks at our Gramma Lucia and Grampa Frank's house in Galisteo. I am so excited because we get to play with JoAnne, Gloria, Joe and Freddie, our aunts and uncles who are the same age as we are. Gramma and Grampa's old adobe house is nice and cool, and always smells of fresh tortillas, caldito and coffee. "Hola, ninos!" Gramma and Grampa say as they greet us with big hugs and kisses. JoAnne, Gloria, Joe and Freddie are just as excited as we are, so off we go to play.
It's morning. Time to get up, but I am so snuggly and warm under Gramma's homemade quilts. We have chores to do before we can play again so we better get moving. We chop wood so our grandparents can cook, take the chill out of the early mornings, and heat water for our baths. We draw the freshest water from the old well, chase and feed the chickens, and take their precious gift of fresh eggs in for our breakfast.
All done! It's time to play! Off we go to our special place. "I'm going to get to the store first," we say to each other as we race through the dirt roads past the few houses, the restaurant, the community center, and the old grey church. Terry, JoAnne and Joe win the race! There's Grampa with his dark grey Fedora tilted up on the right side of his head, sitting on the bench up front at the tiendita, waiting for customers. "Here comes the Red Clay Gang," he says. "Ready for your treat?" He always lets us pick a candy to take to our special place.
"Race you to the bridge," I say. Around the corner is an old, one-lane, wooden bridge that the villagers call El Puente. I close my eyes and I see horse-driven wagons, families walking to church, horseback riders, and old and modern cars crossing the bridge throughout the many years. Thirty-foot trees growing on each side of the bridge offer shade and the most wonderful green apples ever.
Off go the shoes! Off go the socks! Our toes say aahh! The river and the pebbles in the riverbed are so cool and fresh. This is our special place in the summer. The red clay that lines the sides of the riverbed is moist and ready for our next project. What shall we make today -- farm animals, a village with houses and people, or clay pots? The sun is so warm that it bakes our creations while we lie on the bank and eat our snacks - candy, green apples with salt, and water. We stretch out our arms and legs to dry off before we head home.
The frijoles are ready. We make fresh tortillas and red chile and wait for Grampa and Gramma to get home from work. Gramma says, "Well, my Red Clay Gang, what did you do today?" She oohs and aahs at our creations and then gives us a special treat. Once a week Gramma is allowed to bring home a leftover container of ice cream from the restaurant she works at. What a delicious way to end the day. Even though our prayers are said and lights are out, Gramma still has to tell us several times to stop talking and go to sleep. But we are already planning what we will do tomorrow. Buenas noches!

title: Judy Tuwaletstiwa Exhibition
body: On June 7th, Judy Tuwaletstiwa's major show "The Dream Life of Objects," opened at the Center for Contemporary Arts. A violin performance and discussion (July 14) and a panel (August 30) are scheduled around the show, which is up until Sept. 15th.

title: Patrick McFarlin Exhibition
body: Patrick McFarlin's Downtown Club Revival at SITE Santa Fe was featured in The New Mexican (June 8) and doubled as an 80th birthday celebration. His solo exhibition of oil paintings in monotypes at Webster Collection (541/2 Lincoln Ave, above the Plaza Cafe) continues until July 8.

title: Conservation Voters Environmental Scorecard
body: Conservation Voters of New Mexico's 2019 environmental score card just came out, and our Rep Matthew McQueen got a grade of 100%, up from his lifetime score of 96%.

title: Sina Brush Letter
body: Sina Brush wrote a letter to The New Mexican (5/20/19) questioning the wisdom of adding more Margarita drinking (and driving) on the Margarita Trail in Santa Fe.

title: Deborah Madison Publications
body: Two articles by Deborah Madison appeared in Heritage magazine (Winter/Spring 2019) on "Chimayo's Chile Culture" and Estevan Restaurante in Santa Fe.

title: Roberto H. Valdez Publication
body: "Living Down Country People: Names of the Galisteo Basin" by Roberto H. Valdez was published in the recent issue of Land Water People, which also included an article on Lone Pinon, the lively conjunto band that played at La Sala last month.

title: Lucy Lippard Curated Exhibition
body: Lucy Lippard has curated a show ("Alicia Stewart: Unfinished....") at the Harwood Museum in Taos of the remarkable paintings of a young Santa Fe artist who died at the age of eighteen. It's up until Nov. 10. (And this is a good time to go to the Harwood; the featured exhibition is Judy Chicago's Birth Project from New Mexico collections and there is a small show of beautiful colchas and amazing mega-drawings by Afton Love.)

title: Magazine Features and Art Coverage
body: The June issue of The Magazine includes a painting of Agnes Martin's former Galisteo home by Eleanor Ray and a discussion of Harmony Hammond's older work in Shane Tolbert's "West by Southwest: Considering Landscape in Contemporary Art," and a New Mexico Women feature on your editor. Hammond's paintings are at Art Basel in Switzerland, described as an integral part of the narrative of modernist abstraction, even as they insist on an oppositional discourse of feminist and queer content. Layering patches of fabric over grommets, Hammond evokes a bandaged body, implying "an interruption of the narrative of the modernist grid and therefore, an interruption of utopian egalitarian order."

title: Bill Mitchell Film and Media Exhibition
body: Former Galistean film photographer Bill ("Billie") Mitchell had one of the most popular pieces in the new media exhibition Currents, at El Museo Cultural. Bike Party was a Virtual Reality experience with stationary bikes, and take it from your editor, it was exciting biking in a herd of other riders in DC, Baltimore and DC. On opening night, outside on the railyard, Bill's Mobile Projection Platform - MPP projected thrilling driving shots on window screens.

title: NM 41 Road Repairs
body: For all those who have suffered the bumps and grinds of NM 41 south of the village after its $20 million plus so-called "improvements," construction has had to recommence because, according to NMDOT, soil testing was inaccurate. Another $4.2 million is being spent to fix the brand-new work.

title: B Anaya Road Spending
body: And speaking of roads, a feature in The Reporter (6/13) and a cover story in The New Mexican headlined "The Fix Is In?" (6/13) reported that over the last few years, the County spent almost $1 million in improvements for the remote B Anaya Road off NM 41 in Stanley, "and crews are out there again, paving away." Named for Basilio Anaya, grandfather of Galisteo's former County Commissioners Mike and Robert Anaya, it leads to their ranch and dead ends at the home of Robert Martinez, the County's Deputy Public Works Director.

title: Saddleback Ranch Sale
body: The New Mexican (6/8) reported that Saddleback Ranch, north of the village on NM 41, was sold in 2008 for $17.45 million, one of the highest priced local properties in this century.

title: Richard Shuff Photo Archive
body: Former Galistean Richard Shuff recently reminded us that he has more than 10,000 digital photos of Galisteo. He photographed "just about every person in Galisteo and many varied subjects."

title: Rattlesnake Encounter
body: This from Judy Tuwaletstiwa a couple of weeks ago: "Rattlesnakes are out .... or in depending on how one looks at it." A small one, c.18" long, slid in under the screen door into her kitchen. "Once we got it in a box, Jim Sloan came down to pick it up." Question: Do baby rattlers pack a bigger venom wallop because they don't yet know how to control it, or is that a myth?

title: Nolo Bait for Grasshoppers
body: And this on another potential pest from Susie Shanklin: Nolo Bait is an EPA-registered biological control for grasshoppers. It contains naturally occurring Nosema locustae spores, uniformly applied to flaky wheat bran. Grasshoppers eating it are infected with the spores. Young ones die more quickly than older ones. Infected grasshoppers are cannibalized by healthy ones and Nosema Locust spreads though the population. This organism provides long-term benefits to landowners without environmental damage.

title: {GVFR News: Don Truax}
body:
My wife Jessica and I moved to Galisteo in August of last year. We became new grandparents in January. I joined the fire department to become an active member in the community. I'm currently in the 16-week Volunteer Fire Academy, with 6 1/2 weeks to go, and hope to still be standing at the end. I have a whole new appreciation for the skills and knowledge that firefighters possess.
I also like to fish and love horses. I worked at a horse shelter for 3 years prior to moving to Galisteo, and have been volunteering at The Horse Shelter in Cerrillos since October. I look forward to learning how to fly fish and exploring the lakes and rivers of New Mexico and beyond. Lastly, I love the chile, both red and green, the hotter the better.

title: {GVFR News: Deirdre Africa}
body: After barely getting settled in my sweet hacienda, I started wondering how to contribute to the wonderful village of Galisteo. It is important to me to be useful and to learn new skills so I volunteered for truck maintenance at our fire department. One thing led to another and now I'm a wildland fire fighter and licensed to drive fire trucks. Every week I learn something new at the training sessions and I feel like I could offer my skills in an emergency. When I'm not at the firehouse, I'm sewing aprons and digging holes at Rancho Bueno.

title: {Snake!}
body:
Plain and simple, I am fascinated by and attracted to SNAKES. I want to read about them, see them, and observe all species, venomous and non-venomous. Don't get me wrong, I respect them and prefer to keep my distance while learning their natural history. I also understand that you, the reader, might be phobic or have an aversion to scaly critters that possess venom and fangs like hypodermic needles. A bite from one of our local rattlers, serious and painful, is to be avoided at all costs.
On the other hand, a snake that comes in contact with a human usually ends up dead, and that bothers me because all snakes occupy an important niche in healthy ecosystems while at the same time providing pro bona rodent control. And since recent fossil discoveries indicate that snakes have slithered our earth for more than 150 million years, just maybe we should admit to their right to slither on for a long time to come. After several months wrestling with just the right tone and tack to take in writing about snakes, I happily shelved my efforts to make room for the following Best Snake Story Ever:
As has been their habit for many years, Dianne and Vernon Wilson dropped their Toyota truck off to Michael, their favorite mechanic, to have the shocks replaced. When they returned to reclaim the truck, Michael greeted them with a big smile and the words "Your truck has a tenant." He then presented them with a large plastic, lidded bucket containing a rather beautiful Bull Snake, adding that their job was to return the snake to Galisteo where it clearly wanted to be. So, Dianne and Vernon put the bucket in the Toyota and returned to Galisteo where they released, quite near their house, all four feet of snake.
According to Michael the Mechanic, while underneath the Toyota working overhead to replace the shocks, he realized he was staring up into two round beady snake eyes. He didn't panic since he knew a thing or two about snakes, most importantly that venomous Rattle Snakes have cat eyes (vertical pupils), and therefore he must have been nose to nose with a harmless non-venomous Bull Snake. Michael carefully removed it from the wheel well (as his crew "freaked out" at the sight of the harmless snake), and carried it quite a distance away to a vacant lot filled with weeds, rock and rubble-a perfect spot for a constrictor that preys on rats and mice.
Once freed from his armload, Michael returned to the Toyota to pick up where he left off. Glancing up a short time later, Michael was surprised to see the Bull Snake slithering straight for him and the Toyota. He stopped work, gathered up the now all-too-familiar Bull Snake, and once again walked "way far away" from the Toyota -- twice as far as before-until he felt certain it was safely ensconced in a perfect Bull Snake habitat, never to return. He walked back to the Toyota, closing the garage bay door behind him.
Well, the old adage "Never say never," fits nicely into this story because (and I promise I am not making this up), when Michael finished the maintenance and raised the bay door, that Bull Snake was waiting right outside.
Clearly this cannot be the end of the story since the burning, unanswered question remains: Why did the Bull snake repeatedly return to the Toyota and what was it doing in the wheel well in the first place?
Friends and family offer the explanation that the Bull Snake must have eggs back in Galisteo, although for any snake to "think" that returning to the Toyota was the way back to Galisteo and its eggs is asking a wee bit too much of a tiny reptilian brain. Additional research reveals that Bull Snakes don't lay eggs until June or July, but they do inhabit a small territory to which they are faithful. Could it be that the Toyota is this Bull Snake's territory?

title: {Editorial}
body:
I returned from a working vacation a couple of weeks ago to fall into a local controversy around the coming improvements to our Community Center. At the heart of the disagreement was some people's perceptions that the GCA Board was acting above and beyond the community without proper transparency. This group feels that plans for upgrades at the Community Center were crystallized long before the March meeting to inform the community, and that suggestions for a different plan proposed by a long-time Galistean with expertise in green building were ignored, although his objections were heard over a series of two meetings. While some of his suggestions were convincing, the Board finally chose to confirm the original plan. Hard feelings ensued.

It is of course the Board's responsibility to present a fully considered plan and as far as I can tell, it had met the required steps for transparency after the hard work of jumping through all the bureaucratic hoops necessary to receive the lucrative grant from the USDA. (I spoke at an event at the GCC on Sept. 8th, when the audience was practically fainting from the heat, which convinced me that a cooling system was necessary; heating rarely is, because the passive solar system set up some forty years ago is still effective.) Questions have been raised about whether agenda and minutes of Board meetings have been regularly posted on the mailbox bulletin board; they have admittedly been irregular, corrected in the last three months.

The main protagonists have shaken hands, but the issues remain contested. Rumors and misunderstandings spread fast in our pueblo chico. Check them out before reacting. At the core of these problems is the fact that too many of us do not attend the meetings that make these major decisions. (And, in my case, I fail to understand many technical issues.) It would be great if there were a system by which people unable to attend meetings could engage with the issues ... but nothing can take the place of open dialogue. If we cannot serve or attend meetings, for whatever valid reasons, we can contact a Board member with questions. Letters to El Puente are another public forum ( c.150 words max).

It is difficult to criticize those good souls who volunteer for the GCA Board and other responsible positions on our entirely volunteer-run village. And thanks as well to those who don't have the time away from work to serve or even make it to many meetings, but are concerned enough to enter the fray. So here's a hearty Gracias to them and to those on the GCA Board, the Fire Department, The Water Board, La Sala, and the Studio Tour. Where would we be without you?

title: Newcomers: High on Altitude
body:
You may have noticed some new corredores locos in Galisteo this summer. My husband Paul Davis and I (photo at below) moved from Philadelphia into our home on La Otra Vanda in the late Spring. We both have enjoyed running on the east coast near where we lived and raised our children. When we sold our home we decided to travel in our van while looking for a new place to settle. Running as we move around helps us explore and connect more intimately with our surroundings. Santa Fe was a pleasure to find so we parked our van and ran trails both in town and in the mountain ranges.

After deciding to stay and buying our new home we thought it might be nice to sign up for a race to keep us motivated. We settled on Pikes Peak Ultra on July 27th, in Colorado Springs. This gave us close to three months to train. Many mornings we would enjoy running in the Galisteo neighborhood, combining streets and trails. The Galisteo Basin Preserve and rail trail were perfect for longer runs and the mountain trails helped with our altitude adjustment. Moving from sea level to 6,500' had already been difficult and our first attempt at Mt. Atalaya was not pretty. Many stops and starts with gasps for air. We knew it could only get better. By the end of July we were feeling confident with our training.

Thankfully we both survived the race in Colorado. It was a beautiful day with only one epic hail storm at the top of Mt. Rosa. Paul has since hiked the Cape Wrath Trail in Scotland with his brother in August. Julie stayed home and did the Santa Fe Endurance trail run, where she met some fast Tarahmuara Indians. Now we are back in Galisteo with a home and community to settle into and probably more races to run. Let us know if you want to join us. When we're not running, Paul continues to develop his software for recording, editing and mixing sound (ardour.org) while I mix up my roles as a mosaic artist ( often in residence), licensed massage therapist, and short-term rental host.

title: Seasons and Memories
body:
I guess some individuals prefer cooler weather, but I can't wait for spring. There are many signs of spring. When the seasons are changing there is something in the air that is a sure indication that we are about to change our wardrobe, maybe get our barbecue grill ready for outdoor cooking, or that annoying urge to begin spring cleaning. For me, it has always been the fragrance of new blooms on the fruit trees, those lovely lilacs, and even the new, tiny vegetation peeking through the ground which is our natural landscape.

It is amazing how different aromas can trigger a memory from the past. As a youngster, I can recall walking to school. If we had extra time we would look for chimaja, an herb that we used to pick for tea. It grew in the early spring and served as a medicine for stomach ailments. It had a very distinct fragrance, pleasant tasting, and we ate it fresh right after picking it. My mother would let it dry, then save it in jars for future use. We were still a little ways from the school, and I caught the smell of alcohol coming from the school house. Well, to me this meant that the school nurse was there. It was vaccination time once again. I hesitated for a moment because I was not very fond of needles, and I knew that I would be at the other end of that needle. Ouch!!! To this day I still cringe when I have to get a flu shot. I'm not alone. I had to get my flu shot recently, and an individual waiting there asked the pharmacist about the size of the needle.

Each season brings a special memory for me, with a certain fragrance. I've always had a strong sense of smell. In the winter, there is a chill in the air accompanied by the strong smell of firewood. I can remember staying under the blankets until someone else built a fire in our potbellied wood stove. Springtime has that wonderful aroma of little tiny wildflowers, and cool mornings filled with that the damp smell of an approaching rain storm, or someone has recently mowed their lawn. For me, springtime reminds me of my Mom transplanting her favorite petunias, and how I need to get started with my flowers. I always have petunias in my flower garden because they were my mother's favorites. Early summer brought the wonderful aroma of lilacs. Warmer air carries the smells of tree blossoms, strawberries ripening on the vine, my mother baking fresh bread, and our white sheets hanging on the clothesline to dry. We must not forget those sounds of summer, after thunderstorms, when the tadpoles came into the puddles, and later tiny frogs hopped around the yard. Let's give those crickets some credit too. As a child I can remember searching under furniture for that annoying cricket that kept me awake. What triggers your memories?

title: Clafoutis, Cicadas, and Chablis
body:
At times Mother Nature can be a Mean Mother, but this past summer she lovingly nurtured Galisteo with copious showers of nitrogen-rich rain. The basin vistas greened-up as blooming wildflowers, yucca and cholla created a virtual garden of Eden. Galisteoans greeted each other saying Isn't this rain wonderful!? Have you ever seen a summer so green? Don't you just love it? The rains came down, the river overflowed its banks, and the Spade Foot Toads croaked out their annual invitation to females to show up for the mating party. A covey of Scaled Quail was sighted crossing the highway just north of town. An errant Prairie Rattler that slithered under the screen door into Judy and Phillip's kitchen was bravely corralled in a cardboard box until it was whisked away by Sloan's Live Rattlesnake Removal Service. Early one quiet morning, a beautiful Red Racer, looking for all the world like a Sea Serpent, swam 'round and 'round in my bird bath. The blooms on Scott and Florence's Century Plants shot skyward like Jack's Beanstalk. Corey's garden that Grow Y'Own built flourished with herbs and greens as she "grew her own" soup. Maria's hens produced eggs through the summer.

For me, the bounty was first evident in the ample fields of Needle and Thread grass flashing silver, waving in the wind. On my walks with Grappa through damp, sandy arroyos, I found things growing and blooming I had never noticed before, like Mormon Tea. Coming upon hidden gardens of blooming mounds of pure white Loco Weed was a pleasant surprise. By July, Catherine's orchard, snuggled behind brick walls, was a smorgasbord of fruit—cherries, apricots, pears, peaches, plums and finally apples. Friends came to pick, and still the boughs hung heavy. Picking cherries one day, Maria declared that she had never in all her life in Galisteo seen such a harvest. Bears and coyotes tempted by fallen fruit came at night to leave their sign to be found in the morning. Butterflies and hummingbirds gorged on the nectar generously offered by wide-open blooms. Abundant proof of Persephone's presence was everywhere. It was a delicious time.

I loved the days when turquoise skies billowed with enormous cotton-white clouds swollen with moisture. Clear nights flaunted both Blue Moons and a Blood Moon. In August a super-bright full moon threw shade on the Perseus meteor shower. Common Night Hawks circled low in evening skies scooping up insects in their gaping mouths. I reveled in time spent outside walking Grappa or tending my garden. When I could, I found my way to the porch swing to read Craig Childs' House of Rain about the importance of rain to the Early Puebloans. Looking up from my book, out across the long fetch of the lush Galisteo Basin resting beneath dark monsoon clouds heavy with moisture, I understood the blessings of this summer of rain.

And so, as the summer ends, Catherine and I savor the last Cherry Clafoutis, prepared with cherries from her orchard frozen in July. The rhythmic droning of Cicadas calling from the proud old cottonwoods along the Galisteo river provides the perfect soundtrack. We raise glasses of Chablis in a toast to the summer that was.

title: In Our Own Back Yard: Jeffrey Epstein and Zorro Ranch
body:
National news has been having a field day with the saga of Jeffrey Epstein, the billionaire financier and convicted sex offender accused of trafficking and abusing teenaged girls in Florida and elsewhere, who committed suicide in jail last month. This is close to home for Galisteans, several of whom had interactions (no, not that kind) with Epstein when he visited his 7,559-acre Zorro Ranch on the top of Clark Hill, some of which extends down into the Basin. At least one Galistean has been interviewed by the media since Epstein's suicide in a New York jail. Although El Puente had reported on his earlier conviction, your editor once received a call from him bragging that he had bought more copies of her book Down Country than anyone else. (I demurred on an invitation, and refrained from saying I was probably a bit old for his tastes.)

A local real estate appraiser remarked that Zorro "is not big enough to be an actual working ranch. Nobody would build a house that big on land used for a cattle ranch. This was not an investment property" (New Mexican 8/13). There is a ranch manager and "nominal cattle," as well as a stable and airstrip. State Land Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard has now terminated two grazing leases dating back to 1993 (renewed in 2017). New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas noted that the acreage meant for cattle grazing should not have been granted, and accused Epstein of leasing state land simply to build privacy around his multimillion-dollar estate. Balderas is continuing to investigate whether girls were trafficked or abused there. Several female names were listed in his "little black book" under "Massage-New Mexico." No news on that so far, although one of Epstein's accusers has alleged that former governor Bill Richardson, among others, enjoyed "privileged" visits to the ranch, which he denies.

Zorro land was acquired from former governor Bruce King. Epstein's name was on County records in 2012 but in 2013 (or 2016?) it was transferred to Cypress, Inc., based in the U.S. Virgin Islands, a notorious tax shelter where Epstein owns an island. (Tax evasion and huge political contributions in NM are also known.) The house is 33,000 sq.' (or merely 26,700' in another report), intended as the biggest house in New Mexico, to surpass that of another local rancher. (I once talked to a contractor working there who said when Epstein found out the kitchen wasn't the biggest in NM, he tore down a wall to add 1,000 feet.) The fate of the ranch (valued in the recent trust at $17.2 million) is unknown. Selling it may not be easy. Tom Ford's ranch has been for sale since 2016; first listed as $75 million, it has since come down to $48 million.

title: Vernon Wilson (9/24/1934 - 9/18/2019)
body: Vern Wilson was a friend to many of us in Galisteo. His smile welcomed all. His sense of humor brightened our lives. As a husband and father, dear friend, painter, print maker, wood worker, baker, cheese maker and gardener, he was a "hands on" experimenter. Vern loved to learn and to make things, including an amazing collapsible sawhorse for cutting the winter's wood. George Vernon Wilson was born in Las Vegas, NM on September 24, 1934, and at twelve years old he traveled by train with his family to live in Florida. Vern was so modest many people did not know of his service in the U.S. Army in post-war Korea, where a whole new world of art and culture opened up to him. For thirty-plus years, he taught painting, drawing, and print-making privately as well as at the Art Center College of Design in Pasadena. In 1970, he was a founding member of the 7th Street Gallery, the first Artists' Cooperative in LA. Dianne recalls, "We found Galisteo on one of our trips to our mountain home in the Pecos. Vern has roots in the Las Vegas valley. We bought our land not knowing the future but hoping we could build a sweet place with sunsets in mind. In the late '90s Vern needed a private place to work. He designed our home and studio and here we lived our lives in gratitude." Vern participated in the Galisteo Studio Tour for fifteen years. Friends and tour goers came to see Vern's creative work and to share his love of life and his smile. Vern and Dianne, partners in life, creativity, and fun, were married for 58 years. On September 18, 2019, Dianne, sons and daughters-in-law Mark and Shelly, Kevin and Pia, Matthew and Stephanie and grandson Ben quietly and lovingly said Fare Thee Well to Vern. In our own ways we may all say Fare Thee Well to our dear friend and wonderful neighbor Vern. - From Dorothy Victor and Sam Sloan. (Photo: 1989).

title: Eric Thomas (9/9/1949 - 10/6/2019)
body: Dr. Eric Sekator Thomas died of heart failure on October 6. A member of the Narragansett tribe, he was born in South Kingston, Rhode Island. In his youth, Eric's activism in Native affairs was renowned as he fought the federal government and won recognition and compensation for the Narragansett ancestral land. After the establishment of the tribal organization, Eric was recognized for his strong and wise leadership by the University of California at Berkeley, where he received his PhD. in Cultural Anthropology, rowing on crew at middle age and on the dean's list throughout. Eric was an effective and committed leader, a gifted artist, exhibiting in Indian Market, a joyful friend, companion, and a pleasure to be with. Resident of Galisteo since 2006, Eric was instrumental in spearheading the revitalization of La Sala de Galisteo. He led and supervised the youth construction training as vice president. His hard work in fun will be missed by all who knew him. Eric's ashes will be buried on his tribal land in ceremony, and a Galisteo memorial is planned for a future date. Eric was a gentle giant spirit man whose missions were all accomplished and done well. RIP ERIC! (Photo: Bahia Kino, Mexico, 2006.) Editor's note: Galisteo knew Eric as an active community member and especially the creator of Bob the Cop and other imaginative productions. His generous, fun-loving presence will certainly be missed.

title: The Flour Dress
body: It is the first day of school (August 1941). I'm so excited! I am going into the fifth grade at the Galisteo elementary school. We have to walk over the big hill called "La Loma del Tejano" and then pass the cemetery. Mama made me a very special dress to wear today. It has a big, bright yellow sunflower in the front and smaller sunflowers all around the rest of the dress. I slip it over my head and it slides easily down to my knees and fits perfectly. It has one small loop tie on the back of the neck and a cloth belt Mama made from the same material. I am so happy that I spin around and around, sending my flour dress twirling. As I spin, sunflowers appear to be flying all around the room, and suddenly the room starts to smell like lavender. Mama made dresses for my sisters and shirts for my brothers but I know that my flour dress is the most special of all. You see, during the day, Mama did all the household chores while caring for a two-month-old infant and three toddlers; and although she was exhausted, she stayed up late into the night sewing this special dress. Before sewing it, she washed the material by hand in lavender water and hung it on the outside line to dry, and then she designed and stitched together my beautiful dress. Do you want to know why I call this dress my "flour" dress? Well, you see, we had a very big family there were eight Sandoval children in the house, and my Papa and Mama, and we had very little money. We could not afford store-bought material, sewing patterns, zippers and buttons. After making tons of tortillas and biscuits, Mama used the multicolored flour sacks to make our clothes. She designed and stitched the most beautiful and fashionable clothes out of these "flour" sacks. Thank you, Mama! I learned so many lessons from you, including how to make beautiful clothes for my own children and I remain a very talented seamstress today. (This story is based on a childhood memory from Connie Sandoval Valencia about her Mama, Lucia Mora Sandoval.)

title: Community Center Park Establishment
body: The GCA Board is pleased to announce that a new Galisteo Community Center Park is being established in the area of the existing basketball court and the mostly-defunct children's playground, with a small perimeter area around the two. It was established with the former lease from the County, an addendum to the Watts Park, approved by the Board of County Commissioners. We took this approach as the NM Anti-donation Law does not allow for funds or labor from public sources to private organizations, but it was made possible by a leasing arrangement thanks to our Commissioner, Rudy Garcia, and to P.J. Montoya of Public Works. For those who were unable to attend the discussion on this activity at the Board election last March or the Town Hall meeting on June 25th (or do not recall the several community emails and notice in El Puente), the lease arrangement allows for provision of the following: ongoing repair and maintenance of the court and playground, as well as the costs of liability and facility/equipment insurance; and management of the $50,000 grant from State Capital Outlay for the initial court repairs (infill of surface cracks and fissures, re-painting of boundary lines), replacement of backboards & nets, replacement of playground equipment as well as a shade structure to cover it, and a rubber mulch ground cover for the playground. Over the next several weeks, the County Works Dept. will begin cleaning, pruning and preparing these two areas. Playground equipment and shade structure(s) will be installed later this Fall or early Spring. Galisteo and the GCA board will retain control and scheduling of the court and playground for the use and enjoyment of Galisteo residents, their families and visitors, just as we do today with Watts Park. Looking forward, we have completed a request for additional Capital Outlay Funds in the fiscal year 2020 and 2021 budget cycles for a water fountain, another shade structure, and some perimeter trees and a drip system. Capital Outlay Funds are from State and County, completely separate from USDA grant funding. The USDA funds are for repairs and upgrades to the Community Center, and a progress report on that project will be issued soon. As always, if you have questions, please contact your GCA Board members directly.

title: Wannabe a Tree Doctor?
body: Peach-burdened, two branches of my trees severed, fell, snapped to the ground. Nothing to do but saw them off neatly, dress the gaping wound, and mourn. But when one of two main trunks of a third peach tree splintered almost in two, I determined to save this beloved tree that I planted twenty years ago -- the tree that survived being chewed almost to the ground by Donna and Jim Sloan's horses when first it was planted, the tree that produces the sweetest fruit. Only a third of its trunk was still partially attached. With Michael Anaya's help we trimmed the heaviest laden branches. A floor mop propped outside the kitchen door became my inspiration. Grabbing a pair of scissors, I cut off a handful of its cotton strands, and after soaking them, laid them like water carrying veins inside the tree trunk's gaping wound. Using all our strength we torqued the broken limb in place as best we could, before binding on a sodden towel and two splints of wood. A month later the leaves stand spry and its fruits are ripe. Should I? Shouldn't I paste the repair with protective goop to get it through the winter?

title: From the Water Board
body: The Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Association Board met on Sept. 30 to tackle an unexpected shortfall in the new construction despite the major grant/loan we received. The only two bids came in very high and we are re-bidding the entire project to allow us to continue without incurring debt. Hopefully we will receive help on capital outlay from our County Commissioner, Rudy Garcia, and State Senator Liz Stefanics, and Rep. Matthew McQueen. The priorities are: to bring the second well on line, improve the pressure, and extend the system to several households north of the village, west of NM 41.

title: Another Snake Story
body: This is Bully on your editor's Georgia O'Keeffe icon (gift from a Galisteo friend). The friendly bullsnake lived in my workroom for a few weeks last summer, a surprise visitor when s/he stuck her head up over a shelf of books. I was leaving for a family visit in Maine and Walt Stevens, staying with my dog, was aware of her/his presence but only found her in the bathtub much later. She was thirsty and probably hungry and he scooped her up and evicted her. But this summer s/he wanted in again. I found her on the doorstep, under a nearby bush, almost in the house having pushed the screen door open. After a few weeks, s/he gave up -- back to nature. title: Nancy Helle (1944 - 2019)
body:
My mother was born on August 16th, 1944, in Lakewood, Ohio. Breaking familial and societal bonds, she left the U.S. at age twenty, going to Ireland to work at a hunting stable. She sang in bars and taught English across Europe, travelled extensively in North Africa and the Middle East, and spent seventeen years in Jerusalem.

She was incredibly industrious and hard-working, a self-taught carpenter, leather worker, and talented gardener. She was quick-witted and gregarious, always willing to help a friend or neighbor. Never one to turn down an adventure or challenge, she whitewater rafted with her beloved sister and rode her horse from Saint Louis to Galisteo [with another former Galistefia, Linda Rice].

She is survived by sister Connie Mouradian, daughter Rebecca Hayes and grandson Liam, and daughter Caitlin Helle and granddaughter Alma Mendoza, as well as countless friends around the world. Even in dying Nancy kept her sense of humor. She said the thing she was looking forward to most was "not having to hear that bloated orange shitbag anymore."
