title: A New Life for Former Lamy Depot
body:
In the ten years I have lived in Galisteo, I was never aware of Doc Ferneau's house. Although I check the real estate listings regularly, I never saw it listed and there was no For Sale sign. When I got a call from my friend Muriel Fariello, I saw where it was, loved the views, and decided to make an offer. I thought they were willing to hold it for me for a week until I could get out to view it, but they wouldn't send me paperwork. So I called Galisteo broker Elayne Patton and asked her to represent me.

Of course it was in many times worse condition than the pictures showed. My friends wanted me to knock it down. What I found out is that it was an old yellow Atkinson, Topeka and Santa Fe Railroad [Depot and later] "Section House" that was moved from Lamy in 1975 to its present site by Elmer "Doc" Ferneau, who lived there until his passing in 2018. [See El Puente, No.19, Nov. 1998, for Marie Ferneau's account of the hist01y and the move.]

The Railroad reached Lamy in February, 1880. Until the 1920s, a train could only travel so far in a day; initially about I 00 miles, then it doubled. Prior to electricity being available on a train, passengers and crew disembarked daily. The passengers would go to a hotel while the crew stayed in a Section House, which typically had a big room and an attached kitchen. It would also be used for storage. I measured a few pieces of lumber in the house, which were much larger than today's. It wasn't until 1924 that the first national lumber size standard was set.

The red tin shingles -- we found two samples in a drawer-- were of the classic "Gothic Arch" pattern common in the 1920s. The house had large interior beams and seemed to be supported by the outside frame, which meant we could make interior alterations without affecting its structural integrity. The floors were cedar and Antonio Chavez told me the exterior siding was redwood, resistant to both pests and fire. Two sections of the floor had been replaced, presumably so that big RR tie beams could be placed to lift the house to its new site in Galisteo.

Also good for a gut rehab, there was a crawlspace and an attic, which made it easier to replace/add plumbing and electricity; they both had to be totally replaced. And all the electrical and telephone lines were underground -- another positive.

There weren't many positives, to be sure. The house had a cesspool, so a new septic had to be installed; just a small holding tank, so we added a 1700-gallon cistern, reworked the well, etc., etc. But the roof did not leak and we could keep the roof tiles, replacing only about five of them.

When I thought over what to do with the property, "industrial farmhouse" came to mind and I decided that would be the style, keeping as much and as true to what was there as possible but making the infrastructure all new, all modern. With my casita tenant Rod Forslund, an interior designer, we walked the house several times while I told him I'd like to end up with three bedrooms and two baths, minimal hallways, reusing as much material as possible. We came up with a plan and Rod measured and drew it up on the computer. This being my twenty-first rehab, I had AutoCAD but prefer the drafting kit my father gave me for high school graduation.

We started demolition on March 20th, first removing a non-structural wall so the kitchen was now open. We had the Bobcat remove all the trees and stumps that were choking the house and hiding the views. Walking the property I found the perfect beam to go where the wall came down; we only had to cut it 7" and it looked like it had been there forever.

On the outside, in keeping with our industrial farmhouse scheme, we placed rigid insulation over the redwood siding, which would have been too costly to restore and paint and needed insulation. Over that we have corrugated galvalume, which looks white from the road, is not reflective, and has minimal maintenance. We reconfigured the outside entrances. A workman fell through one of the landings and was shaken but not hurt.

A deck open to the views was added. Everado used leftover rebar as sidebars on the railings in keeping with the spirit of the house and to keep costs down. The master bath was fitted with a deep whirlpool tub with a large window looking out on the Ortiz Mountains.

I worked with Everado Andujo as I had with a few other projects. On a gut rehab you can't really have a firm budget or timeline but it came in about 5% per square foot over my optimistic estimate and about four weeks longer than expected. We were able to price it for rental just a tad over my first analysis. My dream was to rent it to someone who would appreciate the views and the design. I am pleased to introduce our new neighbors: Geninne Zlatkis, an artist (see her work in the Georgia O'Keeffe museum store and online) and Manolo Benitez, an architect just completing a new studio in Galisteo for Jenny Stocker.

title: Dollar Store or No Dollar Store?
body:
The Santa Fe County Planning Commission has supported the appeal of opponents to a proposed Dollar Store on the northeast side of US 285 near Eldorado. The land is owned by developer Joe Miller, who for decades has faced vehement opposition to his various projects. The store would be part of the first phase of his mixed-use development called Cimarron Village.

Edgar Catanach, a mail carrier who with his wife has owned a home near the project site for more than thirty years, filed the appeal after helping gather c. 1,200 petition signatures. "I'm not opposed to development," he said. "But I want responsible development, things that serve the community. If they had offered to put an organic market right there, that would have been fabulous." He has no problems with other parts of the master plan, which also includes park space and residential uses.

State Rep. Matthew McQueen was among those who spoke against the project. Noting the site's proximity to an I-25 interchange, he said, "People come off that ramp too fast. To introduce a bunch of cross traffic right there concerns me .... I pointed out to the commission that as a commuter I drive through that intersection at least twice a day, and we've had some really awful accidents in that corridor, including some fatalities .... I think there are safety issues to consider."

The next step for opponents will be to plead their case before the Board of County Commissioners.

(Adapted from an article by Howard Houghton in The New Mexican, 11/22.)

title: Potter Home Burglary
body: Thieves broke a glass door and ransacked the Potter home on San Cristobal in Ranchitos on November 10th. Police are investigating. It looks like a professional job. This is a sad reminder that if you are away or have a second home here, you may want to consider a lighting and/or sound-programmed system so the home looks occupied, and you should have someone to check on it. title: Pipe Dreams or Pipe Nightmares
body:
A frozen pipe burst can cost thousands of dollars for repair, mold, or water damage, and freezing weather is here early this year. Here are some recommended precautions: Keep temps around 60 degrees or above. Keep interior doors open. Disconnect water hoses. Buy a water leak alarm (not expensive at Home Depot).

If you tum on a faucet and water just trickles out you probably have a frozen pipe. If there's no leak yet, run warm water thru the pipe or wrap it with a towel soaked in hot water. Do not use a hair dryer or anything with an open flame that could damage the pipe or start a fire ..

Call a plumber if you can't thaw the pipe, it's cracked or leaking, or it's in the wall or ceiling. Good luck!

title: Newcomers (More or Less): A Toyota, a Tesla, and a Truck or Why We Live in Galisteo
body: The rental Corolla nosed over the crest of 285 and we saw it. The basin stretched out before us looking just like it had for the past million years. Majestic, expansive, untouched. And it was calling our name. By the time we pulled into the village, we were sold. We began looking for houses and quickly discovered how small Galisteo was. Nothing was for sale. At this point, we were all in, so we decided to build. We found a lot and Kirsten designed a small, beautiful house. She found a traditional adobe builder who did one house a year. We got on the waiting list. 18 months later, it was a reality. We pulled into the parking lot of our favorite Mill Valley restaurant. Spaces were scant, but we located one up front. I began to pull in, when a Tesla rushed by me and grabbed the spot. The license plate said "PRE-IPO." Kirsten looked at me and said, "We have to get the hell out of here." Twenty years earlier, we had met at a San Francisco design magazine, fell in love, had twins, and moved to Marin. In the course of those twenty years, we watched Marin's sleepy towns tum into traffic-jammed playgrounds for tech billionaires. When our kids left for college, we left too. We chose Santa Fe because amazing culture, food, and weather were all packed into a small, friendly town. It felt like a sort of off-the-grid secret ( compared to the Bay Area anyway). But after looking at dozens ofhouses, we couldn't bring ourselves to pay top dollar for finishes and details we didn't really like. "Santa Fe? Why would you move there? It's too touristy. Now if you said 'Galisteo,' I'd get it." That's Tom Jenks, an old friend I worked with at Esquire forty years ago. He teaches writing and, it turns out, had a student named David Snyder who lived in Galisteo. So after another unsuccessful Santa Fe house hunt, we headed back to the Albuquerque airport and decided to drive through Galisteo. 16 The Hill is done now and we both happily work from home. Kirsten worked at a top landscape architecture firm in the Bay area and now continues to work remotely. I do remote content marketing for Amazon, Intel and other folks. But I'm mostly excited about starting LAWLESS, a small press. (Look for our first book on Sam Shepard in New Mexico coming out this spring.) Our dog Stella likes the landscape so much that she ran away for three days last summer, apparently touring the entire village and (amazingly) dodging coyotes. (Denise Lynch found her when she nonchalantly rolled in through her dog door-accompanying Denise's dogs.) The one thing we never counted on were Galisteo's amazing people. We have met more interesting people than anywhere we've lived. Our kids tease us that we are more social here than we were in San Francisco. We are part of a monthly supper club, involved with La Sala, the GCA, and the Studio Tour, and have been invited to some great dinner parties. For us, it's the perfect blend of being hermits and having great community. And we get to drive a 1986 Jeep Comanche, which Nick Anaya told me was "cool." What else could you want?

title: Water Table Decline in Eldorado Area
body: According to Steve King (manager of the Eldorado Area Water and Sanitation District), the water table in the Eldorado area is declining. Hydrologists report that more water is being taken from the aquifer than can be naturally replenished and it is not clear how efficiently the state monitors private wells. The district has about 3,000 customers served by a dozen wells; extensions to new properties cost $15,000 each. But they are "pursuing a connection to the Santa Fe County water system and a long-term service agreement" (New Mexican 12/8/19).

body: Bobby Anaya of Santa Fe passed away on November 26. He was born September 30, 1938 in Galisteo, son of Abel and Mary Anaya. Bobby (according to the obituary in The New Mexican, 12/8) was a well-known musician from the age of ten until his death, performing with his father, his brothers Henry, Leo, and Jimmy, and his son Rick. Since the early 1980s he was in a group called Mariachi Encanto.

title: Artist Geninne Zlatkis and Family Settle in Galisteo
body: Artist Geninne Zlatkis, her architect husband Manolo Benitez, and their dog Zorro (!) who are renting the restored Ferneau home, moved to New Mexico from near Mexico City five years ago. They lived in Lamy and are now building a new home there, renting here until it is completed. "I am in love with Galisteo!" says Geninne. "Ever since we drove around the first time. It feels like one of those old Mexican towns that I love so much. I was born in New York. My dad was from Argentina and my mom from Chile. They met in Manhattan. Manolo is from a beautiful little town in central Mexico called Bejucos, but he grew up in Mexico City."

title: A Galisteo Hero
body: Tristan, Christy O'Connor's eight-year-old Westie, was the subject of an article by Hirsch Wilson in The New Mexican (1/9). Tristan is an emotional support dog (and a champion surfer!), on the road a couple of times a month to visit Marine veterans through the Wounded Warrior Project. Atypically small for his role, he is nevertheless eminently qualified. He makes eye contact, hops up in laps and proves a good listener to those who are wounded, depressed, or suicidal. One Marine credited him with probably saving his life. Christy calls him her Zen dog - (hero) "calm, empathetic and friendly to all .... There is something about having a silent friend, who listens, loves unconditionally and doesn't judge. The recovering Marines feel safe and heard. Walls break down when they talk to a dog. Dogs have a healing power that can transform a life." This has been confim1ed by a Purdue University study.

title: Sixty Years Ago - Las Marias Ranch Stock Move
body: The caption reads: "In northern New Mexico a major spring ranch job is moving stock to summer pastures. These pictures (courtesy of the New Mexican, Santa Fe) were taken a few weeks ago on the Las Marias Ranch near Galisteo. The ranch, operated by Frank Ortiz y Davis & Sons (and their fathers and grandfathers before them for a couple of hundred years) is in excellent shape and the cattle will gain 250 pounds or more this summer. Pictures at top right show the yearlings cautiously crossing a paved road, then going through the gate to their new home. At top left are cowboys Sarapio Montoya (horseback) and Antonio Chavez; the latter has worked for the ranch more than 35 years, as did his father. Bottom photos show a rebellious yearling trying to flee the herd; snagged by an accurate loop, and undergoing an examination he could have avoided." (From West Texas Livestock, July 3, 1958.)

title: How We Met: Heidi Johnson and Craig Fulmer
body: Craig and Heidi met 23 years ago under a rare star-filled night in the Pacific Northwest. Craig had been mowing his lawn when the neighbor, Susie, appeared at the fence with a friend in tow. She introduced the two and invited Craig over that evening to preview their new house. Heidi said "nice to meet you" and went on her way. Craig threw the lawnmower into the garage and ran for the shower while shedding grass-stained clothes and leaving muddy footprints everywhere. He showed up at the neighbors with two bottles of wine (they didn't drink) and a keen eye to meeting the friend, who was nowhere to be seen. Craig handed over his business card to Susie with the request to pass it on to Heidi. After a week of no response, he returned, with another business card in hand, and again asked Susie to pass it on. Heidi did finally get the card, called, and on their first date, they spent five hours drinking coffee and another three over pizza. As Craig and Heidi like to say "It all begins with friendship, loyalty, and trust."

title: How We Met: Annika Kaplan and Alex Amend
body: Annika and Alex first met in the spring of 2008 at a punk show in Minneapolis. Without speaking, they found themselves dancing together. At the end of the act, Annika remembers clearly the first thing Alex said to her: "Hey, partner." They dated that summer before Alex went to Washington D.C. for his first job after college. A year later Alex returned and they reconnected before Alex moved again to New York City for another job. Fast forward nearly 10 years and Alex is in Minnesota for a friend's wedding. He reached out to Annika and she agreed to meet for lunch. They found themselves on a long walk talking about their lives and their former relationships. Annika invited Alex to her apartment to meet her dog Una. They kissed there and, as they say, the rest is history. They married in September of 2018, moved to Galisteo in late winter 2019, and welcomed their first baby, Gilda, on 1/11/20.

title: How We Met: Cecile and Kevin Smith
body: In 2014 I was moving from Massachusetts to South Carolina to be close to my father after my mother's death. I got my house in Carlisle MA ready for sale, but even before it was listed my realtor, a good friend of mine, brought a good friend of hers to look at it. I thus met Cecile, recently divorced, who bought my house in MA as I was moving 1000 miles away. We were immediately attracted to each other, and started dating behind our realtor's back as she had told each of us separately not to have any contact until after closing. After three years of long-distance relationship, and a lot of long-distance driving, we were married at that same house by our realtor friend who is also a justice of the peace. This was just after we had bought our new home in Galisteo, and we have been here ever since.

title: How We Met: Denise Lynch and Captain John Shannon
body: During the 2017 winter holiday break Denise and her Saluki were in the KSFR Radio Station to record her monthly volunteer underwriting spot. She is the voice of UPAYA Zen Center. I had recently begun working there as a reporter/producer, focusing on Santa Fe's art scene. I found her in the kitchen area and began asking questions about her beautiful dog, Wells. The conversation proceeded with ease and we discovered a shared love of film. We are both graduates of the SFCC film school and Denise is a graduate of IAIA Cinematic Arts and Technology -- plus we had both made independent films featuring the Galisteo Basin as a main character. In the course of our conversation I mentioned I was a retired US Army Captain and a paratrooper with over 400 jumps and she shared that her son, Sean Sohn, was an Airborne Ranger. Denise recalls, "Men who jump out of planes was an interesting shared topic." During our brief encounter we learned that we also had an appreciation for the Belgian Malinois breed. We now have a two-year-old Malinois named Scout who is a PTSD Service Dog and is in scent and personal protection training. After Denise told me about her art and that she mined her own clay in the Galisteo Basin, I requested her contact info for an interview about her bowls. (Here's the link to the interview that started it all: https://www.ksfr.org/post/ksfr-talks-regional-artist-denise-lynch.) Well-bred dogs, films, jumping out of airplanes and beloved Galisteo were the building blocks of our unique start.

title: A Tragic Week in January
body:
On the morning of January 14, Pedro Allan Sandoval (2003-2020) and his brother Mateo Francisco Sandoval (2005-2020) died in an automobile accident on NM 41 between Stanley and Moriarty. They are Stella Maestas's great nephews and related to many others in Galisteo.

Both brothers were on the Moriarty High School football, basketball and track teams, members of 4H, the Sociedad de San Jose, and the National Junior Honor Society, and had won many sports and academic honors. They loved the outdoors, gaming, and working with kids. They are survived by their parents, Ernie and Alexandra (Lexi) Sandoval, and their sister Camille.

Memorial Services, attended by hundreds, were held on Jan. 22 at the Moriarty High School Gym. Banners read "#Sandoval Strong" and "60+40=100 percent" (for the brothers' football team numbers). Honorary pallbearers were the entire student body. The Pintos won their next game, an emotional moment. The brothers are buried at the Stanley cemetery. A GoFundMe account for the family was over $40,000 within a few days.

Two days earlier, Galisteans Deirdre Africa and Heidi Johnson lost an only son and brother. The Joplin, Missouri newspaper reported: "Colby Tait Africa, 45, a senior programmer for Projility, passed away Sunday Jan. 12, 2020. He is survived by his son Parker Africa of Monett, MO, his mother Deirdre, and sister Heidi, both of Galisteo, NM." Deirdre adds, "With generous donations from the community, I'm planting a Liberty apple tree to remember the person he was."

title: The Return of Netflix
body:
The large number of vehicles at the Silverado movie set on Cerro Pelon Ranch is due to NetFlix filming through May 15th. Representatives met with GCA officers Roger Taylor and Anna Cardenas to review Galisteo filming guidelines. All filming will be at the movie set; the crew will respect the night sky ordinance as well as limit sound disruption; all crew and cast will be reminded regularly about speed limits through Galisteo; heavy equipment will travel I-40 to NM 41 to the set.

After current construction at the set (6:30 AM to 6:30 PM), filming will begin 3/13 to 4/20 (c. 5AM to 10PM, mostly weekdays) with 100-150 actors and a crew of around 250. Traffic will increase. Expect drones and one night of simulated dynamiting and fire (hopefully avoiding the almost disastrous Wild Wild West fire years ago). From 4/21 to 5/15 there will be remediation on the set (6:30AM to 6:30 PM).

Please direct concerns or questions during this entire period to Roger or Anna and we will address them with the Location Managers. Silverado, of course, is private property. The set will be closed to the public.

title: GCA Election and Census Information
body:
The GCA election on March 7th (see p.1) will fill four GCA Board positions: three Director positions and the Treasurer.

The Census is coming! Look for a post-card in your mailbox around mid-March giving you options (a website link, a phone#) to complete the ten-question survey. Remember: every person not counted means $3,700 in Federal funds goes to another community or to the State. New Mexico receives c.$60 million in Federal funds for assistance programs. Senator Liz Stefanics reports that a mere 1% under-count of New Mexico's population in 2020 would result in a $780 million loss of federal funds over a 10-year period, so it is absolutely critical that we help ensure that everyone be counted. We need every dollar!

title: Guatemala
body:
A kaleidoscope of warm tropical colors in a volcanic landscape with a population of 50% indigenous Maya speaking 21 Pre-Hispanic languages, embedded in a cultural and religious mosaic and woven into the bright fabric of an experience enough for two lifetimes - these define my recent trip to Guatemala.

This year I traveled once again to the pueblo of Santa Catarina Bobadilla on the outskirts of Antigua at the base of El Volcan de Agua to work as an interpreter for Baby's Breath Project as part of a team prepared to train indigenous, rural midwives (Comadronas) in the use of the neonatal resuscitation bag and mask to assist babies born not breathing. We were a team of neonatal nurses, interpreters, and two Guatemalan doctors.

In twenty days, we taught, tested and certified 112 rural Comadronas, each of whom received a certificate and a Baby's Breath Backpack filled with the supplies necessary to put their training to use. Guatemalan Comadronas are estimated to attend 50 to 75% of births in indigenous populations. In Mayan culture their job is a sacred calling, as the skills are often passed down through generations within a family. These dedicated women are experienced and skilled in the home delivery of babies and care of the mother. However, without the training and supplies provided by Baby's Breath Project, a baby born not breathing has little chance at life.

For the second week, my team consisted of one English speaking nurse, her interpreter (me) translating her English to Spanish, and a second Guatemalan interpreter translating my Spanish to the K'iche-speaking midwives. The animated teaching and enthusiastic learning sprinkled with smiles, jokes, and laughter from nurses, midwives, and interpreters alike spoke to a surprising lack of language barriers. To the delight of the Comadronas, Shannon, my nurse partner, and I both learned to speak a few encouraging words in K'iche.

On Graduation Day, along with hugs, smiles and tears, we all expressed the joy of connections, friendship, and a job well done. For me the takeaway is that I've got friends in Guatemala and the "Comadronas" know they have friends in the United States. For this experience I am forever grateful.

*Baby's Breath is a nonprofit organization teaching the program developed collaboratively by the American Academy of Pediatrics and the World Health Organization. On Face book at Baby's Breath Project. www.babysbreathproject.org.

title: Now That Corona Is No Longer Just a Beer
body:
The caring community of Galisteo is a good place to be "sheltered in place." For those of us who already work from home, things are almost normal, aside from the sense of a dark cloud over us all, but many are suffering economic woes as a result. And many are busy sewing masks and gowns for the GVFR, the County, and anyone else who needs them.

News that a zoo's tiger got COVID sent a shudder through pet owners, but as John Watson-Jones informs us: "the bottom line at this point is that you cannot get COVID from your pet, however you can give COVID to your pet, so if you test positive, you should use all the precautions you would use to prevent transfer to another family member. Human to pet transmission is rare, symptoms are usually short lived and the animal recovers." Up to date information can be found at IDEXX.com/COVID19.

Here's how a few of us are coping:

From Chan Anaya: Vernon and I are so happy to be back home in Galisteo with his mom Mary Alice. We were on 14-day quarantine after a trip to Alabama to celebrate my dad's 93rd birthday, which of course was canceled. Came back early to be with Mary Alice. We did exercises across the lawn with her while still on Quarantine. She is the only other person in our tight circle right now. The perfect time to try crazy things with our hair. My daughter and I both shaved our heads. Helps me stay focused as a prayer warrior as the Dine taught me while I was working with them for ten years: Up to greet the sun with a com pollen blessing each morning. As new gardeners in this area, we would love to see who all is farming/gardening and wants to share their wisdom.

From Greg Salustro and Wayland Wong: Before Covid 19, Wayland and I spent three or four nights each week going out to dinner at everything the area has had to offer (hello Paper Dosal hello Mampuku Ramen! hello Legal Tender!). But what we've turned to in these times of anxiety and stress is good home-made comfort food. In our marriage, for Wayland, a Chinese American, this means anything made with rice, and for me, Italian American, it means pasta and more pasta (as Sophia Loren brilliantly put it: "Everything you see I owe to spaghetti.")Wow, we've been married for seven years and food is really teaching us about compromise: rice with tomato sauce and grated cheese and pasta with hoisin sauce! Sometimes our dinners don't work but with help from NYTimes cooking often they do. Also thank you Deborah Madison for our Meatless Mondays and all you've taught us about rice, bread and pasta. Cooking has become our tactic to control this chaos, and it's keeping us positive. We are very fortunate here in Galisteo. Both Wayland and I are volunteering at Kitchen Angels, which prepares and delivers really nutritional and delicious meals to a very at-risk population, especially now. Please support them or the charity of your choice during these very difficult times.

From Fred and JJ Milder: How privileged we still are. Each day, I take our dogs for a walk in our spacious and exquisite surroundings. Sometimes it is a short I-mile loop. Other times it is a multi-mile exploration of some part of the public lands that envelop us and are available to all. The dogs and I love our time together. At this time of year, each day brings new, joyous observations of the myriad wildflowers and newborn life after the winter. Not to make light of anyone's personal struggles at this moment, be they physical health, economic hardship, or the enforced solitude, but humankind has survived through and thrived after times like these before. We will again. Stay strong, care for others, and keep healthy.

title: Sopitas and Pinons
body:
Based on Connie Sandoval Valencia's memories, as shared with her daughter, Michaela Sandoval Valencia

It's a cool October day in my little village called Galisteo. The bedroom I share with my sister is a little cold so I don't want to get out from under the warm quilts, but Grampa Climaco is coming for us this morning to go pifion picking. I nudge my sister, Patricia, to get up and then I run over to get my brothers (Benny, Tacho, Frank and Rudy) up and remind them about our fun day with Grampa. "It's going to be cold up in the mountain, so dress warm," Grampa told us. We pull on our layers of clothes and run outside to get our chores done quickly so we can eat our breakfast before Grampa comes for us. "Hurry," Mama says, "Grampa will be here soon."

Here he comes in his covered wagon, pulled by two, big golden brown horses. They snort and paw the ground as if to say "hurry it up children." Off we go with our empty flour sacks and coffee cans, and big dreams of bringing them back full to the brim with big, fat pifion seeds. It gets colder as we start to climb the mountain so our cheeks and noses turn red, but we are not chilled because Grampa covered us with thick, warm quilts. While I'm enjoying the puffy clouds and beautiful blue sky, my brothers are arguing about who will bring home the most pifion.

Grampa finds the perfect spot where there are several trees clumped together, with lots of pifion on the trees and on the ground. We are itching to jump out of the wagon but he tells us to wait a minute while he unties the horses fom the wagon and secures their leashes to another set of trees. While we wait, the boys are eyeing the trees that appear to have the most pifion and proclaiming which tree is theirs. When we toss off the quilts and jump down, the cold bites at us but we don't give it no mind because we're off and racing at full speed to claim our tree. In no time we have all filled our bags and cans and it's time to head home. Even though all the bags and cans are full to the brim, the boys are still arguing about who won the contest.

When we arrive in Galisteo, Grampa does not direct the horses to our house. Instead we head towards his house because he tells us he has a treat to give us. While he and my brothers unhitch the horses and give them food and water, Patricia and I run into the kitchen. Gramma Kika (Francisca) has the wood stove going so the room is so nice and warm. Mmmm, it smells like coffee brewing and freshly baked bread. Gramma helps us wash off the sticky tree sap and dirt from our hands and then Grampa and the boys come in and wash up also. Gramma sets seven coffee cups on the table, along with milk and sugar. We sit at the long, old oak table full of anticipation, wiggling in our chairs, because we think we've guessed what our treat is. Grampa fills each cup with coffee, handing one to each one of us. Then he passes around the milk and sugar. Gramma hands us each a plate with a slice of bread, still a bit warm from the oven. We look at Grampa Climaco and Gramma Kika with the brightest eyes and the biggest smiles as we say altogether "Ah! Sopitas," and proceed to dip chunks of bread into our sweetened coffee.

To this day, occasionally, when I smell fresh coffee and fresh bread, I remember the pleasure we had eating "Sopitas". You see in those days (about 1944, when I was 13 years old), we didn't have much, so treats were very rare and very special.

title: Spring 2020: Bluebirds.... and More
body:
February was tough. A cold, windy one-day-longer-leap-year month that lingered long after the brightness of Christmas lights and the warmth ofValentine's Day kisses faded. But spring is near. I'm sure. American Robins and Red-winged Blackbirds audition for the Bosque 's dawn chorus, my overly anxious tulips are risking frost, allergy season is two weeks early, taxes are coming due, and the dog is shedding.

March gamboled in soft as a lamb, bringing us longer days, more sunlight, and warm "spring-like" temperatures. And best of all, dozens of Western Bluebirds carrying the sky on their wings crowding my birdbath, brightening my day, and bringing a considerable improvement to my attitude. They are, after all, "The Bluebirds of Happiness."

Here's my take, thus far, on Spring 2020:

The Great Homed Owl pair that called in February is now busy feeding owlets, pushing them to maturity ahead of the flood of baby rabbits, prairie dogs, and packrats that will be their prey later in the spring.

A female Northern Harrier already hunts the sage south of Corey's porch.

I watched as a Golden Eagle circled the Bosque, flying higher and higher to disappear into a deep blue sky.

Catherine reports American Goldfinches at her feeder.

From the telephone wires along 42, American Kestrels scan the fields for small reptiles, insects and mice.

Northern Mockingbirds repo1ied last week in Las Campanas may soon find their way to Galisteo.

Say's Phoebes have arrived to nest under our portals. Barn Swallows will follow.

Sandhill Cranes are calling from high over the Basin as they migrate northward.

Turkey Vultures will be roosting in the Bosque before the end of March. (Editor 's note: I was awaiting them with bated breath and the first ones I saw at last were on March 26, a bit late.)

Both Western and Mountain Bluebirds have arrived to nest in Galisteo. As members of the thrush family they feed primarily on insects supplementing with fruit and Juniper berries. Bluebirds are cavity nesters in stiff competition with aggressive non-native English Sparrows and Starlings. Providing nesting boxes is the best thing we can do to boost our Bluebird population. (See Cornell site:www.nestwatch. org/learn/all.about-birdhouses/birds/westembluebirds.)

I remind myself to clean out birdbaths, fill feeders, offer meal worms for nesting phoebes and bluebirds, remove old nests from boxes, and place brushed-out-dog hair where birds can find it for nest building material.

While I was putting the finishing touches to this offering, rains and hail arrived to spoil more than a week of beautiful "spring-like" weather, proving the point ofMark Twain's quote, "In the spring I have counted 136 different kinds of weather in 24 hours." But spring is near ( or here). I'm sure.

title: Barbara Beals Cooper (1933 - 2020)
body:
From the family: Barbara Beals Cooper, 86, passed away March 25 of natural causes after a brief stay at a nursing facility in Albuquerque. She grew up in Syracuse, N. Y., with her childhood sweetheart Joseph Morgan Cooper Jr., whom she married in 1956. Her Smith College junior year abroad in Geneva, Switzerland awakened her love of travel and other cultures, pursued with Joe as they raised their family in the Philippines and Mexico. Later the proprietor of a travel agency in Rowayton, CT, she travelled extensively. Moving to Galisteo in 1987, Barbara found her true home, restoring, with Joe, a traditional adobe house [the Lucas Anaya property on The Hill]. Intensely creative and intellectually curious, she was an accomplished self-taught artist in many media and served as a docent at the O'Keeffe Museum in Santa Fe and volunteered with the Friends of the Library in El Dorado.
Her family was central in her heart. She is survived by daughters Betsy Mackey, Molly Damron, and Amy Sherwill, son Joseph M. Cooper III, sister Judy Beals, brother-in-law Walter Cooper, eleven grandchildren and two great grandchildren. Her beloved Joe pre-deceased her in 2015 and son Christopher Cooper in 2018. A celebration of life is planned for a later date.
From the village: Barbara and Joe and were active in the community for decades, working with the Studio Tour, serving on the Board of the Galisteo Community Association, leading and supporting many local issues. And they helped found El Puente de Galisteo in 1996-97. Their love of the village was always evident. Their many friends and neighbors here mourned Joe five years ago, and are now mourning Barbara.

title: Basin Hummers
body:
Ever walk outside on a beautiful spring day and as soon as your foot touches the earth, a rich, fruity scent wafts up to envelop you in the warm aliveness of the living, breathing earth body itself? Well, it happened to me this morning at the same moment a trilling Broad-tailed Hummingbird buzzed by my nose, opening my mind to a strong connection to all life and sending me running home to once again research Hummers. Here are some interesting facts I discovered about our four species found in the Galisteo Basin:
Broad-tailed: As a high-mountain jewel, this bird (like most Hummers) is equipped to survive freezing nights by slowing heart rate and lowering body temperature in a state of torpor. Their brilliant magenta throat feathers will make you look twice. The metallic trill produced by wing tip feathers adds pizzazz to their spectacular courtship dives, after which the male trills back to central Mexico leaving the female to raise the babies alone.
Black-chinned: The most adaptable, wide-spread, and numerous of our four Hummers, this tiny bird is at home in deserts as well as mountains. Nests built by the female to hold her coffee-bean sized eggs are made of plant fuzz and spider silk that expand to accommodate the growing babies whose tummies she keeps full by catching insects in midair. Adult birds feed on flower nectar using their forked tongue to soak up nectar at the rate of up to twenty licks a second. As the tongue is withdrawn, the nectar is squeezed into the mouth.
Rufous: Straight out of Mexico, this brilliant orange Hummer glows like Aztec gold as he flies off his perch to make life difficult for all Hummers who dare enter his territory. All ages and sexes are aggressive protectors of their nectar rights. One reason for the feisty attitude just might be their almost 8-thousand-mile migration from Mexico to Alaska and back- the longest of any bird relative to body size. Rufous also get the prize for the most northernly breeding site of any Hummer in the world. After breeding, the males fly down the chain of the Rocky Mountains, stopping here in the Galisteo Basin for a few days to tank up for their return to the tropics, making life challenging for all other Hummers.
Calliope: The smallest Hummer in North America that is also the smallest long-distance migrant in the world barely weighs as much as a ping pong ball. They migrate through here north into Colorado and as far as Canada to breed and nest. These dainty, inconspicuous, and non-aggressive birds fly under the radar of the more aggressive Rufous as they quietly slip in to sip alongside the big boys. Watch your feeders later in the summer to catch a glimpse of the much-smaller male with the bright, rosy-red gorget refueling for his return home as far south as Central America after breeding.
While I was researching, a friend called wanting a reminder of how to prepare nectar for the little Black-chinned Hummer that just showed up at her window. In case you, too, have forgotten the sugar water recipe, here it is:
4-parts H2O to 1-part cane sugar. Heat the water to boiling, add the sugar and stir until dissolved. Do not add coloring. Fill feeder with the amount Hummers will drink in 3- 5 days. Store unused sugar water in the refrigerator. Remember to monitor feeders carefully-a dirty, moldy feeder can kill Hummers. Clean feeders regularly in hot soapy water. Hint: I recommend the easy to clean Best Feeders from El Dorado Country Pet or Wild Birds.
By the second week of April, three species of Hummers present in the Galisteo Basin had come calling at my feeder- Black-chinned, Broad-tail and Rufous. If you don't like caring for feeders, planting Humming Bird blooms is always a winner. Hummers have amazing memories and will return to hover over the site of last year's feeder, waiting for you to get with the program. These precious pollinators depend upon you to make your patio a Hummer friendly place to help mitigate the effects of Climate Change and loss of habitat. According to the 2014 State of Birds Watch List, some Hummers declined 62% between 1966 and 2014.
"So much Beauty we need to look after." (Charlie Mackesy, The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse).

title: {GVFR/Water Board/GCA Updates}
body:
Under the able guidance of Chief Jean Anaya and Craig Fulmer, the Fire Department is fully operational. Truck maintenance is accomplished within Covid-19 regulations. Chief keeps us informed on the latest developments. Monthly business meetings are on Zoom (and we even got a glimpse of wide-eyed baby Gilda Amend, the GVFR's unofficially adopted mascot). The GVFR sends out a whopping thank you to Deirdre Africa for making the reusable gowns for our Rescue, Squad, and Med 80. Craig reports, "When I delivered the gowns to Med 80, their jaws literally dropped. That's how Galisteo FD rolls!"
And remember, given the threat of drought, high winds and fire season, there are currently NO BURN PERMITS.
The 2019 Water Quality Report for the Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association came out in April. Nothing to worry about (we're not Flint), but for those interested, a link to the full detailed report will be posted on the Galisteo Community website.
The GCA Board is pleased to announce that the red shade sails are installed at the Community Center (see below). We are getting close to the end of the USDA Equipment Grant project, with only a storage shed remaining to be installed. Last month the new ceiling fans and lights were installed, and prior to that was the installation of the new hot water heater, water softener unit, RO undersink drinking water unit, and the 3 mini-split heating/ cooling units plus compressor. Hopefully we'll be able to gather at some time in the months to come to celebrate!

title: {Need Still More COVID Advice?}
body:
One respected local physician recommends that when you return to your home after being in contact with the public, remember to inhale steam for extra protection. Boil water in a pan, then turn off the heat. Put a towel over your head and inhale the steam for two full minutes. (Be sure not to burn your mucous membranes!) You can add a couple drops of eucalyptus essential oil to disinfect the airways.
If you think you are getting sick, start the steam inhalations right away, several times a day. Drink hot ginger tea all day, take hot baths, use your sauna if you have one, and use a heating pad on your chest. Don't forget to stay hydrated. You could also take high doses of vitamin C throughout the day. The fatty envelope of liposomal vitamin C allows us to take huge doses which otherwise would cause severe cramps and diarrhea.

title: Conservation News
body:
548.56 acres have been added to the existing 250-acre easement at the Galisteo Basin Preserve, for a total of 798.56 acres at its heart. This amended conservation easement expands protection to a contiguous 6, 150.5-acre conservation area that permanently protects wildlife habitat, migration corridors, scenic vistas, cultural resources and publicly accessible trails. It also creates more of a buffer on the west side of the Galisteo Springs conservation easement, the source of water for generations of ancient and modern peoples. And it grants public access to up to five miles of future trails connected to the Preserve's 30-mile trail network. Ted Harrison and Gretchen Grogan at the Commonweal Conservancy have, once again, made possible the protection of this wonderful area.
The Rio Grande Agricultural Trust newsletter reports that "retired school administrator Johnny Pack [husband of the late Linda McKee] joined three neighbors to place an easement on 600 acres including riparian wetlands a few miles north of the Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge. Between tax breaks and funding raised by the land trusts that now hold the easement, Pack, who owns just over half of the total acreage, realized as much per acre about $1,300 - as he could have expected from an outright sale. "It was the best of both worlds," he said. "I could recoup money and put land into an easement that protects birds."

title: Susan Rothenberg (1945-2020)
body: The internationally renowned painter Susan Rothenberg died at home in Galisteo on May 18 after months of complications from back surgery. She was born in Buffalo, NY, graduated from Cornell University, and studied for two weeks at the Corcoran School of Art before moving to New York City in 1969. From 1973 to 1980 she was known for her horse paintings, which have been credited with a resurgence of figurative art, or New Image Painting. "I had been doing abstract paintings, using a central dividing line so as to keep the painting on the surface and call attention to the canvas," she told New York magazine: "The horse was just something that happened on both sides of my line. The image held the space and the line kept the picture flat." One of these paintings was hung in the Obama White House. Her first marriage to sculptor George Trakas ended in divorce, after which she married Bruce Nauman, moving with him to their Las Madres ranch just north of Galisteo in 1990. Her work had expanded to striking paintings of fragmented Galisteo poker players, figures in motion, birds, dogs, and artifacts from the Galisteo Pueblo, which is on their property. (The ruins are preserved through an easement to the Archaeological Conservancy.) Susan is survived by her daughter Maggie, and Bruce, her husband of 32 years. Alfred MacAdam wrote in The Brooklyn Rail about her show this past January at Sperone Westwater in NYC: "The only thing we can ask of this great artist is that she never stop working and never abandon the commitment to radical ambiguity that fuels our own creative and imaginative responses to her images."

title: The Talk of the Town: Baby Great Horned Owls
body:
Baby Great Horned Owls fledglings in our Bosque got the attention of birders from far and wide. Unfortunately, too many overly eager pairs of binoculars gathered beneath the nest tree possibly stressed the vulnerable owlets during the most dangerous time in their life.

Catherine and I first spotted the nest on April 6 when a raucous raven with mischief on his mind called our attention to the tall, leaf-less cottonwood tree where Mama owl sat stoically protecting her brood. Ravens, crows, hawks and other owls aren't the only threat the babies must survive. Snakes, raccoons, and misbehaving humans will all be fended off by the devoted, mated-for-life owl pair.

Adult Great Horned Owls armed with razor-sharp talons are equipped to take on all comers, aiming for the face and eyes of the intruder. Powered by a wingspan of nearly five feet and backed by a body weight of three to almost five pounds, their attacks are swift, silent, and effective. Capable of killing, but not lifting prey two to three times their own size, Great Horned Owls are the top nocturnal avian predator in the woods.

Earlier this spring while we anxiously awaited the arrival of Hummers and Warblers, Mama owl was already busy sitting day and night on her borrowed nest brooding her owlets. Papa owl, hunter-in-chief, was busy finding food for himself, mama, and the extremely fast-growing, ridiculously cute babies.

Once the owlets are able to thermoregulate to maintain their own body temperature, the female may move to perch on the side of the nest or nearby in the tree making room for her growing babies. By six weeks the owlets' talons are strong enough to enable them to begin "branching" as they move out of the nest to cling to tree limbs or climb up and down the tree trunk using beaks as well as talons. By seven weeks they are experimenting with short flights and numerous crash landings, at times ending up on the ground and in danger.

A good rule of thumb when near the nesting tree is: Look up. Look down. Leave fledgling owls where they are unless wounded. The owl pair will continue to feed and defend the fledglings. By 9-10 weeks the owlets are flying with their parents. The steep learning curve of these next few months is a critical time during which they must perfect their flying and hunting skills to defy the statistic that 50% will die before their first year.

Over millennia, Great Horned Owls have diversified, evolving attributes that help them beat the statistics. As adults they have no natural predators, eat almost everything that moves, nest in a wide variety of habitats, earlier than any bird in North America, and hunt after dark with silent stealth aided by large eyes and radar-like hearing. Successful owls typically live thirteen years and as long as twenty three in the wild. A Great Horned Owl in the San Francisco Zoo made it to fifty. With any luck, our owlets will reach adulthood as members of the most common and widespread of the nineteen species of owls in North America.

I wish for you the experience of being in the woods and suddenly becoming aware of a Great Horned Owl, staring down at you with the calmness of a Buddhist Monk who has reached the highest level of enlightenment. It will surely deepen your conviction that nature is full of wonder and meaning.

"Every night the owl -with his wild monkey-face calls through the black branches, and the mice freeze and the rabbits shiver in the snowy fields- and then there is the long, deep trough of silence when he stops singing, and steps into the air." (Mary Oliver)

title: Steve Moya Steps Up: A New (Interim) President for the Water Board
body:
On April 3, Phillip Tuwaletstiwa sent this communication to members of the MDWCA: "I have served as President of the Water Board for approximately five years. It is time to turn over the Presidency to someone else. We are fortunate that Steve Moya, a Board Member [and former President of the Board years ago], will assume the duties of President effective April 5, 2020. Steve will serve until the upcoming water improvement project is complete. After that he will step down. I shall remain on the Board to assist in the project.

"Normally, we would hold a Board Meeting to sanction the change of officer responsibilities, but current health and safety guidelines prevent public meetings. For the same reason, we must cancel the Membership meeting scheduled for April 8th.

"Under the circumstances arising from the Coronavirus Pandemic it is necessary for the Water Board Officers to make administrative and executive decisions to keep the water system functioning and oversee our obligations to improve Galisteo's water system. It is equally important to inform the membership of significant administrative and operational issues. If any member of the Galisteo Water Association has questions, please contact a Board member.

"Galisteo is fortunate to have our Water Board, which has worked diligently to serve our community. We have secured approximately $670,000 in funding to improve our water system, and if all goes well, construction will start in the next couple of months."

The Board is also concerned about the recent $150K we received from the Capital Outlay appropriation. In March, Tuwaletstiwa thanked Senator Liz Stefanics for her support in that funding. However, the legislature is now in the process of modifying the budget at the special session and "Galisteo's water improvements could well take a back seat to urgent state health essentials. Other concerns are the uncertainty of construction during Covid-19 and state approval for our pending new bidding process." However, Craig Fulmer is optimistic about his communications with a state contact.

title: Bosque Trail
body:
A small group of appropriately masked community members have removed some of the log "bridges" across the Galisteo Creek. Two of them crossed over to private property which the owners prefer people not trespass upon. Please remember the walking path goes from the entrance gate at the wooden bridge adjacent to the Griscom property on that side of the creek down to Laura Yeats' property. Walking north from the wooden bridge, the path crosses the creek on wooden ground pilings towards the former Agnes Martin property.

Please do not replace these logs. When we have higher flows of water they become dams catching debris washing downstream - you can see piles of debris several feet high against some of the older cottonwoods - causing water to move towards the banks and enabling erosion. In the dry season those debris piles become fire hazards. During the restoration work several years ago, much of that debris was removed and burned under the supervision of the GVFR. Let's continue to support the health of our bosque in an environmentally friendly manner.

title: LONG AWAITED WATER PROJECT BEGINS
body:
From Craig Fulmer
The Galisteo Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association
Board meeting on Sept. 8th was attended by Apple Mountain
Constructors and our representatives from the NM Environment
Dept., Walker Engineering. The most pressing issue was the
date for beginning construction on the long awaited updating
of our water system. Our project will begin mid-to-late October
-- sooner if AMC's other jobs wrap up ahead of schedule.
The first phase will be new underground water supply
lines. The second will be a new pump house by the water tanks
on CR 42. While AMC's crews are trenching and laying new
supply pipes, the major components of the new pump house
will be ordered and fabricated. With Covid part of our life now,
the lead times for factory orders of industrial equipment is
running long. AMC anticipates all phases of our water system
improvement project to be complete and operational early in
2021. As we approach a start date, we will notify the village of
effects on individual roads.
I's been quite a while in the making, but we are finally ready
to begin construction to bring pressurized water to Galisteo.
Ed.note: Special thanks to Phil, Craig, and Steve for a huge
amount of work on this project.

body:
From La Sala
Two members persisted in their pursuit by having their cousin,
John Benjamin writes to correct and amplify the account
John Benjamin, sign their

What follows has been lightly edited.

I started working on starting a fire department in Galisteo
Fighting these people would have destroyed what we
in the fall of 1991, with the help of Dave Ahman and Moira
had worked four years to build. I chose to walk away SO our
Walden. I wrote a letter to the village proposing the idea. We
fire department would survive. I left a fully trained and fully
collected well over 100 signatures and then I went to the County
equipped organization, the new pumper truck had been ordered
Commission and asked for a Fire District to be created. It was

I then called for volunteers. We had our first organizing
I resigned as the roof was going up.
meeting in March 1992. In June we had sixteen committed men
The fire department was the best thing I have done in my life.
and women members and commenced to get everyone trained. I
was the only member already a state certified fire fighter from my
time at the Las Cruces fire school in 1977 and as a volunteer for
Cerrillos in what soon became the Turquoise Trail fire department.
We worked hard to get everyone certified and to collect the
months. In June 1993 we became a New Mexico Certified Fire
Department. Besides the endless list of hand-me-down equipment
I found, I took advantage of a federal program that gave first-
year fire departments first choice of any free federal surplus
equipment. I found a 1953 military 6x6 in Fence Lake, and a
1000-gallon water tank in Madrid. With a $3,200 Forestry grant
we bought a brush pump and welded the tank onto the 6x6 truck,
installed the pump, and the result was a great brush truck/tanker
which could go anywhere. Madrid also gave us an old ambulance
which became our Rescue unit.
From Chilili, we acquired a 1980 military 4x4 Dodge
Power Wagon with a Forestry brush pump attached. This was
an adventure requiring the State forestry man Louis Casaus to
draw his gun in order to hold angry Chilili citizens at bay while
I worked on the ignition system. Chilili had lost its right to the
truck as they had not maintained it and it was non operative. I
have not been back to Chilili since.
Our Class A fire truck, which we needed to become State
Certified, came from Fort Wingate as Government surplus. It was
a 1971 International, 1200-gallon-per-minute class A pumper, the
truck in the "No Pants" photo in Pueblo Chico. It looks like a
1948 because of the body style, but it was a 1971 and in great
condition. I believe the 1948 truck you mention is the one that
Mike Levis of Santa Fe Brewing donated during the earlier
1970s attempt to start a fire department. Lack of leadership
unfortunately resulted in the truck freezing solid and being ruined
during its first winter in Galisteo.
After being appointed Chief by the County Commission I
was elected Chief in the spring of 1992 at our first membership
meeting. I was the Fire Chief for 3 1/2 years and a year and 10
months as the Chief of a State Certified Department. I resigned
in the spring of 1995, after Ian was born.
1994 was our first complete year as a certified department
and qualified members received a year of retirement credit.
Being State Certified was the key to succeeding. It brought a
yearly stipend to the department -- about $17,000. In 1992-93,
we had raised about $15,000 per year with cider sales and the
Valentine's art auction. We were certified quicker than any
previous department.
Unfortunately some of the members wanted to be given a
year's credit for the PERA retirement fund without having made
the contribution of attendance and training required.

title: COMING DOWN THE PIKE: MORE ROAD WORK
body:
In 2019 the New Mexico Department of Transportation did
extensive surveying along NM41 from La Vega to the intersection
of NM41 and US285. Now they are creating a final plan to
submit in Spring 2021 for project funding from NMDOT and
the Federal Highway Administration. Actual work could start in
late 2021 or in 2022. To see the draft, visit www.nm4
galisteo.com, and explore the website's StoryMap. The public comment
period ended 9/14.
Some highlights: Between La Vega and Mile Post 7 (Linda
Vista Stables) the driving lanes will be 11' wide, with a 4'
shoulder on each side, posted speed limit 30MPH; lanes will be
11' wide, with a 4' shoulder on each side and 2 center medians
for traffic slowing, posted speed limit 35MPH;

title: FROM LA SALA
body:
We are pleased to welcome a new board member, Pamela
Clapp, to our volunteer group that operates the building and
programming of La Sala de San José. Here she introduces herself:
My husband Jeff and I lived and worked in New York City
for many years. When we retired we spent six years in Paris
before coming to Galisteo three years ago. My career in the
arts began in the 1980s at New York's Robert Miller Gallery,
which represented Louise Bourgeois, Lee Krasner, Robert
Mapplethorpe, and Alice Neel, to mention just a few.
In 1994 I became the program director at the Andy Warhol
Foundation for the Visual Arts where for the next seventeen
years I was in charge of the grant-making program. Recipients
included a wide variety of institutions from large museums to
small artist-run spaces. The foundation also provided grants to
individual artists through a national regranting program. In its
early days the foundation supported historic preservation projects
such as Cornerstones in Santa Fe and a restoration project at
Acoma Pueblo. This is where Galisteo comes into the picture.
Over the course of my work at the foundation I visited all
fifty states. New Mexico, where I had never been, was the most
memorable. It really felt like another world, especially if one
came from the east coast. Jeff and I stayed at the Galisteo Inn
several times, never dreaming that one day we'd be living right
here in Agnes Martin's former home.
We're so fortunate to have such a unique cultural resource
like La Sala in Galisteo. I hope I can be of help to the board as
it continues its great work.

title: Absentee Voting and Early In-Person Voting Information
body: Many of us received a postcard from the USPS regarding Absentee Voting by mail. If you plan to vote by mail in Absentee Ballot you DO NOT want to follow these guidelines. If you wait may be too late to receive and return your ballot. Request your ballot as soon as possible and return it immediately. If you wait to mail it until 7 days before November 3rd it may arrive too late to be counted. Complete and mail it as soon as you receive it. If you have not mailed it 7 days prior to November 3rd, you should concerned about your ballot not being counted, then vote early: the possibility of viral exposure is probably no more than when sanitizer to clean your hands after you exit the polling location. Although anyone can vote in-person at the Galisteo to vote early as agreed. title: Summer of 2020
body: The summer of 2019 found me writing of Galisteo orchards hanging heavy with peaches and cherries and rainy evenings filled with the songs of Spade-foot Toads. Now in the Summer of 2020 -- no fruit, no toads, no rain. Masked, gloved, and quarantined, we sweated through searing heat, disappointing monsoons, and wind-driven dust. Acerola and yucca declined to bloom. My patio petunias struggled while despicable Bindweed and Itbush flourished. The mid-summer ninety-six degree heat persisted until mid-morning. Up in Ranchitos our Saye's Phoebe pair managed to raise three broods of four chicks each -- only because we kept them supplied with worms served up twice a day under the pons. The Mountain Bluebird nested successfully in their bird house out near the bird water. An act of vandalism occurred the other day in the Village that was inexcusable and unnecessary. All of us are weary of the toxic discord in our politics these days, however when we react we cannot make good decisions, especially since there are other recourses. At the back playground the Bank Swallows plied the skies for insects to feed three broods of healthy ones, only to drop out of the sky dead for all adults and young alike -- during a state-wide "bird kill" following an unnatural cold snap and insect demise at the end of August. But now it's Fall. Mountain Lion tracks and Mule Deer are seen in the Rio Galisteo bosque, the beastly heat has disappeared, Rio Grande Cottonwoods are tinged with gold. Fedchor warplers are migrating through the sharp call bird call sound track. The sweet lament of White-crowned Sparrows fill our Indian Summer days outside of village homes this summer. What a wonderful service! Jim Sloan removed some twenty-one rattles from in and outside of village homes this summer. What a wonderful service! According to the journal Science, the pandemic-induced slowing of human activity leaves us with a quieter world in which we see more wildlife, hear more birds. For the White-crowned Sparrow males, the decreased competition from environmental noise offers an opportunity to sing softer higher-quality bird song, more appealing to the opposite sex. In a quieter world we hear up to four times as many bird songs, improving our own quality of life and enjoyment of the brief but spectacularly pleasant fall weather Mother Nature decided to send us to beg pardon for our Summer of 2020.

title: Letter: Community Email Editor Response on Political Discourse
body: From Your Community Email Editor Roger Taylor, GCA President and Vice-Chair Democratic Party of Santa Fe County. Last night someone deplorably tore down our neighbors sign supporting Trump/Pence. (We have a Biden/Harris sign in front of our house.) Our neighbor is a combat veteran and, as a veteran myself, I implore everyone to respect him, his views, his rights, and his property. As American Citizens we are obligated to uphold the Constitutional principles of free speech and protection of private property. Galisteo is a small but refreshingly diverse place of race, religion, politics, gender, heritage, and beliefs. We can agree and disagree on many issues, but in the end, we must stand up for our neighbors, help when we can, be generous, show tolerance, and have respect. A more constructive way to express our beliefs is to use the power of the vote to elect candidates who will work on behalf of those beliefs. Let's remember that communities thrive through civil discourse and action, whether or not we share the same opinions.

title: Un Cambio en el Viento/A Change in the Wind
body: The author of this book, a fictionalized history of early New Mexico, Larry Anaya (aka Labriano Alfredo Chavez y Anaya), was born in Galisteo in 1948, son of Don Lucas Anaya and the sweet lament of White-crowned Sparrows fill our Indian Summer days. Ellen Jenkins and Fray Angelico Chaver, studied theology at the College of Santa Fe and became Curator of the Galisteo Historical Museum (now the home of Woody and Dianna Gwyn) under the auspices of Jose Ortiz y Pino III and his father Frank Ortiz. Living now in San Antonio, he recently found El Puente and Pueblo Chico, thanks to his cousin Michelle Robles, and sent us his book. Here is a brief excerpt from his introduction: "GALISTEO...a name that conjures up wonderful visions. Growing up in the little New Mexico village, I was always fascinated with its past. As a youth I would ramble the hills and discover traces of a long-forgotten people. I would walk the same paths my ancestors marched across 500 years ago as they struggled to make their way through the high desert into uncharted lands. As I explored the ancient ruins of Pueblo de Galisteo I could swear I heard whispers among the scruffy junipers and sounds of distant drums echoing from the surrounding sandstone hillsides. Like most young boys, I had a very vivid imagination and I envisioned my ancestors -- the grand conquistadores searching for treasures that were never found. Legends filled the hills as I recalled stories told to me by my parents... tales of both sadness and intrigue. Ancient petroglyphs carved into the gray-black basalt rocks of 'El Creston' filled my head with figures of ghostly beings...The mysterious images displayed on the rocks made my mind run rampant as I put myself in the place of the artist."

title: Bandits in the Bosque
body:
New directories will arrive by mail in January. Thanks and Stay Fire Safe! Donations $75 and over get a snazzy t-shirt, Glancing high up into the old cottonwood near the river, we saw the mother racoon hanging dead, half out of the nest hole, her three helpless babies clinging to the tree trunk next to her.

Our rescue mission swung into action. A quick call to GVFR produced a ladder. My daughter Madge, shopping bag slung her shoulder, climbed up above our heads, plucked three little kitten-like babies off the tree, scooped three more out of the nest, dropped them all into the bag, and climbed safely to the ground.

A foster care volunteer from Espanola Animal Hospital accepted the orphan racoons and our job was done.

The back story revealed that the mother racoon, using her dexterous paws, jimmied open a bait box of rat poison, pilfered the contents, and returned to the nest to nurse her babies. Able to open ninety per cent of locks designed to stump human intruders sensitive racoon "fingers," packed with nerve endings, are a force to be reckoned with. Enhancing these masked mammals' ability to "see" with their paws, a highly developed neuron-dense cerebral cortex interprets messages received through touch. Researchers believe that racoons' signature habit of dousing their food in water softens the pads on the ends of their "fingers" making their nimble forelimbs even more sensitive. When tested in the lab, racoon memory and puzzle-solving ability scores just below primates and well above cats and dogs. Our Bandits in the Bosque with a reputation for mischief are creative problem solvers capable of competing with Aesop's Crow.

In the Bosque with a reputation for mischief are creative problem solvers capable of competing with Aesop's Crow. Now one of the interesting things about the winter is that there are bees called heater bees that specifically are used within the hive to keep the hive and the rest of their hive mates warm. So they've adapted really well to being on Earth. They're amazing. They're amazing little creatures.

Racoon Coats of the have and Davey crocker Coons Cap are cultural icons. Calvin Coolidge kept his pet racoon in the White House. The Beetles sang of "Rocky Racoon" who checked in to his room only to find Gideon's Bible." A recent movie feature an animated "Rocket Racoon" (Ask your grandkids.) with "Rocket Racoon"? Ask your grandkids.)

In spite of their popularity, racoons as pets are on the Do Not Recommend list of wildlife experts. These capricious wild animals have a notorious sweet tooth guided by an acute sense of smell and will guzzle your hummingbird juice, trash seed feeders, and loot your candy stash with the stealth of a cat burglar. We learned the hard way while camping along the Canadian River near Tucumcari one hot July. After dropping our sleeping bags next to the food tent, we slept under the stars while a furtive band of masked marauders quietly unzipped the tent, opened plastic wrappers, ate the middle out of our loaf of bread and the creamy filling from an entire package of Oreo Cookies. Having cashed in their five-finger-discount, the racoons disappeared into the night, leaving mayhem and disappointment behind.

On the serious side, while not denying their "cuteness", racoons can transmit fatal (if not treated) rabies and are capable of killing my dog in short order. In today's time of Covid-19 caused by the transfer of zoonotic diseases, I would think twice about inviting a wild animal to share my home. If you are out at night and lucky enough to pick up their yellow-green eye-shine in your flashlight, best to maintain your social distance and leave the bandit to its mischief.

title: Little Joe vs. the Wringer Washer
body:
Well, that was a crazy laundry day! A story to tell for years to come!

This story is based on a memory shared by Joe Sandoval about his beloved sister, MaryLou Sandoval Baca. It is written as though MaryLou -- 17 years old at the time -- is telling the story. Little Joe really lost the fight with the rollers of the wringer washer, and MaryLou really came to his rescue. Some of the story was made up to make it a little more interesting.

It is so quiet and peaceful early in the morning in our little vegeOseothesing bat soon it will be mehoten outdoors. I have just finished hanging some towels and sheets on the clothesline. It's so nice outside that for just a minute I close my eyes and I can hear the birdsongs in the nearby trees, and the leaves moving ever so gently with the morning breeze.

The sheets and towels are dancing on the clothesline, sending off' a scent of lavender.

Mama and my sisters and brothers are in the kitchen eating breakfast. Daddy left early to open up the local general store. After breakfast, Mama went out to work in the garden, and my sisters, Stella (10 years old) and JoAnn (7), stayed in the house watching over my younger siblings (Fred, 2, Gloria, 4, and Joe, 5). When they are done eating, Fidel (15) and George (12) go outside to chop wood and haul in buckets of water from the well.

Joe loves to hang out with Fidel and George. He wants to go out with them to chop wood but he knows he can't because he is too young and it is not safe.

Well, I better stop dreaming and get the next load of dirty clothes washed and ready to hang up. With seven kids in the house, and me, Mama and Daddy, there are always a lot of dirty clothes. I get more hot water from the stove and dump it into the washing machine, add a little more detergent and another load of dirty clothes, and then turn the machine on. I add more clear, cool water to the big silver washtub for rinsing. While that load is washing I go outside to fold the now dry sheets and towels.

Suddenly, I hear "ayudame, ayudame, por favor, MaryLou!" (help me, help me, please!) Oh no! That sounds like my little brother, Joe. What has he gotten into now! I drop the clothes into the basket and run into the washroom to find him crying.

His arm is stuck in the rollers that ring out the wet clothes. "Aye, Diés Mio (Oh, my God), what am I going to do? How am I going to get his arm out? I'm so scared. What if his arm is broken? I start yelling for Mama. In the meantime, I remember that there is a latch that opens up the rollers, so I lift the latch and gently pull out Joe's arm. I wrap my arms around my little brother and hold him tight so he'll stop crying.

Within seconds, Mama runs in and pulls Joe into a hug while I tell her what happened. She tells Stella to get a cold, wet towel to wrap Joe's arm in to stop the swelling. Fidel and George come running into the house so fast that they almost trip over each other. They love their little brother Joe so much, and are always so protective of him. They feel so bad that he got hurt. They give Joe a big hug and then Mama tells them to run quickly to get the doctor. Daddy and Mama take Joe to Santa Fe because there are no doctors in Galisteo. Luckily, he only has bruises and swelling. No broken bones. The doctor laughed, saying, "in all my years he have never heard of someone getting their arm stuck in the rollers of a wringer washer."

When Mama and Daddy get home, they tell me, "hijita, que suerte que tu sabias que hacer" (daughter, it's a good thing you knew what to do). Joe says, "MaryLou is my hero forever!" Even now, at the age of 69, Joe remembers his big sister as his hero.

title: Captain John Shannon & the Galisteo Bee Sanctuary
body:
(excerpted from La Sala's "Buzzing Interview" by Tessa Miller.)

How long has the bee sanctuary been in Galisteo?

JS: The Bee Sanctuary is really in its second year now. Last year we started with one hive, and we added another two because we caught a feral swarm of bees. It was quite an experience, we were very lucky. We had one swarm land in a tree right behind our hive so we were able to get them very easily. And then what happened was our hive actually swarmed and we caught that and made a third hive with it. So we were very fortunate. We sort of had an outer organic expansion of our existing bee stock.

Okay, I wasn't aware that there were feral bees roaming around Galisteo!

JS: Oh yeah, absolutely. They're out there. But this year has been very different. It hasn't been conducive to hives swarming. So we didn't see any this year, which you know, was a little disappointing. Because we would have loved to have caught some new ones, but no luck. But we're in our second year.

So what was your inspiration for starting the sanctuary?

JS: Oh, well, a couple of things. One, we have the hive right here on Denise Lynch's Quartermill Farm. So there was a beehive on the property I'm renting. This hive has been in Galisteo since around 2007. So these bees are long time Galisteo residents. The motivation was the hive, and we are really cognizant of how important pollinators are in regard to everything that we do. It's very important for food production in particular and with the die offs that we've been seeing of bee colonies, primarily due to the use of pesticides in everything, we decided to create an area where bees could thrive. And since we knew this hive had done really well here, and we're right by Galisteo Creek, and we have an orchard on the property, there's an orchard across the street, there's an orchard up the hill, so the bees have plenty of pollen and opportunities to get pollen and water. We just said, okay, let's set up here and cultivate this spot for them. Let's make this their little sanctuary, ...It's nice that I have the honey that I do, but it's really good that other people are going to do this, not just for the honey, but for the pollinators themselves.

Do you know approximately how many bees you have? Is there any way to track that?

JS: Right now, we're at one hive. Two were abandoned. What I think happened was they ended up going over to our like two and a half hives itself. In that hive, I don't know, it's a large, large amount. An average hive can have anywhere from 10,000 to 60,000 bees in it, this one probably has more than that, and it's probably more like a 100,000....The queen in this hive is very active. We just checked her yesterday, she's laying around 2,000 eggs a day. It's going to start slowing down a little bit as we get into the winter and they're putting up honey and they're getting their larva set. It's not really a hibernation, but they've definitely slowed down during the winter.

More questions? See the La Sala website for full interview.

Want some honey? Contact john@galisteobeesanctuary.com.

title: {From the GCA: Keep Galisteo Clean}
body:
In years past when there were a number of vacant and unsold properties, it was not unusual for residents to dispose of construction materials (mostly dirt and concrete chunks) at certain locations where there were erosions or holes. However, in the past year these properties have been sold and are now privately owned, and the County has stepped up maintenance of its roads. In fact the County has removed much of this dumped debris and is now enforcing a $1,000 fine for illegal dumping. Please bring your debris to the appropriate waste and recycling centers.

And speaking of "dumping," there have been a number of complaints in the village about people not cleaning up after dogs. We have narrow roads, dense housing clusters, and lots of walkers, which does argue for picking up poop. And please don't leave the bag on the side of the road.
