title: Epstein's Victims Not Forgotten
body: On March 8, International Women's Day, carloads of villagers (and Julie Deery on a bike) caravanned south on NM 41 to the protest at Jeffrey Epstein's former Zorro Ranch, organized by Albuquerque Women's March. Staged just north of the new Ranch gates (under construction halted for lack of permit), the rally was within view of the isolated mansion identified by some as the site of the Epstein circle's worst criminal offenses against women and children, possibly even including murder. Protestors numbered in the hundreds and varied from elderly women in sequined hats to young men with neck tattoos. They cheered as speakers called for full investigation of the Ranch, un-redacted Epstein files, and demolition of the Zorro mansion, but there were also moments of tears and hugs. Speaker Daniel Wilson, brother of the late prominent Epstein accuser and victim, Virginia Giuffre, spoke of her love of New Mexico land despite the horror that came with it. (Giuffre died by suicide last spring.) US Representative Teresa Leger Fernández spoke about Virginia's Law, her proposed legislation to eliminate the statute of limitations for civil claims regarding sexual abuse and trafficking, named for Giuffre. In an interview with a Japanese journalist, Caroline Hinkley said nothing felt comparable to the Ranch rally in her lifetime of human rights advocacy demonstrating at nuclear sites and prisons. Ezra Sage, who remembers scary stories of Zorro Ranch from his Galisteo childhood, was quoted in The Santa Fe New Mexican saying he was glad Epstein's New Mexico history was finally getting attention.

title: 25 Years of Zorro Ranch in El Puente
body: A couple of months ago I (your editor) started to write a short update on the Zorro Ranch when suddenly all hell broke loose. It seems that the Feds had told New Mexico not to investigate here; they were taking care of it, though they never searched the Zorro ranch. Now, years later, Attorney General Raul Torrez has reclaimed the Zorro investigation from the do-nothing feds. Two Democratic state representatives -- Andrea Romero (Santa Fe) and Marianna Anaya (Albuquerque) - have announced a "truth commission" to investigate Epstein's activities at the ranch, six years after his alleged suicide in a New York jail on August 10, 2019. The Women's March rally on 3/8 (see p.1) provided an opening salvo. The recent release of millions of documents relating to Epstein's crimes (with millions more to come) offers glimpses into his time overlooking the Galisteo Basin, including those men invited to Zorro Ranch, none of whom has been accused of any crime. The Department of Justice's sloppy redacting has covered up some participants while criminally disclosing the names of some victims. I decided to look back at El Puente's coverage, which began innocently enough in Feb. 2001: "the huge yellow house that looms over the southern edge of the Galisteo Basin.. belongs to New Yorker Jeffrey Epstein, who acquired the property from Bruce King in 1993 and named it the Zorro Ranch. Complete with airstrip, the spread is now valued at $33 million, a figure the owner is disputing in court, since his property taxes amount to $183,502.64. The house is thought to be the largest in New Mexico." In 2006 El Puente reported that the ranch was listed on the tax rolls as the "largest and highest-valued residence in the county," with a main house at 23,105 square feet. "It is appraised at a record $16.6 million for structures alone (New Mexican, June 11)." I wish I could remember the name of the guy I met ages ago who was working on building the Epstein mansion; he said that a wall was torn out so Epstein would have not only the biggest house but also the biggest kitchen in the state. I can't help wondering if this was the anonymous tipster who told Albuquerque radio journalist Eddie Aragon that there were two girls' bodies buried on the ranch. Further El Puente references, thirteen of them in "Pedacitos," introduced us to Epstein the "financier." In Sept 2006: "Owner Jeffrey Epstein was just arrested for allegedly having sex with five minors in Palm Beach. Gov. Richardson and other New Mexico politicos have returned or donated his contributions to their campaigns." In Nov. 2008: "New York Magazine reported in July that Epstein, owner of the Zorro Ranch south of the village, has begun a prison term for soliciting sex from minors." In Feb.2009 it was reported that he gave $50,000 to Richardson's gubernatorial run. A long-gone Galistean scolded your editor for "saying bad things about a rancher"! Today Epstein's bad things are all over the news. He had petroglyphs chiseled from their sites for ranch decoration and some of the wilder reports involve body burials and baby farming at Zorro. The New Mexican (2/8/26) reported a rumor that Epstein had acquired an ancient bell from the San José de Gracia church in Trampas, stolen a century ago. In Feb. 2016: "Jeffrey Epstein, a convicted sex offender, who owns the Zorro Ranch.. is the subject of ongoing litigations from at least a dozen of his then-underage victims. He is also a pal of Donald Trump, who told New York Magazine in 2002 that Epstein 'likes beautiful women as much as I do, and many of them are on the younger side. No doubt about it, Jeffrey enjoys his social life.'" (I don't know why this quote has not surfaced in recent discussions.) In April 2017: "One of the names mentioned in a nefarious deal perpetrated by Trump's second Labor Secretary nominee was ...billionaire and ex-con Jeffrey Epstein, owner of the Zorro Ranch." In December of that year: "Also in the news is our neighbor to the south - - Zorro Ranch owner Jeffrey Epstein. A civil suit has been filed against him by three teenage girls. Steve Terrell (in The New Mexican 12/10) noted that the opposing lawyer has agreed not to refer to Epstein as a "billionaire pedophile" or "convicted child molester" and assumes that he will also refrain from calling Epstein "a creepy scumbag" or "despicable perv." In Sept. 2021: "Looking for a haunted house? Sotheby's is advertising Jeffrey Epstein's [7,588-acre] Zorro Ranch for a mere $27,500,000, no mention of Epstein or its lurid past. The main residence (still the biggest house in NM?) includes a large indoor pool, a gym, library, and exceptional kitchen.." In 2023 the ranch sold for only $18,000,000 (quite a cut-rate!) "Jeffrey Epstein's New Mexico sin den has been rebranded The Stanley property is now known as Rancho San Rafael." We were told the new owners were "oil people." We now know, thanks to reporter Clara Bates, that the planned Christian retreat is owned by Donald Huffines - currently the GOP candidate for On March 1st of this year, The New York Times reported on the re-opening of investigations into Zorro Ranch, including quotes from Mike Anaya, Kevan Saunders, and Jim Sloan, who noted he turned down a Zorro job because he refused to sign a non-disclosure document. The Internet is full of videos refuting the media's reportage. They range from detailed analyses to a glamorous mortician's analysis of Epstein's "dead" body. What next? Tune into El Puente.

title: {Letter to the Editor: Chip Conley}
body: For the past five years, MEA has appreciated being a harmonious Galisteo neighbor. Some of you work with us, others have come to a workshop, and a number of you have your art exhibited at our two retreat centers. For this reason, I wanted to respond to the article in the last issue of El Puente that characterized MEA as a profit-maximizing developer. Here are a few facts: In the eight years MEA has been open in Baja and New Mexico, the company has never made a profit and is aligned with a non-profit that assures that about half of our MEA midlife students are on full or partial scholarship. I've never paid myself in these eight years and I'm the sole investor so I can exert decision-making control without external investors' typical capitalistic tendencies. In our five years of owning the 2,566-acre Rising Circle Ranch (formerly Saddleback), the only buildings we've built are additions to two existing homes, using regenerative design and construction practices to house our retreat centers. As we stated at the GCA community meeting in November, we're using less water on the ranch than is allocated, partly due to our conservation efforts. As for our real estate activities, we've recently bought two homes in Lamy and Eldorado (which will have 5 and 3 renters each) as "Golden Girls" homes, for older women who want to age with other MEA alumni. Some of our older employees may also be housed in these homes. And we've applied to subdivide three lots on the ranch, ranging from 7.4 - 14.8 acres, to build homes for MEA alumni over the next five years. If we ever choose to create additional lots on the ranch, our subdivision application would be subject to BCC approval at a public hearing so we welcome your questions at that time. Please note that preserving abundant open space is a core part of our MEA ethos since nature is the best teacher.

title: Air Quality Testing Results
body: Results are in from the 2025 Galisteo road testing by the State and County which culminates almost thirty years of concern for the safety of our road materials -- first by John Benjamin and later also by Rep Matthew McQueen. Last August, Santa Fe County tested samples from seven locations in the village east of Hwy 41. Their findings show roads at five of the locations rated Good to Excellent, while two locations rated Fair to Poor with higher levels of lead and silt. All locations met EPA standards. The state's final 152-page report incorporating the County results, is unequivocal: "The data suggests... no measurable health risks to the Galisteo community under current conditions. No additional mitigation or monitoring is currently recommended." We have nothing to worry about? John Benjamin still hopes to see the road in front of his house sealed and finally an end to his battle with dust, toxic or not. And for the rest of us, consider keeping your speed down to single digits when driving past your walking neighbors. The dust from our roads may not be killing us, but it is still unpleasant and guaranteed to be more so in the upcoming heat wave.

title: I found an arrowhead on my land today
body:
behind my house
a gate swings useless
from the broken fence post
give a little push and it gaps wide
enough for me to step through tread
dirt no different from the patch surrounding
the desert home I claim no trespassing allowed
the fence wire warns though coyote on his hunt for
prey derides the delineation with his scat following the
unbroken line-evidence of his nocturnal exploring I came across
a dangling papery overcoat discarded on a rock in the arroyo
by a rattler
a place where heel-toe imprints left by cottontails and leaping
jackalope
pattern the sand each day I walk the walk I walked yesterday
the walk I walked the day before jumbled footprints
prove our nomadic desert comings our daily goings mocking
ownership last night the wind blew hard erasing all
existence of mine of yours

And the data center Project Jupiter in southern New Mexico will require a million gallons of water a day. As this is more than its local utility can provide, additional water will have to be bought and reallocated from the Santa Teresa LLC, which acquired an annual 2,600 acre feet in 2017. In addition the Trump administration has stripped mining protections from the Upper Pecos, threatening a beloved recreational area. Happy Earth Day?

title: GUNSHOTS
body: Around 11:30 PM on March 30th, and again the next morning, Galisteans were treated to the unmistakable sound of intermittent gunshots. The sheriff was alerted. According to a witness, two ambulances, six sheriff's deputies, a sniper, a crisis person, and the GVFR convened and "did an amazing job of handling it all." No one was hurt. The shooter was taken away in an ambulance to get the psychiatric help he needs. Two village residents were subpoenaed to testify at a hearing on April 21.

title: WATER BOARD ANNUAL MEETING
body:
On March 26th the annual meeting of the Galisteo MDWCA took place at the GCC. Thanks to proxies, a quorum was reached though only five Community members attended. Treasurer John Watson-Jones deserves our gratitude for the vast amount of work involved after the major leak that cratered the Association's funds. Nevertheless a 2.8% cost-of-living raise for our contractors was unanimously approved.

Notice of Violation: The NM Environment Department identified the broken tank gauge last year but it was not repaired Even though there is an electronic gauge in use, NMED wants an external gauge. Rudy Martinez is scheduling tank divers who could possibly fix the gauge inside the tank.

President Gregory Hart moved to reelect the four Board members whose terms expired in March 2026. All agreed to remain for another term: Paul Davis, Vice President; John Watson-Jones, Treasurer; Deirdre Africa, Secretary; Antonio Chavez, Board Member. Freddie Cárdenas nominated Anna Cárdenas to the Board, but due to a procedural glitch her election will have to be revisited at the June Board meeting.

Hart has been diligently scanning decades of Water Board documents which will eventually be organized and stored on the cloud. He is also discussing with the Eldorado Water District the decommissioned water tank they have offered us.

A member has requested a leak adjustment; Ana Berry worked it out and it was approved by the Board. Discussion of the draft leak adjustment policy by Paul Davis will be finalized at the next meeting. We can also decide whether the proposed Leak Adjustment Policy should be added to the Rules and Regulations.

Responding to a query from community member Janice Wall, Davis agreed to write a brief basic set of instructions on what to do if you get a water leak, and submit it to El Puente. It will appear in the May issue.

The deadline for Capital Outlay applications is July 1, 2026. Galisteo's MDWCA wish list includes hooking up the second well, getting a replacement tank, and acquiring a generator for the pump house.

County Commissioner Camilla Bustamante spoke about a possible Water Authority to comprise the County and the City of Santa Fe which other public water utilities might also join or benefit from. Apparently our Association would have options as to our level of involvement, should we decide to participate. (Thanks to Board Secretary Deirdre Africa for access to the minutes on which this coverage is based.)

title: AIR QUALITY TESTING
body:
Last year, having just read newly published 20-year old studies on the dangers of environmental micro-particles, I am more concerned than ever about the health hazards of our Galisteo roads. I contacted the Santa Fe County Health Department and County Commissioner Camilla Bustamante, who put me in contact with County Public Works. Road samples were taken and tested. The results were released March 2026 in a report along with air quality test results, which El Puente reported last month. The "good to excellent" rating of our roads from the County is misleading. It stems from just one of fourteen categories of the road samples and pertains only to the Sub-Grade material — the native soil under the road or Sub-Base material meant to be used under a finishing seal— and has NO relationship to the current surface material we drive and walk on every day.

The only things that do affect us are the Base-Course (road surface) samples. Of the seven tested only two are within NMDOT and County standards. Five of the seven samples exceed the allowed amount of fines by over twice as much. (Fines are defined as the percentage of material which will pass through a #200 screen.) The standard for fines is 8% - 12%. We have 27% - 39% fines on these five roads.

Most importantly, a base-course should have little or no silt, whereas five of our base-course samples are 23% - 29% silt. This is the dust we are seeing and breathing from our roads, which has been proven by EPA, WHO and NIH research to cause head, lung, and heart issues over time.

These samples prove that the gravel we drive on is not qualified as surface material, especially as it continues to degrade. I believe we need to formally request Public Works to bring our roads up to standard by chip-sealing, which involves a liquid binder and new top of crushed gravel. The County is willing and able to do this. The base-course we have is perfect to support a chip-seal coat, which requires almost no maintenance and should last at least 20 years. Examples of chip-seal roads can be seen on Demora Road in Eldorado and on Camino de los Cabreros in Ranchitos. Using a brown-colored aggregate will match the aesthetic of Galisteo- and greatly improve the quality of our lives.

I will share my analysis of the road samples at the April 2 GCA board meeting and with anyone else who's interested. My hope is that residents affected by Via La Puente will lead the way, make this change for one street, and show the rest of the village that we don't have to live with dangerously dusty roads.

title: EL PUENTE INDEXED!
body:
Most of us take El Puente for granted, and why not after almost thirty years? But others out in the world see something special about our newsletter. Last year, journalist Lucy Schiller wrote an article on El Puente for the Columbia Journalism Review in which she calls it "an extraordinary (mostly solo) work of journalism, a map of history in progress, revealing a shifting landscape." And this year, El Puente received a unique tribute from journalist, data geek, and Galisteo resident Ted Alcorn. Using Claude.ai, Ted has created an El Puente searchable index. What good is that? Well, imagine you think there's a scarlet tanager at your bird feeder and want to make sure. The index pulls up nine El Puente articles relating to scarlet tanagers. Or you want to know who was Studio Tour President before Lesley Dyer or why the bosque bridge is named for George Michael Anaya? Is highway traffic a new issue? Has there ever been a murder in Galisteo?

There's now an index for that, with a box for word or name searches; an alphabetical list of all the 3205 people ever mentioned; and a section of topics covered over the years. Ted, who recently built a similar index for the New York Times that has drawn tens of thousands of visitors, says, "My intention was only to make the archive of all El Puente's work more accessible and live and useful." The Index is online at https://tedalcorn.github.io/el-puente-archive/ or find it at galisteocommunity.org/el-puente. Ted asks that you use the index's feedback button for suggestions or errors. Lucy Schiller's piece on El Puente, "Monumental Tiny News," is also online.

title: {Galisteans Running for Office: Matthew McQueen (Land Commissioner)}
body:
Major issues? The good news is that the State Land Office earns over $2B/year for public schools, universities, and hospitals. The bad news is that 97% of that revenue comes from oil and gas. I think the challenge for the Land Office is to diversify their revenues. The Land Office holds nine million acres in trust for the people of New Mexico. We can do more renewable projects (wind, solar, geothermal), commercial projects (on appropriate parcels), and affordable and workforce housing projects (again, on appropriate parcels). And we can do all of that while we protect land for conservation, agriculture, and recreation (including hunting and fishing).

How to block Project Jupiter and other data centers? Data centers need guardrails, preferably adopted at the state level: (1) use renewable energy; (2) use reclaimed water; (3) no adverse local impacts on water use, electric rates, and air quality; and (4) local/union labor.

What's in it for Galisteo? Because of the existence of the Land Grant Permanent Fund, which most State Land Office revenue pays into, the average New Mexico taxpayer saves $3,000/year. Plus, we support public schools, which are essential to our democracy.

It's been an honor to serve the village and all of House District 50 for twelve years. I'm going to miss that role, but I think you'll be in good hands with Sarah Boses as your representative.

title: Galisteans Running for Office: Sarah Boses (State Rep District 50)
body:
The major issues I'm focusing on are: Healthcare should work for people not just insurance companies. I'll support efforts for lower costs and make sure everyone can get the care they need. Strong schools start with strong educators and supported families. That means better pay, safer schools, and addressing the challenges students face every day. We need more affordable housing. I'll support practical solutions that help young people and families to stay in our communities.

Community Safety means the right response at the right time, supporting law enforcement while also using proven approaches for non-violent emergencies. Water & Environment are critical. I'll work to protect our natural resources and support responsible planning so our communities can thrive, even in times of drought. I support diversifying our sources of clean energy.

I think it's pretty cool that the village of Galisteo could continue to be represented by someone who lives here. I grew up in Santa Fe, lived in Eldorado for four years, and we've lived right outside of the village since November, 2020. No place has ever felt so much like home. I've learned a lot about the issues facing rural communities: reliable access to water, high speed internet access, mail delivery, emergency services, and roads. I understand the importance of protecting health, safety, and the environment - including our water - while preserving the historic character of Galisteo and other rural communities.

I'm running for State House District 50 because I believe our government works best when it focuses on the people it's supposed to serve. I believe my experience will bring an important perspective to the Legislature and I look forward to the work ahead!

Right now I'm working a full-time office job in town and helping my three kids get through the last few weeks of school. My husband is also an extra busy educator. I will have an event or two in the village before the general election, so that I can sit with folks and talk more directly - my very favorite part of the campaign!

title: Ambient vs. Local Air Pollution: Part II
body:
We have a quality of life and health problem. It has been a problem for 27 years. I am working with the GCA to present our case to our County Commissioner. Last month I wrote about the 2025 Galisteo Road Material Study results. This month I'm addressing what I learned from the New Mexico Environmental Department's Ambient Air Quality Testing done last fall. (See El Puente #286). NMED only tests for "ambient air pollution" and cannot test for "localized vehicle-generated road emissions," according to two different anonymous sources at NMED.

The dust produced on Via La Puente and 33A/Avenida Vieja from 41 to the bridge is localized air pollution. It affects the health and quality of life of those of us who live and work close to the road and of the dozens who daily walk the road and the Bosque. Localized air pollution flows with the prevailing winds and settles into low-lying areas nearby. The homes along the Bosque, west of Avenida Vieja, are considered to be in a low-lying area. Ambient air monitors cannot be sited in low-lying areas. (According to an anonymous source, a scientist at NMED, the strict ambient air testing criteria set by the EPA are designed to avoid "localized air pollution.")

The contractor's conclusion in this very expensive Ambient Air Quality Testing states that there are no health concerns for the Galisteo Community and no mitigation is necessary. But because of the north to northwest prevailing winds during the study and the strict siting rules, the three air monitors were placed upwind or far from dust-producing 33A/Via La Puente, making the results and conclusion meaningless. The more correct conclusion would be to state that there are no health concerns for people living upwind or far away from our dusty road, but we already knew that by simple observation.

Sadly, the Ambient Air Quality Testing did not address our localized air pollution. But the Road Material Study does prove that the material on Via La Puente, 33-A is an unsatisfactory road surface material because of its excessive fine particles and silt.

For more detailed knowledge of either study, please contact me. We need the dusty roads material to be removed and replaced with good, brown Type I-B base course or to be chip-sealed. The costs of either will be much less than the cost of an NMED study.

title: Mosquitos, Be Gone!
body:
The GCA and its Bosque Volunteer Guild is sponsoring a mosquito abatement program to focus on a problem that many residents have brought up. On May 9th, GCA volunteers distributed Summit Mosquito Bits (SMB) over standing water on GCA property. It is important to do this now, as mosquito larvae start hatching when the weather approaches 80 degrees.

According to the manufacturer, SMB is an organic and environmentally safe product, harmless to beneficial insects, pets, birds, fish, horses, and livestock. (See https://mosquitoreviews.com/mosquito-larvicide/summit-bits/)

To be effective, we'll also need willing Galisteo homeowners with areas of standing water to distribute these pellets on their own property. Eight ounces of pellets will treat 2,000 square feet of standing water and will effectively stop mosquito larvae from hatching. Longer term treatment products, such as mosquito dunks, may be necessary over the course of the summer. The GCA had a limited quantity of pellets available for distribution, but you can buy the product directly through Amazon.

title: Not Up to Camping? Try Glamping
body:
The commercial development off Highway 41 a few miles north of the village continues, lucky for us, in kinder gentler formats. Our newest neighbor is UnderCanvas, a nationwide glamping company known for its "upscale outdoor accommodations" and dark sky certification. (Glamping is a portmanteau of Glamorous Camping) UnderCanvas's PR firm declined to give any details, but we can assume their new Santa Fe location next to Haciendas Tranquilas will resemble their other locations from Yellowstone to Acadia National Park in Maine: probably thirty luxury safari tents clustered around a hospitality center, replete with bathrooms (real plumbing), designer furniture, and decks.

A night will run you around $350. UnderCanvas/Santa Fe is not near a national park or forest like the other sites, but it is near the railroad tracks, which should provide a novel outdoor experience when the Southwest Chief roars by. Snark aside, UnderCanvas is a media darling with overwhelmingly positive reviews, and it will provide another option for your visiting family and friends. No mention yet of Santa Fe on the UnderCanvas website and no word on an opening date.

Wondering about water? El Puente asked Chip Conley of MEA if he knew anything about it and he replied: "Their water attorney approached us but my impression is that they're planning to truck their water in, but I don't have any verified confirmation of that."

title: {Marking the Margins at Duende Gallery}
body: The exhibition -- a collaboration with UNM's Tamarind Institute, open from May 30th to Nov.30th -- brings together artists examining the social, racial, and political conditions shaping their time. Working across generations and mediums, they approach lithography not simply as a tool to create multiples, but as a means to question and rework established systems of power. The outstanding roster includes Galisteans Harmony Hammond and Judy Tuwaletstiwa and former Galistean Fritz Scholder, as well as a healthy percentage of indigenous, African American, Latinx, Asian, and feminist participants. Hours are Friday, Saturday and Sunday, noon to 6.
